title: Strictly Come Dancing review – delighted new hosts helps show feel genuinely fresh | Strictly Come Dancing | The Guardian
description: The presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joy
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: The presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joy
Content: New hosts, from left, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe look genuinely excited to be presenting the show.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAView image in fullscreenNew hosts, from left, Josh Widdicombe, Emma Willis and Johannes Radebe look genuinely excited to be presenting the show.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAStrictly Come DancingReviewStrictly Come Dancing review – delighted new hosts helps show feel genuinely freshThe presenters look terrified and some of the celebs are hard to identify, but Strictly remains a rare refuge of joyEmine SanerSat 19 Sep 2026 18.16 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt this point,Strictly Come Dancingcannot be allowed to fail. When we’re all living off our Wes Streeting-mandated prepper rations, it’s the only thing that will keep us going, linking us to a time when joy, sparkle and diversity brought the nation together. Enshittification stalks the show – it has long felt too repetitive, its celeb lineups seem to get feebler each year, and the departure of longstanding presenters Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman threatened to be a lethal blow – so there’s a lot riding on this new series.“Strictly Come Dancing – still fabulous,” said the continuity announcer introducing the launch show, not sounding entirely sure.‘I was on the loo when I got the news!’ Strictly Come Dancing’s new hosts spill their scandalous secretsRead moreOn early impressions, it just might be. The new presenters Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe look not a little terrified, but the vibe they’re going for is can’t-quite-believe-we-got-the-gig humility combined with superfan credentials, which is absolutely the right note. In all the shots of them watching the action – the pro dancers’ routine, the return of last year’s winner, former footballer Karen Carney – they look so thrilled it’s endearing.View image in fullscreenThe launch show is often tedious – not much dancing and not much from the judges.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PA“It’s a little bit overwhelming to be here, but we are so delighted,” says Widdicombe, after the brilliant opening number. It’s an “honour”, coos Willis, who also says she feels as if she should be curtsying when the judges enter. Radebe, until now one of the show’s professional dancers, brings some elegant restraint. He may not have their presenting experience, but he’s not as dazzled by the glitter as his co-hosts.From a Gavin and Stacey star to Dani Dyer’s return: every Strictly Come Dancing 2026 contestant ratedRead moreThe launch show is always tedious – not much dancing, not much from the judges and gnawing irritation at all the “celebrities” you’ve never heard of – but you get the sense they’re all giving it everything. Everyone laughs a bit too hard, previous series are heavily referenced, and the word “journey” is mentioned more times than I care to hear it.Not much can be done at this stage, barring some minor injuries, about this year’s pitiful celebrity lineup – a fact that will, unfortunately, become even more dazzling when the BBC’s new favourite show, Celebrity Traitors, starts again in a few weeks – though at least, unlike the year before last, there’s nobody who is famous for being in an advert.The pro dancers must now be better-known than some of their celebrity partners,including a hairdresser to the stars (Chris Appleton), a TV presenter (Will Best from Big Brother, but not even the good Channel 4 version) and more than a few others to which the response can only be “no, me neither”.View image in fullscreenThere are five new pro dancers for this series, and a new way of setting up the couples.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PAThere are some gems, among them Dame Sarah Storey, Britain’s most successful Paralympian, former footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips and actor Jaime Winstone.Still, Strictly has always been greater than the sum of its stars, and so it keeps hoofing along. It’s been rocked by affairs and accusations of bullying, but it’s also been a rare refuge of joy and progress.Actor Bethany Antonia – familiar to anyone who watches HBO’s House of the Dragon – grew up with Strictly, now in its 22nd year, and tells her fellow contestants that watching boxer Nicola Adams dance with Katya Jones in the show’s first same-sex pairing in 2020 “was such a big part of my coming out journey”, encouraged, she says, by watching the positive reaction of her family every Saturday night.Antonia gets to dance with Nancy Xu, and they both look ecstatic to have been given each other, though this is also the default setting of every pairing. Nobody is allowed to look disappointed.There are five new pro dancers for this series, and a new way of setting up the couples, which is, as everyone keeps saying, a bit like speed-dating – they keep swapping partners, brave for a show which has been blamed for many a ruined marriage, until a couple is called. It’s only slightly less dull than the old way.View image in fullscreenStrictly has always been greater than the sum of its stars.Photograph: Guy Levy/BBC/PASo the couples are set (it’s Winstone and last year’s pro winner Carlos Gu all the way for me), and the new presenters have had their soft launch – this show is pre-recorded, but from now on it will be live – and although I’m not convinced it takes three, the signs are good.Willis is a class act, Widdicombe is best when he’s given the space to gently rib the contestants and Radebe brings such an air of gentle benevolence to otherwise shouty primetime TV that it feels genuinely fresh. Maybe I just really want it to work.Explore more on these topicsStrictly Come DancingBBCEntertainment TVReality TVTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I feel like I’m cancelling out her life’: the wrenching work of clearing out a parent’s home | Death and dying | The Guardian
description: From old love letters to pieces of string, our homes are stuffed with stuff. When it comes time to empty a parent’s home, sorting the junk from the memory can be overwhelming
Author: Stephanie Wood
Headline: From old love letters to pieces of string, our homes are stuffed with stuff. When it comes time to empty a parent’s home, sorting the junk from the memory can be overwhelming
Content: ‘My apartment has become a museum of family stuff and stories. Once, I couldn’t bear to let the stuff go; now I feel suffocated by it.’Illustration: Victoria HartView image in fullscreen‘My apartment has become a museum of family stuff and stories. Once, I couldn’t bear to let the stuff go; now I feel suffocated by it.’Illustration: Victoria HartDeath and dying‘I feel like I’m cancelling out her life’: the wrenching work of clearing out a parent’s homeFrom old love letters to pieces of string, our homes are stuffed with stuff. When it comes time to empty a parent’s home, sorting the junk from the memory can be overwhelmingStephanie WoodSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 19.14 EDTShareSoon after her marriage in 1952, Ellen Rogers’ mother, Fay, bought a coordinated bedroom ensemble – a floral dressing gown and matching bedspread. The day I talk on the phone with Rogers, she has made a tough decision – she is putting the gown and bedspread in a garbage bag to be sent off to a charity shop. “I feel so bad,” she says.Fay died in May aged 97, and had lived in the same terrace house in Camperdown in inner Sydney her whole life. Rogers grew up in the house and returned three years ago to be a live-in carer for her mother. Now she’s cleaning out the house so it can be sold. The decisions she must make are endless; which pile for what item – family, rubbish or charity? “It’s overwhelming – there’s so much,” Rogers says, “including every bloody card she ever received.”Through winter, Rogers moved through the house alone, trying to focus on the task but not always succeeding. Her three brothers are elsewhere. “It’s quite lonely and I hate this house because it’s so cold. I just wish I could speed up the process but I can’t. Some days I’m right on to it, and then other days I just can’t, because it’s very emotional – and I’m not really an emotional person.”I’ve been in a similar situation. I know the emotion and loneliness of emptying a family home.After my father diedin 2010, my mother moved to a smaller place on the Queensland coast. The large family home in Toowoomba where I grew up remained – overflowing with my parents’ household items, their collections (beer steins, fabric, books, Royal Doulton figurines), as well as every last item from my grandparents’ home which arrived in a large removal truck when they came to live with us.View image in fullscreenEllen Rogers in her mother’s kitchen in inner-Sydney Camperdown.Photograph: Joel Pratley/The GuardianIt took me 12 years to empty what came to feel like an emotional halfway house; I flew up from Sydney for a fortnight or more a couple of times a year. My mother was with me, but absent too, lost in memories and completely incapable of making decisions about anything. We argued over everything. We argued over a piece of string. “That’s a perfectly good piece of string,” she said one day of a fragment maybe 10cm long.I moved through the silent house feeling the ghosts of the family’s past, the grief-filled shadows, the immense weight of possessions, ofstuff.double quotation markA house full of things is not a house but a memory machine; things are not things but layers of recollection of selfBut Rogers and I are not alone in the challenges we’ve faced. The global population is ageing and members of the so-called “Silent Generation” – those born before 1945 – are now in their 80s and 90s and either moving into care or dying. (Deaths in Australia have risen by 20% over the past decade.) This is the generation that came of age during the increasingly affluent decades after the second world war. They bought stuff – lots of stuff. And now, emptying out their homes is becoming a rite of passage alongside weddings, anniversaries and funerals. (Are Australia’s charity shops ready?)The four women I spoke to for this story (research suggestswomen are more likely than men to manage estate admin alone) use similar words to describe the grief-edged process: “wrenching”, “gruelling”, “overwhelming”. For others, especially in families riven with tensions and fractures, it can be explosive.View image in fullscreenFamily photos in Fay’s house. The exercise of emptying out a family home has come to reveal a generational gap in attitudes towardsstuff.Photograph: Joel Pratley/The Guardian“Get a skip [bin], clean it out while your mother’s not there,” a close family member who made no contribution to the clean-uptold me. (I was enraged.) “Throw it in a skip,” people told Anne (she asked that only her first name be used) as she and her siblings started to clean out her mother’s home in Sydney’s southern suburbs in July.Anne’s feelings about the presence of a skip on a footpath are similar to mine. “The earth’s too fragile” to just toss things into landfill, she says. Among my many recycling triumphs, I found a charity to take a pile of old spectacles that emerged during my cleaning; Anne has organised for more than a hundred of her mother’s X-rays to be recycled for their silver and PET plastic content. “I would do that for every single item in the house if I could.” But she has had to compromise with her sisters and allow some things to be discarded. “The stress for me is looking over my shoulder all the time and monitoring what’s happening; my sisters are wonderful but they have a different approach.”What end-of-life experts know about living well: love your wrinkles, celebrate birthdays and don’t obsess over workRead moreKathy, a former Sydney public servant who asked that I not use her real name, inherited her late mother’s house after she died in 2024 and has been living in it while trying to clear it out. She has also found herself unable to simply toss things away. “The problem with getting rid of Mum’s stuff is I look at it and think, ‘I can’t just throw it into a skip’ … It’s like, someone will want this.”She thought she’d found a home for her mother’s extensive collection of vases when a friend said her Japanese floral arranging group was looking for big vases for a demonstration. “Have I got big vases for you!” Kathy told her. She pulled them out of a cupboard. Her friend looked at them. “Oh no, none of them are suitable,” she said.The women I interviewed have all had another concern: paying respect to possessions that carried layers of meaning for their parents. A house full of things is not a house but a memory machine; things are not things but layers of recollection of self.Melbourne woman Adrienne lost her mother in 2022 (she asked that I only use her first name). But even before her death, she had already started to tackle her mother’s house. “I completed a ‘Swedish death clean’ at my mum’s house over three stifling January days,” Adrienne wrote in an email to me. Her motives were pure – to make things easier for her mother, who was expecting visitors to stay – but she regrets now her vigour.double quotation markFrugal memories and habits, and a sometimes almost reverential respect for material possessions, were embedded in the Silent Generation’s psyche“She watched me, sat forlorn at her kitchen table, while I ruthlessly moved things on. I did not empathise with how much meaning might be attached to stuff I was basically calling worthless. I see now that objects can store all sorts of nostalgia including several versions of self – old interests and enthusiasms, even unrealised aspirations. I store the picture of her sitting at the kitchen table and can see her grief during the process. I wonder if she was also reflecting on her eventual end as well?”My mother also bore witness to the moving on of things invested with meaning. Like Adrienne, I was ruthlessly efficient through the process, driven by a wild rage at the staggering physical and emotional scale of the job left to me, the absence of my sibling, and my mother’s shifts between pigheadedness and shilly-shallying. But an image of Mum sitting at her kitchen table, looking lost, remains with me too. As is something she said as we went through a pile of Dad’s old clothes: she remembered, she said, the feeling of his dinner-suit jacket brushing her arm as they walked down the aisle on their wedding day.But a parent present in spirit only can still exert a powerful psychic influence. Anne, as the oldest child, felt responsible for ensuring that her mother’s possessions received “due acknowledgment” as stitches in the fabric of her life. As Rogers builds piles in her late mother’s Camperdown home, she is flushed with guilt. “Well, I said to my brothers when I was getting cranky the other day in a group [chat] … I feel like I’m cancelling out her life.”View image in fullscreenEllen Rogers goes through a box of family photos: “This would have been at Australia St, a women’s community group. Everyone would be dead and gone now in this photo.”Photograph: Joel Pratley/The GuardianThe women’s stories reveal something else: the exercise of emptying out a family home has come to reveal a deep generational gap in attitudes towardsstuff. What’s frequently described as “brown furniture”, for example, holds no appeal for members of the Ikea generation. But frugal memories and habits, and a sometimes almost reverential respect for material possessions, were embedded in the Silent Generation’s psyche. Frequently, a shiny new item signified status, a step forwards and upwards.My mother, born in 1936, reminds me frequently how little she had growing up. I heard the old lessons as we waged a battle over kitchen cupboards and linen closets. “When sheets wore out, we’d cut the sheet down the middle and sew the outer edges together to give it new life,” Mum told me more than once. Soap, she said, was removed from its wrapping paper so it hardened and lasted longer.Kathy has also found that her mother’s lessons are sticky. “There are still things in the kitchen that she used before she was married in 1967, and the good wedding china does not have a broken or chipped plate amongst it; everything she had is in good condition because we didn’t grow up with much money.”She thought clearing out her mother’s things so she and her partner could make the house their own would be straightforward. “It just isn’t.”View image in fullscreenOne of Rogers’ nephews wanted her mother’s Charles and Diana tea caddy and a couple of her grandkids took some figurines, but her brothers seem not to want anything.Photograph: Joel Pratley/The GuardianKathy found that dealing with her late father’s hoardings – old speciality books related to his profession and “a garage full of things to fix stuff or build stuff” – was simple. But in the kitchen, she came to a screeching halt over casserole dishes.“I unpacked them on to the bench, and I just thought, ‘right, which of these will I keep?’ And then I just looked at them and thought, ‘I can’t,’ … it was just like a whole shutter came down in my head,” she says.“They’re so tied up with memory; I thought, ‘I know what she used to put in each one, I know the difference between the one she made lemon delicious in and the one she made chocolate pudding in, the one that was always out at Christmas with the tomato casserole.”Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before | Gaby HinsliffRead moreFor Rogers, the emotional trigger was discovering cards her father had written to her mother. “He passed away when I was six. I’d never seen his handwriting. That gave me a little cry.”The clean-up has made Anne realise that she places little store by possessions. “I’m not really interested in the jewellery or anything expensive, I just want the mementoes,” she says.“In Mum’s knitting bag, for example, I found a bunch of letters that Dad sent to Mum and vice versa, when they were courting. I don’t particularly [want to] read them but I fished those out – they’re important and special.” She has kept one of her mother’s childhood books in which she found an inscription: “my favourite book – do not throw out”.I still have nightmares about the process of clearing out my family’s Toowoomba home, fever dreams in which endlessstuff– books, bags, china, chairs, figurines, forks, photographs, paintings – hurtles towards me. But what madness is this – at the end of it, I took ownership of hundreds of items from the house – my great-grandmother’s sideboard, hundreds of my father’s books, my great-aunt’s dinner service, my grandmother’s old mixing bowl, my mother’s 1950s cocktail shaker … and on, and on …My apartment has become a museum of family stuff and stories. Once, I couldn’t bear to let the stuff go; now I feel suffocated by it. I look around and feel panicky. My nieces and nephew are unlikely to be interested in anything I’ve kept or the stories attached to them.I think of Rogers: one of her nephews wanted her mother’s Charles and Diana tea caddy and a couple of her grandkids took some figurines, but her brothers seem not to want anything. I think of Kathy, who says her brother and niece only took away a box or two.And I think of an elderly relative who never married, did not have children. After he died, family members went to clean out his home. There was almost nothing left. The man had released them from the burden.

title: ‘Everyone assumed it represented a poo emoji!’ 27 writers on the greatest cake of their life | Cake | The Guardian
description: From the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressions
Content: Catherine Shoard’s eerie-looking Sorting Hat cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Catherine ShoardView image in fullscreenCatherine Shoard’s eerie-looking Sorting Hat cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Catherine ShoardCake‘Everyone assumed it represented a poo emoji!’ 27 writers on the greatest cake of their lifeFrom the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressionsSat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Sorting Hat sponge cakeThe Sorting Hat sponge I made for my son’s Harry Potter party is not the best cake I’ve ever tasted. That would be anything baked by my granny, or the coffee religieuse (a choux pastry puff) I ate in Boulogne-sur-Mer with my mum. But it’s the most surprisingly edible cake I’ve ever made – a vaguely Jamie-Oliver recipe with buttercream filling and tinned mandarin slices. It didn’t only work; it tasted great, and wasn’t quite as teeth-screechingly sweet as expected. My one regret is that I over-pimped the decoration: it looked so sinister in the fridge with its cold, Sorting Hat stare that the next day I stuck on googly eyes and further sparkles. This perhaps explains why everyone assumed it was a poo emoji cake, despite it being a Harry Potter party with heavy-touch theming. That people thought I actually wanted children to eat shit is a shame, but it still remains my greatest culinary success.Catherine ShoardA perfectly piped 35th birthday cakeView image in fullscreenA knockout 35th birthday cake from Lily Vanilli.Photograph: Courtesy of Hollie RichardsonMy dreams of a cake fit for Marie Antoinette came true on my 35th birthday: with a single baby-blue tier, whimsical white piping and glace cherries for a welcome dash of gaudy. After taking it home in a taxi from Lily Vanilli bakery in London, I proudly displayed her for all to marvel at. Inside, the vanilla sponge had a raspberry and buttercream filling. It felt like my wedding day when I cut the first slice. By the end of the night, after everyone had tucked in and I was about 10 tumblers of prosecco deep, I fulfilled another lifelong dream: face-planting a cake. (Well, half of one.) I picked at those sugary remains for days afterwards.Hollie RichardsonAn orange cream gateauMy most treasured Christmas present of 1992 was the Hamlyn All Colour Cook Book. While I don’t remember cooking any of the savoury recipes – sherried kidneys and turkey in aspic weren’t quite to my 10-year-old tastes – the “family favourite cakes” chapter was a different story. I started with Mary Berry’s classic Victoria sandwich and graduated to her triple-decker chocolate button cake. But I found the ultimate in sophistication, decadence and all-round deliciousness in Audrey Ellis’s “fancy cakes” section: a glorious orange cream gateau. I lovingly baked two orange-zest sponges, sandwiched and smothered them with orange-juice buttercream, and decorated the top with jellied orange and lemon slices. It looked, and tasted, like pure sunshine.Rachel DixonNigella’s pear, pistachio and rose cakeView image in fullscreenA post-dip Viv Groskop with her 51st birthday cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Viv GroskopThe monumental creation is Nigella’s pear, pistachio and rose cake, expertly reinterpreted by my friend Sian. This entity represents the three all-important ingredients of the perfect bake. First, it was made by someone whose cakes always taste as good as they look (a difficult achievement), the kind of person who is tired of everyone saying to them: “You should go on Bake-Off. No, but really, you should.” Sian very much ticks this box. (She really should.) Second, it is part of the grand tradition of “birthday swim” cakes to be eaten with friends at 7am after a freezing cold dip. And third, it features the inventive use of a single candle to represent the numeral “one”. (It is a 51st birthday cake.) No cake could compete on taste, suitability-for-occasion or creativity.Viv GroskopAn iced gingerbread cakeBefore my father died, I had never had to organise a funeral. The strangest element was choosing items for a funeral buffet when I was so choked with tears that I could barely swallow. But my mother was keen that we offered a good spread for my foodie father’s send-off. I chose iced gingerbread mainly because my dad loved ginger. But a mass-catered cake sounded unpromising. Imagine our surprise when it turned out to be one of the most heavenly bakes I’ve ever eaten. Tasting as if it was homemade, it was perfectly moist, with a good kick of ginger and cinnamon. The showstopper was the melt-in-the mouth lemon icing. There was loads left over and it offered us some solace in the gloomy days afterwards.Anita ChaudhuriThe Forg meme cakeView image in fullscreenMadévi Dailly’s generous Forg cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Madévi DaillyThe best cake I ever had was a replica of the notorious “Forg cake” meme, surprise delivered to my door by a friend who had never baked before. I was in the middle of a full nervous breakdown, and had been hooked up for a 24-hour blood pressure test the day before that had brought me to the edge of sanity – so this gentle, generous act of friendship restored my faith in better things to come. It was delicious, too: a superlative victoria sponge hidden underneath droopy pastel icing.Madévi DaillyA Swiss-meringue buttercream chocolate cakeView image in fullscreenThe ‘vintage’ cake at Cafe Lewi, Sydney, Australia.Photograph: Courtesy of Yvonne C LamIt’s not my fault I’m not a cake person. When I was growing up, after the birthday kid had blown out the candles, my saturated-fat-fearing aunties (it was the 90s) would scrape off the cream before serving the naked cake slices to my unimpressed cousins. One upside of adulthood is cake (and cream) whenever I want. On a recent child-free day with my husband, we went to Cafe Lewi, a tiny venue in Lewisham, Sydney, where they serve homemade bakes and pastries, as well as enticing meals and drinks. Their “vintage” cake is a thing of beauty – layers of chocolate sponge with a sultry crumb, sandwiched together with a chocolate ganache and raspberry curd, and thickly slathered on all four sides with a snow-white Swiss meringue buttercream, all embellished by someone who knows their way around a piping bag. We ate it for breakfast.Yvonne LamA Kirby birthday cakeEvery year since my son’s third birthday, I’ve put together a fancy fondant based on one of his fleeting interests: on my first attempt, when the theme was Pokémon, my Pikachu was so lumpenly misshapen that my son burst into tears. It turns out, though, that if you practise something once a year (with a few clay modelling sessions) and watch alotof videos, you do improve. This cake, made by my wife, was a victoria sponge with buttercream and jam filling, but the wrapping – modelled, of course, on video game hero Kirby when he turns into a car – was all me. It tasted like triumph.Joel SnapeMy mum’s chocolate hedgehog birthday cakeView image in fullscreenRich Pelley’s mum, with her hedgehog cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Rich PelleyAs a child, I had one currency: chocolate. The more the better. Nowhere offered a better exchange rate than my mum’s cakes, not least her chocolate hedgehog birthday cake: chocolate sponge, chocolate buttons for spikes and a chocolate-icing face. It became the best bit of birthdays, until I got too old for candles, left home and somehow went 30 years without a birthday cake from Mum, hedgehog or otherwise. Luckily, I’ve corrected this terrible injustice by telling her that all Guardian journalists are now required to have their mum bake them a cake … and she believed me. Thanks, Mum. Happy birthday to me.Rich PelleyThree fourth birthday cakesIn April 2000, I turned four while on a family holiday to Nepal to visit my grandparents, who were living there. My parents had explained that it might not be possible to get me a birthday cake while we were away. For an almost-four-year-old, this was a huge tragedy, a fact that I shared with almost everyone we met. When the big day arrived, the hotel staff surprised me with a huge cake decorated with green, pink and yellow icing. I was overjoyed. I can’t remember what it tasted like, but I know I’ve never been so excited about eating a cake. My tiny mind was blown again soon after, when it turned out that my grandparents had also arranged a cake for me. Then my mum baked another when we got home. I couldn’t believe my luck –threebirthday cakes! I was on a high for weeks.Lucy KnightThe perfect vegan chocolate gateauView image in fullscreenAnastasia’s handmade vegan chocolate gateau.Photograph: Courtesy of Ann LeeIt was my friend Anastasia’s birthday party. We were watching Eurovision and had just finished stuffing ourselves with pizza when she brought it out. A vegan chocolate cake, covered in edible purple flowers, plump strawberries and juicy blackberries, it was more a work of art than a simple gateau. She had baked it using a recipe by Nigella (who else?) and the glossy chocolate icing oozed on to the plate. From the first spoonful, I knew I had finally found it – a vegan cake that didn’t taste like a vegan cake. As someone with an extremely sweet tooth who is lactose intolerant, I have tried many over the years. Usually, they’re too dense, too dry, or taste too virtuous to feel like a treat. But this was rich, creamy, and ridiculously indulgent, even without all the sinful dairy. I savoured each chocolatey bite.Ann LeeA cafe’s lemon drizzle cakeI was 16 and on a school trip to Westminster. During our lunch break, I visited Caffè Nero, which, in the early 2000s, still had an exotic Italian appeal and a hint of sophistication. In a hurry, I made an impulse purchase – an individually packaged slice of lemon drizzle cake. It was so delicious that I still think about it all these years later. The cake was moist, with candied lemon peel, topped with fondant icing, and contained what I can only describe as bursts of lemony icing sugar balls within the sponge. I can’t remember much about the trip except for that slice of lemon heaven. I have yet to find a lemon cake that matches it.Georgie WyattA tarta de galletas birthday cakeView image in fullscreenEsther Gomez (left), on her fourth birthday with her no-bake tarta de galletas.Photograph: Courtesy of Esther GomezFor decades, this no-bake wonder has beenthebirthday cake in every Spanish household. It’s perfectly sweet, moist and beautifully balanced, with alternating layers of milk-soaked biscuits, velvety vanilla custard and the smoothest chocolate ganache. Easy to assemble and incredibly forgiving with measurements, it is the perfect introduction to cake-making for little kitchen helpers. I’ve enjoyed it hundreds of times (I have a very large family), and it remains my favourite – not just for its wonderful taste and lovely texture, but for the fond memories attached to every bite.Esther GomezA book made out of cakeView image in fullscreenFrances Ryan’s uncanny, edible facsimile book cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Frances RyanI’d worked for four years to write my second book and, like every author, was looking for attention. What I received from my mum was more than I could have hoped for: a facsimile of my bookWho Wants Normal?made entirely in cake. The real cover was recreated in orange and yellow icing wrapped around sponge pages, and even the endorsement was piped on. It was akin to that episode of the Bake Off where contestants make roast dinner gravy out of chocolate, except that this was baked by a professional my mum had hired. Was it a book? Was it cake? I could never write anything so delicious.Frances RyanA black forest gateauMy very first memory, at the age of two and a half, is of a black forest gateau. No chocolate cake could have prepared me for it. It stopped me in my tracks; a vast slab of dense, dark chocolate-and-purple-stained cream dotted with posh, burgundy cherries – all far more sophisticated than the sticky glaces I knew from fairy cakes. And it was on wheels (a dessert trolley). I told the waiter I wanted a “big slice”. He tapped me on the head and said I had to wait. Strangely, my memory doesn’t stretch to eating it. Perhaps it remained a feast for the eyes alone. Either way, it set the cake bar for life.Emily Retterskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA baklava cheesecakeView image in fullscreenThe delightful baklava cheesecake at Nuba in Vancouver.Photograph: NubaWhile I’m not a big fan of cakes, there was one that bucked the trend: a baklava cheesecake. I tasted this melt-in-the-mouth delight when I was working at Nuba, a Lebanese restaurant in Vancouver. Its flaky filo pastry pistachio base was perfectly complemented by a soft cheesecake centre. Three years on, I’m still waiting for the pastry chef to send me the recipe.Gabriel StewartMy mum’s tea loafIn terms of looks, this cake is pretty underwhelming. It’s brown on top, and brown inside. There’s no icing, decoration or fireworks. But it tastes fantastic. It was the cake my mum always made growing up: a simple loaf with sultanas and raisins inside and, crucially, tea. The fruit gets steeped in it. Not surprisingly, it pairs well with a cup of tea and sends me back to the Sunday afternoons of my childhood. I think this cake’s feelgood vibes have seeped in deep, because whenever I want cheering up – not being much of a cake maker – I put the kettle on.Paula CocozzaA coconut cream cakeView image in fullscreenLana Crowe’s coconut cream cake, with the backup lemon number.Photograph: Courtesy of Lana CroweOne of my best friends baked me a coconut cream cake for my 26th birthday. I’m dairy intolerant, so this type of whippy treat usually sends a shiver down my intestinal tract. But she made it vegan by replacing all the milk ingredients with coconut, even using coconut milk powder in the icing. It was buttery, subtly sweet, featherlight but satiating, with toasty, nutty notes. Five years later, my family still talks about it. My friend had been so nervous it would be horrible that she also baked me a backup cake. A fine testament to friendships in your 20s.Lana CroweSchwarzwälder kirschtorteCan there be anything more thrilling to a child than a cake trolley? The anticipation as it works its way towards you, pushed by a smart and austere waiter, laden with cakes lavishly decorated like something out of a children’s picture book. My sister and I, both about 12, were with my dad, who was working in Salzburg for the summer. One day he took us to this grand cafe, all retro Mitteleuropean magnificence and good manners. I chose a black forest gateau, probably because it was the biggest. I actually don’t remember eating it, so perhaps I was underwhelmed. It’s the delight of the trolley I remember, and – rare for a child – being able to choose what I wanted. I remember its name: schwarzwälder kirschtorte. The words still pop into my head, on repeat, like a spell.Emine SanerA popcorn mermaid cakeWhen I was growing up, I was allowed to choose the cake I wanted for my birthday each year. At five or six, that meant a mermaid cake. Chocolate-coated popcorn “rocks” covered the sponge, on top of which perched a (non-edible) Ariel doll, her legs obscured within the cake itself and a mermaid’s tail fashioned from “scales” painstakingly cut out of icing. I seem to remember she also wore a shell-shaped icing bikini top. It possibly wasn’t the most sophisticated cake in the world, but I had chosen it from a recipe book and my mum had somehow made it real. I was thrilled.Leah HarperA burnt Basque cheesecakeView image in fullscreenBurnt Basque cheesecake at La Viña in San Sebastián.Photograph: Nathaniel Noir/AlamyI was in San Sebastián for the night – though it felt more like a week as we hopped from one pintxos bar to another. Ending the evening at La Viña, we joined a 20-strong line for Basque cheesecake from the restaurant that invented it. Sitting on a shop stoop with violently coloured Patxaran cocktails in hand, we carved our way through the slab. It was a dreamy custard mousse with a caramelised cut-through from the burnt outer layer, descending into a centre more liquid than solid. A rare dessert that felt both light and decadent at once.Emma ElsworthyNigella’s chocolate Guinness cakeView image in fullscreenNigella Lawson’s classic chocolate Guinness cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Louis StaplesFor my birthday earlier this year, my bestie Alix baked me a cake that I’m still dreaming about (and drooling over). Nigella Lawson’s chocolate Guinness cake brings together the three defining features of any of her recipes: it’s indulgent, unpretentious and sumptuous. The sticky cocoa sponge balances the subtly bitter taste of Guinness with enough sweetness to give an elephant a sugar high. And the sponge’s delicate hint of chocolate is offset by the sourness of the unfussy cream cheese topping dolloped on the top – making the cake look like a creamy pint of Guinness.Louis StaplesBettys’ Dougal the dog cakeView image in fullscreenThe Yorkshire standard Dougal cake at Bettys in York.Photograph: BettysIn 1970s York, children’s birthday cakes came in one shape (round) and in one of two colours (yellow or brown). Then, one day, there was Dougal. Bettys tearooms’ version of the character fromThe Magic Roundaboutblew my mind – I had no idea a cake could be dog-shaped. Dougal was also a taste sensation: his shaggy coat skilfully fashioned from feather-light butter cream; his innards from sophisticated dark chocolate sponge; his face from a meringue disc with a cheeky, pink piped-icing tongue. Although now tragically discontinued, this exquisite cylindrical trailblazer will long remain in the hearts of many York children. Dougal walked so Colin the Caterpillar could run (crawl?).Emma BeddingtonA grilled banana cakeView image in fullscreenKieran Yeow’s beloved grilled banana cake, at Milk.Photograph: Courtesy of Kieran YeowThe grilled banana cake at Milk in Balham, south London, was the ray of warmth I was looking for last winter. Paired with silky whipped halva and pumpkin seed tahini, it worked divinely with a slightly smoky, yet delicate, sweetness that melts in the mouth almost instantly. Who knew a banana milkshake came in cake form?Kieran Yeow‘Death by chocolate’ cakeCake was never on the menu when I was a kid. My mum was, and remains, an anti-sugarist, who ran a tyrannical campaign of snack and confectionery suppression. But a memorable exception was made when I was around nine years old. I was invited to a friend’s birthday party at the local swimming baths, but my folks muddled the dates and brought me a day late. Not only did I miss out on flinging myself around an inflatable assault course, but I also missed a rare chance to get my paws on a slice of birthday cake. I felt crushed, but I leveraged my disappointment to manipulate Mum into taking me to a local cafe, which served the legendary “death by chocolate” cake. A large slab of multilayered indulgence thudded on to the table. After years of substitute confectionery, I felt its name was a legitimate warning. The warm, buttery fudge at the top was sprinkled with milk chocolate flakes, complemented by layers of sponge as soft as cloud, smooth salted caramel, chocolate ice-cream, and a final layer of sponge stacked on top of a dark chocolate base.Daniel LavelleA buttercream Victoria sandwichView image in fullscreenDale Berning Sawa’s elaborately embellished Victoria sandwich cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Dale Berning SawaWhen a traditional sponge cake – known as pound cake in the US andquatre-quarts(describing equal measures of butter, eggs, sugar and flour) in France – is done right, there’s no bettering it. I wouldn’t usually ice it: that dense crumb (from using plain flour, rather than self-raising) defies decoration. Turn it into a Victoria sandwich, though (as I have for my kid from the age of four), and all that air you spend seven minutes beating into the butter and sugar sets the mind afloat with possibility. I’ll bake multiple layers, then sandwich them with raspberry jam into a tall stack, which I lightly buttercream all over (I like a vanilla or white chocolate Swiss meringue buttercream) and cover with rolled-out fondant. Sometimes, I add sculptural elements – Matisse-like chocolate trees with moulded marble leaves, candy-stained-glass shards, misshapen meringue mushrooms, sidings of chocolate bark. I can say these are the best cakes I’ve had, not because I get to taste them but precisely because I usually don’t – no matter how thinly I slice the portions, the cake is simply inhaled before I get the chance.Dale Berning SawaA lemon drizzle and earl grey traybakeSometimes, the most delicious treats are the ones you’re not supposed to eat. At 15, my friend and I baked and donated cakes as part of the volunteering section for our Duke of Edinburgh awards. On this occasion, what came out of the oven dazzled and, for once, wasn’t burnt. It was the most delicious, golden, glistening lemon drizzle tray bake. As I sliced our masterpiece into bite-size pieces, I snuck a few into my mouth. It was the perfect balance of sweetness and tangy lemon, with a hint of earl grey tea. It was a guilty pleasure, but so worth it.Charlotte SmithExplore more on these topicsCakeFoodBakingFamilyDessertfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: When friends become good neighbours: the Melbourne families who transformed one home into three townhouses | Architecture | The Guardian
description: In a novel approach to urban housing, some residents have pooled their time and finances into redeveloping single dwellings. It’s a herculean task – with feel-good results
Author: Doosie Morris
Headline: In a novel approach to urban housing, some residents have pooled their time and finances into redeveloping single dwellings. It’s a herculean task – with feel-good results
Content: Liam Wallis (right) with resident Jerry O’Sullivan and his partner Lucia (left) at the Davison Collaborative, in in the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLiam Wallis (right) with resident Jerry O’Sullivan and his partner Lucia (left) at the Davison Collaborative, in in the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianArchitectureWhen friends become good neighbours: the Melbourne families who transformed one home into three townhousesIn a novel approach to urban housing, some residents have pooled their time and finances into redeveloping single dwellings. It’s a herculean task – with feel-good resultsDoosie MorrisSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.43 EDTShareMelbourne architect Chris Gilbert had run out of eggs. He texted a neighbour and within minutes, he says, their child arrived with some. “Then I made brownies and my kids took some over to the neighbours’ house.”Australia’s best apartment designs for 2026 – in picturesRead moreIt sounds like a flashback to a bygone era, but this neighbourly exchange took place this month, at the Davison Collaborative, a novel housing project in the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick. In 2020 the townhouse development replaced one past-its-prime brick veneer house with three architecturally designed three-bedroom family dwellings, trebling the lot’s density and future proofing it “for at least the next 50 years,” says Liam Wallis, from the sustainability focused property development and consultancy company Hip V. Hype.In 2018, times weren’t so idyllic. Gilbert was being outbid at auctions week after week. Each Monday he’d arrive despondent at his shared working space with Wallis, and Wallis’ business partner Peter Steele.Wallis had already been mulling whether pooling resources to redevelop single home lots into multiple dwellings could increase density, while saving families money.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Sarah Birthisel, Sarah Cosentino and Stephen McGarry at Northcote Townhouses.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The Guardian“I said ‘hang on a minute, let’s just do a project. Let’s see if this works. Let’s figure out how hard it is,’” Wallis says.They eventually bought a postwar home, owned by the same family for 50 years, at auction. The parents had died and their children were selling. Two years later, the three couples moved in. “And each of those homes were the same size as the original dwelling,” Wallis says.As Wallis, Gilbert and Steele were moving in, a similar plan was unfolding in another inner-north Melbourne suburb. During lockdowns, a close-knit group of friends and colleagues (with experience in architecture, interior design, project management and a tradie among them) who lived within walking distance of one another in Carlton North, were spitballing ways to parlay their collective professional wisdom (and their finances) into a similar proposition.double quotation markThose incidental interactions are so beautiful and bring such a buzzSarah CosentinoFour years later, Sarah Birthisel and her husband, along with couples Sarah Cosentino and Stephen McGarry, and Tanya Smith and Neil Clarke, moved into their tri-townhouse venture, Northcote Townhouses.Sitting down with Birthisel and Cosentino, the pair are obviously pleased with how things turned out. Knowing such an endeavour wouldn’t be feasible in Carlton North, the group looked to the adjacent municipality of Darebin. Fewer heritage overlays, larger lots and cheaper prices, they explain, made the area far more suitable.View image in fullscreenNorthcote Townhouses consists of three homes on a 638 sq metre property that backs on to the Mernda train line.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianAfter agreeing on their vision and drafting contracts, the consortium bought a 638 sq metre property that backs on to the Mernda train line in Northcote. Their first order of business was to make their intentions known to other residents on the street. “It was really important to us to connect with our neighbours, to make them aware that this wasn’t going to be something that we would be flipping … That this would be our home, and that resonated really well with the community,” Cosentino says.Then they went to the council with a strategy that Birthisel says was “very sympathetic to the streetscape and continued the rhythm of the streets”. Development approvals went smoothly and they broke ground in 2022. When it came time to move in, they staggered that process so each couple had some time to settle in.Cosentino and Birthisel say that while the communal aspects of the arrangement were alluring, each family also wanted a sense of privacy. Two years into their experiment, they feel as if they’ve achieved that.View image in fullscreenThe Davison Collaborative was a finalist for the Victorian premier’s design awards.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The Guardian“I love the security of knowing I’ve got friends at my doorstep. I also equally love that sense of retreat and sanctuary; we could be in the house the whole weekend and feel like we’re not around everyone else at all,” Cosentino says. On the flip side, last summer, they say, was full of plenty of balmy evenings where private gatherings with family and friends spilled into common areas, and impromptu alfresco meals were shared, with their children playing in the communal garden. “Those incidental interactions are so beautiful and bring such a buzz.”These two projects have been nominated for a slew of awards – the Davison Collaborative was a finalist for the Victorian premier’s design awards, while Northcote Townhouses received a commendation in the Houses awards. While they underline how collectives with the right professional and financial capital can leverage their resources into remarkable housing solutions, they were no small undertaking.“It’s very difficult for just anyone to do it, unfortunately,” Wallis says. Their project was stalled at planning, and then at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (Vcat), for a year. And, like the Northcote venture, the professional experience of the members made all the difference.View image in fullscreenThe entire process of establishing co-housing, from forming the group to moving in, takes on average four years, one consultant says.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianIn an effort to keep friendships intact, the Davison Collaborative deferred broad spectrum project management to Hip V. Hype because “it’s impossible to run a complex project if you have to go back to someone with every decision, but there are select, important decisions that need collective agreement and so we carved those out [early on],” Wallis says.For less prepared consortiums, Tim Riley is in the business of filling knowledge gaps. His company Property Collectives has worked on 11 collaborative housing projects around Melbourne and charges a fixed management fee to guide groups of families, friends and occasionally strangers through the process of property development, right through to final fixtures.He says the kind of people who use his service “aren’t seeing the sort of homes on the market that they would want to live in, at a price point that makes sense to them”.View image in fullscreenTim Riley says co-housing consortiums are most successful when participants share a clear vision.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The Guardian“There’s an acknowledgment that if we want to create this little co-housing community of 10 or 20 households, we need to do it ourselves.”While participants often save upwards of $100,000 compared with buying a similar home in a similar area, Riley says these homes are not “capital-A affordable”. But beyond design and financial imperatives, he believes there is something deeper at play.Repaint, curate trinkets and go ‘curtain crazy’: how to give personality to a boxy, bland apartmentRead more“I think it is all rooted in a belief that having more meaningful social connections with your neighbours is a really valuable thing to have in life,” Riley says.“For the young families that are involved, the desire to have a place where their kids are growing up in a supportive community with a range of people in different life stages is really attractive. And similarly for the older generation, they’re not wanting to go to a retirement village, they’re wanting an intergenerational community.”Riley says his company keeps contracts as standard as possible “so that lenders, builders and the whole ecosystem doesn’t see it as being terribly strange”.On an interpersonal level, Riley thinks consortiums are most successful when participants share a clear vision. Typically they employ “sociocracy”, which establishes from the outset which decisions need to be unanimous and which require majority approval. Each household has one vote. “And that can reduce a lot of friction through the process.”View image in fullscreenSarah Birthisel at home at Northcote Townhouses.Photograph: Charlie Kinross/The GuardianThe company then walks all participants through aplan of workthat has seven decision gates, starting with strategic vision and ending up in operations. He says that “chunking” the herculean task makes the process less daunting. The process from forming the group to moving in takes on average four years.While no longer a resident of the Brunswick project, Wallis believes every block on Davison Street could easily accommodate similar ventures, turning nine homes into 27.“We did a bit of an exercise and looked at, within a kilometre radius, how many blocks of land were on laneways in Brunswick with the same attributes as our site. There was something like 500. We could turn 500 family homes into 1,500.“We don’t need to build 20-level buildings to increase density. We just need to use what we have more effectively.”

title: ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners | Transport | The Guardian
description: Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group
Content: The Blade Runners group began attacking traffic infrastructure in 2023.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Blade Runners group began attacking traffic infrastructure in 2023.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyTransport‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scannersSensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ groupEsther AddleySat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, inDevon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers.A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.”Posted to social media after the incident on 28 August, the footage rapidlyattracted attention. To some, it was an act of straightforward vandalism; a woman in her 60s and man in his 70s werelater arrestedand bailed on suspicion of criminal damage and causing danger to road users.Others, however, believed the woman should be lauded. “Not all heroes wear capes,” reads one Facebook comment on a supporter’s page. “Bideford and Barnstaple next, please,” reads another.Most people view traffic lights as helpful landmarks that keep road and pavement users safe. To a group who call themselves “Blade Runners”, however, the traffic scanners installed above them increasingly conceal a sinister purpose: to install “phased array electronic assault weapons” on city streets that they claim can carry out mass surveillance and even cause cancer, dementia and sudden death.Previous activists claiming affiliation to the movement havetargeted Ulez camerasin London, resentful at their surveillance and the resulting emission zone charges; there have also been sporadicattackson 5G mobile network towers, inspired by conspiracy theories that include the suggestion theyspread Covid.View image in fullscreenA vandalised Ulez camera in west London targeted by ‘Blade Runners’ in 2024.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyIlfracombe is not the only town where traffic scanners have been attacked. In May, police in Cambridgeappealed for informationabout a suspect after nearly 200 traffic detector units were damaged. In the same month inSleaford, Lincolnshire, 10 units were vandalised in a week, with the council describing the conspiracy claims as “ridiculous”. In County Durham, apensioner is facing trialafter allegedly damaging units on eight sets of traffic lights.To Susan Grant-Muller, a professor of technologies and informatics at the University of Leeds’s Institute forTransportStudies, hostility to traffic scanners is puzzling because “this technology, in its most basic form, has been around since the late 70s”. Activists targeting traffic lights do not generally damage the familiar green, amber and red stop-go systems, but instead target additional sensors installed on top that monitor vehicle volume and, in some cases, pedestrian numbers, to allow lights to be phased to help traffic flow smoothly.“The cameras aren’t recording any personal information at all,” says Grant-Muller. “They aren’t recording faces or any details about the car. They just detect that there is something there, a car or person, and the length of the queue that people are waiting in.”They are generally only installed at junctions with a history of traffic flow problems, she says – often at the request of concerned local residents – and are welcomed byLiving Streets, which promotes pedestrian safety. “Better monitoring technology improves pedestrian safety at traffic lights and crossings, [particularly] when enforcement technology is used as part of a wider approach to road safety,” says Tanya Braun, the charity’s director of external affairs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDrivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues ‘wilfully putting lives at risk’Read moreNone of this convinces those who see a more nefarious purpose behind them. Conspiracies about these scanners fits into a broader fear of surveillance and limits to individual freedom. This is part of a“super-conspiracy” that believers call “the great reset”, says Clare Birchall, a professor of contemporary culture at King’s College London, who has written extensively on technology and conspiracist thinking.“These super-conspiracies draw all sorts of different things together to give some kind of shape to a whole bunch of different anxieties and fears,” says Birchall. “We’re all worried about technological overreach. Lots of people are worried about datacentres. And I often read conspiracy theories as a vernacular form of critique. It’s an everyday version of what we’re all trying to grasp.“I’m not surprised at all that [some] people need to find a narrative to find their way through it, because we’re so disenfranchised when it comes to the collection of our data or what happens to that.”Conspiracies often form in response to frightening events, agrees Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor and chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, “and if you can assign that to a bunch of evil-doers who are responsible, that can provide psychological comfort for certain people, because they’d rather have bad people do bad things, then realise that the world contains effectively random events that you can’t control”.Explore more on these topicsTransportCrimeRoad safetyMotoringDevonLondonSurveillancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A losing battle’: will UK public service broadcasters survive amid US onslaught? | Television industry | The Guardian
description: Jobs and programme budgets in firing line at BBC, Channel 4 and ITV as they are outgunned by YouTube and Netflix
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Jobs and programme budgets in firing line at BBC, Channel 4 and ITV as they are outgunned by YouTube and Netflix
Content: Filming for the upcoming BBC series The Detection Club. The corporation’s licence fee income has fallen by 38% in real terms since 2010.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenFilming for the upcoming BBC series The Detection Club. The corporation’s licence fee income has fallen by 38% in real terms since 2010.Photograph: British News and Media/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.Television industry‘A losing battle’: will UK public service broadcasters survive amid US onslaught?Jobs and programme budgets in firing line at BBC, Channel 4 and ITV as they are outgunned by YouTube and NetflixMark SweneySat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Iwouldn’t be surprised if the BBC orChannel 4disappeared,” says one of the thousands of TV staff at risk of redundancy, as British broadcasters face what has rapidly become a fight for survival against US digital rivals.“My generation grew up with Netflix and YouTube … Honestly, I feel like it is a losing battle.”Over the course of the summer the crisis facing the UK’s biggest public service broadcasters (PSBs) – theBBC, Channel 4 and ITV – has reached fever pitch amid announcements of deep job cuts and talk of business models unfit to face up to the deep-pocketed streamers.Earlier this month, Priya Dogra, Channel 4’s new chief executive, announcedthat 28% of its staff are to be cut, the biggest round of redundancies in the broadcaster’s 43-year history, amid a slump in advertising and increasingly stretched finances.Meanwhile the BBC’s new director general, Matt Brittin, a former top Google executive, ispushing through up to 2,000 job cutsas he attempts to negotiate a dramatic overhaul of its licence fee funding model with the government to secure its long-term future.And four years after ITV announced an £800m-plus plan tocreate a streaming “national champion”to take on Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon, chief executive Carolyn McCall has raised the white flag, arguing that acut-price £1.6bn sale of its broadcasting arm to Skyis the only way to survive.“What is happening is not unique to the UK, it is all across Europe and beyond, it relates to ‘local’ broadcasting operations,” says Sir Peter Bazalgette, the formerITVchair who has also sat on the board of the culture department. “I cannot see a future Europe where there are four or five domestic broadcasters in each country with viable financial models.”View image in fullscreenFormer Google executive Matt Brittin is is pushing through up to 2,000 job cuts at the BBC.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersUS tech companies such as YouTube owner Google, Facebook and Instagram parent Meta, and streamers such as Netflix, have deployed their billions in funding to develop their businesses into viewing, subscription and advertising juggernauts.The Silicon Valley behemoths are forecast to take almost $50bn (£38bn) in UK ad revenues by 2028 – two-thirds of the $74bn total – at which point 90% of all ad spend will be digital, according to eMarketer.That expansion leaves a shrinking pool of funding for commercial PSBs, which have struggled to untether from their reliance on traditional TV advertising – a market that is forecast by WPP Media to shrink by 2031 to just £2.4bn, 60% down on 2015 levels.Meanwhile, the predominantly publicly funded BBC’s licence fee income hasfallen by 38% in real terms since 2010,owing to a combination of freezes or below-inflation increases to the licence fee and increasing non-payment.The BBC has lost 2.7 million payers of the £180 annual charge since the beginning of the decade. Last year it lost afurther 539,000, taking the total who still contribute to 23.3 mllion, the lowest level since 1999.Brittin, now spearheading negotiations with the government over the terms of therenewal of the BBC’s royal charternext year, has called the model a “busted flush” and “insufficient to sustain a universal public service”.View image in fullscreenWriter Jack Thorne, director Philip Barantini and actor Stephen Graham celebrate their Emmy wins for Adolescence. The British-set drama was commissioned by Netflix.Photograph: Daniel Cole/ReutersThe increasingly financially stretched PSBs face competitors with huge financial resources for programme-making. Netflix alone has a content budget of $20bn this year, and enjoys a larger share of UK TV and streaming viewing than ITV, Sky, Channel 4 or Channel 5, while YouTube is close to overtaking the BBC to become the most popular platform in Britain on the same metric.“If you think about the shrinking money and budgets I feel we are heading toward a two-tier system,” says a senior executive at a leading TV production company. “It is great that the big US corporates like Netflix, Amazon and Disney have these mega-budgets and do produce great ‘British’ shows like Adolescence, Black Doves and Slow Horses but they are becoming in a class of their own.“My fear is we end up with a system where the UK public service broadcasters will diminish to such an extent, while facing such big budgets wielded by rivals, they will become a bit like a cottage industry.”The crisis in which Channel 4 finds itself has renewed talk of whether those whoadvocated privatisationto ensure its long-term survival may well have been right, or whether atie-up with the BBCmight build the scale needed to survive.“Channel 4 has always punched above its weight and being a challenger is nothing new,” said a source at the broadcaster. “But it was never meant to operate in isolation – it was designed to be part of the creative ecosystem. So partnerships will be a defining feature of the new era. They’re a way for the channel to compete on reach and scale while maintaining its independence.”The UK’s PSBs have a patchy record on collaboration, although notable successes include the development of Freeview, and have not been able to come together to map out a streaming future as viewing moves beyond linear TV.Earlier this year, Carolyn McCall, the ITV chief executive, expressed her frustration that talks to create a British streaming champion comprising the original three PSBs had failed because“we all have such different business models”.However, as the reality of the scale of the crisis facing the industry becomes ever more apparent, a new wave of collaboration is taking place – some say helped by a change of top executives.View image in fullscreenChannel 4’s Derry Girls. The broadcaster is in talks with the BBC to run its content with ads on the iPlayer.Photograph: Peter Marley/PABrittin has said the BBC is intalks to enable Channel 4 content to run with ads on the iPlayer, having told MPs that the commercially funded PSB looked “very subscale” given ITV and Sky are merging.This week, Channel 4, which relies on advertising for 90% of its income, made a significant move to try to address this scale issue bypoaching the £300m-plus contractto sell the TV and digital ads for Paramount UK properties including Channel 5, Nickelodeon and Comedy Central from Sky.And although ITV, Channel 4 and Channel 5 now make a little over £1bn annually in revenues combined from their respective streaming services, which continue to grow at pace, it is not fast enough to bridge the gap from lost legacy TV revenues in the short term.“Despite the attention that video sharing platforms receive, public service streaming is the untold success story of the year so far, outpacing viewing growth to YouTube and subscription video-on-demand services,” says the Channel 5 president, Reemah Sakaan. “Audiences and advertisers alike still want trusted, relevant and distinctly British content, and they are choosing our platforms as go-to destinations.”The UK’s PSBs had realised as far back as 2009 that coming together was necessary to ultimately compete, but the British streaming platform, called Project Kangaroo, wasblocked by the competition regulator. Three years laterNetflix led the US expansionof the international streaming era to the UK.View image in fullscreenChannel 5’s All Creatures Great and Small. The broadcaster’s president says people want ‘trusted, relevant and distinctly British content’.Photograph: 5 Broadcasting LimitedThe BBC’s Brittin has warned that the issue of scale is now more acute than ever saying UK broadcasters risk being “underweight” as global players dominate content creation and distribution to audiences.“What is at stake? It is about the criticality of local content, and independent impartial news about our country,” Bazalgette says. “Content made for us, by us about us. There are some marvellous programmes [made by the global streamers] but that is not the same as an absolute commitment to sustained investment in local content.”The quest for scale extends to working more with rivals, exemplified by the BBC’s recent deal tocreate bespoke content for YouTube to expand its reachwith younger audiences. However, none of the UK’s PSBs have yet pushed collaboration as far as France’s TF1, which has made all its channels available on Netflix.As the fight for the commercial survival of Britain’s biggest broadcasters continues, many of those affected by a brutal summer of restructuring remain unconvinced there is a bright future for the TV industry.“I would say it is a watershed moment,” says one TV executive. “Our sector of the media industry has peaked, we are definitely in decline.“If you are young enough your next job will most likely not be with another broadcaster. It is all about downsizing; it is where your skills and experience might fit into another industry. It is bleak, very bleak.”Explore more on these topicsTelevision industryPublic service broadcastingITVTV streamingBBCITV plcChannel 4featuresShareReuse this content

title: UK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surge | Party funding | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Exclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals
Content: There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThere is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with some Labour MPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersParty fundingUK politics increasingly funded by billionaires as mega-donations surgeExclusive: A total £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research revealsRowena MasonWhitehall editorSat 19 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish politics is increasingly being funded by individual billionaires with a wave of mega-donations having flooded into UK political parties over the past two parliaments.A total of £179m has been donated by wealthy individuals since 2019, research reveals.The figures from the IPPR thinktank show how big money is playing an ever more influential role in Westminster, with a particular rise in mega-donations of more than £1m.The research found that contributions from individual donors have accelerated since the Brexit party received £10m from the Thailand-based billionaireChristopher Harborneand the Liberal Democrats were given £8m by David Sainsbury, the supermarket tycoon, who has now returned to Labour.Between 2001, when donation records began, and 2018, the total donated by individuals giving more than £1m averaged £3.9m a year.But between 2019 and 2025, that figure rose to £13.1m a year, almost three-and-a-half times as much, and far outstripping what would be expected with inflation.The research found 72% of all £1m-plus donations from individuals since records began had come since 2019.Guardian analysis found that in some years, such as 2023, almost £7 out of every £10 in reported private donations to political parties came from wealthy companies or individuals who gave more than £1m in a calendar year.The figures are likely to raise fresh concerns about the influence of a small groups of wealthy individuals, which have already been heightened since two crypto billionaires, Harborne and Ben Delo, said they had each given £36m toReform UKthis month.Reform UK has said it is trying to redress the balance as the other parties have taken millions in mega-donations in past years. The Conservatives’ biggest donors include Frank Hester, who gave more than £20m before the 2024 election, and Labour’s Gary Lubner, who has given more than £9m in total.The IPPR figures draw on Electoral Commission data since 2001 and Transparency International analysis, plus the two record donations of £36m each to Reform UK from Harborne and Delo.There is increasing concern among Reform UK’s rivals about the issue of donations of more than £1m, with someLabourMPs pushing for a cap of £100,000 or £500,000 a year.Some Labour members are intending to push the issue at the party’s autumn conference, and proposals for a cap are likely to be tabled when the government’s current elections bill goes to the House of Lords this autumn.No 10 has been reluctant to include a cap amid opposition from some trade unions who fear it could lead to restrictions on them being able to donate so much in future.However, the government has recently pledged to deal with the issue of mega-donors having an outsize influence on politics. It has already introduced a cap of £100,000 a year for donations from overseas voters.Harry Quilter-Pinner, the executive director ofIPPR, said:“Something fundamental has changed in how British politics is funded. Million-pound donations were once exceptional. However, since 2019, mega-donor money has become a much bigger part of our political system.“Reform’s extraordinary fundraising has accelerated that trend, but this is much bigger than one party or two enormous cheques. This is the Americanisation of British politics, where political parties can become dependent on a handful of people with exceptionally deep pockets.“Britain should draw a clear line. The government should introduce a £100,000 annual cap now and bring it down over time, so that no individual can bankroll a political party simply because they are incredibly wealthy.”Civil society groups have urged the government to fix the issue for good, after the government said earlier this month a new taskforce would examine the issue of mega-donations.Dr Susan Hawley, executive director of Spotlight on Corruption, said: “Without urgent action to limit the amount that wealthy individuals can give to political parties, we’re going to continue to see a staggering inflation of money – and the influence it buys – flowing into the coffers of political parties … The taskforce needs to take decisive action to get big money out of our politics in a fair and even-handed way, so that power and influence is returned to ordinary voters, where it belongs.”At the time of the £72m in donations to Reform UK, Duncan Hames, senior director of policy at Transparency International UK, said the situation with big donations was “completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast”.Explore more on these topicsParty fundingReform UKChristopher HarborneLabourLiberal DemocratsConservativesFrank HesternewsShareReuse this content

title: Camilla praises ‘life-enhancing power’ of books amid Earl Spencer memoir controversy | Queen Camilla | The Guardian
description: Queen speaks of love of reading at festival for charity she founded after success of her Instagram book club
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Queen speaks of love of reading at festival for charity she founded after success of her Instagram book club
Content: Queen Camilla with Gyles Brandreth speaking to author Reeta Chakrabarti during the Queen's Reading Room festival at Chatsworth House.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenQueen Camilla with Gyles Brandreth speaking to author Reeta Chakrabarti during the Queen's Reading Room festival at Chatsworth House.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAQueen CamillaCamilla praises ‘life-enhancing power’ of books amid Earl Spencer memoir controversyQueen speaks of love of reading at festival for charity she founded after success of her Instagram book clubYassin El-Mouddenand agencySat 19 Sep 2026 19.06 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQueen Camilla has spoken of her love for books with a “life-enhancing power” after a series of allegations were made about King Charles in extracts from Earl Spencer’s memoir about the life of Diana, Princess of Wales.Camillawas welcomed to Chatsworth House in Derbyshire for the first day of the festival for the Queen’s Reading Room, a charity she founded after the success of her Instagram book club during the pandemic.She told the guests: “I created my Reading Room simply because, like all of us here, I love books and their life-enhancing power and I want to share that love with others.“In those early days, I had no idea if anybody would be interested but six years on, we are a global community of millions from over 180 countries, swapping recommendations, undertaking research and donating thousands of books to women’s refuges and homeless shelters.”Camilla’s speech about her love for reading comes after Spencer madea series of damning claimsabout the king in a new memoir chronicling the life of his sister, Diana, that prompted an “unprecedented” response from Buckingham Palace, which said: “The pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason”.In further developments on Saturday, Spencer accused Charles of “gaslighting” in the palace’s response to the claims and said “Diana would be cheering from the rafters at this book”.Speaking to the Mail on Sunday, Spencer said “it was not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king”.He added: “It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said.“I also thought it was a rather poor imitation of the ‘recollections may vary’ quote, which was a much more elegant way of putting things, but in these circumstances entirely out of place.”The BBC is scheduled to broadcast its full interview with Spencer on Sunday.Camilla will also feature in the BBC Arts programme The Book That Changed My Life, which is due to air next month as part of theNational Year of Reading 2026.The BBC has said the documentary film will follow Camilla as she meets four remarkable people whose lives have been changed by books at moments when they most needed them. The latest details of the show were revealed on Saturday at the Reading Room festival.During the event, she spoke to Ian Kirby, one of the contributors to the documentary, asking him about his experience of finding community and hope through reading.Kirby, from Gateshead, fell into depression after a traumatic incident at home, but discovered a new perspective on his own experiences after joining a local book club and reading the autobiography of local boxing champion Glenn McCrory.Speaking in the documentary, he says: “That is the beauty of a book.
