It can give you experiences you’ve never experienced, but they can also be an inspiration.”The BBC has previously said the documentary would “feature individuals from a wide range of backgrounds who all share one thing – moving stories of resilience and renewal, fostered by reading”.“From finding solace in a book while in prison, to overcoming deep depression through the connection of a local book club, or finding the inspiration to completely change their life, these stories reveal how books offer salvation, hope, joy, deep connection and fresh perspectives when people need them most,” it added.It said the film would also explore the growing scientific evidence that reading can improve health and wellbeing.The documentary was first announced by Camilla during a Clarence House reception celebrating the fifth anniversary of her Queen’s Reading Room book club in March.In a speech, Camilla described how her literary project was launched to share her “lifelong conviction that books make life better”.At the festival, alongside the journalist Reeta Chakrabarti and broadcaster Gyles Brandreth, Camilla revealed her four book recommendations for autumn – Finding Belle by Chakrabarti, The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde, Whistler by Ann Patchett and Sashenka by Simon Sebag Montefiore.In the Sculpture Gallery, Camilla also attended a reception with literary figures taking part in the festival, including Lee Child, who wrote the Jack Reacher novel series, and Turkish-British novelist Elif Shafak.The Book That Changed My Life is expected to air on BBC Two on 14 October.Explore more on these topicsQueen CamillaMonarchyShareReuse this content

title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’ | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spending
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spending
Content: Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had to ‘stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said the prime minister had to ‘stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAKemi BadenochKemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spendingYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of “fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning”, as she repeated her call for the prime minister to cut the welfare budget to fund increase spending on defence.Speakingto the Telegraph, the Tory leader said that “Burnham may be a people pleaser but difficult choices cannot be avoided through dither and delay”.She said the government had to “fund our defence properly” at a time when former military chiefs have raised questions about Britain’s preparedness for war.Badenoch said: “Our government is fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning. In France and Poland, leaders are taking action now against the growing Russian threat. What is our government doing? Has anyone heard from Wes Streeting, the former head of the National Union of Students, who has rocked up as defence secretary?”Discourse on the “welfare v warfare” debate has grown louder in recent days since Burnham’s comments during prime minister’s questions on 9 September that national security could not “come at the expense of social security”.John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bankRead moreTheTory leadersaid Burnham was sending a “dangerous” message that he would not cut welfare to fund the military, which was “heard loud and clear in Moscow as well as Manchester”.She added: “We have to stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history when Russia is testing our resolve week after week. It’s time to get serious.”The UK has promised to commit 3.5% of national income to defence by 2035, in line with a pledge by Nato members, but there isgrowing pressureon the chancellor, John Healey, to outline how further increases will be achieved before next month’s budget.Adm Lord West, a former security minister under Gordon Brown, said Britain’s military was in “quite a parlous state”.“In many ways, one could argue we are already at war. We are certainly in the grey zone – whether it’s cyber-attacks, drones getting near the edge of somewhere or threats to underwater cables,” he added.Lord Dannatt, a former chief of the general staff, said: “My bottom line is thatAndy Burnham, and regretfully I would now add John Healey, are playing fast and loose with the nation’s security.”The Conservatives have proposed capping housing benefit to raise £4bn to spend on defence. The party has rejected suggestions that the policy would make people homeless but suggested some would have to “move somewhere cheaper.”The Tories will hold their annual conference in Birmingham in two weeks.Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamDefence policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins | Liberal Democrat conference | The Guardian
description: Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton
Content: Ed Davey urged delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope ‘that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down’.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEd Davey urged delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope ‘that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down’.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PALiberal Democrat conferenceEd Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference beginsLeader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in BrightonYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying Lib Dems would not give up the fight to defeat “nasty populism” and Reform UK’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”.On stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”.He also praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight” and contrasted this with Reform, which, he said, “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72 million quid”.Davey,who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.He spoke of his “visceral shock [and] overwhelming anger at seeing human beings treating other human beings with total contempt” and drew parallels between that experience and the need to not look away “when we see human dignity under attack”.Lib Dems have ‘moral responsibility’ to block Reform, says Ed Davey as party gears up for snap electionRead moreDavey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest.“The fight to stop the world’s richest man who learned racism in apartheid South Africa from funding racism around the world.”He also referred to the “fight to defend the Royal National Lifeboat Institution after volunteers for the coastal rescue charitywere recently targeted online amid anti-migrant protests”.He said “Reform know they don’t speak for the real United Kingdom” – and what Farage was “counting on to get him to No 10” was that people would get “tired, depressed, fed up with seeing Zia Yusuf on BBC Question Time week after week”.But Davey said he hoped Reform were watching and would see “a party that won’t be ground down. That won’t be deterred. That won’t give up the fight.”Also during the first day of the conference, Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan set out a £600m plan to improve maternity care, including proposals to bring in one-to-one midwifery for every woman in labour backed by a round-the-clock senior consultant.The party said the measures will pay for themselves by reducing how much the NHS has to spend on compensation for maternity negligence claims every year – totalling £1.3bn in 2024-25.Munira Wilson, the Lib Dem education spokesperson, said the party would introduce a guarantee to provide 100 hours of work experience for students from GCSE age to 18 to tackle the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training.Explore more on these topicsLiberal Democrat conferenceLiberal DemocratsEd DaveyReform UKThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: George Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’ | George Osborne | The Guardian
description: British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewing
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewing
Content: George Osborne also defended the British Museum taking money from firms such as BP to keep it free to visit.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAView image in fullscreenGeorge Osborne also defended the British Museum taking money from firms such as BP to keep it free to visit.Photograph: Aaron Chown/PAGeorge OsborneGeorge Osborne ‘thought Peter Thiel’s Bayeux tapestry visit would be secret’British Museum chair tells Big Brue festival he thought no one would find out about the private viewingHelena HortonandNadia KhomamiSat 19 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorge Osborne has said he thought no one would find out about a private viewing of theBayeux tapestryhe organised for the tech billionaire Peter Thiel at the British Museum.The former chancellor, who is chair of the museum, told the Big Brue festival in Somerset that he had been on holiday when Thiel was shown the medieval artwork.Thiel, who supports Donald Trump, is the founder of PayPal and Palantir, a software company that builds data integration, analytics and artificial intelligence platforms for government agencies and large corporations.Palantir has a swathe of British public contracts, including, most controversially, a£330m deal with the NHS, which it has held since 2023.The company also works for the US, Israeli and UK militaries. Its use of AI-powered software to support military strikes in Gaza and Iran, US Ice immigration raids and its access to NHS data has stoked concern.Of the viewing, Osborne said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.The visit wasrevealed in the Guardianshortly after it happened.When asked what the museum might have got in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is he hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”Osborne, who lives in Bruton, near where the festival is taking place, complained that people treat theBritish Museumlike the Foreign Office when they protest about donors who are thought to support the Israeli government.He said: “The critique was that [Thiel] was a supporter of the Israeli government … I mean, this is the most difficult, and almost all the protests that happen at the museum … When I started five years ago, they were climate protests, Just Stop Oil and that kind of thing. Now they’re almost universally Gaza.“You know that is the moment I would say the most sensitive, difficult political issue for the museum, and you know we try and navigate it, and I keep trying to point out we’re not actually the Foreign Office.”He said the museum has to take money from companies such as BP to be able to operate.“You cannot say we want museums to be free, and then one of the biggest British companies offers us £50m, BP, and we go, oh, don’t, because we object to oil exploration. Where is the money going to come from?“You’d shut down the British Museum. People do say this. They say you shouldn’t take tech money, you shouldn’t take oil money. You can’t take any money from the banks. We want the museum to be free. The museum would shut down.”Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. title: Footballers and fans pay tribute to Noah Woods after toddler’s death in Suffolk | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Players in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applause
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Players in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applause
Content: Ipswich Town's Leif Davis joined a search party to look for the toddler before his body was found. He later donated £2,000 to the boy’s family.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenIpswich Town's Leif Davis joined a search party to look for the toddler before his body was found. He later donated £2,000 to the boy’s family.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersSuffolkFootballers and fans pay tribute to Noah Woods after toddler’s death in SuffolkPlayers in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applauseYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlayers wore black armbands duringEverton’s home match against Ipswich Townon Saturday, as part of a tribute to three-year-old Noah Woods, whose body was found after he went missing in Suffolk this week.A photograph of the boy was shown on the big screen before the Premier League game in Liverpool, and three minutes after kick-off both sets of supporters stood to applaudin memory of Noah.The toddler, who was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism, became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Brantham on Tuesday afternoon,Suffolkpolice said.About 1,300 members of the public joined a search which ended on Wednesday whenpolice divers recovered a body from a nearby lake.On Thursday, Noah’s father Rhys Woodspaid tribute to his sonin a message shared on a community Facebook group.He wrote: “There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.”View image in fullscreenA photograph of Noah Woods was displayed on the big screen at Everton’s Hill Dickinson stadium on Saturday afternoon.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersIpswich Town’s captain Dara O’Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton were among a delegation from the Suffolk club who laid flowers at the playground where he went missing.Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 toa fundraising appealset up by Good Dads Club, a group of fathers in Colchester, Essex, to support Noah’s family. It had already received more than £100,000 in donations from more than 6,000 supporters by Saturday evening.Suffolk constabulary said the child’s death was not being treated as suspicious but that the force still has a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file to the coroner.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkIpswich TownEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker | Israel | The Guardian
description: Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country
Content: Elor Azaria, pictured in an Israeli military court in April 2016, was 20 when he was sentenced.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenElor Azaria, pictured in an Israeli military court in April 2016, was 20 when he was sentenced.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APIsraelIsraeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attackerElor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide countryAssociated Press in JerusalemSat 19 Sep 2026 16.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case thatdivided the countrya decade ago.Elor Azaria’sconviction in 2017 for manslaughterand his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. Amobile phone videocaptured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence ministerIsraelKatz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreHerzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon,to resign.After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahucalled for Azaria to be pardoned.After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.Explore more on these topicsIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaWest BanknewsShareReuse this content

title: Dutch riot police break up violent far-right protest in The Hague  | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Authorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre park
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre park
Content: Police made several arrests as they dispersed hundreds of activists.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice made several arrests as they dispersed hundreds of activists.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press/ShutterstockNetherlandsDutch riot police break up violent far-right protest in The HagueAuthorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre parkAssociated Press in The HagueSat 19 Sep 2026 15.43 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDutch riot police dispersed several hundredfar-rightprotesters in The Hague on Saturday after violence erupted and local authorities banned a planned march in the city against immigration and asylum policies.The Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that 24 people had been arrested, after some protesters threw fireworks and other projectiles at police.Justice minister David van Weel called on X for an “extremely firm” response to what he described as “disgusting scenes” at the protest, organised by the far-right We Are the People organisation.He said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, and attacked and threw fireworks at police.“Thanks to all the police officers who are once again standing up for our democratic rule of law,” he wrote.View image in fullscreenThe march was organised to protest about immigration and asylum policies in the Netherlands.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Hague municipality banned the march after violence broke out among demonstrators gathered at the Malieveld, a park in the city centre, and later ordered the crowd to disperse.Those arrested were detained for various offences, including failing to comply with the order and illegally possessing weapons.Police reportedly used pepper spray and a water cannon on the rioters.Saturday’s unrest came a year afterrioting erupted during a rightwing demonstrationin The Hague.A police car was set on fire during the clashes between black-clad protesters and police. The headquarters of the centrist D66 party – whose leader, Rob Jetten,is now prime minister– was also attacked.Jetten said on X that the demonstrators deliberately sought confrontation with the police and chanted “abhorrent” far-right and antisemitic slogans.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsThe far rightProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: The president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it
Author: David Smith
Headline: The president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename it
Content: Trump has no legal right to demolish the Kennedy Center, which was established by Congress.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump has no legal right to demolish the Kennedy Center, which was established by Congress.Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpAnalysisTrump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at riskDavid Smithin WashingtonThe president has threatened to block renovations and suggested the landmark could be demolished after courts ruled against his bid to rename itSat 19 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 20.24 EDTShareIt was born with the world premiere of Leonard Bernstein’s Mass. “Young people will come here and they will see this cultural centre,” Rose Kennedy, the mother of slain US president John F Kennedy,said at that opening night gala. “They will carry some of these ideas back to their different communities.”More than half a century later, the potential death knell came just after 4.30pm on Tuesday witha perfunctory announcementon the public address system: “The centre is now closed to the public. Please exit the centre by way of the Hall of States.” Soon barricades had been erected and security guards were blocking access.TheJohn F Kennedy Center for the Performing Artsin Washington DC, once filled with the buzz of audiences and children, had fallen as silent as a mausoleum. Now a high stakes legal battle is under way to prevent Donald Trump from taking a wrecking ball to the building that is both national arts complex and living memorial to the 35th president.The current White House occupant, incensed that courts have prevented his name being added to the Kennedy Center, told reporters this week: “I think that theTrump administrationshould certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down.” On social media, Trump declared the venue “destined to doom” without his intervention.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump looks down from the presidential box in the Opera House at the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts as he participates in a guided tour and leads a board meeting on 17 March 2025.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesThe once unthinkable threat became more thinkable when an Agence France-Presse photographertook a picture of Trumpaboard Air Force One, holding a placard with ominous red text: “Kennedy Center DEMOLIS...” The rest of the word was obscured by the plane’s window frame. Below was a big picture showing a yellow heavy construction vehicle scooping rubble from a torn-down building.Trump has no legal right to demolish the facility, which was established by Congress. Critics say he is acting out of spite because he cannot get his way.Kerry Kennedy, the former president’s niece , said: “Like a child who can’t play with a toy, he wants to stomp on the toy. But this is not a toy. This is the living memorial to a slain president.“It would be like adding the Trump name to the Trump-Lincoln Memorial or the Trump-Jefferson Memorial or Trump-Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The courts have spoken, he cannot demolish it, he cannot put his name on it and he should be focused instead on his job.”The Kennedy Center did not respond to requests for comment.The 100ft structure opened in 1971 on the banks of the Potomac River. Since then it has presented ballet, children’s theatre, comedy, contemporary dance, hip-hop, jazz, international festivals and educational programmes. The annualKennedy Center Honorshave hosted past presidents and a who’s who of US arts and culture.View image in fullscreenPresident John F Kennedy looks at a model of the Kennedy Center on 8 October 1963.Photograph: National Archives/Getty ImagesTrumpseized control of the facilityin February 2025, claimed its finances were in dire straits and fired board members who did not align with his “vision for a Golden Age in Arts and Culture”. Deborah Rutter, the centre’s president, was ousted and replaced by Ric Grenell, a Trump loyalist and former ambassador with no experience in arts management.An initiative created in 2020 to promote anti-racism and community outreach was shut down and its 10-person staff dismissed. Citing “drag shows specifically targeting our youth”, any programming perceived as “woke” was purged. It was a commercial disaster as audiences, performers and philanthropists deserted the centre in droves.Lawyer Norm Eisen, who has litigated against the administration’s attempts to impinge on institutional independence, said: “He slapped his name on there and destroyed the lifeblood of the Kennedy Center: audience and artists.”In January, the Kennedy Center hosted the world premiere of Melania,a documentary about the first lady, with the Trumps in attendance. Three days later, the president announced that he would be closing the facility for two years for $257m repairs and renovations.View image in fullscreenReflected in the Potomac River, the exterior of the John F Kennedy Center of the Performing Arts building is lit up in multiple colors in advance of the annual Kennedy Center Honors on 1 December 2024.Photograph: J David Ake/Getty ImagesThe Trump-appointed board backed the move and also voted to rename the venue the “Trump-Kennedy Center”. Trump’s name was duly added to the exterior marble facade, before the US district judge Christopher Cooper intervened and ruled that only Congress has the authority to rename the memorial. The name was removed but the result remains hidden by giant scaffolding and tarpaulins.Asked about Trump’s motivations, Eisen ofDemocracy Defenders Actionadded: “You would need an authority in abnormal psychology to get the answer to that question but he appears to have developed an obsession because he’s not used to hearing the word no.”On Tuesday this week, Judge Cooper again ruled that the Trump administration could not put a new Trump sign on the Kennedy Center’s facade or rename its plaza for the president “without Congress’s blessing”.Hours later, the centre’s board voted to close the facility for two years, citing the need for $257m of repairs and renovations. The centre’s executive director, Matt Floca, ordered an immediate seven-day emergency closure, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration”.But Democratic congresswoman Joyce Beatty and Senator Sheldon Whitehouse allege that the closure is a “pretext” to hide a financial “death spiral” caused by artist boycotts and dwindling ticket sales.View image in fullscreenConstruction workers build scaffolding near the sign for the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts on 12 June.Photograph: Anna Moneymaker/Getty ImagesIn an interview on Friday, Whitehouse, the top Democrat on the environment and public works committee and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board of trustees, said the events represented three phases of Trump’s assault on the complex.“One is what I call the mob bust out gone wrong, in which they tried to take over and run the Kennedy Center,give themselves and their friends big contracts, charge expensive goodies to Kennedy Center accounts, do political favours using Kennedy Center facilities for Trump allies, and that was extremely damaging to the business of the centre,” he said.“Then they moved into the renaming fiasco and that seems to have struck a lethal blow to the centre’s business model – a predictably damaging blow that they failed to consider at all. Now they’ve moved into a third stage in which they are threatening the actual destruction of the Kennedy Center if they don’t get their renaming.”Whitehouse added: “It has gone from bad to worse but the through line in all of this is that these trustees are under a legal duty to put the welfare of the centre itself first and, if they fail in that duty, they create a legal environment in which courts can and ultimately likely will step in to make sure that the centre is run lawfully.”The legal battle intensified on Thursday, when Judge Cooper issued an order requiring the Kennedy Center togive at least 30 days’ noticebefore making any major physical changes to the building, including demolition.Whitehouse said: “There’s a contrast between the thuggery and bullying world in which you could countenance a threat to tear down the Kennedy Center if your name doesn’t go on it and the actual legal world in which actions have to be approved by a board that has a fiduciary duty to put the welfare of the institution first. Those two are irreconcilable at this point.”View image in fullscreenDonald Trump threatened to keep the Kennedy Center closed for good after a judge ruled his name cannot be added on to the famed arts institution’s facade on 15 September.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesStill, Trump ordered the demolition of the White House East Wing to make way for a ballroom, despite opposition from preservationists and questions over the administration’s authority to proceed without Congress. He is now threatening to cancel the renovation of the Kennedy Center, and warning of its possible demise, if his name is not restored to the building.Chris Raleigh, an organiser theHands Off the Artsmovement, which is mobilising grassroots resistance, said: “That’s what you do when the hostage takers can’t get what they want. There comes a point where the hostage is inconvenient. Look at it: the people who have fought back have pushed Trump to the brink here.“In no way at all is he winning. His name is not going up on the building. There is somebody in the White House every day who says, before they walk in that building, ‘Oh god, please don’t let there be another Kennedy Center story today.’”Raleigh added: “Everyone in Trump’s life should be telling him: ‘You gotta to get out now. This is not going to help you.’”And even if the current peril passes, it will be difficult to restore the centre to its former glories. On Friday it laid off about a dozen staff,the Washington Post newspaper reported.Michael Kaiser, who led the centre from 2001 to 2014, warns that even a two-year closure will be damaging. He said: “When you don’t have audiences and you don’t have donors participating for two years, those individuals go elsewhere. When you have no staff, even if there’s a time in the future where we can return to a more sense of being normal, it’s not going to be so simple to reopen a building of this size and complexity.”Some critics see the attack on the Kennedy Center as part of a broader assault on institutions and freedom of expression. On Friday, Trump announced that the media outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico would bebanned from the White Houseand, with health secretary Robert Kennedy Jr standing behind him in the Oval Office, railed against the Kennedy Center again.To Kerry Kennedy, who has worked in thehuman rights arena for 45 years, the president is a “petty tyrant”. Asked to consider the possibility of the Kennedy Center being lost, she reflected: “It would be devastating for my family because we love Uncle Jack but in the end Trump is not going to hurt my family. He is hurting our country and he’s hurting our world and he’s giving permission to tyrants everywhere to shut down arts centres and silence critical voices.”On Friday evening thousands of protesters gathered outside the Kennedy Center in view of the marble facade that remained concealed by scaffolding and tarpaulins. The speakers included a drag queen.Against the setting sun, protesters beat drums and waved signs that read: “Keep your tiny hands off our Kennedy Center”; “You’re no Jack Kennedy”; “Our center not DJT’s”; and “Wicked starring DJT”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpThe KennedysJohn F KennedyWashington DCTrump administrationArts fundinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: Don’t be afraid to be masculine, laugh more, and phone your mum: letters to our sons, by Stephen Graham, Riz Ahmed, Danny Dyer and other wise men | Men | The Guardian
description: The Adolescence actor and the psychologist Orly Klein asked fathers to write to their sons. The results – from famous dads to the wisdom of strangers – were moving and motivating. Here’s a selection
Author: Romesh Ranganathan
Headline: The Adolescence actor and the psychologist Orly Klein asked fathers to write to their sons. The results – from famous dads to the wisdom of strangers – were moving and motivating. Here’s a selection
Content: All illustrations: Sandra Navarro/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAll illustrations: Sandra Navarro/The GuardianMenDon’t be afraid to be masculine, laugh more, and phone your mum: letters to our sons, by Stephen Graham, Riz Ahmed, Danny Dyer and other wise menThe Adolescence actor and the psychologist Orly Klein asked fathers to write to their sons. The results – from famous dads to the wisdom of strangers – were moving and motivating. Here’s a selectionStephen Graham, Danny Dyer, Goldie,Romesh Ranganathan, Tom Daley,Riz Ahmedand othersSat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google’ello champWhat can I say? From the moment you and your sister were born my heart has been full of a love I never thought was humanly possible. As a baby you were filled with wonder and so much energy. You had a beautiful, mischievous and inquisitive nature, which has always made me smile. You were climbing, running and jumping everywhere. You’d walk into a room wearing shoes that were four times, five times, 10 times too big for you … Sometimes they were ye mother’s.The sound of your laughter is one of the most beautiful compositions made by nature. I am so blessed to be a part of your life, and our friendship is something I hold dear to my heart. That beautiful bouncing boy has grown into a man who brightens up a room whenever he walks into it.I have had the pleasure of watching you grow, of watching you learn the lessons of life, like how you conducted yourself when your heart was broken for the first time. To watch you navigate that pain with compassion and come out the other side appreciating your worth without holding on to any resentments, showing your vulnerability to me and your mother and allowing us to guide you through – that was truly admirable.View image in fullscreenYou’re the glue that holds friendships together – you give 110% to all of your relationships. You are a fantastic listener, never judgmental. You have the humility to sit with a prince or a pauper and treat them both equally with dignity and respect. I think one thing I’ve passed on to you is the quality of a proper hug, and anyone who knows you would completely agree.You’ve got funny bones. The little voices you do, your silly impressions, and I love watching the double act you and your mum have created, especially when yous take the piss out of me (Iam5ft 6in). One of my fondest memories is when you and me went out to play football. We climbed over the school gate, wheeled out the goals and had the best game of shootie the world has ever seen (I think I won 10-9). When we got home and knocked on the front door we were covered from head to toe in mud. I’ll never forget your mum’s reaction: “What the hell have you two been up to?!” You and me looked at each other and burst out laughing.View image in fullscreenStephen Graham with his son, Alfie, in 2025.Photograph: Mario Cartelli/Sopa Images/ ShutterstockMy hopes, dreams and aspirations for you are already being fulfilled. Keep being you because you are brilliant. You constantly embody what your nana used to say: “No one is ever above you and no one is ever beneath you.” Always be true to yourself and to who you are. The only advice I could ever give you is to keep doing what you’re doing, always be willing to learn, always be open-minded and always be honest.I love you so much – you’re one of my best mates. I love you to the moon and back for ever.All my loveDadStephen Graham, actorCount your blessings and phone your mum more.Drew, actor, MerseysideThis is a letter …View image in fullscreenDanny Dyer with his son, Arty, in 2016.Photograph: Trevor Leighton/Camera Pressa few words to you, my son. My only son. My son and heir. Unfortunately for your sisters, you get the lot. All my readies. My hard-earned dough. What a result.Just wanna thank you, really. For being a brainy little fucker. The smartest in your class. Never something I could claim to be. The way you can think logically is amazing to me. The way you can retain information brings a tear to my eye. Yes, you’re on the spectrum but ain’t we all. It’s what makes us unique.There’s a lot of wrong ’uns in this world. I know that you won’t be one of ’em. I’d call you my prince. But as we’ve learned, princes can be noncy fuckers.So proud that you’ve come from my nuts. It’s the greatest thing my testicles have ever done.Don’t ever be afraid to be masculine. Always be considerate and kind and thoughtful to anyone you meet coz you never know what they’re going through.Love you, my boy. More than you’ll ever understand.DadDanny Dyer, actor and presenterReject behaviour that devalues women, even when it’s disguised as humour, habit or frustration. Challenge it in yourself first, and in others when needed. How you treat women will say more about you than any success you ever achieve.Martin, retired, HampshireA gentle soul is not there to be chipped away at until hard edges form; it should be polished until the armour of confidence is built.Marc, project manager, BristolHello NikNow that you are 21, I feel as if I can speak to you as one adult to another. I have dozens of reasons to write this letter, but one outweighs them all: the constant sirens and explosions that can be heard in the city every week. Even back when I was working as a journalist at the front, recording interviews right in the trenches, I had already accepted the possibility that I might die. But what frightened me most was something else – that I might not have time to talk to you again, to tell you what truly matters.I no longer live on the frontline, but hundreds of kilometres away from it. Yet rockets and Shahed drones reach this far every week. I’m afraid I won’t be able to do everything I’ve planned in life. And I’m afraid I won’t be able to tell you what truly matters to me. That’s why I’m writing.First and foremost, you might be wondering why I remain in Ukraine, knowing that my life is at risk. Indeed, I had the chance to leave. But I would have lost all respect for myself if I had. It’s as simple as that. An enemy has attacked our country. And it wants either to destroy us or to turn us into slaves. It’s just like in The Lord of the Rings – the orcs have come for the people. I have taken up the fight. My weapon is not a gun, but words. I want to tell people the truth about this war. I truly believe that it is the truth that will help bring it to an end.That is why I stayed. That is why, for two and a half years, I risked my life, travelling along the frontline, helping foreign journalists cover the war, and writing reports and even a book on what I saw. That is why I joined the army, to serve my country. Once again: I could have left.Menof conscription age are not allowed to leave the country, but I have an exemption because I am a father of three children. One thought always stopped me: what kind of life would await me in Europe? The life of a refugee, odd jobs in a restaurant, canteen or care home – just to keep a roof over my head and food on the table? I wouldn’t even be able to support our army. Right now in Ukraine, everything comes down to one simple truth: you are either in the army, for the army, or against the army. That’s the reality of war. It’s as simple as that – there are no grey areas; there isn’t room for doubt or debate.So, there you have it – that’s what I believe. This doesn’t mean I think our country is perfect or wonderful. There is much I dislike – the way things are run, the behaviour of some politicians and commanders. But I remember John F Kennedy’s words: ask not what your country can do for you – ask what you can do for your country. I stayed to fight for my country’s freedom. So that one day, when the war is over, you can come back home and live in a peaceful and free country. In the country for whose freedom your father fought. It may sound a little grand. But you cannot speak about values and faith without a certain grandeur.Sometimes I look at our old photographs and recall the past. Sometimes I remember the first days after you were born. Your mum and I invited many friends over. We were the first in our circle to have a child, and it felt like everyone wanted to congratulate us. One of my friends asked me, “Do you feel like a father yet?” I didn’t know what to say. I was overwhelmed. There was suddenly a new person in my life, a person born out of your mum’s love and mine. My first feelings as a father were wonder, awe and anxiety. I was afraid to hold you in my arms, afraid to bathe you. You were a tiny baby, completely dependent on us. You cried – and your mum nursed you. You fell asleep – and she could finally rest. For a time, her entire world revolved around caring for you. I will never cease to admire this almost sacred power in women – the ability to create life, nurture it and sustain it.It makes me sad that I have to write this letter at all. It is yet another visible and obvious confirmation that I am not with you. After all, if you were living with me, I wouldn’t have to write any letters. I would simply talk to you every day; you would see how I live, how I interact with people, what I do and why – and that would be enough. Children don’t remember our words, but our actions, and they adopt our way of life. Or they leave it behind, if we behave unworthily. The hardest thing about these years of separation isn’t the shelling, rockets or power cuts. The hardest thing is opening the front door after work and not hearing, “Daddy’s home!”I wanted to write to you about raising children – but you know more about that than I do now. You’re training to be a nursery teacher; you’re with children every day. All I ask is that you don’t repeat my mistakes with your own children. Spend time playing with them while they’re still small. Be there.We parents like to think we know which moments shaped our children. We’re usually wrong. It turns out the things that stay with you are the ones where you were watching and we didn’t even know it. Let’s talk about this soon. I have a fortnight’s leave coming, and I’ll be there to see you. I don’t know what you think you’ve learned from me, but I know what I’ve managed to give you: how to read, think and explore the world. And smaller things, like how to ride a bike. We went swimming together, and I decided to find you a coach. Now your breaststroke is faster than mine. You’ve learned languages and left me behind. That’s the greatest joy for me as a father: when my children become better and stronger than me.Your ever-loving fatherVladVladyslav, Kyiv region journalistTranslated from Ukrainian by Marta GosovskaI used to be obsessed with material things. All of those things don’t matter. You can still be miserable in a Ferrari!Gareth, chef, BedfordshireDear JamieI don’t even know where to start this letter, son. I’ve never written to you in prison. It never felt right. Maybe because deep down I didn’t know how to. Maybe I never really learned how to be a father. My mum and dad were never there for me, and I guess I carried that on without meaning to.But I need to say this straight. I’ve always been proud of you. Always. From the day you were born.When we first had you, life was mad, but there were beautiful moments too. You walking round the estate in that little denim outfit, beanie on, that bit of baby jewellery I brought back from Miami – you looked the part, proper cool. Maybe that was my ego a bit, but you really did light up the place.View image in fullscreenGoldie DJing in 2001.Photograph: Sal Idriss/RedfernsWhen me and your mum fell out, everything changed. It was chaos and I didn’t handle it well. I thought by leaving, going to America, searching for peace, chasing art, I was doing something right. But really I was just running. I thought you’d be safe with your mum on the estate, but I didn’t see how fast things were changing.I still remember painting that walkway by your school, the same path you used to walk down every day. When they shut that school, it broke me. That place was the heart of the estate, and when they closed it, it felt like watching the soul of the place die.And, you know what, Jamie, that’s where so much of this started, I think. The pressure. The madness. Kids from different estates suddenly turning on each other. It used to be a few scuffles, a black eye, a busted lip, and you’d move on. But it changed. Somewhere along the line it went from fights to life and death. From 0 to 100. Either him or me. I never really saw it for what it was until you said it yourself: it was either him or me, Dad. That hit me hard. Because I realised it wasn’t just about violence or choices. It was about there being no alternative. No space. No outlet.When I was your age, we had youth clubs, breakdancing, graffiti, music. We had places to put all that energy and pain. That’s what saved me, Jamie. Art saved me. It gave me somewhere to throw all that chaos inside me. That’s why I’m still here. But when they closed the schools, shut the youth clubs and cut the funding, what did they expect was gonna happen? They ripped the heart out of those communities and then blamed the heartbeat for bleeding.So yeah, there’s blood on our hands. But it’s not just yours, son. It’s a whole generation failed. A country that turned its back on you kids and then acted shocked when the streets turned to fire. I don’t say that to make excuses. I just want you to know I see the bigger picture now. And I see you in it, not as a monster, not as a mistake, but as part of something much bigger that went wrong.Then came the call. The one that said my son had taken someone’s life. Jamie, that broke me in half. My heart just sank. All I could think about were two doors: one with your mum answering, hearing you were wanted for murder, and another mother opening hers, being told her son was dead. Two mothers gone that day. That weight has never left me.I didn’t visit for a long time because I was angry, not just at you, but at myself. Because when I looked at you, I saw that bright kid who used to paint beside me, the spark in your eyes, the laughter. There’s a photo of us, me leaning over you while you’re painting in your little pyjamas. That one still gets me.When you came to stay with me in Hertfordshire, I tried to show you my world: the records, the dogs, the art. I thought maybe I could keep you out of trouble, get you into something new. But the streets were always calling, same as they called me when I was young. And when the police came, asking if I’d seen you, saying you were on the run, I can’t even describe the feeling. All that success, the house, the money … none of it mattered. I’d failed where it mattered most.You know that old saying, you can drag a horse to water, but you can’t make it drink. That’s how it felt. I tried, but maybe I didn’t try in the right ways. Maybe I just didn’t know how.But I’ve seen you changing in there, Jamie. I’ve felt it when we talked. There’s more calm in you now, more understanding. The groups you’re doing, the reading, I can tell it’s helping. That’s why I wanna send you more books. Things that might speak to you like art spoke to me.You said something the other day that stuck with me, about feeling anxious about getting out. I understand that now. Freedom’s a strange thing after you’ve been trapped for so long. It’s gonna feel weird, but you’ll find your feet. One step at a time, son. You’ll get there.You’ve always been the stamp of me. Everyone says it. The look, the laugh, the way you move. You’re my son through and through.And I love you. I’ve always loved you. Even when I was silent. Even when I didn’t show it.Maybe next time I’ll start my letter with that, instead of ending with it.I love you, Jamie, from the bottom of my heart.Goldie, musician andartistYou can’t put toothpaste back in the tube. Mistakes will happen – face them, fix them, learn from them. That’s how life is lived.Stewart, East Sussex, trainerskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo my boysWhen I was your age, I remember being really let down by my dad, because of the way he had let down my mum, and it shook me to my core. Up until that point, I didn’t think that dads could make mistakes. We didn’t speak properly for a while after all that, but then my relationship with him got a lot better, because I then saw him for what he was – a flawed human being who loved us very much. It is partly because of this that I have tried to be as open and as honest with you as I can about my mistakes, flaws and doubts, and many of my flaws I have demonstrated without meaning to – but it all helps!You mean so much to me. I have seen all three of you grow into different strong, funny, charming, kind and loving personalities, and every single day I look at you and can’t quite believe that you are my sons. While I worry about how you are going to get on, and what pain you might feel in the future, and what heartbreak you might suffer, I never worry about what you are going to put into the world. You are three people who I couldn’t be prouder of.View image in fullscreenRomesh Ranganathan with his wife, Leesa, and their sons, Theo, Alex and Charlie, in 2019.Photograph: Justin Goff Photos/Getty ImagesI have been lucky enough to spend most of my working life doing something I love, and I would implore you to do the same. Work is hard even if you love it, but doing something you love or care about is one of the best ways to spend your life in contentment. I have never dreaded a day’s work, and I really wish that for you. Choose something you care about and chase that thing until you make it happen, at whatever level that may be. We all get caught up in successes and triumphs, but the greatest triumph is doing it at all. The greatest gift I can hope to give to you is to get you to stop caring about outcomes, and throw yourself completely into what you’re doing. That is much more enriching than any awards, fame, money or recognition.More than that, though, the best advice I can give you is to show love and respect to everyone you come across. If you only think about bettering and helping yourself, I promise you, you will find life unrewarding. If you instead spend your time looking to make connections, supporting people around you, showing people love whether they’re your friends or not, celebrating their successes as if they were your own, you will find happiness follows. What you give to other people will come back to you many times over. That has been my experience, anyway. But please remember, most of the time I’m not sure I’m right.I am sorry for every day that I spent not being with you. I am sorry for every moment that anything took me away. You are my best friends and I would trade every single achievement I have ever made at work for a breakfast together. Maybe not a breakfast. A holiday. An all-inclusive holiday.My sons, you have become what you are not because of me, but hopefully not in spite of me. A happy accident maybe. Plus, let’s be honest, Mum is the better one, isn’t she? I know it’s easy to forget, but please make sure you find some way to show gratitude to her. She has spent every waking moment since you were born thinking about the best and most supportive ways to love you. And I think we can agree, she’s smashed it, despite being slightly obsessive about tidiness. I often agree with you on that, but don’t tell her I said that as she and I have to present a united front.Thank you for being who you are – kind, loving and almost-as-funny-as-your‑dad boys who I’m so beyond proud I played a small part in bringing into the world.With all of my loveA flawed human being who loves you very muchRomesh Ranganathan, comedianTry to switch off. From work, but from screens in particular. I know it’s hard and I don’t say this as a nagging parent; I say it as a parent addicted to bloody screens. I love you.AnonymousRobbie and PhoenixOne of my biggest dreams growing up was to become a parent. I imagined reliving what I had with my dad and hoped that one day I could be even half the parent he was to me: someone who was always there for me at all of my competitions, waving a massive union flag.As I learned more about myself, I thought that dream might never become a reality. But the two of you have brought so much love and joy into your papa’s and daddy’s lives. With so much love, and with the help of your amazing “tummy buddy”, what once felt impossible became real.View image in fullscreenTom Daley and his husband, Dustin Lance Black, with their sons, Robbie (on right) and Phoenix, in 2023.Photograph: Meg Oliphant/Getty ImagesWe have always tried to be as honest and open with you as possible, answering your questions whenever they come. And if we have one piece of advice to give you, it’s to continue to stay close to your incredible tummy buddy, the wonderful woman who helped make our dream of having a family come true.I cannot wait to see the people you grow to be, although not too quickly, because time already feels like it’s moving far too fast. You make me so proud to be your papa every single day.I love you both so much.Your papaTom Daley, OlympianThis letter is my hand on your shoulder. Proof that even when I’m quiet, I’m here.Alex, creative, LondonView image in fullscreen1 Always read the question.2 Measure twice; cut once.3 Think carefully before replying – doubly carefully before posting.4 Do a smaller number of things brilliantly, rather than more things well.I love you so much.John, scientistTo my sonThe place I would always rather be is with you.I know it can be hard to feel that when I have to be away so much to work. I can’t promise to always be there physically, but I promise you’re always on my mind and in my heart. You are what drives me forwards, and brings me back to anchor me.No matter what, I am always with you. Always.View image in fullscreenRiz Ahmed in 2026.Photograph: Robby Klein/Getty Images for IMDbThe love that I feel for you is unlike anything else. Putting you on my back is my deepest joy. Long after you’re too big for me to carry you, I hope I can still give you that feeling. That you are able to stand taller, see further and climb higher, because of the love that supports you.Being a man means many different things. You will work out what it means to you. You don’t need to follow anyone else’s template. Just remember the non-negotiables. Self-respect, respect for others, respect for our environment.It also means facing challenges. That’s part of life. And when you do, remember it’s OK to share your feelings and reach out. Draw strength from your family, friends and community. Vulnerability is brave, beautiful and powerful. We aren’t supposed to pretend it’s all OK. Taking off the armour helps us connect.Each obstacle is an invitation to deeper connections with others, but also to grow, and to unearth the deepest parts of yourself.More than anything, our challenges are a reminder that life’s river is one we don’t control, and that there is a greater current guiding our lives. Surrendering to its flow, swimming with the current, can sometimes bring us more peace, power and purpose than fighting it.I’m always here for you, proud of you, and grateful to be on this adventure with you.Please make time for joy. Seek it, share it, create it for yourself and others.You are beloved and worthy of love.BabaRiz Ahmed, actor and rapperYou have two ears and one mouth.Use it in the right ratio.Chris, BerkshireLads, boys, fellas, chaps, menIt’s all right being a bloke. Let’s face it, we don’t have the odds stacked against us like women do. But it can still be confusing. So here’s a few wise lessons I’ve learned through 50‑plus years of being stupid.The first thing is, you can be who and what you want. It’s all good. Life is much more fun if you try things out from different angles and ignore the voices of the cool, telling you, “Nah, no way!” I’ve passed on to you a few things that you’ve accepted already. You know to respect others and to care about the world around you. This is good. I wonder how this will manifest itself as you grow and change, and the world grows and changes around you?You stand up to prejudice. You’re basically decent and kinda leftwing. You don’t like the Tories. Which is good, because that really is a red line. But back to the first point. I do like football. I also like motorbikes and beer and mountain climbing and other bloke stuff. And I know you quite like some of that, too.But I also like cheerleading and pole-dancing, long walks, drag, books, foreign films, fake eyelashes, art galleries, socialism, fur coats … I know you hate some of that and can be mortally embarrassed by me, but, believe me, my life is much more fun and interesting for all of it. Try anything you might be intrigued by and sod anyone who tells you it’s weird. Weird is good.My dad once told me that he realised too late that he was actually a good guy – someone he could like and be proud of. And actually quite good-looking. He told me that I was, too. He told me too late and I believed him even later. I hope I haven’t told you too late and I hope you believe me now.Believe in yourselves. Love and respect yourselves and others. Stand up to injustice and ignore ignorance. Be who and whatever you want to be.I love you.Mick, trade union organiser and cabaret performer,SussexGet a dog.JamesThis is an edited extract from Letters to Our Sons by Stephen Graham and Orly Klein, published by Bloomsbury (£22) on 24 September. title: The moment I knew: On a bike ride, she did a bunny hop over a speed hump – her pure joy for life delighted me | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Anna Malos and Georgie bonded over their shared love of travel and horses. By their third date, an awkward encounter cemented their relationship
Author: James Norman
Headline: Anna Malos and Georgie bonded over their shared love of travel and horses. By their third date, an awkward encounter cemented their relationship
Content: Anna Malos and Georgie at Lands End in 2010View image in fullscreenAnna Malos and Georgie at Lands End in 2010The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: On a bike ride, she did a bunny hop over a speed hump – her pure joy for life delighted meAnna Malosand Georgie bonded over their shared love of travel and horses. By their third date, an awkward encounter cemented their relationshipFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesAnna Malos, as told toJames NormanSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGeorgie and I met at a kick-boxing club in London in 2004. We sparred together in a few beginner classes, just hitting soft pads. Although I didn’t pay her too much attention initially, I immediately recognised she was tall, elegant and very good looking.It wasn’t until the club’s Christmas drinks that things kicked off between us. We started talking and couldn’t stop. We’d both travelled and worked in Latin America, and also loved horses – Georgie had volunteered with a horse-riding business for tourists in Ecuador. The sparks were flying all over the place.A friend of mine was deejaying at a gay club nearby so we headed there and continued chatting, dancing and flirting. About 2am we found an all-night cafe and talkeduntil daybreak, then went our separate ways. But we planned to meet again.On my way to our third date, my housemate called saying we’d been burgled. I had to return home and call the police. When I explained this to Georgie she suggested coming to mine instead. When the police finally arrived, many hours later, I introduced myself as one of the occupants. One of the constables asked Georgie who she was. There was this awkward silence – on date three was she my girlfriend? I think we went with “friend”. But she didn’t go home that night.View image in fullscreenThe couple on a horse-riding trip in Kyrgyzstan in 2011Things moved quickly from there. One morning in early spring we took a bike ride through a nearby park that had little speed bumps. Like us, our bikes were very different – mine was a lightweight touring bike and hers a hard-tail mountain bike.The moment I knew: I had planned to break up with him – then he snuck out of school to buy me hot chipsRead moreI was riding just ahead of her but when I looked back I saw her doing this funky bunny hop over the speed hump. I can picture the jacket she was wearing – dark grey, heavy canvas – and her focus as she flicked her bike over the hump. It was that joie de vivre that delighted me. Her embarrassment when she realised I’d seen was also so very her – wanting to be cool, but so much more than that. This was someone who couldn’t contain her enthusiasm. It crystallised what I loved about her.After a couple of years of living together in London we moved to Melbourne. She loved the city and fitted right into some sports and footy clubs here. But she found it hard to get work for her niche in sports community development. So she went back to the UK for work and our relationship became long-distance.Nearly a year later, in 2009, she found out she had breast cancer. She was only 32. Within a fortnight, I gave up my job and moved to the UK to be with her. She absolutely knew I would upend my life to support her at a time it really mattered.She did recover well initially. A couple of years later we made it back to Australia and this time we both found work that suited us. We also took many great trips – camping in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, cycling trips all over including from Cairns to Cape York.View image in fullscreenAt their commitment ceremony in the UK in 2016View image in fullscreenIn the backyard of their home in Rye, East Sussex, in 2020But a couple of years later she was diagnosed again, and a bit later the cancer metastasised. At the tail-end of 2019 her doctor advised her that she may only have six months to live. It was time for her to head home to the UK and I went with her. It coincided with Covid lockdowns, so we got to spend a tremendous amount of time together in a small town near her family.Georgie seemed to be improving but then she started to get breathless and her specialists couldn’t work out why. She was in hospital for scans when she had a brain haemorrhage and lapsed into unconsciousness. Two days later, in July 2020, after some intensely moving times in ICU with her family, she died.I feel so much gratitude for the time we spent together. Just three days before the brain haemorrhage she had cycled to see her GP – so fitting, being active was so important to her. It was her irrepressible energy I loved, and I am a better person for having known her.Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: Suzi Quatro: ‘It is absolutely crazy I’m not in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. But I’m in good company!’ | Music | The Guardian
description: The 76-year-old rocker on her pre-gig routine, the one reality show she’d go on and who she’d cast as herself in a film about her life
Author: Andrew Stafford
Headline: The 76-year-old rocker on her pre-gig routine, the one reality show she’d go on and who she’d cast as herself in a film about her life
Content: Suzi Quatro: ‘I always just did what I felt, and I like that about me.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSuzi Quatro: ‘I always just did what I felt, and I like that about me.’Photograph: Sarah Lee/The Guardian10 Chaotic QuestionsMusicSuzi Quatro: ‘It is absolutely crazy I’m not in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. But I’m in good company!’The 76-year-old rocker on her pre-gig routine, the one reality show she’d go on and who she’d cast as herself in a film about her lifeAndrew StaffordSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYour new album is called Freedom and the title track interpolates The Girl Can’t Help It. You’re going to be rocking until they take you out in a box, aren’t you?When I was 35, a journalist stupidly asked me, “When are you going to retire?” I said, “I will retire when I go on stage, turn my back on the audience, shake my ass, and there’s silence.” This followed me my whole career, so when I got to 65, I said, “I will retire when I go on stage, turn my back on the audience and my ass shakes by itself.”I’m 76 now but at 75 I gave my final quote on this subject, and it was serious – I will retire when I go on stage and do not deliver to my standard. When I feel that, I’m done.There’s also a cover ofMC5’sKick Out the Jams, with Alice Cooper. Tell me a bit about Detroit in the 60s, where you had Motown on one hand and yourself, Alice, Iggy andMC5 on the other? What a time to be alive!What a city! We had Motown, which we all bowed down to, we were weaned on it. But all the white rock’n’roll groups, they all had that danger, that edge, that foot-on-the-gas desperation. I’ve talked about it with Brother Wayne Kramer, who passed not long ago, and Alice, and we don’t know why that is, but we can never get rid of that. It was a special time.What’s the most chaotic thing that’shappened to you on stage?Tove Lo: ‘The rumour I hear the most is that I’m either pregnant or in rehab. I want both of those to not be true’Read moreWe were doing a show once, going down a storm, and I have a section with the drummer where we’re both playing, because I’m a trained percussionist, so it’s likeGene Krupa and Buddy Rich. Then the PA blew, and all the audience could hear were drums. We looked at each other, and went, right, let’s go!So, we did a 15-minute drum solo together, because whatever happens on stage, the golden rule is you use it – you have to make it work. Finally, somebody from the side of stage put his thumbs up, and we went back into the song. Everybody thought it was part of the show.You’re a veteran road hog. What’s the first thing you do when you get to your hotel?I set up my room. The computers go on the table. My diary gets opened. My stage clothes get hung up on the hooks. My boots get put out. My pyjamas go on the bed. I turn the bed down, then before I leave the room for the gig, I close the curtains and check all the lights to get the correct ambience. That way, when I come in after the show, it feels like home.View image in fullscreenSuzi Quatro in Amsterdam in 1973.Photograph: Gijsbert Hanekroot/RedfernsHow about your most chaotic encounter with a fan?Most of them are great but this wasn’t nice. A couple of years ago I was coming out to do my final song, and everybody had their hands up for a high-five. So did a little bit of that, and one girl grabbed my hand, held on to it with a death-grip and tried to pull me off the stage. I tried to pull back and my entire jumpsuit ripped, right across my ass.I finally got free and I walked backwards to my monitor – very professional! – and I sat down and did the rest of the song, not moving. As soon as the song was over, the monitor guy came and put a towel around my waist, and I walked off. I wish I could find that girl because I would love to give her a piece of my mind. I was really upset.There has already been adocumentary about you. If there was a biopic of your life, who would play you?Suzi Quatro review – at 75, her signature scream is still thrillingRead moreWe’re working on that right now, we’re doing the screenplay as we speak. Scarlett Johansson springs to mind. But whoever plays me, I would have to meet them, because I would need to feel something that you can’t act, and that’s theSuzi Quatrovibe. Don’t ask me to explain it but I would have to feel they have that vibe about them.If you had to appear on a reality TV show tomorrow, which one would it be?There’s only one — Strictly Come Dancing.Before you went solo, you were in a group withyour sisters, the Pleasure Seekers, whose best-known song isWhat a Way to Die. Was that inspired by the Who’s My Generation?I don’t know who inspired that; it was just about getting drunk and crazy. But what I love about that song is that I was only 15, and my style was set right from the beginning. It wasn’t something I developed through the years. Nobody ever told me how to stand, how to sing, how to play, what to do. I always just did what I felt, and I like that about me.What’s an album you always return to?I’ve got a few. Bob Dylan’s Blonde on Blonde. Jackson Browne’s Running on Empty. And Tom Petty’s first album. Those are the three that just popped to mind that I will play nonstop and never get tired of.Tell me why you’re not in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.It is absolutely crazy. It used to bother me but now I’ve read up on lots of people who aren’t in it, and I’m in good company! I always thought it was a no-brainer, because there was never a woman playing an instrument in a rock’n’roll band with world success before me. I just hope they’re not waiting for me to die so they can do it posthumously.Suzi Quatro is touring Australiabetween 14 November and 6 December. Freedom is out nowExplore more on these topicsMusic10 Chaotic QuestionsPop and rockSuzi QuatroDetroitfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hunk – or ‘unc’? What magazine covers of Michael B Jordan and Tom Cruise tell us about manhood | Men | The Guardian
description: Images of two actors on front of Vogue and GQ land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlines
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Images of two actors on front of Vogue and GQ land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlines
Content: Covers from Vogue magazine of Michael B Jordan and Tom Cruise in GQ.Photograph: Vogue/GQView image in fullscreenCovers from Vogue magazine of Michael B Jordan and Tom Cruise in GQ.Photograph: Vogue/GQMenHunk – or ‘unc’? What magazine covers of Michael B Jordan and Tom Cruise tell us about manhoodImages of two actors on front of Vogue and GQ land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlinesChloe Mac DonnellSat 19 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom Cruise andMichael B Jordanshare many similarities as box-office powerhouses known for their death-defying action hero stunts. But this week the two stars went head-to-head, or more accurately chest-to-chest, on magazine stands.In one corner there’s 64-year-old Cruise on the cover of GQ, his first for the magazine in 20 years. Posing in an unbuttoned shirt, one hand running through his tousled hair, the other gripping his belt buckle, this is Cruise playing the role of sexy Cruise.Despite his efforts, and Cruise previous having beencrowned the sexiest man alive, the internet, usually a place of deep division, has unanimously agreed that the resulting image is deeply unsexy.“Never sharing Tom Cruise GQ cover because I have compassion for others,” reads one comment on GQ’s Instagram. “What horrors did I do to get this in my algorithm,” adds another. Others have nicknamed him “unc” –internet slang for someone out of touch.Meanwhile, 39-year-old Jordan makes his Vogue debut (the sixth man to be given a solo cover) lying down and laughing on a bed of flowers, the blazer of his suit unbuttoned to showcase his many, many abs and a flash of his right nipple.Most of the comments are NSFW (not suitable for work). An example from the tamer offerings: “I aspire to be a flower.”The covers land at a time when masculinity is increasingly dominating headlines. From toxic masculinity tolooksmaxxingand performative males, the conversation is being driven by increasing concerns over the manosphere and what exactly being a man means and looks like today. Cruise is a boomer. Jordan is a millennial. Both have added further fuel to the masculinity fire.Dr Ashley Morgan, a masculinities scholar at Cardiff Metropolitan University, says despite there being “a massive range of masculinities”, people tend to focus on one type: the white male patriarch.“That is what Cruise is selling on this cover,” she says. In contrast, “Jordan presents a range of masculinities including ideas around Black masculinity. He’s wearing a suit but it’s very suggestive. His cover is more universally attractive to men, women and others.”For Andrew Groves, director of the menswear archive at the University of Westminster, there is a clear fashion distinction. “Everything in the Cruise image is constructed to make it appear sexy, yet somehow it isn’t,” he says. “Cruise is given clothes rather than fashion. The worn shirt and old Levi’s belong to a masculine language of work and labour. Jordan is allowed fashion, decoration, jewellery, and softness. His masculinity is constructed through a much wider set of codes.”When Adam Baidawi was named the new editor of GQ last year, he said he wanted to restore the magazine to “its rightful place as the North Star of masculinity”, and that GQ would be “a magazine for and about men”.His debut cover in September featured the actor Jeremy Strong wearing a hoodie and holding a steel archery bow. It chimed heavily with what Baidawi’s predecessor, Will Welch, set out to do. One of his most popular issues was “The New Masculinity” edition in 2019, which starred Pharrell Williams on the cover in a gown-like coat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA year later, Harry Styles appeared on the cover of Vogue wearing a dress. Six years on, Styles has ditched his signature sequined jumpsuits for suits and ties on his world tour while Trump’s Maga movement is being driven by tech bros and a model of manhood that champions traditional patriarchy.Alona Pardo, who previously curatedan exhibition exploring masculinities in photography at the Barbicanin London, says the two latest covers highlight “how the media continues to codify and reinforce normative ideals of manhood”. Pardo says the image of Cruise defying ageing is particularly reductive as it reinforces “the standard that a man’s worth is linked to physical vigour and perpetual dominance”.Jessa Crispin, author of What’s Wrong withMen, says Cruise’s cover reflects his role as “the dad of Hollywood”. In the accompanying interview he talks about teaching young actors how to navigate the business, including giving actor Glen Powell a six-hour instructional film. “It’s a very kind of traditional man-as-steward masculine role,” Crispin says. She compares the “tame” Jordan cover to Cary Grant, “masculine with a sense of humour, and not really anything revolutionary”.Pardo says both are disappointing. By using the visual language of virility they reassert “traditional patriarchal authority”. Framed against social movements including #MeToo, Pardo says the images “function as a reactionary bid for male solidarity” and ultimately reassert “traditional patriarchal authority in direct opposition to movements challenging systemic power dynamics”.Explore more on these topicsMenMagazinesTom CruiseMichael B JordanNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

agonisingly difficult and ambiguous situation to the next – each a terrifying point of no return, each the awful occasion of things seen and said that can’t be unseen or unsaid.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewPick of the restShaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy BottomIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenThings that go baa in the night … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph:
