description: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Author: Anna Ivanenko
Headline: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Content: Illustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianOpinionUkraineMeditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missilesSometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming backAnna IvanenkoSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTShareSometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours afterUS Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow.Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time.I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen

title: Maga wants more babies. But they don’t seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detention | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Officials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they need
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Officials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they need
Content: ‘It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance.’Photograph: AlamyOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Maga wants more babies. But they don’t seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detentionArwa MahdawiOfficials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they needSat 19 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareMaga men have babies on the brain. They may not all be interested inchanging diapersor hands-on parenting, but they’re very keen on population growth. “[W]e want more babies, to put it very nicely,” Donald Trump saidlast year.Trump, who has called himself the “father of IVF” andjokedthat he will be known as the “fertilization president”, surrounds himself with people who profess a similar fondness for children. Only afew daysafter being sworn in as vice-president, JD Vance declared he wanted “more babies in the United States of America” and went on to make pronatalist policies a theme of his time in office.Meanwhile, the administration’s favourite moneyman, Elon Musk, is doing his own part to increase the population. Ashley St Clair, the mother of one of his many offspring, has claimed he once told her hewanted to have“a legion of children before the civil war”. At least one of Musk’s kids hasdenounced him, so I’m not sure he’s considered that they might not all be fighting on the same side.While the Trump administration may want a baby boom, it won’t shock you to hear that, when you take a closer look at their particular brand of pronatalism, they don’t actually seem to want “more babies”. What they really want, judging by the way in which pregnant immigrants are being treated, is more of the “right” type of baby.AGuardian investigationpublished this week revealed that ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers. These detained women are reportedly not receiving the prenatal healthcare they need and, alarmingly, ICE does not seem to have records of how many of these women have suffered miscarriages.“ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration,” the Guardian writes. “[B]ut the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.” Let me just reiterate that: we have no idea how many women in ICE detention have lost their babies over the past 11 months.It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers;the agency, and theTrump administration, is normally very big on surveillance. Last year, the Guardianreportedthat pregnant immigrant women were turning up to hospitals to deliver their babies wearing location-tracking smartwatches as part of an ICE monitoring program. One of these women was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, which can cause major swelling, and hospital staff were worried that the smartwatch would cut off her circulation. “She was in tears about [the idea of taking the surveillance device off],” a hospital staffer told the Guardian. “She had this deep fear that ICE was going to come to the hospital and take her baby.”Surveillance also extends to the broader pregnant population. When Dr Erica Schwartzwas confirmedby the US Senate as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) earlier this year, sheemphasized: “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.” While the CDC doesn’t require states to collect data on abortions, 44 states plus Washington DC have some sort of mandated abortion reporting, according to theGuttmacher Institute. This isn’t necessarily sinister but, following the overturning of Roe v Wade, there has been growing concern that this data might be weaponized to punish abortion patients and providers, who are increasingly being treated like criminals.And that concern is hardly unfounded. In the first two years after Roe was overturned, prosecutors in 16 states charged more than 400 people with pregnancy-related crimes, a2025 reportby the group Pregnancy Justice found. The report also noted that there are likely far more cases of miscarriage criminalization than have made headlines.Funny, isn’t it? If you suffer a miscarriage in ICE detention, possibly because of systemic medical neglect, the US government will apparently shrug and look the other way. But if you have a miscarriage in a state that hasfetal personhood languagein its abortion laws, you may find yourself facing a police investigation and criminal charges. Once again, there is nothing pro-life about this administration. They are solely pro-control.FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” an internalFBI memo warns. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online.” Oh dear, my heart bleeds for these poor ICE agents.Turkey is targeting LGBTQ+ activists and journalistsStarting last Sunday, Turkish police raided the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organizations and HIV-advocacy groups. Then they arrested peopleprotestingagainst the raids and journalists covering the protests. “This is thewidest crackdownon LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch. Homosexuality isn’t illegal in Turkey, but the government seems to be weaponizing “obscenity” laws to target the community.Israeli ‘double tap’ strike kills child and medic in GazaThe “ceasefire”continues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’ than men with the same conditionNew research from the University of St Andrews found that women have significantly unequal medical care. Men are far more likely to be offered treatments such as strong painkillers or surgery,according to the analysis.Joe Rogan calls Trump supporters ‘nuts’ and ‘rabid’Does thepodcasternot realize that his supporthelpedget Trump elected? Lack of self-awareness aside, it’s amusing to watch some of Trump’s former supporters turn on the president.Michigan high school asks girls to share details of menstrual cyclesFemale students who miss swimming because of their periods need to have a parent submit a note “stating the length of the menstrual duration” so they canmake up the day. If you don’t comply,your grade is at risk.Indonesia’s all-female firefighting team are battling peatland blazes and patriarchal attitudesOne hundred and forty-six women, aged between 20 and 58,make up the Power of Mama, which protects the biodiverse region of Indonesian Borneo. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most,” one member said of what motivated her to fight fires. “I thought I had to do something about it.”Kash Patel defends new FBI bestiality policyPatel told a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing that the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” byautomatically disqualifying them. At one point of this absurd hearing, a senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. Just when you thought US politics couldn’t get any more stupid, it goes and surprises you.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)OpinionSurveillanceFBITurkeyLGBTQ+ rightsIsraelGazacommentShareReuse this content

title: I live in the ‘coolest neighbourhood’ in the world. It’s not as great as you’d think | Raphael Rashid | The Guardian
description: A wave of tourists and visitors has changed the character of the Seoul neighbourhood I live in and helped create a place that no longer feels like home
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: A wave of tourists and visitors has changed the character of the Seoul neighbourhood I live in and helped create a place that no longer feels like home
Content: A rainbow walkway laid for an LGBTQ+ night event in the backstreets of Jongno 3-ga, June 2022. Seoul, South Korea.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA rainbow walkway laid for an LGBTQ+ night event in the backstreets of Jongno 3-ga, June 2022. Seoul, South Korea.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianSouth KoreaI live in the ‘coolest neighbourhood’ in the world. It’s not as great as you’d thinkRaphael RashidA wave of tourists and visitors has changed the character of the Seoul neighbourhood I live in and helped create a place that no longer feels like homeFri 18 Sep 2026 23.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 23.22 EDTShareIn 2021, I was asked by Time Out to nominate a Seoul neighbourhood for its annual list of the world’s coolest. I didn’t think much of it and put forward the one I live in, Jongno 3-ga, in the old centre of the city. Somehow, it got ranked third.This week, the same area was named thecoolest neighbourhood in the world. I should be pleased, but instead, I’m devastated.All these lists seem to celebrate the same idea of “cool”: expensive conceptual art galleries, high-end restaurants, and the sort of places that cater to a narrow demographic of people who read lifestyle magazines. Most cities have these places.But when I moved to Jongno 3-ga, I chose somewhere that was the opposite: humble, raw and completely unpretentious.‘The vibes, the food, the people’: a night out in Burwood, Australia’s coolest neighbourhoodRead moreI was first drawn to the neighbourhood 20 years ago, fresh out of school. I recollect with sweet nostalgia being one of the few tourists at a time whenSouth Koreawas not “cool”, and people often advised me against travelling there, confusing South Korea with North Korea.There were no English menus, but restaurants were welcoming. Shopfronts were rusty but full of artisanry, while alleys that went nowhere and were slightly dilapidated felt cosy. There were men getting drunk over bottles of soju who occasionally got into a brawl, but nothing that ever felt particularly threatening. I felt at home and eventually made it my home.View image in fullscreenDiners eating at street barbecue restaurants in Jongno 3-ga.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianIt was a refuge for society’s rejects: people with nowhere to go, some of the poorest in Seoul, residents of the city’s tiny-room settlements and people with disabilities. In Tapgol Park, elderly women sold sexual services to older men in plain sight. Outside the park, pensioners played janggi, Korean chess, on the pavement. Around them lived musicians and artists. In Jongno 3-ga, everyone was welcome.For years, thepojangmacha, the street-food tents that serve everything from fried squid to kimchi pancake, catered to older people drinking through to the early evening. Then at some point – around 9pm – there was an unofficial handover to the gay scene.South Korea is socially conservative and the LGBTQ+ community isstill very much frowned upon. But come the weekend, hundreds of excited men of all ages came to let off steam out in the open, as well as in one of the area’s more than 100 gay bars and karaoke rooms. Jongno 3-ga was a place where people could be themselves, without fear of being outed, harassed or judged.Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with antsRead moreNone of that was cool. But that was the entire point: people could mind their own business in a safe haven amid a culture addicted to consumerism and keeping up appearances.That all changed after Covid. The street barbecues andpojangmachaare still there, but now they have queues, some up to an hour long. People line up for a seat, take their Instagram shots, and the neighbourhood that used to hide people has become a place to be seen.With the crowds came the displacement. Gay patrons no longer take over the streets at night. The older drinkers have largely gone. The sex workers have been pushed out. The chess boards outside Tapgol Park were cleared away. Rents have risen sharply.View image in fullscreenJongno 3-ga station, in a neighbourhood long home to Seoul’s gay scene and a gathering place for its older residents.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianThe area is now littered with kitschy tourist shops, claw-machine arcades and unmanned photo-booths, and, in the streets nearby, bakery after bakery, coffee shop after coffee shop. One by one, the small merchants have left, to be replaced with another dessert shop. It’s now hard to find the humble rice-and-soup places that fed this neighbourhood for decades. The once shabby and unremarkable place is now heavily curated, and doesn’t feel very “Korean” any more.Locals complain about lost identity and gentrification but put on a brave face for the hordes of tourists, both local and international, who come to gorge on this area.None of this is the fault of the visitors either. They were told the place was worth seeing, and they are buying exactly what they were sold. K-culture has never been more popular. From the likes of BTS to Squid Game, the whole world is looking to South Korea and keeps coming – and things are changing to accommodate for these tourist dollars.But in a way, I feel part of the problem. I highlighted a place I loved for being overlooked, and feel I helped create a monster. Now, as the neighbourhood becomes almost unrecognisable, I wonder what effect these rankings have on the people who live in the listed destinations.Jongno 3-ga becoming the “world’s coolest neighbourhood” is nothing to celebrate. I feel guilty for calling it cool. I’d take the word back if I could.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreacommentShareReuse this content

title: After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly | Jamie Oliver | The Guardian
description: This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful, says chef and campaigner Jamie Oliver
Author: Jamie Oliver
Headline: This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful, says chef and campaigner Jamie Oliver
Content: Children wait to be served dinner at a school in Swindon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreenChildren wait to be served dinner at a school in Swindon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyOpinionSchool mealsAfter 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properlyJamie OliverThis week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful!Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTShareMore than 20 years ago, when I started thecampaign and TV series School Dinners, I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our children at school. I have never, and will never, stop banging that drum – even after this week’smomentous announcement on school food standardsin England. Because it is so important we remember where we started from.Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, buttwice the recommended sugar, school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’ssocial connection and sense of belonging. Well-fed kidsare happier, have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, andtheir learningandbehaviour improve, too.It’s no surprise that80% of teachers agreethat unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.But we didn’t need scientific evidence to tell us that – who doesn’t feel and perform better when their bellies are full of the good stuff? Get school food right and the prize is massive. Not just for children today, but for the adults they will become. Feed children well and we give them a better chance of healthier lives, greater productivity and less long-term pressure on the NHS and social care from diet-related disease. That’s no small change when current estimates are that obesity, and its knock-on consequences, costs the UK economy about£126bn each year.That is why it’s so great to see the government announce new standards, based on the latest science. It’s the first time in a decade. And it means, for this generation of kids, they will be nourished with more fruit and vegetables, fibre-rich proteins and whole grains. Beautiful stuff.It’s a big and much-needed update, but we know that amazing schools, caterers and chefs can rise to the challenge. Through myGood School Food awards, we have shown amazing school food is possible and affordable, and it’s happening right now in schools across the UK.TakeChef Russ in Bournemouth. Working out of a cupboard-sized kitchen, he has transformed the food at his school. Not only has the school increased the uptake of meals from 28% to 98%, there’s a waiting list of parents keen to nab their kids a place there.We see this pattern in schools up and down the country, and we have to keep telling these stories again and again because it goes against what many people think they know – that kids simply won’t eat the “good stuff”. We have heard that for decades. And we get it, because the food environment we all struggle with makes it hard to eat well, and so this seems to chime with our experience. But school is different. It’s a rare, protected space where that noise can be stripped away.And when it is, remarkable things happen. Children eat – and enjoy – delicious, nutritious food. The evidence is clear: when the food is good and the environment is supportive, over time school meal uptake increases.View image in fullscreenJamie Oliver serves up a healthy school dinner.Photograph: Andy Butterton/PAWhat makes me excited is these standards won’t just sit on a piece of paper. There will be proper monitoring to make sure they are actually followed. Not to nit-pick. Not to catch schools out. But so we know what’s working, where schools are doing brilliantly, and where we need to deploy care, love and support to help them get it right. That’s where theSchool Food Projectcomes in. We know not all lunch trays are created equal, which is why we are partnering with Bite Back, Chefs in Schools, School Food Matters and the Food Foundation to help to make sure these new standards can really be for everyone.These new school food standards will finally fix what is on children’s school plates, but it’s only half the job we have to do. A delicious lunch nourishes a child for the afternoon, but teaching them how to cook nourishes them for the rest of their life. You can serve the best meals in the world, but if a child leaves school without knowing how to feed themselves, that’s where it stops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionServing up salad success at school dinners | LettersRead moreThat is why food education must be absolutely central to transforming school food. And it’s why I’m passionate about giving kids (and adults) the skills, knowledge and confidence to cook from scratch. My dream has always been simple: I want every single child to leave school knowing 10 core skills that will save their life.My free10 skills food education programmeteaches kids basic, bulletproof culinary foundations – how to chop safely, balance flavours, cook a nutritious staple meal from scratch, and stretch simple, fresh ingredients into something delicious. If kids leave school knowing how to cook a fast vegetable stir-fry, a simple soup, or how to make a loaf of bread, not only will they be healthier now, but they have options in the future.With this cooking superpower they can feed themselves, and their future families, on a budget. That isn’t just a life skill: it’s health insurance for life.Jamie Oliver is a chef, restaurateur and campaignerExplore more on these topicsSchool mealsOpinionSchoolsObesityNHSHealthNutritionHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: Twenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking out, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: Twenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking out, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at Coachella in California on 19 April 2025.Photograph: Timothy Norris/Getty Images for CoachellaView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at Coachella in California on 19 April 2025.Photograph: Timothy Norris/Getty Images for CoachellaOpinionEd SheeranEd Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he wasJason OkundayeTwenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking outSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 07.14 EDTShareIt must have come as a surprise to Ed Sheeran when all of hissupport acts withdrewfrom the remainder of the US leg of his tour. The American rapper Macklemore had triggered the walkout when he gave an impassioned speech calling for a “free Palestine” on stage and was dropped for doing so. The decision by the remaining acts to drop out in solidarity exposed a deep divide in the modern music industry.Some artists still insist on keeping politics out of music, while others expect music to speak to our perilous times.After he was dropped,Macklemore wrotethat Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before”, to which Sheeranresponded: “I am not complicit” and “those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum”.Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row - The LatestRead moreI think that the concept of expectation is worth probing. The idea that artists should make their political sentiments known is often dismissed as a parasocial delusion, one particularly rampant among young people on social media who “call out” musicians for their silence (indeed, young people are far more likely to be in favour of musiciansusing their concerts to make political statements). Artists aren’t politicians, the criticism goes, and to consider them as such distracts from, even compromises, the purpose of art as a forum for personal expression and of escapism. In other words, why not just enjoy the music instead of expecting activism from musicians, too?The problem with that idea is that it treats a separation of art and politics as natural rather than something determined by historical convention. It wasn’t so long ago that expectations were quite different. There used to be a neater division between countercultural musicians who were relegated to the periphery and mainstream artists who would be disciplined if they spoke up.The MTV era of music in the 2000s prioritised blockbuster, spectacle and glamour, while avoiding political, social and economic controversies. Artists were generally expected to keep politics out of their music. When Madonna challenged that idea in 2003 with her single American Life, which opposed US foreign policy and jingoism at the onset of the Iraq war, the backlash was heavy: she wasforced to dumpits “un-American” music video, and faced heavy radio blacklisting. It took years forthe Chicks, then known as The Dixie Chicks, to recover commercially from the backlash they faced to their criticism of the Iraq War and George W Bush around the same period.Today, theexpectations that audiences have of artistsare different from two decades ago. Partly, this is because the economics and the technology behind the music industry has changed. In the age of streaming, it is harder to silence artists who have made politically problematic statements – radio station blacklisting is far less fatal than it was before people discovered music through their phones and algorithms.Interestingly, this greater political autonomy also means that the biggest artists take less of a commercial hit in their worst moments. After Kanye West’s antisemitic rants (which the rapper apologised for), his albumVultures still reached No 1on the Billboard charts in 2024. On his most recent tour, he performed at AT&T stadium in Arlington, Texas, one of the venues that banned Macklemore from performing.In any case, this greater autonomy pushes young fans to ask: why not take the risk? Why not speak? Particularly in the case of Palestine, it has often been smaller and less influential artists who have done so. Think of how the scale of Sheeran’s commercial reach, by contrast, dwarfs that of the artists around him who have risked more by speaking out.Artists, both alternative and mainstream, have also set this expectation for each other. The stances a musician has taken on pressing issues are no longer just cudgels used against them. Rather, silence on these matters has become a source of shame.Billie Eilishrebuked her fellow celebrities for not taking a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the US and itskilling of civilians. The Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, who I saw at Glastonbury last year leading a “free Palestine” chant on the Pyramid Stage, had this to say while receiving the award for best album at theIvor Novello Awardsthis year: “I have a very specific idea of what songwriting is supposed to be for, and I think it is to reflect the times through your own personal view so that everybody can have something to connect to and something to learn from years later. And now I would compel my fellow artists in the room, it is not the time to sit on the fence.”The political shift in music also reflects a tonal shift. Artists have become more emotionally intimate with their audiences. I was struck by ananalysispublished earlier this year by the music data company Musixmatch for the Economist, which assessed lyrics from the Billboard charts to conclude that pop music has become “gloomier”. The most popular songs increasingly invoke sadness, angst and heartbreak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA study in the Times also found that the musical mood hasbecome more downbeat. This is in itself not surprising – listeners increasingly wantauthenticityfrom musicians and depend on it for a sense of connection. Think of the music of Eilish and CMAT, both of whom are popular with young audiences and praised for filterless emotion. They invoke that gloom, vulnerability and emotion – in other words, they communicate pain as a central tenor of their sound.As CMAT said of her music, which muses on isolation, capitalism and disillusionment: “Everyone has the same wants and desires, and if you’re really honest as an artist with your pain, it will always connect.” For many young people, part of the pain they have felt in the past few years has been in witnessing the events in Gaza, as well as the rising global tide offar-right populism, the climate crisis and instability. So for a generation that is increasingly accustomed to having their despair made audible through gloomier music, why would they not increasingly expect artists to draw connections between their personal pain and what is causing it?Artists, then, cannot assume that the old bargain still holds. Sheeran’s insistence on an apolitical arena of music is increasingly anachronistic – a position that has exposed the faultlines of modern music. Many listeners increasingly seek emotional clarity as well as moral clarity. Whether popular music has risen to that moment will be judged by history. But for now, as the expectation changes, it is down to artists to decide if they change with it.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answer | Timothy Garton Ash | The Guardian
description: Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Author: Timothy Garton Ash
Headline: Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Content: A protester holds up a placard reading ‘Nazis raus’ (Nazis out) during rival rallies at Koenigsplatz in Munich, Germany, 12 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protester holds up a placard reading ‘Nazis raus’ (Nazis out) during rival rallies at Koenigsplatz in Munich, Germany, 12 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answerTimothy Garton AshInstead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watchingSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.08 EDTShareFar-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a littleregional electoral victoryfor one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (NaziGermanyuntil 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.Then there’s the fact that Germany is Europe’s central power. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel says that when her party gets into government after the federal election scheduled for 2029, Germany will abandon the euro and leave the Schengen border-free travel area. What would be left of the EU then?The great German liberal social and political thinker Ralf Dahrendorf,who died in 2009, told me more than once that he would only feel really confident of the resilience of German democracy when it had withstood the test of a big economic crisis. Well, the country is close to that now.The final segment of “because it’s Germany!” is perhaps the most interesting. The federal republic’s entire constitutional, political and educational system is designed to prevent anything like the collapse of the Weimar republic into Hitler’s dictatorship in 1933. The federal republic should be awehrhafte Demokratie– a democracy capable of defending itself.So how Germany will defend its democracy is a question not just of European but of global significance. Looking at all the answers being frenetically canvassed in Berlin, I think the most convincing formula is: neither ban the AfD nor embrace it, but instead constrain it legally and fight it politically.The German constitution provides for political parties that are “hostile” to its basic liberal democratic principles to be banned. Senior German politicians have called for an application to be made to the constitutional court to ban the AfD, or at least its most extreme parts, on those grounds. But it’s too late for that. The AfD has been a major force in the Bundestag since its success (off the back of the migration crisis)in the 2017 general electionand, like Reform UK in Britain, has led nationwide in opinion polls. To suddenly tell so many citizens “you’re not allowed to vote for the party you support!” would itself be an assault on democracy.But this is not democracy as the tyranny of the majority: the people have spoken, off with your head! It’sliberaldemocracy, meaning the outcome of any popular vote is constrained by the rule of law, human and minority rights, and pluralist, anti-majoritarian institutions. The real threats to German democracy today are less like Weimar in 1933than Budapest in 2010(when Viktor Orbán took over) and Washington DC in 2025. The mini-Donald Trumps of the AfD have reportedly been quietly exploring Trump-like executive and administrative devices they might use toconsolidate their control. The Federal Republic of Germany has the right, the power and the duty to stop them.Article 37 of the constitution, which allows federal authorities to overrule anti-constitutional behaviour by the states, has never been used in the 77-year history of the republic. Assuming, as now seems likely, the AfD forms the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, all federal powers, up to and including article 37, should be used wherever necessary. For example, they should prevent sensitive intelligence about Russia’s increasing aggression being shared with a Saxony-Anhalt branch of the domestic security service controlled by the pro-Russian AfD; secure the independence of courts and prosecutors, as well as the neutrality of police and civil service; and, I would add, stop any extreme politicisation of education and public service broadcasting. Of course, AfD politicians will cry “foul!”; tough. If, as they say, they want “another republic”, they can go and live in Russia.Yet even more important than these legal and administrative constraints is the political response. At the opposite end from those calling for the party to be banned are Christian Democrats calling forthe “firewall” to be abandoned and AfD politicians to be embraced as part of the normal political process. Letting them take responsibility in a state government will, it’s argued, expose their incoherence, incompetence and lack of real policy answers.Talking and working with them will end up moderating them, as apparently happened with Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. I’ve been tempted by these arguments myself. But evidence collected bypolitical scientistssuggests that a strategy of inclusion is just as likely to put more wind in the nationalists’ sails. And AfD activists are themselves warning against the danger ofMelonisierung(Melonisation).So Christian Democrats should not be tempted to get half into bed with the AfD, like a middle-aged man nervously edging into an extramarital affair. Instead, starting already this weekend with elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, they should more effectively combat it politically. Rather than defining Christian Democracy by what it’s against (the AfD and the far-left Linke), they should say what it’s for. To renew Germany’s social market economy, they should implement all the labour market, pension, tax and other reforms agreed this summer with their Social Democrat coalition partners – and more. Faced with huge external challenges, from Russian aggression to US and Chinese AI, the Christian Democrats – historically the party of Europe – should boldly advocate the European-scale answers which alone will give any European country the strength to stand up to giants.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut besides AI, Germany’s mainstream parties badly need EI (emotional intelligence). The key to the success of the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund in Saxony-Anhalt, as with Trump and Britain’s Nigel Farage, is a kind of emotional communication. I’m here with you; I hear you and see you; I share your anger. With me, you can say what you really think and be yourself, because – whether or not I’m a millionaire – deep down I’m a normal bloke like you. So let’s all have a beer and march forward to an imagined past.It’s fascinating to re-read the exiled German political scientist Karl Loewenstein’s influential1937 articleon “militant democracy” and find him insisting that democracy cannot “devise emotional formulas capable of competing with the fascist Pied Pipers”. Hence the emphasis on constitutional constraints. But in our transformed information environment, with its premium on attention, drama and passion, democracy can’t be defended simply by legal constraints and rational policies. Democrats everywhere need to compete with today’s Pied Pipers on the emotional plane, too. Constant presence on social media and physical presence on the ground are both essential.Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, and to some extent the UK’s, Andy Burnham, have shown how it can be done. So much will now depend on German democrats, and especially Christian Democrats, proving they can do the same.Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book,Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters, is published in OctoberDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Nine women in South Africa have been murdered since July. We are being told to be vigilant – but where are the warnings to men? | Nolethu Ndude  | The Guardian
description: The country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter it, writes Nolethu Ndude, founder of We Mattah
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter it, writes Nolethu Ndude, founder of We Mattah
Content: Crowds gather near the site where a murdered woman’s body was discovered, Boksburg, Ekurhuleni district, South Africa, on 17 September.Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCrowds gather near the site where a murdered woman’s body was discovered, Boksburg, Ekurhuleni district, South Africa, on 17 September.Photograph: Emmanuel Croset/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionGlobal developmentNine women in South Africa have been murdered since July. We are being told to be vigilant – but where are the warnings to men?Nolethu NdudeThe country has one of the highest femicide rates in the world, and women are yet again being asked to remove themselves from public life to counter itSupported byAbout this contentSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTShareWhen I heard the authorities advising women in and around Kempton Park, the site of a recent spate of femicides, not to walk or run alone, to avoid isolated places and to “remain vigilant”, my immediate response was anger. Remain vigilant. How groundbreaking.Women are already vigilant. We photograph number plates before entering vehicles. We share Uber details with friends. We phone one another while walking. We watch the driver’s route and notice every unexpected turn. We avoid certain roads, certain times and certain conversations. We scan parking areas before getting out of our cars. We check the back seat. We listen for footsteps. We carry pepper spray where we can. We hold our keys in a way that makes us feel slightly less defenceless.Women have informal safety systems built into our friendships. “Please let me know when you get home” is not simply a polite farewell. It is a survival protocol.Yet women are still being killed.‘What’s happened to us? Where did we get lost?’ Zimbabwe reckons with the reality of violence against womenRead morePolice are investigatingthe deaths of nine womenwhose bodies have been found across the Ekurhuleni district, east of Johannesburg, since July. Some were found naked or partially clothed, and several had visible injuries.One of the women wasElizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo, a 38-year-old who disappeared after leaving her home in Kempton Park for an afternoon run on 9 September. Her body was found three days later.Now running must be approached like a security operation. Choose a group. Share your route. Check the time. Avoid quiet roads. Stay where people can see you. Keep one earphone out. Carry your phone. Remain visible. Remain alert. Remain vigilant.But women cannot “vigilance” themselves out of gender-based violence and femicide.Where are the instructions to men? Where is the urgent public warning telling them not to harm women? Where is the nationwide mobilisation asking men to confront their friends, brothers and colleagues? Where are the campaigns teaching men that affection does not create ownership and that rejection is not humiliation?Where is the same relentless attention on perpetrators, effective policing, prosecution and prevention?The truth is, women are not safe anywhere.In 2019, 19-year-old University of Cape Town student Uyinene Mrwetyana went to collect a parcel from a post office in Cape Town.She was raped and murderedinside that post office by an employee. Her murder shattered the idea that danger is limited to badly lit streets and isolated fields.If we must avoid every place where another woman has been attacked or killed, where are we allowed to exist?We are told to stay indoors, although many women are abused in their homes. We are told not to trust strangers, although women are killed by husbands, boyfriends, relatives and former partners. We are told to choose better, as though abusive men introduce themselves honestly and arrive carrying warning labels.South African women were killed at a rate of12.2 per 100,000 in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime. That figure should stop the country in its tracks. Instead, it becomes another statistic repeated during interviews, marches and annual campaigns.Afterprotests ahead of the G20 summitin Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared gender-based violence and femicide a national crisis. Women had already spent years explaining that it was one.The issue is not whether government has heard us. It has. The issue is hat actually changes after gender-based violence is declared a national crisis?Which institutions become accountable? What additional resources are committed? Are police stations properly equipped to act when a woman is reported missing? Are officers trained to respond to survivors with care rather than suspicion? Are investigations adequately resourced? Are protection orders enforced? Are shelters funded? Are survivors protected while cases move through courts?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWho answers when commitments are not fulfilled?The Commission for Gender Equality has called for an urgent safety audit of the affected areas. It wants attention given to lighting, surveillance, public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance. That is necessary.But the response cannot end at Ekurhuleni’s borders. Women are being killed nationally, therefore prevention strategies must implemented at a national level.We also need to stop treating every killing as an isolated tragedy with no relationship to the culture around it.Femicidedoes not begin when a body is discovered. It develops along a continuum.Through my work with young people, I see why intervention must begin long before violence reaches the criminal justice system. We need sustained education about consent, bodily autonomy, healthy relationships, emotional regulation and positive masculinity.That is not an excuse for violence. It is part of preventing it.Men must confront misogyny in their own circles. They must challenge the jokes, controlling behaviour, coercion and entitlement before somebody is dead. Silence is not neutrality. It protects the conditions in which violence thrives.This responsibility does not belong only to activists, police or women’s organisations. It belongs in homes, schools, churches, workplaces, sports clubs, taxis, universities and friendship groups. It belongs wherever boys learn what manhood means.I am not arguing that women should ignore immediate safety warnings. I am arguing that those warnings cannot be presented as the solution. There is a difference between sharing information about a specific risk and building an entire response around women limiting their lives.The state’s responsibility is not to teach women how to stay alive around violent men. Its responsibility is to prevent violence, investigate cases properly, pursue perpetrators and build a country in which women can collect a parcel, go for a run, leave a relationship, take a ride home and simply live.We have restricted ourselves. We have changed our behaviour. We have remained vigilant. We are still being killed. It is time the authorities, and men, tried something different. Accountability would be a good place to start.Nolethu Ndude is a South African social entrepreneur, speaker and founder ofWe Mattah, a youth-centred organisation working across sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender-based violence prevention, mental wellbeing and youth empowerment.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentOpinionFemicideSouth AfricaAfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Denmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereignty | Greenland | The Guardian
description: Statement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Statement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s security
Content: Denmark's prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland's prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, in Nuuk, Greenland, on 7 September 2026.Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/APView image in fullscreenDenmark's prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and Greenland's prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, in Nuuk, Greenland, on 7 September 2026.Photograph: Mads Claus Rasmussen/Ritzau Scanpix/APGreenlandDenmark and Greenland say US military agreement will not compromise Arctic territory’s sovereigntyStatement sought to clarify Trump’s announcement that US will have ‘permanent control’ over Greenland’s securityEdward Helmoreand agenciesSat 19 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDenmarkandGreenlandhave said any agreement with the US to develop a significant military presence in the strategic Arctic territory will not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty.In a statement on Saturday clarifying an announcement byDonald Trumpthat an agreement had been reached to give Washington “permanent control” ⁠over Greenland’s security, Denmark and the semi-autonomous territory ⁠expressed hope that a deal would end friction with the US over the issue.Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, said he was pleased with the proposed deal. “The agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and ​the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination,”he said ​in a post.US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over GreenlandRead more“Next week could be a good week – forGreenland, ‌Denmark and the United States,” Denmark’s foreign minister, ‌Lars Lokke Rasmussen, said in a statement.“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NatoEurope– while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said.The US,Denmarkand Greenland said late on Friday they had reached a deal to allow the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their ⁠own bases on the island.The deal is expected to be signed during the UN general assembly next week.Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the degree of theUS militarypresence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.Trump said on social media that under the deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America”.He added that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all ‌other needs, in Greenland”.The security and mineral resources of the vast northern island have been subject to Washington’s foreign policy and attention since the start of the secondTrump administration, with officials citing national security, access to valuable natural resources, including rare earth minerals, and control over emerging Arctic shipping lanes.The island had a significant US military presence in the 1950s, when fears of annihilation in a US-Soviet nuclear exchange required that long-range nuclear bombers and early-warning systems be based on Greenland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe US still maintains a reduced military presence at the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, on the island to monitor for missiles.Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen, told Reuters that the Denmark-US deal “is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources”.Rasmussen added that if Copenhagen cedes any formal power to Washington over Greenland, which it has held for 1,000 years, it would raise questions for Greenlanders of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States”.US ambitions for greater sway over the Arctic island have strained relations with Nato. In January, European member nations sent military personnel to Greenland to demonstrate military readiness. Eight European allies issued a joint statement confirming their commitment to Arctic security. Negotiations followed.A Nato spokesperson ‌on Saturday said the alliance ​welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, ​stability and cooperation in this vital region”.Reuters contributedreportingExplore more on these topicsGreenlandDenmarkUS militaryDonald TrumpTrump administrationEuropeUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy ex-husband says ‘I think I did the best I could’ | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trial
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trial
Content: Lindsay Clancy in court earlier this month.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy in court earlier this month.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersMassachusettsLindsay Clancy ex-husband says ‘I think I did the best I could’Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trialEdward HelmoreSat 19 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are set to describe their experiences of theMassachusettstriple-murder trial of his former wife Lindsay Clancy, with Clancy telling 60 Minutes: “I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.”The couple will on Sunday night make their first public comments on the case. CBS has been trailing excerpts of the broadcast.The interviews with the pair marks a second significant media “get” for 60 Minutes since it came under new leadership earlier this year. Last week, it secured an interview with a pilot who was rescued by special forces after being shot down over Iran.The Clancy interviews come as Massachusetts prosecutors are set to decide later this month whether to retry Lindsay Clancy over the killings of the couple’s three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in January 2023. A hearing is slated for 29 September at Plymouth superior court.A trial over the summer riveted public attention and ended in a mistrial when a single juror rejected the Clancy’s defense position that she had carried out the killings because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that meant she could not be found criminally responsible for her actions.The trial shed light on the little-understood mental health condition, and the resulting mistrial sharply divided public opinion. The single holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, came forward last week to say he thought enough physical evidence and key witness testimony presented at trial proved Clancy “knew exactly what she was doing and planned [it]”.Patrick Clancy, who testified in the prosecution phase of the trial but has supported his former wife, has been subject to intense speculation outside the courtroom from online content creators and conspiracists.Earlier this month, an attorney for Clancy threatened legal “consequences” over what he called a “relentless, escalating and destructive defamation campaign” targeting his client.“Enough is enough – this spread of blatant and baseless falsehoods must stop,” attorney Howard Cooper said. “Those responsible should understand that there will be consequences, and every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.”According to excerpts of the 60 Minutes interviews released ahead of airtime, Patrick Clancy talks about his grief, his memories of his children, and conspiracy theories.Clancy tells correspondent Ross Douthat he still talks to his kids “all the time” and asked them for help. Asked if they do, Clancy responds: “I like to believe they do. It’s a way I stay connected to them.”Clancy, who discovered his three children after finding his injured wife lying in snow below a second floor window and is now paralyzed from the waist down, also told the news program: “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time, and I live with the outcome. I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.”The Clancys repeatedly sought psychiatric and mental care for the young mother in the months before the incident, and have since filed a civil lawsuit alleging negligence and over-prescription of medications on the the part of two health professionals and healthcare providers.In the released interview excerpts, Danis, 37, discusses how she met Patrick, their marriage, and defends her husband against the theories that have appeared online.“I don’t understand how the story’s been so twisted, but I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner,” Danis, an infertility specialist, tells the program.The couple met while jogging and Patrick moved to New York and married earlier this year, she says. “I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Unease in ‘newly independent’ Piddington as world media and Danny Tommo descend  | UK news | The Guardian
description: As villagers take stock following symbolic vote, some fear far-right weaponisation of asylum dispute and influx of ‘masked people like in Dover’
Author: Amelia Gentleman
Headline: As villagers take stock following symbolic vote, some fear far-right weaponisation of asylum dispute and influx of ‘masked people like in Dover’
Content: In a symbolic referendum, villagers in Piddington voted 285 to 26 to become an independent state over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn a symbolic referendum, villagers in Piddington voted 285 to 26 to become an independent state over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers nearby.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianUK newsUnease in ‘newly independent’ Piddington as world media and Danny Tommo descendAs villagers take stock following symbolic vote, some fear far-right weaponisation of asylum dispute and influx of ‘masked people like in Dover’Amelia GentlemanSat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first significant event in the newly independent principality of Piddington was a decision to select the newt as the national animal, reflecting optimism that the amphibian’s endangered status might help block plans to open a centre for 1,250 asylum seekers on neighbouring land.The choice was announced on Thursday morning, the day after Piddington announced that villagers had voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK. Parish councillors were also thinking about asking local children to design a flag and considering whether the new principality’s national sport should be cricket or football.The second noteworthy event was the arrival of Daniel Thomas, who prefers to be called Danny Tommo, the leader of thenew balaclava-wearing anti-migrant movementPatriot Platform, with an offer to rally his masked supporters, if the site is opened, “to protect women and children” locally.By the end of the week, some residents of this pretty Oxfordshire village were still struggling to interpret Tuesday’s symbolic ballot of 358 villagers, and the announcement on Wednesday that Piddington had voted to “secede from the UK and pursue self-determination” by a margin of 285 to 26, in protest at plans to convert a former military base near the village into housing for asylum seekers.View image in fullscreenAfter expressing unease over the vote on Newsnight, Rachel Marsh, a Piddington resident for 20 years, said she’d received ‘violent threats online from a lot of very toxic keyboard warriors. I’ve never encountered anything like this before.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianFor many, the vote was a demonstration of plucky British eccentricity in the face of adversity, with Ealing comedy Passport to Pimlico vibes. The day after the independence vote there was still a summer fete atmosphere: Battle for Britain bunting was hanging over the doorway to the village hall, “I Am Spartacus” placards stood by the roadside alongside new signs telling drivers that they were entering the Principality of Piddington, “The Village That Roars”. Journalists from Japan, Norway and Ireland arrived, puzzled by the lack of public transport and functional wifi; they scrutinised the community noticeboard in search of clues to explain the village mindset (“Tortoise Found”, “Harvest Coffee Morning”, “Pilates for All Abilities”).For others, the week’s events have more troubling outcomes. Chef Rachel Marsh, who used to run a livery yard in the village where she has lived for 20 years, was meeting police officers on Friday to discuss her safety. She received death threats and her family was targeted with racist abuse online after she expressed uneasein a Newsnight interviewthat fear was being used as means to “rally and activate people” locally.The determined jollity of the village independence movement left a sour taste, she said, in the light of the backlash she had received both from local residents and online activists.“Given that their aim is to protect women and children it is quite ironic that they are using aggression like this towards me for speaking up against racism,” she said. Originally from New Zealand, Marsh has lived in the UK for 40 years; her husband’s parents were Windrush generation arrivals from Jamaica. Messages posted online this week suggested that she and her husband should leave Britain. “We’ve had violent threats online from a lot of very toxic keyboard warriors. I’ve never encountered anything like this before.”View image in fullscreenA sign near the MOD base in Piddington where the government plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers. Villagers’ reasons for opposing these plans range from concerns over environmental risks and treatment of asylum seekers to hostility towards immigrants.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianMarsh, like everyone else in Piddington, opposes the government’s asylum housing plan, announced in June. Residents were particularly dismayed at the government’s decision to submit a fast-tracked ‘Urgent Crown Development’ application, designed for projects deemed to be of national importance, allowing ministers to bypass local authority planning processes, as they race to meet a commitment to shut down asylum hotels entirely “in this parliament”.But village harmony has fractured in places, over disagreements over how best to oppose the decision. Some locals back a Wrong Plan, Wrong Site campaign, primarily focused on the legalities, cost and environmental risks of the proposed housing. Other activists have highlighted the perceived risk to local women of the site. One local, asking not to be named, said the rhetoric in the village had become markedly “more hostile to asylum seekers” over the summer. “The tenor has changed,” he said.The leader of the parish council, Tim McNally, who led theindependence movement, said he was happy that the village had “sent a message to the political jugular”, adding that he was now talking to other village leaders elsewhere in Britain, sharing a blueprint with advice on how to object to unpopular decisions imposed by central government.In interviews earlier this week he said he would consider renaming the village Trumpington if the Donald Trump agreed to adopt the principality as the 51stUS state. Since June he has been filming video appeals for support, speaking direct to the camera as he walks around the village onhis @piddingtonroars X account. The campaign has attracted Elon Musk’s attention,prompting the SpaceX CEO to tweetto his 241.6 million followers: “Soon, this will happen to your town”, above a description of the plans for housing for asylum seekers in Oxfordshire. McNally responded: “Thank you, Elon, for helping our little village roar around the world.”View image in fullscreenLocal parish councillor Joe Marshall, who said that a meeting was being held with the far-right group Patriot Platform ‘so we can open a dialogue’.Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianOn Thursday, parish councillor Joe Marshall was cheerful about the ballot result, if still wrestling with the practicalities of independence. The village would continue to view King Charles as their monarch, he said. Councillors were wondering if “someone’s son’s under-11 cricket team” might agree to represent the principality. “Ultimately we’re not going to be culturally any different from Britain,” he said.He saw nothing problematic about the swift visit from a nationalist activist leader, stressing that all politicians, environmental campaigners and political figures were welcome to visit. “We’ve not written to these people to invite them but with the high profile of what we’re doing right now, these people will want to come. Our responsibility as a parish is to ensure the safety and the security of the village,” he said, adding that a private meeting with Patriot Platform was being held “so we can open dialogue”.“I assume that their intent is to offer protection, which right now we don’t need because there is no one on this site,” he said. “We’d rather engage with people, walk them around the village, have a cup of tea and a chat, rather than say: ‘We don’t want you here’.” Villagers were disappointed, he said, that there had not been any similar visits from Home Office ministers or government officials. “They haven’t sent a representative even to have a private conversation with the parish council.”Thomas arrived without an entourage of men in balaclavas on Thursday afternoon. On Friday morning he posted a video of himself outside the gates to the Site A military base, standing outside the village hall, on the village green and interviewing two villagers.View image in fullscreenRobin Smith, who lives near to Piddington, says the asylum seekers who would be housed at the MOD site ‘are humans. This camp is not the right place for them.’Photograph: Alicia Canter/The GuardianRobin Smith, who runs an IT consultancy in Bicester, was sorry to have missed him on the whistlestop tour. “I would have liked to have met him and to have heard him explain his manifesto. The people who are coming over are humans. This camp is not the right place for them.” Andrew Smith, a Network Rail employee from Bicester, was less upbeat: “We don’t want to see masked people like there were in Dover – that’s not really the view of the local people; we are concerned to do the right thing. These people have got to go somewhere, but it has to be properly resourced with the proper facilities.”The Liberal Democrat leader of Oxfordshire County Council, Tim Bearder, said it “was disgraceful the way the far right are weaponising” the dispute. But he was encouraged by a Wednesday evening planning committee meeting, where district council officials were critical of the government’s proposed plans for the new site. “It was considered in 2005 and rejected. There is no electricity, no water, and no footpath. There have been two fatalities on the nearby road. It’s not in the best interests of local residents or the asylum seekers,” he said.Calum Miller, Lib Dem MP for Bicester and Woodstock, said the interference of external groups was not welcomed by the majority of people in the local area. “The events of this week have shown the power of local opposition to this proposal,” he said. “Local councillors, local people, and a local legal challenge are taking the government to task for this proposal.”Rachel Marsh was one of the 26 people who opposed the independence vote. “This is just a publicity stunt. It’s complete theatre,” she said. She was uneasy at the arrival of Patriot Platform’s leader in the village. “My feelings about the appropriateness and suitability of Site A are exactly the same as the rest of village – I object, like everyone else – but you don’t need to base objection on a fear-based rhetoric.”Get in touchContact Amelia Gentleman about this storyIf you have something to share about this story, you can contact Amelia using one of the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailamelia.gentleman@theguardian.com.For other options, see our guide attheguardian.com/tips.Show moreExplore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery  | Reparations and reparative justice | The Guardian
description: Leaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resists
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Leaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resists
Content: An emancipation statue in Bridgetown, Barbados. Leaders told the conference that reparations needed to be realistic and set over decades.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn emancipation statue in Bridgetown, Barbados. Leaders told the conference that reparations needed to be realistic and set over decades.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesReparations and reparative justiceCaribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slaveryLeaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resistsNatricia Duncanin BridgetownSat 19 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said.Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options.Earlier this month, a spokesperson forAndy Burnhamreiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”.Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said theCaricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser forthe Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice.He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said.On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice.“The fact is that the consequences of slavery fall squarely under the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which obliges states to help address the consequences of native genocide and slavery,” Gonsalves said.Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research findsRead moreIn March this year, 123 nations voted for a landmark UN resolution that described chattel slaveryas the gravest crime against humanity. The UK was one of several European countries that abstained from voting in the resolution. But, last month, a UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination said countries werelegally obliged to consider reparationsfor the transatlantic slave trade and take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.David Comissiong, the deputy chair of theBarbadosNational Task Force on Reparations, said the Caribbean nations were considering “several legal strategies”.“You’ve hadJamaicatrying to engage with the national legal judicial system of the UK, the privy council – that is one strategy,” he said, adding that going to the international court of justice for an advisory opinion was another option.Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the CRC, said reparations was a matter of justice, adding that countries in the region were forced to create viable democracies “out of the mess” of colonialism, which was still having an impact today.“When Jamaica took its petition to the UK, we had to surround that petition with the fact that when Jamaica became independent in 1962, 80% of the black people in Jamaica could not read or write. After 300 years of British colonisation, they moved into independence with 80% illiteracy. How do you build a modern nation, not even a competitive economy, with 80% illiteracy?”Speaking at the conference, Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said the Caribbean had “no desire to bankrupt anybody”.“But we have a desire for justice,” she said.Earlier this year, Barbadoscommissioned a report which showedthat Britain stole 25 million years of life and labour through slavery in the country.She added: “The British government took almost 200 years to repay the debt that it incurred when it paid the slave owners £20m.” Mottley pointed to the fact that Germany paid $95bn (£71bn) to the Jewish community because of the horrors of the Holocaust.Mottley said that she did not want “anybody to diminish the fact that in this country here, which I have the honour to lead, that from settlement in 1627, 400 years ago next year, for 211 years, not six, people were treated as chattel”.“If they dared to speak or to do things that were displeasing, their lives and limbs were put at risk. The evidence is clear. What is absent is the will,” she said.Explore more on these topicsReparations and reparative justiceBarbadosCaribbeanAmericasJamaicaAndy BurnhamShareReuse this content

title: Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims sue California museum over Nazi-looted art | Holocaust | The Guardian
description: Pasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world war
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world war
Content: Adam and Eve, painted in 1530 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, on display in the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.Photograph: Gerard Vuilleumier/Norton Simon Art Foundation/APView image in fullscreenAdam and Eve, painted in 1530 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, on display in the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.Photograph: Gerard Vuilleumier/Norton Simon Art Foundation/APHolocaustJewish heirs of Holocaust victims sue California museum over Nazi-looted artPasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world warAssociated PressSat 19 Sep 2026 10.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJewish heirs ofHolocaustvictims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits inCaliforniastaking their claims toNazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums inLos Angelesand Auschwitz.This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws byCaliforniaand the US Congress, which strengthen US-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during the second world war.One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles superior court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair, Daniel Gryczman, against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of painting Adam and Eve. These are two lifesize oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.Nazi-looted painting must be returned to Jewish art dealer’s heir, Argentina court rulesRead moreThe other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dina Gottliebova Babbitt, aHolocaustsurvivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz.
