It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death”, from the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum in Poland.Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotionally, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered intergenerational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history.Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing more than 600,000 works of art acrossEuropefrom Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command, and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of ModernArt, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the approximately 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.Von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi-era atrocities,” she said.The Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the US supreme court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin, where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research “must remain in the memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”Explore more on these topicsHolocaustPaintingNazismArtSecond world warPolandCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil’s wind farms have been a huge success. So why isn’t everybody reaping the benefits?  | Global development | The Guardian
description: While the country’s ambition is to be the ‘Saudi Arabia of green energy’, communities in the north-east are bearing the cost in diminished health and livelihoods
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While the country’s ambition is to be the ‘Saudi Arabia of green energy’, communities in the north-east are bearing the cost in diminished health and livelihoods
Content: A local farmer’s horse stands in a field next to one of Serra do Mel’s windfarms in Rio Grande do Norte state. Brazil has about 35GW of onshore wind capacity in commercial operation, the fifth largest in the worldView image in fullscreenA local farmer’s horse stands in a field next to one of Serra do Mel’s windfarms in Rio Grande do Norte state. Brazil has about 35GW of onshore wind capacity in commercial operation, the fifth largest in the worldSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanGlobal developmentBrazil’s wind farms have been a huge success. So why isn’t everybody reaping the benefits?While the country’s ambition is to be the ‘Saudi Arabia of green energy’,  communities in the north-east are bearing the cost in diminished health and livelihoodsSupported byAbout this contentAlice Lima and Marilia Gurgel. Photographs by Marco ServentiSat 19 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBeneath the power lines cutting across Antonio de Souza’s property in Serra do Mel, in north-eastBrazil’s Rio Grande do Norte state, rows of cashew trees once stood – until the clean energy company ordered them to be cut down.De Souza cannot plant crops in the affected area and the tractor cannot be driven through it in bad weather, as the driver risks an electric shock. Cattle, another source of local income, are forbidden from grazing near the cables.The contract says the infrastructure occupies one hectare (2.5 acres); yet, the farmer counters, four hectares have become wasteland on a 50-hectare plot that was the family’s livelihood.The story of Serra do Mel is one often heard in places where wind has provided energy and development, a model now moving offshore. But still rarely discussed is how the benefits can also harm local communities’ health and livelihoods.Wind turbines in Serra do Mel, BrazilBrazil has about35GW of onshore wind capacityin commercial operation, thefifth largest in the world, according to the Brazilian Association of Wind Energy and New Technologies(ABEEólica) and the Global Wind Energy Council. In November 2023, in Riyadh, Brazil’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, summed up the nation’s ambition: within 10 years, Brazil would be known as the“Saudi Arabia of green energy”.Nine in 10 of Brazil’s wind turbinesare in the north-east, thanks to the constantly strong winds, which engineers often describe as the “best in the world”. It is also among the regions withBrazil’s worst social indicators. This convergence could have resulted in a historic redistribution of wealth, but those in the turbines’ shadow tell a different story.View image in fullscreenJosé Cristino da Cruz on his farm in Serra do Mel – he is one of those involved in a community-led lawsuit against Voltalia“If I’d known it would be like this – that I’d be prevented from planting and harvesting – I wouldn’t have signed that contract with them,” says De Souza, who adds that he is not opposed to wind power.When representatives of the French renewable energy multinationalVoltaliaarrived in his village after a year of drought, De Souza signed the contract, as did almost everyone in the area. The promise was a monthly income of 3,000 to 5,000 reais (£430-£720), adjusted annually like a salary, without harming crops.A decade later, the farmer is leadinga public civil lawsuit against Voltalia, filed in May 2025 by three rural workers’ organisations, witha favourable assessmentfrom the public prosecutor’s office and the public defender’s office, which provides legal aid, monitors human rights and has an ombudsman role.The people of Serra do Mel are not calling for the company to leave but they do want to know how much the energy generated on their land yields and to receive what they say was promised to them.They also want to regain the right to retire as farmers, which is at risk because they can no longer work their holdings – land the Brazilian state granted to needy farmers 50 years ago is now leased to a multinational for another 50.The payments, hard to audit, are 1.55% of turnover, which will depend on where the energy is sold. Data from theNational Electricity Agency(Aneel), compiled by the Lavoro Institute, shows that 17 of the Serra do Mel power stationssell all of their electricity on the open market. Most of it goes to Brazil’s south-east and central-west regions, at prices negotiated directly with large consumers.2:05Brazilian farmers describe what it’s like living next to wind turbines – videoThe paradox is that electricity generated in Serra do Mel is sold cheaply to people the residents have never met, while the power that lights their homes costs twice as much.A Voltalia windfarm in Serra do Mel celebrated Brazil passing the 10GW power milestone in 2016. But 10 years on, most streets in the municipality remain unpaved and families have no mains water. One day, Edvaldo Bessa, then 75, returned to his plot of land and got an electric shock from the steel cables of the metering tower, which lacked insulation.View image in fullscreenPower lines in Serra do Mel carry electricity generated by wind turbines to Brazil’s national grid. Farmers are not allowed to cultivate within 50 metres of each pylonData from the Primary Healthcare Information System (Sisab), compiled in the Lavoro Institute’s report, shows a significant rise of people in Serra do Mel complaining of anxiety and panic disorders, sleep disorders and hearing problems from 2022 onwards – when most of the municipality’s 36 windfarms came into operation. In Poço Branco – a municipality similar across all indicators except the turbines – the trend moves the opposite way.View image in fullscreenRelvani de Brito near her land in Serra do Mel. Since her late father signed a 50-year lease with an energy firm for a solar and windfarm on the farm, Brito has not been allowed on her landBrazil has no federal regulation stipulating a minimum distance between turbines and people’s homes. While France requires such equipment to be at least 500 metres from houses, Relvani de Brito lives 250 metres away from a turbine. This is what the “Brazilian windpower miracle” is built on.“During the day, you can barely hear it,” says De Brito. “At night it’s worse because everything is quiet, and that’s when the racket starts.“I take medication for anxiety. I don’t sleep at night; I wake up at one o’clock, right on the dot,” she says.In July 2024, at a packed meeting, hundreds of farmers voted to take legal action against the company. Thecivil class action, filed in May 2025 by a coalition of three workers’ organisations, seeks compensation for collective non-pecuniary damage for health problems or unfair contracts; the suspension of the four windfarms still under construction; the relocation of existing turbines; and a corrective environmental impact assessment, with community participation.It also calls for a review of the contracts, limiting the transfer of rights to 50% of the plot, restoring the farmers’ status as “special insured persons”. This means that farmers should not be able to sign over their entire plot to the energy company.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBy law, if a farmer transfers up to 50%, they do not lose their insurance rights, provided they continue to work the land. The “special insured person” status is a category within the Brazilian social security system created for rural workers on family-run farms.Approached after the lawsuit was filed, Voltalia said it had not been served, that it complied “strictly … with Brazilian legislation” and adopted “a collective, participatory and transparent contractual construction process”, with a “commitment to the social development of the communities”. It denied that the projects caused damage.In a statement to the Guardian, Voltalia said it valued “sustainable development” and “dialogue with local communities … from local in-person assistance to digital channels such as the Ombudsman, as well as regular meetings, and social and environmental initiatives.”Regarding contracts, the company said it “developed the agreements in collaboration with local landowners and diligently addresses any matters concerning these agreements through the appropriate channels.” It added that its windfarms were “managed in accordance with applicable regulatory, social, environmental, and health and safety requirements”.Just over 18 miles (30km) from Serra do Mel, the wind blows towards Areia Branca beach, where boys are playing football. Behind the goal, onshore turbines already form a white fence. Now, what almost no one saw coming has been licensed to be built right in front of them, but this time offshore.View image in fullscreenCristovão, in the Areia Branca region, is the first site in Brazil licensed for an oﬀshore windfarmIn June 2025,Ibama, the federal agency responsible for environmental enforcement, issuedBrazil’s first preliminary licencefor an offshore wind energy project, which will have far greater capacity than onshore turbines.It will be installed off Areia Branca, near the terminal that is the main distribution point for Brazilian salt. The developer is the National Industrial Training Service (Senai-RN), with all the energy supplying the port itself, a test site under a recently enacted law from 2025.At Ibama, more than 100 offshore windfarm licence applications are waiting to be processed. “The way this process is conducted sets a precedent for all others to follow,” says Giovanna Ferreira, an activist monitoring the case on behalf of theSemi-Arid Region Human Rights Reference Centre(CRDH).View image in fullscreenGiovanna Ferreira, a researcher and activist, in her office. The banner behind her reads ‘Energy justice starts with participation’When the CRDH visited the surrounding fishing communities, it found that the people most affected were unaware of what was about to happen. Senai claims the chosen area is in shallow waters far from traditional fishing grounds but the fishers say the towers will be erected where they work.First there were coalmines, then came the windfarms. Why Colombia’s Wayúu people fear the green energy boomRead moreQuestions have been raised about whether further expansion is even necessary. The north-east of Brazil already produces more renewable energy than the grid can handle.In 2025,Brazil wasted 20.6% of the windand solar energy it could have generated, with turbines shut down due to “curtailment” – when grid operators halt generation to prevent it exceeding demand, which could trigger blackouts. This loss is estimated at more than 6bn reais, which the sector association’s president, Elbia Gannoum, called “the worst crisis in Brazil’s wind energy industry”.Out on the beach, time is measured differently. Luis, a fisher from Areia Branca, has heard about the turbines to be put up in the sea where he works. He is fearful, but still believes all will be well. “God and the ocean will always provide the fish we need,” he says.View image in fullscreenLuis on his fishing boat at Areia Branca: ‘God and the ocean will always provide the fish we need’Between Luis’s faith and the legal proceedings lies a decision to be taken far away, as to which of these two forces will shape the future of these waters and the community that relies on it. Local people are waiting for the wind to blow in their favour.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanWind powerBrazilRenewable energyEnergyEnergy industryAccess to energyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Before-and-after images show effects of rain in drought-hit England and Wales | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Much of the UK is still officially in drought after its hottest summer on record, but grasslands are slowly recovering their colour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Much of the UK is still officially in drought after its hottest summer on record, but grasslands are slowly recovering their colour
Content: Clissold Park in north-east London in mid-September.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClissold Park in north-east London in mid-September.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianUK weatherBefore-and-after images show effects of rain in drought-hit England and WalesMuch of the UK is still officially in drought after its hottest summer on record, but grasslands are slowly recovering their colourKatie WardSat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe landscapes of southernEnglandand Wales are slowly regaining their colour after this summer’s extreme heat.The UK’shottest summer on recordleft the south of the country dried out and brown, making the impact of the drought particularly visual.As autumn begins, large parts of the UK are still officially in drought. And even if autumn is wetter than normal, some could still be in drought in the spring, according to the Environment Agency.View image in fullscreenClissold Park, in north-east London, at the end of July.Photograph: Richard Barnes/AlamyBut some rain has returned, and with it the green, to the relief of many. Darren Share, the director of the royal parks, which manages Hyde Park and St James Park among others, recalls: “The grass was completely scorched off across all of our park network, it was quite shocking. The grass level had almost turned to dust.“We’ve had heatwaves in the past but they’ve only been for short periods of time. The grass dies off, we get the rain again and then everything starts coming back quite quickly. This time it was just one [heatwave] after another.”View image in fullscreenPeople playing cricket at Perry Hall Park in Birmingham in mid-August, after the fifth heatwave of the summer.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe cricket pitches at Perry Hall Park in mid-September.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe extreme conditions not only changed the physical features of the parks, he said. “You could see that people were using the parks completely differently.”Visitor numbers decreased significantly during the day and many sporting and volunteering activities were cancelled because of health and safety concerns.The royal parks are not yet in full bloom again, but the difference between now and peak summer is stark. Share attributes the rapid regrowth to the resilience of grass. “I’m looking at the parks and seeing the grass come back to green. We’re very lucky that grass can tolerate that level of heat and will regenerate like we’re seeing now,” he said.View image in fullscreenBrockwell Park in south London in mid-September.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBrockwell Park at the end of July.Photograph: Richard Baker/AlamyIn Wales, whichwas hit by wildfiresin mid-August, the death of grassy areas had a range of social and environmental effects. “I saw really thin cattle because they had no food for grazing,” said Carolyn Thomas, a climate activist and former Senedd member. “Farmers … had to go into their winter stock to keep their animals fed.“Sheep and cows were hiding under the shade of trees barely moving. Some were lying down flat and I was thinking: ‘Are they dead?’”The UK government has pledged £100m to “strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to extreme weather and wildfires”, but Thomas said she did not think this was the solution.“If you have to evacuate your home because of a wildfire you can’t just think: ‘We need a bigger fire service and more helicopters that can drop water’,” she said. “We need prevention.”View image in fullscreenThe Brecon Beacons in Wales in mid-August.Photograph: Leighton Collins/AlamyLike southern England, the Welsh countryside is slowly returning to normal, much to Thomas’s pleasure. “Now I’m walking and seeing green fields,” she said. “It’s amazing. But we still have that loss as well and it’s going to take a while to recover.”Groundwater and reservoir levels remain low and the government has urged water companies to continue their efficiency measures until normal levels are reached.Explore more on these topicsUK weatherDroughtExtreme heatWalesEnglandWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Burning forests, emptying rivers, €180bn in damage: Europe’s politicians face reckoning after ‘summer of truth’  | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?
Content: France recorded its hottest day ever this summer as climate breakdown causes Europe to heat faster than any other continent.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APView image in fullscreenFrance recorded its hottest day ever this summer as climate breakdown causes Europe to heat faster than any other continent.Photograph: Christophe Ena/APClimate crisisBurning forests, emptying rivers, €180bn in damage: Europe’s politicians face reckoning after ‘summer of truth’Amid record-shattering heatwaves and popular demand for climate action, why are politicians often timid or in denial?Fiona HarveyEnvironment editorSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was, according to the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, the“summer of truth”. Climate chaos ripped through Europe and the northern hemisphere, sending heat records tumbling, scorching crops in the fields, burning forests, emptying rivers and reservoirs, warping train tracks, melting roads and killing about 35,000 people in Europe alone.The EU has estimated the damage at about €180bn, and the full bill is yet to arrive: harvests have been depleted, which will probably raise food price inflation, and expensive repairs to infrastructure have only just begun.“All of this is a mere preview,” said von der Leyen in herstate of the EU address on Wednesday. “These were the hottest summer months ever – but probably the coolest of the years to come. Science is clear. Europe is warming at double the global rate. Europe can, must and will stay the course on its climate targets.”View image in fullscreenStreets were flooded in Bangladesh this summer as extreme rainfall fell across Asia.Photograph: Monirul Alam/EPABut while Europe has heated faster than any other continent,no region of the world is being spared. In the US, this summer’s heat eclipsed that of the “dust bowl” years of the 1930s, anddrought gripped 60% of the country from spring, a record for the time of year. Extremerainfall across Asia brought flash floods and typhoons, displacing hundreds of thousands of people and causing severe damage to crops.So what has the political response been? Tepid at best from centrist and leftwing politicians, say campaigners, with few rays of hope to brighten the gloom; denial and dangerous, provocative incoherence from the right and far right.“It was the hottest of summers – it was the meekest of responses,” said Magda Stoczkiewicz, the EU programme director for Greenpeace, of von der Leyen’s intervention. “The EU Commission continues its crusade to dismantle and defund environmental action. It is planning to cut green funding in the next EU budget, continues to support fossil fuels like gas, and is speeding up permitting of environmentally harmful projects.”View image in fullscreenWater levels dropped in Baitings reservoir, West Yorkshire, this summer as more than two-thirds of the UK reached drought conditions.Photograph: Jon Super/APVon der Leyen promised to “double down” on low-carbon energy and to “make Europe’s future electric”, as well as build resilience to climate impacts with a heatwave plan. There have been other positive moves: the Netherlands produced its long-awaited roadmap to “transition away from fossil fuels”, and France adopted a speeded-up plan for electrification. The UK saw the first “down payment” on a promised £1bn community energy programme, and the prime minister, Andy Burnham,committed to “net zero by 2050”.In the developing world, Thailand decided to stop building gas-fired power stations, while Indonesia continued to scale up solar energy under a three-year plan to halt oil imports. India, which has already achieved its2030 target to have 50% of its installed electricity generation capacity from renewables, vowed to push further, to reach 500GW by 2030 from about 260GW today. China’s emissions, meanwhile,are likely to fall this yearunder the acceleration of the country’s switch to electric vehicles and vast build-out of solar and wind energy.Yet, as campaigners have noted, these positive developments are outweighed by governments stalling on climate commitments, or pushing for more fossil fuels. In the UK, the government ismulling the opening of new oil and gasfields. Germany is building new gas-fired power stations; France isfalling behind on its greenhouse gas reduction targets.View image in fullscreenIndia has already achieved its target for renewable sources to fuel 50% of its installed electricity generation capacity.Photograph: Rajesh Kumar Singh/APEven the co-hosts of thenext UN climate summit, Cop31, which will take place this November in Turkey but with Australia in charge of negotiations, are failing to walk the walk on climate. This month,Australia approved the expansion of a coalmine that will continue producing until 2055; the same mine supplies Turkey, which hasrefused to set a phaseout date for coal use.On the right, the record-breaking summer has not slowed US efforts to reverse and remove climate legislation: most recently, the Trump administrationhasrepealed the Environmental Protection Agency rule that cuts emissions from power plants, and pressed ahead withdismantling renewable energy and boosting coal.Populist politicians on the far right are on the rise, and almost all embrace climate denial as one of their key tenets and paint attempts to cut greenhouse gas emissions as economy-crippling. Extreme heat and the coming of climate impacts that scientists have long predicted might be expected to give them pause; instead, their denial has often intensified – as is the case in the US under Donald Trump – or switched focus to clamorous demands for ahuge expansion of air conditioningas the only means of adapting to the heat.Meanwhile, their anti-immigration policies ignore the potential impact of the climate crisis on immigration. Rather than address the root causes of immigration and fund clean energy and development, they prefer to claim that countries should build huge walls around themselves, and to demonise immigrants.View image in fullscreenUnder the leadership of Donald Trump, the US has sought to gut its climate regulations.Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP“Climate has become the central part of the far right’s culture war in defence of the economic and energy status quo that bankrolls it,” says Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead at Oil Change International. “When the brutality of climate impacts has made their previous climate denialism untenable, like in France, theirfallback strategy has been to present adaptation [to the impacts of extreme weather] as a substitute for cutting emissions. All round the world, the far right has weaponised legitimate concerns about affordability and living standards generated by decades of neoliberal policies to protect the fossil fuel status quo.”The populist task is made easier in a world bombarded by threats: from AI, conflicts, geo-politics and rampant inequality. Memories are short, even for significant events. Previous climate disasters were quickly erased from global attention, says Laurence Tubiana, the chief executive of the European Climate Foundation. “We can’t ignore what has happened in Nepal, and we have forgotten what happened in Pakistan just a few years ago,” she says, referring to thedeadly climate-driven floods that affected a third of the country’s population in 2022. “There is a big silence around all this.”Some of the most vulnerable countries are struggling to protect their people, and face avicious cycle of debt, but are seeing little help from the rich world. “Many are being forced to choose between servicing enormous debts and investing in the infrastructure that could save lives when the next disaster strikes,” says Mohamed Adow, the director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank.If politicians in some of the world’s biggest economies are failing to act, it is not for a lack of demand among their voters. John Marshall, the founder and executive chair of the Potential Energy Coalition in the US, says recent polling by his organisation has found that politicians in many large economies are failing to keep pace with their voters on the issue. “The disconnect we’re seeing is not between the public and climate action,” he says. “It’s between what people are experiencing and how much they’re hearing from their leaders about it. People want more clean energy and less of the fossil fuel pollution that’s overheating the planet.”View image in fullscreenA rally held in New York this week calling for an end to the use of fossil fuels.Photograph: Bryan Woolston/APThis calls into question thestrategy of “climate hushing” that some Democrats in the US– and even progressive politicians in other countries – have embraced, amid a widespread perception that voters care only about the cost of living.According to the Potential Energy Coalition polling, that is not the case: about two-thirds of people in the US believe that if public officials refuse to acknowledge the reality of global heating, they are putting people at risk. A similar number said societies could not prepare for extreme weather if they were not willing to talk about the climate crisis.InEurope, polling by Climate Opinion found the shattered heat records elevated the climate to one of the top five concerns in France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the UK. (Denmark, which was less affected by extreme weather, was also included in the poll, but the number citing it as a top concern stayed flat at 28%.) About 68% to 83% of respondents in all countries identified the heatwaves as climate-related.“It’s difficult for the public to get their heads round,” says Michael Jacobs, an emeritus professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield. “And the [far right] are not wrong in one respect, which is that we do need to adapt to the heat. But what we need people to understand is thatnet zero is literally a description of scientific fact. If we don’t reach net zero emissions, we will see temperatures continue to rise.”If weather as extreme as this year’s “summer of truth” fails to make a lasting political impact, we will be doomed to repeat it – over and over, until acting on it is no longer a choice.Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisFossil fuelsExtreme heatExtreme weatherEuropeClimate science scepticism and denialFloodingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to flood-proof your home: from water-thirsty plants to deflated footballs | Flooding | The Guardian
description: After summer’s heatwaves, prepare for winter of storms and heavy rain, with millions of UK homes at risk of flooding
Author: Matthew Taylor
Headline: After summer’s heatwaves, prepare for winter of storms and heavy rain, with millions of UK homes at risk of flooding
Content: Flooding in Pontypridd when the River Taff broke its banks during Storm Bert in 2024.Photograph: Emmawales123/PAView image in fullscreenFlooding in Pontypridd when the River Taff broke its banks during Storm Bert in 2024.Photograph: Emmawales123/PAFloodingHow to flood-proof your home: from water-thirsty plants to deflated footballsAfter summer’s heatwaves, prepare for winter of storms and heavy rain, with millions of UK homes at risk of floodingMatthew TaylorSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe accelerating climate crisis and this year’s record-breaking El Niño mean that, although the summer’s heatwaves are still fresh in the memory, households in the UK are alreadybeing toldto prepare for a potentially destructive winter of storms and heavy rain – leaving millions of homes at risk of flooding.Government action is needed to improve flood defences and build reliance on a national and regional level. But with the UK’s flood season just weeks away, the Guardian spoke to experts to find out what action communities and individuals can take to make their neighbourhoods and homes more resilient, from self-closing airbricks to deflated children’s footballs.Community actionThe first step is tocheckwhether your home or neighbourhood is listed at risk of flooding on the government’s website. If it is, find out if the local council has a flood alert scheme and make sure you and your neighbours are signed up to that and theEnvironment Agency’s flood alerts system.Join any local community flood group – or consider setting one up with neighbours – and approach the council to see what flood plans it has in place, and get involved in making them better. This could include lobbying for more permeable surfaces, rain gardens and tree planting.Identify any vulnerable residents who might need extra support and draw up a street or neighbourhood flood plan to make sure everyone knows what to do in the event of a flood.Tracey Garrett, the chief executive of the National Flood Forum, said flooding can be “incredibly frightening and disruptive” but insists that together, communities, households and councils can make difference to an area’s resilience.“We are seeing increasingly intense rainfall and a growing risk from surface water flooding, and climate change means we cannot assume that the flooding patterns of the past will necessarily be the patterns of the future,” she said. “This makes preparation more important than ever.”Gardens and outdoor spacesAccording to Mary Long-Dhonau, who runs theFlood Mary campaign, protecting your home starts outside. She says now is an ideal time to check brickwork and mortar on outside walls for cracks or weaknesses. These should either be repaired or replaced and external walls can be treated with a breathable waterproof sealant.“Having cracks or crumbling mortar can be like having 20 taps in your wall that will let the flood water straight in,” said Long-Dhonau, who provides adirectory of builders who specialisein flood-related work.Experts also suggest making sure gutters are clear and in good working order. Long-Dhonau adds that residents should consider installing water butts, which catch and store the rain before it reaches the ground. “They are easy and relatively cheap and it means if you get a warning about a possible flood risk you can empty the water butts before the rain arrives, meaning they have full capacity to hold the maximum amount once the rain starts, keeping it out of the drains,” said Long-Dhonau.View image in fullscreenEmptying water butts before a storm arrives will keep more rainwater out of the drains.Photograph: Justin Kase z12z/AlamyThe way gardens, driveways and other outdoor spaces are designed also has a big impact on how quickly rainwater runs into already stretched drainage systems – and how likely your home is to flood.Surfaces such as concrete, paving and artificial grass prevent water soaking effectively into the ground. Instead, you should include planted areas,rain gardensor permeable paving to allow water to drain away.“Even if you have a paved area, just taking up one or two paving stones and planting some water-thirsty plants can make a big difference,” said Long-Dhonau.Improving soil health and increasing plant cover also allow gardens to better absorb and hold water, reducing the risk of flooding.“The trick is to work with nature wherever possible,” said Long-Dhonau.HomesFlooding can happen quickly and be stressful, so experts advise having a “flood to-do list” spelling out what needs to be done should the worst happen, including how to turn off the gas and electricity supplies and which treasured belongings need moving out of harm’s way.With this in mind, experts advise having a “flood box” to keep a few flood essentials in, from a head torch to flood tape, plastic sheeting to absorbent flood cushions.“No one can say exactly what this winter will bring, but you don’t need to wait for a flood warning before taking action,” said Long-Dhonau. “After all, you don’t want to be hunting around for your insurance details or wondering which belongings to move first when the water is already rising.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRising temperatures may increase flood risk through river ‘whiplash’, study findsRead moreIn emergenciesIn terms of stopping the water getting in, the house experts warn that a standard airbrick can let thousands of litres of water in to your home every hour, so it is crucial to identify where they are and have a plan in place for what to do if a flood hits.Long-Dhonau says that ideally they should be replaced with Kitemarked self-closing airbricks, which seal when the flood water comes. Alternatively, temporary covers are available that have to be manually installed before the flood hits.Flood water can also come through doors or windows. Flood doors can be fitted, which, although expensive, are effective at keeping water out. Alternatively, floor barriers can be installed outside the door, which need to be put in place before the flood water arrives.In an emergency, Long-Dhonau suggests having flood tape or aluminium tape in the house, which can be used to seal up airbricks, doors and windows.“People always think of sandbags when floods happen, but having some good-quality flood tape on hand is not only a more effective way to better protect your home but also much, much cheaper.”One of the most distressing and destructive impacts of flooding can be waste water and sewage being forced back up into the house through the toilet system.Ideally, flood-risk properties should have a non-return valve fitted to the drainage system, which will stop this happening. Alternatively, toilet bungs and stoppers are available, which also work but need to be fitted manually.In an emergency, Long-Dhonau suggests a child’s football can be deflated, pushed down the toilet and pumped up again. The toilet seat can then be taped down using flood or aluminium tape.“Obviously, it is about being as prepared as you can be but also using whatever is to hand to limit the damage,” she said.Other tips for flood-prone homesLong-Dhonau suggests raising furniture off the floor by propping it up on upturned buckets or decorators’ trestles. She also says curtains can be tied up with scarves or tights and table legs put in buckets, or even wellies, to protect them from rising flood water. Precious objects should be put in plastic clip boxes and moved somewhere safe.“You want to go into your room and look around at everything below waist height and think, what is really precious to me?”In properties that regularly flood, experts recommend moving plug sockets higher up the walls and installing flood-resilient flooring and materials, which can make a property easier and quicker to clean and save thousands of pounds.Kelly Ostler-Coyle, from the government-backed Flood Re reinsurance scheme said: “No one can predict exactly where or when flooding will happen, but there are practical steps that people can take to make their homes more resilient … A little preparation can make a real difference – helping to protect the things people care about and making it easier to get back into their homes and back to normal if flooding does happen.”Explore more on these topicsFloodingExtreme weatherHomesClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit | Jim Ratcliffe | The Guardian
description: Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
Author: Daniel Lavelle
Headline: Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
Content: ‘At the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it,’ Ratcliffe said.Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAView image in fullscreen‘At the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it,’ Ratcliffe said.Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAJim RatcliffeManchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quitSupporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empireYassin El-MouddenandDaniel LavelleSat 19 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview.SirJim Ratcliffedescribed the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.In what was described as a “statement of no confidence” posted on X, MUMSC said: “Our players, staff, stewards, security teams and supporters come from different countries, cultures, ethnicities, religions and backgrounds. Manchester United would not be Manchester United without them.“Manchester United does not belong emotionally to investment funds, shareholders or billionaires.“After years of decline, broken promises and repeated failure, Manchester United Muslim Supporters’ Club has lost confidence in the current ownership structure of Manchester United Football Club.“Enough is enough. It is time for change. The Glazers [co-owners] and Sir Jim Ratcliffe must go.”Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giantIneos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain was in decline because of high taxes and immigration.His latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country wasbeing “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.MUMSC said it had challenged those remarks earlier this year, adding: “We hoped a lesson had been learned. Clearly, it has not.“This week, Sir Jim has again placed immigration and people receiving benefits at the centre of his explanation for Britain’s problems, arguing that nobody is ‘tough enough’ to deal with either.“We find these latest comments deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable.”The billionaire told BBC News’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline.He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk.“But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident.“And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuardian view on Sir Jim Ratcliffe: Britain does not need political lectures from a billionaire tax exile | EditorialRead moreWhile the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, theOffice for Budget Responsibilitysays it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such asthe 1958.The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.Ratcliffe also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”In response to the criticisms, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.A spokesperson told the BBC they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”Explore more on these topicsJim RatcliffeManchester UnitedIneosIslamBritish empirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Small boat arrivals are ‘wealthy men’ who do not deserve help, says Reform’s Danny Kruger | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: The fact that some migrants pay people smugglers thousands of pounds makes them well off, MP claims
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: The fact that some migrants pay people smugglers thousands of pounds makes them well off, MP claims
Content: Danny Kruger’s claim was immediately dismissed as false by charities who support refugees.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenDanny Kruger’s claim was immediately dismissed as false by charities who support refugees.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAReform UKSmall boat arrivals are ‘wealthy men’ who do not deserve help, says Reform’s Danny KrugerThe fact that some migrants pay people smugglers thousands of pounds makes them well off, MP claimsHelena HortonSat 19 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsylum seekers who arrive on small boats across the Channel are “wealthy men” who do not deserve the help of the British state, according to theReform UKMP Danny Kruger.The former Conservative,who defected last year, said the fact that some migrants were paying people smugglers thousands of pounds – often using their life savings or borrowed money – made them well off. The claim was immediately dismissed by charities who support refugees.Speaking at the Big Brue festival in Bruton, Somerset, Kruger said: “By the way, most of them [are] comparatively wealthy and fit young men who’ve crossed safe countries to begin the journey to the UK.”Asked by the event’s moderator, the editor of the Independent, Geordie Greig, how he knew these men were wealthy, Kruger said: “Because they’re paying thousands of pounds. They’re paying thousands of pounds to people smugglers to get here. Comparatively wealthy, compared to the people who I think most of us can regard as really deserving of the compassion of the British taxpayer.”Seema Syeda, a Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants spokesperson, said it was untrue that most asylum seekers who arrive on boats are wealthy.She said: “The reality is that most asylum seekers who arrive here are denied the right to work, live off as little as £8 a week, and can end up in destitution. But in the end, whether rich or poor, people fleeing war and persecution deserve to be welcomed. The right to safety is a human right.“Many people arriving here have been forcibly displaced due to war, genocide or imperialism that the British state has, past and present, funded or supported.”Earlier this month, Reform politician Matt Goodwin, the party’s unsuccessful candidate at the Gorton and Denton byelection, caused outrage when he said at the party’s annual conference that the “best and the brightest” of the British population had been replaced by “drug-dealing goat-herders” through immigration.Kruger said Goodwin was correct to make these incendiary remarks. He said: “There are some drug-dealing goat-herders who we’ve admitted to this country, so I mean, it’s factual.”Asked by Greig if he accepted that language, he said: “Yes I do.” He added: “And they don’t like our country.”Kruger said he was concerned “about kind of massive cultural transformation. And yes, the admission to our country of many people who do not share the values that we all love, and I’m afraid to say it’s not just recent migrants.”The Reform MP also complained about second- and third-generation migrants.He said: “In fact, I think recent migrants are probably more pro-British because they’ve come here for a reason. They want to be here. We’ve got a problem with second- and third-generation immigrants because they are, and it’s a fault of politics that … this has happened.“We have an alienated generation, many many people, millions of people, for whom they don’t love their country, they don’t think that Britain is great, and they don’t feel that they are part of the mainstream society that we have here, and that is our challenge.”He further claimed that current policies would cause a civil war. “We continue down the path of segregation and of you know elite virtue signalling, pretending we’re all a lovely multicultural diversity is our strength, and it’s rude to even point out any problems,” Kruger added.Rachel Millward, the co-deputy leader of the Green party, said: “Reform is a party funded by billionaires that chooses to attack the most vulnerable in our society – people fleeing environmental breakdown, famine and war.“Instead of stoking division and hatred, just days after anti-immigrant protests brought violence and disorder to our streets, politicians need to step up and offer solutions. We’re calling for more safe routes so that those who need asylum can apply for it before they leave their own country, and never have to face a dangerous crossing in a small boat.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKImmigration and asylumMigrationRefugeesShareReuse this content

title: Kent hotel fire that forced hundreds to evacuate being treated as suspicious | Kent | The Guardian
description: No injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blaze
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: No injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blaze
Content: Inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInquiries into the cause of the fire are under way.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesKentKent hotel fire that forced hundreds to evacuate being treated as suspiciousNo injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blazeSammy GecsoylerandYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA large fire that broke out overnight at a seaside hotel and forced hundreds of people to evacuate is being treated by police as suspicious.Emergency services were called just after 1am on Saturday to the Grand Burstin hotel in Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement,Kentfire and rescue service said.About 280 people were taken to safety and Folkestone and Hythe district council set up a welfare centre.No injuries have been reported and inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way. Detectives from Kent police are also seeking dashcam footage and asking witnesses to come forward.View image in fullscreenFire damage at the hotel.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesTwenty-six fire engines were dispatched to the seafront hotel, the fire service said. According to the BritanniaHotelswebsite, the Grand Burstin overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms.Folkestone and Hythe district council posted on X: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin hotel.“We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected.“We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety.“Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area.”Kent fire and rescue service said in an update: “Ten fire engines remain at the scene of a fire at the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone.“Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots.“It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known.“Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No fire-related injuries have been reported.”A spokesperson for Kent police said: “Kent police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday 19 September 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone.“Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent fire and rescue service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”Explore more on these topicsKentHospitality industryHotelsFirefightersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Students scramble for accommodation after provider goes bust in Dundee | Student housing | The Guardian
description: Case highlights severe financial strain on sector across UK as string of university housing schemes fail
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Case highlights severe financial strain on sector across UK as string of university housing schemes fail
Content: The owner of Marketgait Apartments student accommodation in Dundee filed for administration in mid-July.Photograph: Prestige Student LivingView image in fullscreenThe owner of Marketgait Apartments student accommodation in Dundee filed for administration in mid-July.Photograph: Prestige Student LivingStudent housingStudents scramble for accommodation after provider goes bust in DundeeCase highlights severe financial strain on sector across UK as string of university housing schemes failAre you having problems with your accommodation provider?Julia Kolleweand Amee JoshiSat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 70 students inDundeehave been left scrambling to find accommodation for this academic year after the latest in a string of university housing schemes went bust amid severe financial strain on the sector.Students in the city have been forced to find alternative housing and rapidly move their possessions as term begins this month after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a city centre block.The company filed for administration in mid-July with 68 rooms let. Just weeks earlier it had been urging students to quickly secure its “perfect homes” in online marketing.It is further evidence of a crisis in the UK student housing sector, with companies going bust or disposing of properties owing to to a combination of poor demand or oversupply in different regions.Accommodation providers are grappling withfalling international student numbers, down for a third year; a cost of living squeeze; and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.Whiledomestic student numbers are at a record high, agrowing proportion live at home, mostly because of the cost of renting, in what has been called“the rise of the commuter student”.View image in fullscreenMarketgait is less than a 10-minute walk from the University of Dundee.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/AlamyA boom in new-build student housing in recent years led to too many tower blocks in places such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham. Glasgow, Bristol and London still face shortages, with a general lack of affordable rooms.Modern, purpose-built housing tends to command higher rents than student halls on campus or private rooms, and is out of reach for many domestic students, with wealthier overseas students the main occupants.Three weeks before the then owners filed for administration, Marketgait Apartments in Dundee wasstill being promotedto students.The 116-room building, less than 10-minute walk from Abertay and Dundee universities, had a concierge and a shared lounge with a pool table. The weekly rent was pitched at £199 for a studio and £165 for an en suite room.“Looking for your perfect student home in Dundee?” the operator, Prestige Student Living, wrote on Facebook on 23 June. “Marketgait Apartments still have rooms available – but not for long! Secure your spot today and avoid missing out on a prime location, modern living, and everything you need right on your doorstep. Book now before it’s gone!”On 15 July, however, partners from FRP Advisory were appointed to the Jersey-based special purpose vehicle that owns the redbrick block after its owners, the real estate manager 90 North and Kuwaiti investment company Rasameel, failed to repay a £5.7m loan against the property.Falling student numbers at the building led to financial losses, leaving the company unable to fund essential fire safety remedial works. The building remains closed while its new owner, ATK Property, carries out the work.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJames Elliot says students at at Margetgait had contracts for a year, but now have to leave within a month.James Elliot, 21, who recently graduated from Dundee university, said he knew people living in Margetgait who had to move out and were “anxious, stressed and shocked”.“A lot of the students had contracts to stay there next year, but they were just told they had to leave in a month, you need to be out, you need to move your things out.” Students were helped to book alternative accommodation.Elliot, a housing activist and member of Scotland’s tenants’ and community union Living Rent, added: “Because so many international students were away back home, they couldn’t do that in person. They had all of their belongings there for next year, clothes, pots and pans, everything they needed for uni. So they had to pay a fee for a third party to store their things for them.”Prestige said the lets in place when Marketgait went into administration included 27 students who had renewed their contracts for the 2026-27 academic year. Of those, 17 had already moved out for the summer. Six others asked Prestige for details of a moving company and paid for it themselves.A Prestige spokesperson said the decision and subsequent closure was beyond the managing agent’s control. “Our team took immediate action to notify students, help them secure alternative accommodation in Dundee and return all payments made to us. We deeply sympathise with the students affected by the news and will continue to do all we can to support them.”This is the latest failure in the sector. Amare Students, which ran a 64-room student accommodation block in Birmingham, went into administration in January. Alma Place, a 393-room block in Belfast, was acquired by London-based investors the same month, just over a year after going into receivership.Several struggling housing providers have sought planning permission to open up their buildings to non-students, including a 91-room block in Coventry that is in receivership. Receivers want to let 50 rooms to city workers instead of students.Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, is accelerating a programme of selling off unwanted blocks, with 15,000 to 20,000 beds earmarked for sale, after it slumped to a £418m loss in the first half of the year. Its portfolio will slim down to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities, compared with 29 at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”.Explore more on these topicsStudent housingStudentsHigher educationReal estateDundeeScotlandUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: California warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passenger | California | The Guardian
description: Health authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six counties
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Health authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six counties
Content: Pennsylvania has seen four measles-related deaths as the US grapples with the fallout from increasing vaccine hesitancy.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPennsylvania has seen four measles-related deaths as the US grapples with the fallout from increasing vaccine hesitancy.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesCaliforniaCalifornia warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passengerHealth authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six countiesMarina DunbarSat 19 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaliforniapublic health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure spanning multiple counties after an infected and unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state viaAmtraktrains and thruway buses.The warning comes as the US faces its largest measles resurgence inmore than three decades, fueled largely by growing vaccine hesitancy.TheCaliforniadepartment of public health said the traveler passed through at least six counties – Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin – while making multiple transfers.RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreakRead moreOfficials said the passenger entered California on an Amtrak train that arrived in Los Angeles on 10 September. From there, the traveler continued to Bakersfield before heading through Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville, eventually leaving California for Denver.Health officials said passengers who were onboard thesame trains or buses, as well as people who were inside the stations along the route on the dates involved, have been exposed to measles.The state said it is working with federal partners and local health departments to identify and notify people who may have been exposed.“This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” assistant state public health officer Rita Nguyen said in a statement. “The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated.”Pennsylvania is currently dealing with the country’s worst active measles outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department announced on Wednesday that 731 cases have been confirmed across 38 counties so far this year. At leastfour peoplein the state have died from measles-related illness.Pennsylvania is now seekingemergency assistancefrom the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as the outbreak continues to spread. State officials have warned, however, that the request could be withdrawn unless the CDC publicly recognizes the four measles-associated deaths, something the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, previously instructed the CDCnot to do.And as the death toll from the outbreak continues to rise, Kennedyheadlinedthe Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense earlier this week, an group he led for nearly a decade.He only addressed the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania once during his speech, instead peddling unfounded fears about vaccines at a time when health experts are urgently encouraging people to vaccinate against measles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”The California warning also follows another recent mass-exposure incident involving Amtrak.Earlier this week, it was reported that a person infected with measles traveled onboard an Amtrak train from Sedalia, Missouri, to Chicago, Illinois, resulting inmore than 250 peoplebeing exposed to the virus in Jackson county alone.This month, it was also revealed that the Trump administration changed howmeasles deaths are countedduring the outbreak. The CDC is now relying on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, which is used to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaMMRInfectious diseasesRobert F Kennedy JrTrump administrationHealthWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activists  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
Content: Rita Flores claims that after her recruitment she instigated fights with fellow artists to push them away, and prevent them sharing information with her.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresView image in fullscreenRita Flores claims that after her recruitment she instigated fights with fellow artists to push them away, and prevent them sharing information with her.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresRussia‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activistsExclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSBShaun WalkerSat 19 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst came the blackmail and death threats to secure cooperation, then came a series of tasks, each more sinister than the last: to inform on fellow activists, to elicit personal information from protest-minded artists and – eventually – to help with a plot to kidnap and murder a Kremlin enemy.That is how Rita Flores, a 29-year-old Russian artist, activist and former member ofthe Pussy Riot collective, described her recruitment and three-year handling by officers from Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke when she fled the country last month.Flores made details of her collaboration public in avideo discussionwith her lawyer, Dmitry Zakhvatov, published just days after she left Russia at the end of August. She explained she was coming clean in the hope that others in a similar situation might feel emboldened to break their ties with the FSB.Revealed: how Russia uses mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizensRead moreNow, in her first media interview since leavingRussia, she gave further detail on how she was recruited and run by the FSB. “For the first time in years, I feel calm. All this time I was dreaming about getting out and being able to talk about it all,” she said. The Guardian could not corroborate the details of Flores’s account, but there have been numerous cases of the FSB infiltrating opposition groups over the past few years.View image in fullscreenRita Flores was arrested multiple times for provocative art performances as part of Pussy Riot.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresFlores, also known as Margarita Konovalova, has been associated with Pussy Riot since 2020, when she was detained after a performance near the Kremlin. She had served several short stints in jail and been subjected to surveillance and house searches on numerous occasions, which intensified after the domestic crackdown that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.She was recruited after one of these police searches in February 2023, when two men stayed behind and introduced themselves as FSB officers, she said. They threatened to open a criminal case, under wartime censorship laws, over an Instagram post she had made criticising Russian killings in Ukraine. They also suggested they could arrange for her mother to be killed if she did not sign cooperation papers.“I believed them. I believed they could do everything they said they would … My fear was too great. I was so worried for my family and also for myself,” she said. As a reward for signing, she was given a one-off cash payment of 30,000 or 40,000 roubles (£266 or £355), she said.Her first tasks were to gather information about other opposition-minded artists in the same circles as her and report back to the FSB. The two FSB officers who recruited her became her regular handlers, she said, organising frequent meetings and largely sticking to a classic good-cop, bad-cop routine. She saw the senior officer only occasionally, a crude man in his late forties who introduced himself by a series of different names. In the end, Flores began calling him “the Jacket”, based on the shiny black suit he liked to wear. The junior officer, named Ivan, became her primary handler, and he often tried to be friendly and helpful, leaving direct threats to the Jacket.View image in fullscreenOne of Flores’s handlers promised to ‘re-educate’ her until she became an ‘obedient wife’.Photograph: courtesy Rita Flores“Whenever I met with Ivan and the Jacket together, Ivan was silent. The Jacket would be rude, threatening; he’d insult me as a woman. He was the devil incarnate. Then just me and Ivan would meet, and Ivan would be nice, friendly,” she recalled. “He liked to say, ‘The FSB will re-educate you, I will re-educate you, you’ll have a nice and calm life, and you’ll love Russia, have children and be an obedient wife,’” she said.Flores said she was not supposed to tell anyone about her recruitment, but immediately told “about 20 people”, putting it down to the fact she is a “massive gossip”.Still, she stopped short of telling the people from the art world she was meant to report on, instead claiming that she initiated conflicts with them on pretexts, designed to push them away from her and prevent them sharing sensitive information. Her two handlers kept up the psychological pressure by repeating their threats, and even the friendlier Ivan on occasion made it clear that the consequences for crossing him would be severe, she claimed.“He tried to befriend me, but he could also be threatening. He’d calmly say, ‘they’ll kill your mother and you won’t be able to prove anything’ or ‘if you go abroad they’ll find you immediately and kill you,’ and then he would giggle, like it was all a joke. The Jacket, on the other hand, never joked. His threats were more direct.”In time, there were fewer targets to inform on, as most of the protest-minded artists left the country. She described life in wartime Moscow as an exercise in cognitive dissonance. “Moscow is booming; restaurants, bars and clubs are opening and there are a huge number of events. But those people who understand things have empty eyes and speak empty words,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFlores claims most of the provocative, protest-minded artists have left Russia under Putin’s regime.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresArtists who stayed are careful not to produce any work that could be considered even tangentially political, she said. “People who have stayed in Russia have accepted the rules of a game. You go to a gallery and every artwork may as well come with a sign saying ‘we were forbidden from saying anything’ … there are artists who used to make strong statements, and in 2026 they are drawing flowers in a vase.”Last May, Ivan and the Jacket first started asking her questions about Pyotr Verzilov, an activist previously linked to Pussy Riot who now lives in Ukraine and fights with the Ukrainian army against Russia. A longtime irritant to the Russian authorities, in 2018German doctors saidthey believed Verzilov had been poisoned in Russia.Flores said her handlers wanted her to get information from Verzilov, including his address in Ukraine. Then, they suggested she use her old friendship with him to arrange a meeting in Serbia. There, he would be kidnapped and killed by a waiting FSB squad, they claimed. Ivan began to pay her 50,000 roubles a month as an additional incentive to help with the Verzilov case.Meanwhile, Flores said, she was plotting a way out. She married her partner last September, which she said was partly a way of worming out of the Serbia task, so she could claim to Ivan that her husband would never let her go on a trip to meet another man. Previously, her handlers had banned her from leaving the country, she claimed, and it was only when she contacted the lawyer, Zakhvatov, that she realised there could be a way for her to leave. The pair began scheming in secret over the details.“They created a reality where she felt like they controlled everything, but actually it is not that hard to leave,” said Zakhvatov. In 2022, fellow Pussy Riot activists Lucy Shtein and Masha Alekhina fled house arrest in Moscow bydressing up as food delivery couriersto evade police and eventually leave Russia. Flores’s escape was less dramatic, but both Zakhvatov and Flores declined to give details, citing the need to protect methods for future cases.View image in fullscreenHaving escaped Russia, Flores is now keen to help those in similar situations flee the country.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresAfter Flores’s escape, Zakhvatov announced a secure line for people in similar positions to contact him if they need help. Flores said she would also like to work to help others, and added that she was certain that recruitments in activist circles are a “mass phenomenon”. She said there was at least one person in her own surroundings who had informed on her before she agreed to cooperate, a fact she discovered when it turned out that the FSB had possession of a sex tape featuring her, covertly filmed by the person. Earlier this year, Polandjailed an exiled Russian activistfor seven years, after it emerged he had passed information about fellow exiles to an FSB handler who had recruited him back in Russia.Flores’s video confession at the end of last month was met with praise from some parts of the exiled Russian opposition, who commended her bravery for speaking out and explaining how the FSB operates, but also some scepticism from those who criticised her decision to cooperate for so long. Since then, Flores has been making calls to people she informed on as well as other old friends to explain herself, and said everyone had been supportive in these conversations.“It’s not a big secret that it’s not great to work for the FSB, but fear can change a person,” saidAlekhina. “It’s important that she’s now out of the country and that she said what happened to her out loud. Nobody was killed and nobody went to prison [because of her], so that is good news.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Content: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesNAZAFrom ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryAs Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaignPeter BeaumontSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was theGazadocumentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers –describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly.
