The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.Rightwingpolitical figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he wouldseek new laws to strip citizenshipfrom people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretzwarnedthat their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as didinternational press freedom organisations.The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”View image in fullscreenA protest against the NAZA film-makers in Savyon, Israel.Photograph: Sharon Eilon/Sopa Images/ShutterstockThe rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”At points, the threats of violence have been realised.On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.“The discussion aboutNAZAhas been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towardsdissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry foundIsrael continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreIsrael’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz,wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” hewrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Elderly man allegedly beaten to death in Virginia Walmart by parents of employee | Virginia | The Guardian
description: Bert Atienza and teen worker reportedly exchanged words before parents showed up and allegedly attacked shopper
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Bert Atienza and teen worker reportedly exchanged words before parents showed up and allegedly attacked shopper
Content: The confrontation reportedly began after an argument over a shopping cart.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe confrontation reportedly began after an argument over a shopping cart.Photograph: Charles-McClintock Wilson/NurPhoto/ShutterstockVirginiaElderly man allegedly beaten to death in Virginia Walmart by parents of employeeBert Atienza and teen worker reportedly exchanged words before parents showed up and allegedly attacked shopperMarina DunbarSat 19 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 77-year-oldWalmartshopper died after he was allegedly attacked inside aVirginiastore by the parents of a teenage employee he had confronted over a shopping cart incident involving his wife, according to US media reports.Bert Atienza died from blunt head trauma on 8 June, one day after the attack at the Walmart in Norfolk, Virginia,WTKRreported on Monday. The shocking incident was captured onsurveillance video.Police responded to the store at about 3.20pm on 7 June after receiving a report of an assault.Girl orphaned by Super Bowl reporter’s drugging and a deadly Kansas crash is ‘extreme victim’, granddad saysRead moreAtienza’s wife, Josephine, was left on the floor holding her injured husband in her lap after the attack, according to video from the scene.“My husband was still able to speak, he said, ‘Help me get up,’ but I told him, ‘No, you’re bleeding. Your mouth is bleeding. Ambulance is coming,” Josephine said. “I look at him again. He has no more consciousness.”Atienza was found unresponsive and taken to a hospital, where he died from his injuries the following day. Medical officials ruled his death a homicide caused by blunt force trauma.The confrontation began while Atienza and his wife of 42 years were grocery-shopping after spending the morning at church.Josephine said a 17-year-oldWalmartemployee came quickly down the aisle where the couple was shopping and nearly struck her with a shopping cart. Atienza and the unidentified worker exchanged words before the employee allegedly threw a can toward the couple as they walked away, Josephine told WTKR.The teen then reportedly called her parents, Travis White and Erika Mitchell, who began looking for the couple inside the store minutes later. The store surveillance video shows what appears to be Atienza looking at items on a shelf when White and Mitchell approached and attacked him while their daughter watched.The elderly shopper was allegedly shoved from behind, grabbed and punched as people nearby walked away. He was then pushed into a shelving unit and fell to the floor, where one of the suspects allegedly kicked him.White, 44, and Mitchell, 42, were arrested days later and are being held without bond in the Norfolk jail.Their teenage daughter was also charged with assault and battery, aggravated malicious wounding, and conspiracy to commit a felony, according toWAVY. She is being held at the Norfolk juvenile detention center. Authorities have not released her name because she is a minor.Explore more on these topicsVirginiaWalmartUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies | Google | The Guardian
description: Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models
Content: Google said the hacks highlighted the importance of training its AI models to ‘act responsibly’.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGoogle said the hacks highlighted the importance of training its AI models to ‘act responsibly’.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockGoogleGoogle says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companiesDisclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI modelsJohana BhuiyanFri 18 Sep 2026 20.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a first forGoogle, the company confirmed that its AI model, Gemini, breached the security of three other companies in May. The hacks occurred during a cybersecurity evaluation by AI-security firm Irregular.Irregular, an Israel-based startup that scrutinizes the security of advanced AI systems, was also at the center of some of the recentOpenAIandAnthropichacks of third-party entities, including OpenAI’sbreachof AI software company, Hugging Face.The circumstances that enabled the models to hack other companies in some of these cases are similar: Irregular was testing the models in a closed testing environment with fake companies. The testing environment was not supposed to be internet enabled, but internet access was made available unintentionally,according tothe Wall Street Journal. Once connected to the internet, the models unexpectedly hacked into real firms.Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face. Google confirmed to the Guardian that the hacks occurred, but that the company did not feel it required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies. The Wall Street Journalfirst reported on the breachesand revealed for the first time that they occurred.“In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, vice-president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”In one of the security breaches, Irregular was testing Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities by prompting the AI model to obtain information from a fake company’s software. The fake company had the same name as a real company. When the model unintentionally gained access to the internet, it correctly guessed the password of and breached a real company’s service, Irregular told the WSJ. Google said once it figured out it had hacked a real company, and not the simulated one, it stopped.In two other tests, the model searched the web for and found public repositories containing credentials to two other companies. The model used those credentials to access real companies. When it figured out they were real companies, it stopped, according to Google.Anthropic and OpenAI chose to voluntarily disclose the hacks but Google did not. However, the company said it ensured the three companies that were hacked were made aware.“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins, the Google spokesperson, said.Anthropic and OpenAI’s disclosures prompted the independent senator Bernie Sanders to demand the companies pause development of their technology, saying it signaled the company was no longer able to control their models.OpenAI paused development of their models fortwo weeks, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei hascalled for a collective slowdownof AI development to ensure that its most advanced models are being built with enough safeguards.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)AlphabetnewsShareReuse this content

title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
Content: Alvaro Dominguez / Guardian Design / Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioSilicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanityNick Robins-EarlySat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTShareWhen reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety andthe fate of humanity, he said no. His argument:China.“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic andOpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO,led an industry-wide call this weekto “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it allRead moreThe AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forcesare trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.Amodei’s worst China fearsFew have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEOSam Altmanor Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous propositionRead moreAmodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position,calling export controls a failureand urging Trump to ease restrictions.)But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.View image in fullscreenDario Amodei speaks at Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, California, in September.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAmodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said ata Politico eventon Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, withOpenAIhiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.double quotation mark... Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economyKyle Chan“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”Silicon Valley’s ChinahawksAlthough Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.Several of the tech figures focused on Chinahave connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.Nuclear considered an optionSome leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowskywrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.View image in fullscreenAlex Karp, Palantir CEO, at the G20 Innovation summit in North Carolina, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersOther China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karptold Axioslast year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”The view from ChinaWhile Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab.Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei,accusing himof running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”A race to the bottomWhile the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s modelshacking into outside organizationshave become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.Although experts and diplomatshave expressed little hopethat upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

title: ‘Cost of housing’ crunch looms for low-income families, warns Resolution Foundation | UK cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Thinktank calls on chancellor to end housing allowance freeze with typical two-bedroom household facing £158 week shortfall amid rent rises
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Thinktank calls on chancellor to end housing allowance freeze with typical two-bedroom household facing £158 week shortfall amid rent rises
Content: The average shortfall betwen LHA payment and actual rent can be as high as £300 a week in parts of London.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe average shortfall betwen LHA payment and actual rent can be as high as £300 a week in parts of London.Photograph: David Burton/AlamyUK cost of living crisis‘Cost of housing’ crunch looms for low-income families, warns Resolution FoundationThinktank calls on chancellor to end housing allowance freeze with typical two-bedroom household facing £158 week shortfall amid rent risesHeather StewartSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 1.1 million low-income families in rented homes face a “cost of housing” crunch without action from John Healey in next month’s budget, theResolution Foundationthinktank has warned.Local housing allowance (LHA) has been frozen in cash terms since autumn 2024.In a new report, Saving Private Renters, the thinktank found that rising rents since then have led to a widening gap between what families claiming LHA can afford, and the realities of the market.Thinktank calls for ‘double lock’ England private rent cap to ease living costsRead moreIt said a low-income family renting a typical two-bedroom flat now faces an average shortfall of £158 a week. That rises to more than £300 a week in parts of London.The Resolution Foundation rejects the suggestion that relinking LHA with local conditions would mainly benefit private landlords, by driving up rents.By analysing previous changes in LHA, it finds that 90p of every £1 tends to fall to tenants, instead of feeding through into price changes.Resolution Foundation economist Stephen Hunsaker said: “The gap between average rents and Local housing allowance levels is set to reach a record high this October, and failing to repeg LHA to actual rents in next month’s budget could lock in a freeze for another year, and see the gap reach 30% by March 2028.”He added that “with many tenants receiving housing support already going without essentials to pay their rent today, the government should restore the automatic annual linking of LHA to relieve the pressure on low-income families in the private rented sector.”Relinking LHA to rents would cost £2bn a year by the end of this parliament in 2029-30. The Resolution Foundation suggests funding that change by increasing the “taper rate” at which universal credit (UC) is withdrawn as recipients’ income rises.The report argues this would involve a transfer within the UC system, towards claimants with the most need.The thinktank pointed to survey evidence suggesting one in five working-age adults in families on housing support in private rental accommodation were unable to afford to keep their homes warm, and one in eight were unable to afford three meals a day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen LHA was first introduced in 2008 it was pegged to the median level of local rents, and in 2011 that was reduced to the 30th percentile. It has been frozen for nine of the past 14 years.A chorus of charities and campaigners have called for the restoration of the link, including Crisis, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and Citizens Advice.The chancellor will present his budget on 28 October. He is under pressure to fulfil Labour’s promise of giving voters a “breathing space” amid rising costs, but likely to be constrained by rising inflation and interest rates.A government spokesperson said: “Local housing allowance rates are reviewed annually, and future decisions will be taken in the context of the government’s welfare priorities, and the fiscal context.”Explore more on these topicsUK cost of living crisisRenting propertyResolution FoundationHousing benefitBudget 2026Universal creditHousingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement
Content: ‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Andrew Scott in London earlier this month.Photograph: LounisPhotography/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Andrew Scott in London earlier this month.Photograph: LounisPhotography/ABACA/ShutterstockMoviesAnalysis‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?Catherine ShoardThe Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievementSat 19 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.31 EDTShareThis Sunday, the curtain falls on theToronto film festival, the last of the three big autumn showcases – alongsideVeniceandTelluride– that are launchpads for award campaigns. And as the dust settles on the red carpets, one name rises above the others as destined for sure-fire glory: Andrew Scott.The Irish actor, 50 next month, is now not only considered a lock for a leading actor Oscar nomination but almost certain to take the prize next spring. Should he win, he will become the first out gay actor to do so in the Academy’s almost 100-year history.If that’s a fact that seems astonishing today, it would have felt an inevitability in 1989, when the film for which Scott has been so praised is set. InElsinore, he plays Ian Charleson, the dashing Scottish star of films including Chariots of Fire and Gandhi. Charleson had been given his first role three years before Chariots by Derek Jarman, but excised it from his CV (leading to a lifelong rift, depicted in Elsinore). Muting his sexuality was then considered essential in the pursuit of stardom. Yet despite such curation – and his undeniable talents – Charleson never reached the level of fame he felt he deserved.View image in fullscreenOscar buzz … Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony DickensonUntil December 1989, that is, when he took over the role of Hamlet from Daniel Day-Lewis at the National Theatre, despite secretly having Aids. His performance wasreckoned to be one of the finest ever, and he died six weeks after the final show, aged 40. His family then went public with his diagnosis and sexuality: this was the first celebrity death in the UK attributed to Aids, and did much to boost awareness and acceptance.Elsinore review – Andrew Scott is astonishing as Ian Charleson in devastating Aids dramaRead moreThe film is a passion project for Scott, who also produced and rallied together funding alongside Stephen Beresford, screenwriter of Scott’s big-screen breakthrough, 2014’sPride, another real-life story of 1980s gay history, about an unlikely alliance of LGBTQ+ activists and striking Welsh miners. Scott was galvanised to get Elsinore off the ground by the death of his mother, Nora, in 2023. “When you’re in that grief state,” he said, “you feel like you’ve got nothing to lose.”The actor’s own path to stardom makes for a curious contrast with the man he plays. Born in Dublin in 1976, Scott shot his first film aged 17 before studying drama at Trinity College Dublin and moving to London aged 22. Despite playing gay characters, he, too, was advised to remain silent on his own sexuality, to avoid pigeonholing. Speaking after Elsinore’s Toronto premiere last week, Scott said such a climate gave him “a horrible feeling that I perhaps wasn’t going to be able to speak a language I was desperate to speak”.View image in fullscreenAnother real-life story … Scott with Imelda Staunton, Bill Nighy and Dominic West in Pride (2014).Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyHe came out publicly in 2013 aged 37, shortly after his small-screen breakthrough as Moriarty opposite Benedict Cumberbatch’s Sherlock. In the 13 years since, Scott has arguably done more than any man since Ian McKellen to refute the idea that publicly gay actors cannot plausibly play straight roles. His part in Fleabag is the most lusted after example, yet thehot prieststands alongside numerous other heterosexual characters he’s taken on: Richard Rogers inBlue Moon, Anthony Julius inDenial, 10 different people in hisone-man Uncle Vanya. Still in cinemas is his sturdy and scowling Group Captain James Stagg, meteorological hero of D-day and new dramaPressure.“The war is never over,” said Scott of the debate over LGBTQ+ casting in Toronto, “but there have been significant advances in what I believe is stopping the underestimation of audiences. They’re smart and they want to see representation and also transformation.”Andrew Scott is right – it’s time to retire the phrase ‘openly gay’ | Ryan GilbeyRead moreAnd yet alongside his more conventional career choices, the actor has also consistently sought to engage with the pricklier aspects of the debate – railing against the use of the phrase “openly gay” while doing the rounds forAll of Us Strangersin 2023, for instance. His next role, in Leo Reich’s forthcoming sitcom It Gets Worse, pushes the envelope further.A teaserappears to shows him as a toxic therapist who instructs his much younger client that he’s “just a hole for daddy” before spitting into his mouth.View image in fullscreenA devastating performance … Paul Mescal with Scott in All of Us Strangers (2023).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyFor Guy Lodge, chief critic of Variety, Scott is “essentially carving an unprecedented career path for an out gay leading man in the industry. One where he isn’t pigeonholed into queer roles, but where he doesn’t have to avoid them either, in order to prove his mainstream viability.”While some of his highest-profile roles have been gay or queer men – Pride, All of Us Strangers, the Netflix seriesRipleyand now Elsinore – Lodge points to the lack of other commonalities between these parts. “In defiance of the restrictions and stereotypes that would, not all that long ago, have limited his options, Scott is showing us that there are many ways to embody queerness on screen.”And it is this forward-thinking integrity that has come to mark the actor’s persona. His gentle, uncompromising candour – paired with an elegant discretion about his private life – has meant he is held in high regard and affection both by the public and his collaborators.“I love him,” says Johnny Flynn, who plays the director Richard Eyre in Elsinore, and previously starred opposite Scott in Ripley. “He’s a dear friend and I think he deserves everything for Elsinore. He always puts his whole soul into whatever he does but this was something else. Watching him channel and hold Ian Charleson was such a privilege.”View image in fullscreen‘He puts his whole soul into whatever he does’ … Scott with Ethan Hawke in Blue Moon (2025).Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/APScott, Flynn adds, is “one of our greatest actors. He’s got such a unique quality – a beauty in the deftness of his thinking; darkness and humour and power with heartbreaking fragility. He is such a gorgeous human being – so quick to laugh and wicked fun.”This sort of write-up is seemingly echoed by everyone who works with him. “He is an actor of incredible emotional insight,” says Simon Stephens, who scripted Scott’s one-man Vanya. “His linguistic and physical nuance are balletic. He thinks with relentless curiosity and he works with equal amounts of ferocious energy and care.” Stephens knew he had found a new favourite actor back in 2000, “since I saw him in Conor McPherson’s Dublin Carol. I’m glad I was 26 years ahead of the curve.”In fact, given Scott’s pedigree, his awards run so far has been surprisingly patchy. He won Oliviers for A Girl in a Car With a Man andPresent Laughter, and a TV Bafta for Sherlock, but nothing major for Fleabag – and, at the 2020 Sag awards, shortly after losing, he had to crawl from the auditorium in agonyafter passing a kidney stone mid-ceremony.View image in fullscreen‘I was 26 years ahead of the curve’ …  Scott with Brian Cox in Dublin Carol at the Royal Court in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianFurther indignity came in 2024, when his devastating performance in All of Us Strangers was snubbed at nomination stage at the Baftas (unlike those of his castmates Claire Foy and Paul Mescal). The movie, considered by many to be one of that year’s finest, then failed to score a single Oscar nod – a slight which may end up working in Scott’s favour, as his name will now be synonymous to voters with embarrassment as well as excellence.It may also be worth considering that actors make up the largest branch of the Academy’s votership – and they may respond especially favourably to Elsinore’s celebration of the profession’s inclusivity, courage and camaraderie.The film positions Charleson’s achievement – not unfairly – as a vital fightback against the final curtain that is common to us all, whether or not we tread the boards. “I’d rather die of Hamlet than of Aids,” the character tells his doctor (Olivia Colman), trying to persuade her to help him build up the stamina needed to take on theatre’s most challenging role (1,500 lines, four hours, swordfight in hour three).And in promoting the film so far, Scott has sought to highlight the universal bravery of Charleson’s actions, as well as the sports movie-style achievement of someone weeks from death exhibiting such commitment and athleticism. Those around the actor have, meanwhile, emphasised the sheer graft involved in pulling off a performance of the stature of Hamlet, or Charleson, or both.View image in fullscreen‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus FeaturesAndrew Haigh, who directed him in All of Us Strangers, calls Scott’s turn “simply astonishing. I struggle to think of a better performance. Andrew embodies the character so completely it feels as if we are watching lived experience. But make no mistake, this is a performance of incredible skill. Andrew is completely fearless in the role.”Likewise, Elsinore director Simon Stone says that “every time I rewatch the film I can’t see Andrew – it’s just Ian. The way he surrenders to the character, to the world, the situation, is beyond compare. Sure, it’s also an effortlessly brilliant performance in terms of technique. But what is most astonishing is how he matches this technique with raw truth.“Where other actors may perform an emotion or a state, Andrew presents us with a character surprised by what he is going through. That shock helps the audience be surprised and heartbroken with him and we can feel empathy in the truest sense.”The Academy has spent 98 years giving out leading performance Oscars to gay actors who never or only later publicly spoke their whole truth, as well as to a parade of straight stars for playing LGBTQ+ characters. Their failure to recognise Scott’s remarkable achievements, both professional and personal, seems unlikely.Explore more on these topicsFilmAndrew ScottanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’
Content: Jonathan Franzen.Photograph: Cayce Clifford/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJonathan Franzen.Photograph: Cayce Clifford/The GuardianBooksInterviewJonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’Sophie McBainThe author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen HBO dropped its plan to adapt Jonathan Franzen’s bestselling novel The Corrections in 2012, the author was so relieved he says he performed his first and last cartwheel on the lawn of his home in Santa Cruz, California. There had been an attempted film adaptation before that, but he had been unsurprised by its failure, having warned that it was impossible to condense his densely plotted doorstopper of a novel into a feature-length film. This time, Franzen had signed up as co-writer, with filmmaker Noah Baumbach. He says that HBO was “excluded from the development process. Mistake, because we didn’t know how to do TV.” Franzen himself hadn’t even owned a telly until a few years earlier and certainly didn’t have cable, so as he was wrestling with the script, he began renting box sets. Around three episodes into one drama series, he realised “we have no idea what we’re doing. This is not how you do TV. This is bad,” he recalls. The result, he says, was “one of the worst pilots anyone has ever made”.Franzen used to think TV was the “enemy” of the serious novelist. In a well-known 1996 essay for Harper’s Magazine about the decline of high literature he had complained bitterly about the “banal ascendancy of television”. But after the HBO series failed, he watched Breaking Bad, Nurse Jackie and Silicon Valley and loved them. In the age of social media, AI and the endless scroll, TV has started to look like a “friend”, he says now. And The Corrections is finally being adapted into an eight-part Netflix series, with Meryl Streep playing Enid Lambert, the matriarch clinging to dreams of hosting a perfect last family Christmas, even as her husband Alfred is in terminal decline with Parkinson’s and dementia and their grownup children’s lives are falling apart in terrible, comical ways. Once Streep announced she was in, Franzen felt the “chances of making this show have gone up above 50%”. He says he’s a month away from finishing the script.We are meeting at his home on the edge of Santa Cruz, in his office where the blinds are pulled down low against the bright sunshine. He is 67, tall and slightly stooped, and although his hair has turned white he still looks boyish when he laughs, wide smile and little snub nose, a wicked glint behind his trademark dark-framed spectacles. He has settled into a chair that seems too small for his lanky frame and frequently squirms with discomfort. Should we try switching places, I ask at one point? “No, I’m just physically expressing discomfort with repeating myself,” he replies. He likes to edit his speech as he goes along: “strike that word!” he orders at one point, and “this needs to be underlined”. When he loses his thread he announces, grandly, “you can redirect”.View image in fullscreenMaggie Gyllenhaal and Ewan McGregor on HBO pilot of The Corrections.Photograph: Bang Media International/AlamyThe Corrections, Franzen’s third novel, won the 2001 National book award for fiction in the US, and remains one of the bestselling works of literary fiction of recent decades. It was published a few days before 9/11 and distils the materialism, anxieties and complacency of America’s long 20th century. It is also Franzen’s most “autobiographical novel”, drawn loosely from his own midwestern upbringing: Franzen was raised in an affluent suburb of St Louis, Missouri. Like Alfred, his dad, who was an engineer, developed Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, while Enid is a “cartoon version” of his own mother. “There are not very many incidents from my life in the book but those two: the personalities and the self-deception about the gravity of the mental deterioration – that’s all drawn from my own experience,” he says.Franzen says he learned his “psychology as a novelist” from his family. His parents were “powerful characters”: they were “hilarious” and “terrifying” and also “thoughtful”, with rich interior lives. “They created not only Enid and Alfred, but really the notion of a character … the combination of intellectual substance, emotional wanting, emotional needs and comedy,” he explains. His father died before The Corrections was published. His mother lived long enough to know that an extract had appeared in the New Yorker, as part of a special issue dedicated to American writers under 40.“My annoying aunt, her sister, called her up and said: ‘Irene: do not read Jon’s piece in the New Yorker,’” Franzen recalls. His mother was ill with cancer and had been given months to live. He visited her a few days after that phone call, when inevitably her question was “Why shouldn’t I read your piece in the New Yorker?”. He summarised the story for her, “making some small omissions, but basically just describing what the thing was”. When he was finished, she said: “Thank you, I don’t need to read it.” It was one of their last long conversations. She died 10 days later. “My parents gave us kids everything – including a lot of criticism. But then they just exited, and I was still in my 30s and could write whatever I want,” he says. He could not have published The Corrections had they been alive. Most of his subsequent novels – includingCrossroadsandFreedom, two other big, ideas-filled books – have also centred on dysfunctional midwestern families. “It always puzzles me that people find it remarkable that I have characters who are related through family in my books,” he says, sounding a bit put out. “Because it’s like, well, the Bible is a book of family stories. The Old Testament, it’s all family stories. The Greek myths, Homer …”Franzen initially studied science at university: “That was a bit of a beard to get my parents to pay for college,” he says. They were not happy when he switched majors, “but at least I did something serious like German literature as opposed to a frivolous English major, which they literally would not have paid for.” After graduating from Swarthmore, a liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, in 1981, he won a year-long Fulbright scholarship at the Freie Universität in Berlin. His first novel, The Twenty-Seventh City, was published six years later, in 1988. He has worked full-time as a writer ever since. “I made nothing but mistakes as a young person but actually was lucky enough to realise, this is what you’re good at,” he says.Franzen describes The Corrections as an “angry comedy” and he has a reputation for being, well, an angry guy. Where does his anger come from, I wonder? “It’s still mysterious to me, having so many privileges – not really economic privilege, but every other imaginable kind of privilege – that I was angry for so long. There’s 14 years of being in a marriage that should have ended after two years. That explains a lot, actually,” he says. He married a fellow writer, Valerie Cornell, soon after graduating, and they divorced in 1994. “Then there’s you know, I’m a bright guy, and the stupidity of the world makes me angry.” Oh, and in the 90s, he spent a lot of time “angry that people were seen to be losing interest in the kind of novels that I wrote”. But, he adds, “I don’t know why people think of me as angry now, because I haven’t really been angry in that way since a year after The Corrections was published.”That first year, he concedes with a wry smile, was a little “bumpy”. Many will remember his spat with Oprah Winfrey, who picked The Corrections for her book club and invited him on to her show, only to rescind her invitation after he described her other picks as “schmaltzy”. The pair later made up – she picked Freedom for her book club in 2010, and they hugged on live TV. One of his problems, he points out, is that he cannot “start a thought without injecting a counterthought to it”. Read only half the quote and he comes across like an “asshole”. While criticising her picks, he also praised Oprah for promoting reading, for instance. He can see now that she was right to be annoyed. But, counterthought: “Well, some of her earlier picks were …” theatrical pause “… schmaltzy.”Other spats have followed, with the writerJennifer Weinerover the disproportionate attention given to Franzen’s work. Thought: Weiner is “freeloading” on the gender debate and “asking for a respect that not just male reviewers, but female reviewers, don’t think her work merits”. Counterthought: the gender bias in literature is a genuine problem. He got into trouble for saying he consideredadopting an Iraqi orphanto better understand young people. Counterthought: that mad idea lasted six weeks at the most. Franzen says he has learned to become more circumspect. “I didn’t know what I was doing. I didn’t know how to talk to people in an interview. I didn’t know how to do TV. I would just say whatever I was thinking about and then I would get into trouble and I would feel like: ‘Oh, unfair! I’m getting into trouble.’ Well, you know, dude, wise up, learn how to protect yourself. Don’t say those things.”In 2010, following the publication of Freedom, Franzen appeared on the cover of Time magazine, a rare achievement for any writer. The piece described him as the “Great American Novelist”. He says it was his suggestion that he should be the cover. He got his publicist to contact Time to say they hadn’t had a writer as a cover star for ages, and Franzen would be great. Wait, what, I ask, shuffling through my notes, doesn’t that piece describe you as “singularly ungifted at what you might call brand management”? “Isn’t that hilarious?” he asks, his eyes widening in delight. “It’s hilarious!”He doesn’t think much of the phrase “great American novel”, though. “It’s usually not said kindly. It’s sort of mocking,” he says. He puts on a bullying sneer: “Oh, the great American novelist. Oh, you’re going to write the great American novel, are you?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation mark‘People don’t read Steinbeck any more? It’s sad, but nothing lasts for ever’Franzen is not as down on the future of the literary novel as he used to be. That Harper’s essay? His real complaint at the time was “people weren’t buying books like mine”, he says, pretending to sob. “Actually, they were. They were just not buying my novels. That was my complaint in the 90s, and of course I blew that up into some huge cultural problem.” These days, he thinks those who bemoan the decline of reading need some perspective. “I think the doom-criers about the novel tend to make a fundamental mistake. They imagine some golden age when everyone read Flaubert. There was never a time,” he says. It’s true, he continues, that modern technology does little to help cultivate a love of reading. “It’s easy to imagine a time soon when there is no reason to be able to read, because text can be converted into spoken language and you don’t have to write because you just speak and it can be written for you,” he says. But that hardly feels like the worst thing happening in the world right now. “That’s the other thing I feel about the doom-criers of the novel, it’s like, really, this is a world historical problem? People can’t read Steinbeck any more? It’s sad, but nothing lasts for ever. What do you want?”Franzen says he doesn’t want to comment on American politics because “nobody cares what the novelist thinks”, plus he did an interview with the German newspaper Die Welt before Donald Trump’s second term in which, like many pundits, he predicted that the president wouldn’t follow through on most of his promises and “it’s like no, I was all wrong”. He was, however, on to Trump early. He wrote about the future president in his 1992 novel, Strong Motion, and in various essays that decade. “He symbolised a certain kind of horribleness, a crass, narcissistic, bullying side of American life that, yeah, I noticed early and I hated. I didn’t even live in New York when I wrote Strong Motion and I could feel that odious presence,” he says.He’s more open to weighing in on environmental issues, having written several feather-ruffling essays for the New Yorker on the climate crisis. He angered climate crisis activists by arguing that humankind needs to accept that global warming is going to happen and start refocusing on local projects devoted to conservation and biodiversity. A passionate birder himself, in 2015 hecriticised the bird conservation organisation Audubonfor falsely claiming that climate change is the main threat faced by birds, rather than collisions with glass windows and hunting by cats, two more fixable problems. Audubon responded by accusing him of “extreme intellectual dishonesty”. “They’ve apologised,” he says when I ask him about it, “full stop.”Franzen discovered his passion for birds soon after The Corrections was published. He goes on birding trips whenever he can, but he can also spot a lot from his home: there are violet-green swallows nesting next door, and hooded orioles in the back garden. If it wasn’t so hot, and his blinds weren’t drawn so low, we’d probably see a family of quail running past his office window. “If you want to see quail, this is one of the best places in the world,” he says.He shares his home with his longtime partner, the writer Kathryn Chetkovich. In a corner of his office there is an electric guitar. He picked up the guitar while working on Freedom, and has this morning been practising with the band, Shady Characters, which he formed with Chetkovich’s brothers. It’s a purely private hobby. “I have never performed in public, and I never will,” he announces.Last June, Franzen published a new story in the New Yorker about an aspiring teenage actor suffering an unwanted pregnancy and a crisis of faith. It will form part of his next novel, a sequel to Crossroads, which was published in 2021 as the first book in a proposed trilogy. Does that mean his next book is imminent? “This is not, ‘I’ve delivered the manuscript and we’re getting a little teaser.’ No, this is a ‘I’ve gone deep into the cave and I need to send a sign of life,’” he says. It takes Franzen many years to write a novel, and the years before he has settled on a new project are often “horrible”, he says. He tries to distract himself, often by writing nonfiction, and then “I periodically go back and beat my head against the proverbial brick wall”. “It’s not fun,” he confirms: “Some other day, another idea. Yeah, that one didn’t work either. Wake up in the middle of the night. Yeah, I got it. No, you don’t.”Franzen believes the most difficult part of writing a new novel is that it requires him to change: he needs to become “the kind of person who can write the novel. I’ve had to become a different person in some significant way to get each book written.” To move from The Corrections to Freedom he had to let go of his anger. To write Crossroads, he had to become more forgiving. Right now, he says, “I’m waiting to wake up as the person who is alive again and not the same person he was five years ago.”Does this mean he sees writing as a means of self-improvement? God, no! When he’s working on a scene, trying to capture a character or get the tone right, he’s not thinking in moral terms. “If you’re really engaged with that, it’s not a matter of morality, but a matter of getting at something true. So I prefer truth as a goal to morality, to self-improvement, to the betterment of one’s soul,” he says. “I don’t really care about bettering my soul. I care about getting it right,” he adds. And then, the reflexive edit: “Which is a pretty good ending line.”A 25th anniversary edition of The Corrections is published by 4th Estate.Explore more on these topicsBooksJonathan FranzenFictioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #261: There is so much good telly this autumn you may never go outside again | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like me
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like me
Content: Knowingly trashy and super smart … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreenKnowingly trashy and super smart … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #261: There is so much good telly this autumn you may never go outside againIn this week’s newsletter:From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like meStuart HeritageSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor those of us who like to stay indoors, it has been a bad summer. The World Cup ate up all traditional television scheduling, and the streamers apparently declined to counterprogramme. The Bear came and went before anybody noticed, and House of the Dragon conclusively disappeared up its own bottom.If you’re anything like me then you clung to the good stuff (basicallyDisney’s Furiousand nothing else) like a life raft, eking out new episodes like someone in a desert sucking condensation off the underside of a tarpaulin. But forget summer. It is now autumn, and television is back. In fact, I can’t remember a time when television has come roaring back with quite the same ferocity as it has this month.Everywhere you turn there is something new and unmissable. And I suspect you haven’t even seen your favourite TV show of the year yet.For me, the big one is Sky and HBO’s new divorce dramaWar(main pic). Watching it feels like scratching an itch I didn’t know I had. About the messy divorce between a fading Hollywood star (played by Sienna Miller) and a tech billionaire (played by Dominic West), and the warring lawyers who represent them, it sits precisely at the midpoint between Rivals and Succession – knowingly trashy, but also hugely smart. It’s so unbelievably propulsive, every episode ends with a whopper of a cliffhanger scientifically engineered to give you whiplash. And on top of that, Pip Torrens gets to play the haughtiest lawyer in all of recorded media. It is an absolute joy of a thing.But also –Slow Horsesis back! And that performs a little miracle of its own, too. The show is so long in the tooth that you would probably expect a significant drop off in quality. And yet its new run (its sixth) may very well be its strongest yet (despite theless than enthusiastic viewsof my colleague Jack Seale). Its plot has been slimmed down to its barest essentials – the whole thing is basically just a chase – and it is far more muscular as a result. Everyone is brilliant in it. The writing still sparkles, despite the departure of show-runner Will Smith. There’s a chance that there might not be much more of it to come, especially if Jack Lowdenends up becoming James Bond, so we really need to relish it while we can.View image in fullscreenAn ensemble coming into its own … Domhnall Gleeson, Chelsea Frei, Melvin Gregg and Eric Rahill in The Paper.Photograph: Peacock/SkyEven the remakes and spin-offs are unnecessarily good. I found myself watching the second season ofThe Paper– Greg Daniels’ cousin to The Office – with a mixture of ticklishness and irritation. Ticklishness because it’s warm and funny, and has an ensemble cast (pictured above) that has really started coming into its own; and irritation because it’s only 10 episodes long. The show has the potential to be one of those all-timers, like Friends or Cheers, that you can stick on years from now as you go about your business because you’re so familiar with – and fond of – the characters. At this rate, though, it’ll take 20 years to build up enough episodes to let that happen. There is a possibility that I’m just being greedy, but it’s only because I like it so much.And in the remake department,Reckless(ITVX here, SBS in Australia) is a spin on Neil Forsyth’s impeccable Guilt, that manages to retain all the tension and momentum of that show while adding layers of interesting new dimensions.But there are so many other things to look forward to. Rivals is back soon. So is The Celebrity Traitors. Sharon Horgan has a new show, in the form of Youth. Apple’s Brothers, about Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, looks incredibly diverting. Even if it ends up being bad, Amazon’s Blade Runner 2099 series should be absolutely fascinating. And, if you’re my dad, then the new Reacher spinoff Neagley is essentially the moment your entire life has been leading up to.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have barely scratched the surface here, which is slightly terrifying. For the first time in ages, there might be more good television than spare hours in the day. What an unusual feeling that is.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Youth: Sharon Horgan’s comedy about dating at 50 is utterly hilarious  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painful
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: The perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painful
Content: Adulting … Sharon Horgan and Aran Murphy in Youth.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenAdulting … Sharon Horgan and Aran Murphy in Youth.Photograph: HBOThe watcherTelevision & radioYouth: Sharon Horgan’s comedy about dating at 50 is utterly hilariousThe perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painfulRhik SamadderSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgeing has changed, hasn’t it? There’s a generation of middle-aged and perimenopausal elder millennials and xennials who refuse to do it. We’re young enough to be part of an online world that puts a premium on appearance, too old for such narcissistic self-branding to be achieved without unsustainable effort. Dating apps and social media connect people across generations, so it’s easy to become confused about how old we actually are. Here’s a tip: ask your knees.This brings us to Youth (from Monday 21 September, HBO Max),Sharon Horgan’s dramedy about being 50. That perky title is a quip about the decade being known as “the youth of old age”. Horgan is Alex, a divorcee in her sandwich years, caring for teenage son Ruarí and ageing parents. There’s a lot going on in her life, and some doom. She’s falling forwards in a semi-successful career as a literary agent, getting back into dating under pressure. She needs someone to fall in love with her immediately, as she points out to her best friend. Not for romantic myth-making, but “so there’s a bit of time with the present version of me, before the ‘old me’ is here”.I’ve made it sound not funny; it’s very funny. The world of publishing is ripe for satire, and the show wields more skewers than a kebab shop. On the walls of Alex’s office are posters for prestige titles: Life After Death – A Memoir of Guilt, Babyfingers and Where the Daylight Falls. I’ve seen all of them on the Richard and Judy Book Club. And then there’s Goblin Seed.Goblin Seed is a ludicrous romantasy in the Twilight or Fifty Shades of Grey mould. (I think that title is a pun, too.) It’s written by one of Alex’s former authors, a smug creep who self-published after rejection, and has since enjoyed runaway success with his horny, badly written prose (“The goblin seed was gold, and soon the sheets were glittering”). Tasked with wooing him back, every interaction has Alex looking as if she wants to throw up in her mouth.Youth fires shots across the creative arts. Ruarí’s dad, Lorcan, is an actor. Not quite absent, but so self-involved he’s not so much phoning it in as texting. He’s about to move to Canada to film a lucrative “spaceship show”, and has re-recorded his answer-machine message in its alien language, while feeling above the project. He’s also dating the young landlady he met when he moved out of Alex’s. Oh God, the humanities.‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedyRead moreThankfully, Ruarí has a number of unsuitable father figures to choose from. There’s Alex’s ex, Patrick, a handsome and “institutionally single” 47-year-old who specialises in sending mixed messages. There’s older love interest Michael, played with generous sensitivity byTim McInnerny. He’s stable, kind, attentive. But Alex can’t stop staring at his loose chin, and ducks his kisses like Neo dodges bullets.Sex scenes in Youth are the antithesis of Hollywood gloss, hilarious and penetratingly insightful. “I don’t know you well enough to be selfish in bed,” Alex confesses to one lover. How has the gap between sex and intimacy widened in her lifetime? It’s easy to kid yourself about this at 25, twice as hard at 50.Horgan’s gift is vérité. The friend groups and workplaces are diverse in a way that’s London-real, rather than box-ticking from above. Youth is mordantly funny, yet never betrays character. As you’d expect from the creator of Motherland, it’s superb on mum stuff. Alex often mutters the word “dick” to herself when Ruarí is being particularly teenage, yet their love is clear. He’s played byAran Murphy,son of Cillian, who delivers a beautifully unforced performance. At points I felt as if I were watching Boyhood.Then there’s the parental subplot, which could carry a series alone. A million miles from saccharine depictions of elderly people, Youth shows the uninspiring, Sisyphean grind of care-giving, which is mostly navigating confused, false-crisis phone calls, sibling resentment and travelling 25 miles to demonstrate the position of the volume button on an iPad. However much we deny our age, life has its own plans. Thank God for Sharon Horgan: chronicler of all our journeys, like a foul-mouthed, funnier 7 Up. This painfully relatable, brilliant show made me feel a bit tired at times. Then again, I’m always tired.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe watcherTelevisionSharon HorganDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a new era of Strictly begins in typically sparkling style | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Johannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis prepare their takeover.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAView image in fullscreenJohannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis prepare their takeover.Photograph: Guy Levy/PATV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a new era of Strictly begins in typically sparkling styleEmma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 19 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStrictly Come Dancing7.25pm, BBC OneIt’s time for the new Strictly era to begin, with Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe ebulliently taking over (sparkling) hosting duties. EastEnders stalwart Lacey Turner, footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips, Aussie singer Delta Goodrem, Gavin and Stacey’s Melanie Walters and previous dropout Dani Dyer are some of the 15 celebrities meeting their dance partners in this curtain-raiser. Alongside them, as is now customary in celebrity-based reality TV competitions, there’ll be some “media personalities” you’ll probably need to Google. But it’s not all change: the usual four judges are back with their scoring paddles. All that’s left to do is get ready to rumba!Hollie RichardsonWisdom of the Crowd9.15pm, BBC OneFrancis Galton’s groundbreaking century-old statistics theory is the inspiration behind this new gameshow. (No mention here of him also being widely considered the originator of eugenics though …) John Bishop puts contestants against the audience to ask: is the crowd better than the individual? Anyone who beats the theory could win £30k.HRThe Voice UK6.10pm, ITV1It’s a double Willis weekender, as she returns to host this next round of the singing competition. So far, Kelly Rowland has been left in tears after Aaren James’s emotional performance of How Do I Say Goodbye, while Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones used the show’s first Rewind button to bring back Phantom of the Opera singer Finlay McKillop. Who’s next?HRParis Police 19109pm, BBC FourIt’s the third season of this stylish fact-based French period drama, and the past of courtesan turned informant Meg Steinheil (the charismatic Evelyne Brochu) has caught up with her. However, even as she processes the loss of her husband, her statement isn’t adding up. Meanwhile, Dreyfus has returned, bringing trouble.Phil HarrisonDolly Parton Night9.15pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenDolly Parton wows Worthy Farm in 2014.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAAn evening-long celebration of the country-pop goddess. First, her 2014 Glastonbury triumph. Then, a documentary in which KT Tunstall explores the parallel careers of Parton, Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris. Finally, Dolly’s appearances on the BBC.PHSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneLive from London, the homegrown SNL offshoot roared back last week, with a brand new Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) and a seamless debut from Freddie Meredith. This week sees Stath Lets Flats mastermind Jamie Demetriou on hosting duty, with music from rock duo Royal Blood.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceHamlet (Aneil Karia, 2025), 10.05am, 6pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenRiz Ahmed and Timothy Spall Ham it up.Photograph: NBCUniversal/2026 NBCUniversal All Rights ReservedThere is little Riz Ahmed can’t turn his hand to, so it’s no surprise that he gives a bravura performance as Shakespeare’s tragic hero in Aneil Karia’s modern-day adaptation. The royal Danes are now a wealthy British Hindu family of property developers, but the film retains the Bard’s language while cutting down the text to focus exclusively on Hamlet’s trauma. It’s a bold move that largely pays off, as we follow the heir to the firm as he descends into angst, rage and revenge after discovering his uncle Claudius (Art Malik) murdered his father.Simon WardellLive sportGolf: PGA Championship, 9am, Sky Sports GolfDay three from Wentworth.Premier League Football Tottenham v Aston Villa, 11am, TNT Sports 1Nottingham Forest v Coventry is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Championship Football: Millwall v West Ham, noon, ITV1A local derby from the Den.T20 International Cricket England v Sri Lanka, 2pm, Channel 5The third match, from Old Trafford.Super League Rugby, 5.15pm, BBC TwoWarrington Wolves v Hull KR in the second elimination play-off.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content
