title: John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’ | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete
Content: John Wilson in The History of Concrete.Photograph: Photo courtesy of Magnolia PicturesView image in fullscreenJohn Wilson in The History of Concrete.Photograph: Photo courtesy of Magnolia PicturesDocumentary filmsInterviewJohn Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’Adrian HortonThe creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concreteSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has frequently demonstrated impressive media savvy, but arguably nothing has proved his genius for in-the-know promo more than avideo, released in April, with the documentarianJohn Wilson.The History of Concrete review – John Wilson’s first movie is an absurd triumphRead moreThe spot, in support of the mayor’s plan to reduce the presence of the city’s ubiquitous sidewalk sheds, suggested that either he or someone on his team was a fan of How To With John Wilson, the film-maker’s cult-beloved HBO series that remains a taste signifier for alt-humorous New Yorkers. And for good reason: over three near-perfect seasons, Wilson, armed with his ever-present camera and diffident, memoiristic narration, explored the city’s disintegrating streets with a singular eye for the weird and unintentionally hilarious, turning the most mundane of NYC preoccupations – public restrooms, parking spots, scaffolding – into profound meditations on the glories, indignities and absurdities of modern life.It was because of that scaffolding episode, released in October 2020, that I, like some smart Mamdani staffers, began to perceive the sidewalk shed shadowing my block not as an inevitable fixed entity but an obtrusive, if well-intentioned, symptom of neglect. Shortly after the mayor’s video, said scaffolding miraculously came down – revealing, to my shock, a three square-wide swath of concrete that had not seen the sun in six years.When I credit Wilson for this upgrade, in person at a film office in Manhattan, he reacts with a modest “I’ll take it,” as dry as the dusty footprints of the recently departed metal poles. Fitting, for though that newly revealed concrete, speckled with old gum and anonymous residue, is certainly better, if not exactly beautiful, perhaps only Wilson could see it as cinematic. His debut feature film,The History of Concrete, takes on the granddaddy of all urban materials, tugging wry insights on our terminal human condition out of the crumbling facades of New York’s most pervasive substance.Concrete is many things: a mixture of cement, water, sand and crushed stone; arguably ancient Rome’s greatest invention; the second-most used substance on earth, behind water; the foundation of buildings and bridges and “everything I’ve done before” Wilson says, a “Marvel supervillain origin story” to How To’s many bricolages of unfortunately named streets (“Titman Road”) and sidewalk characters. But it is not what one might call a marketable idea. The general response on pitch calls was crickets – “an absolute emotional flatline,” Wilson tells me during a break from signing film posters featuring a single giant cinderblock.It didn’t help that Wilson, languishing in a post-How To malaise and without the structure of an HBO contract nor writer’s room, didn’t have much of an idea what it would be about, beyond realizing, through a poor DIY attempt to fix the cracked foundation of his Queens apartment, how strange it is to know so little about the dominant element of your visual environment. Wilson initially tried pitching it as an environmental doc, a new riff on the enshittification of American infrastructure. The response was, roughly, “I don’t want to think about this,” he laughs. “And it’s hard to say that I don’t want to make that movie I just told you about either. I want to try, and then experiment and get lost along the way as I usually do.” A strike-era Writer’s Guild of America workshop on how to make a Hallmark movie offered salient advice – “trauma is FINE, if it ends on a high note” – and a pressing question: if Hallmark could make movies about property developers, why not concrete?View image in fullscreenJohn Wilson at the New York Premiere of The History of Concrete.Photograph: Dave Allocca/Starpix/ShutterstockSo goes the 100-minute film, which plays like an extended episode of How To and, in true Wilson fashion, is as much about the difficulty of figuring out your next thing, let alone making and selling it, as it is about the composite material (though he does visit one science lab and, naturally, a corporate meet-up for “the women of concrete”). The film finds Wilson in a strange place after the high of How To’s 2023 – directionless, anxious, famous enough to be the $2,000 Jeopardy question no one gets but not to secure financing for his dream of a feature-length documentary.“I was having a lot of strange thoughts, crazy problems with self-esteem, especially when nobody wanted to take a chance with something like this, at least at first,” he recalls in the same halting, nasally speech of both his How To narration and, as seen in the film, someone’s AI-generated ad to sell gutters on TikTok (“I would’ve done it for free, if they asked,” he deadpans). The pressure to follow but not repeat the show was creatively dead-ending. “There was a lot of frustration when I started to pitch this idea because everyone seemed to want something different than How To, and that just felt like an arbitrary requirement to me,” he explains. The show’s digressive style “wasn’t a shtick. This is how I think. I just think this is the right way to do things. I like essay films, I like shooting things from my perspective.”Resistant to do something different for difference’s sake and in the absence of financing, Wilson went back to basics: pick up camera, leave house. “I just started to do things the way that I always did, and that was the most fluid way to get myself out of the house and, like, have anything to do and work on, because I was depressed,” he recalls. “For some reason, I need to keep reminding myself of the same basic idea, that you should not wait for anyone else to make the thing that you want. You just need to do it.”“I was just caught in this trap again, of thinking that I needed permission,” he continues, eyes grazing the cinderblock poster. So I just went out to try to make it, and then I decided to incorporate all of these voices that were trying to get me to change and do whatever the market would reward.”View image in fullscreenA still from The History of Concrete.Photograph: John WilsonSaid advice includes: make it sexy (he attends a brick-laying competition, where the winner receives a very sleek blue truck); make it a rock-umentary (he meets and follows an aging rocker at a liquor store); make it topical (expert testimony will leave you wary of driving under the crumbling Brooklyn Queens Expressway); make it celeb-adjacent (Wilson is among the few documentarians less comfortable in a room with Kim Kardashian than with a man preserving tattooed human skin). As with any Wilson project, the narrative wanders far away from the initial premise; Wilson wanders from Rome to the Sri Chinmoy Self-Transcendence race in which runners loop around a single block in Queens for a month, from an Ohio driver’s ed class to the set of Marty Supreme (whose director, Josh Safdie, served as an executive producer of Wilson’s doc).All become avenues for Wilson’s sly explorations of far less solid material, from the struggle to find motivation to cyclical self-doubt, our desire to at once move forward and make something last. “I’m thankful for the resistance that I got, because the very thing that you are resisting, or that’s resisting you, ends up becoming the skeletal system or the spine of your work in certain ways, if you let it,” he says, slipping into the show and film’s standard second-person voice.Such challenges could cause you to give up, to quit the project of your dreams for something else, to abandon the sly attempts to convince people to pay more attention to the ever weirder world around them. “There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way,” he tells me, reflecting on the uphill climb to a concrete movie. “But it’s the kind of imagery that I want to see, because I don’t see it anywhere else.”The History of Concrete is out in select US cinemas now and will premiere at the London film festival next month with an Australian release planned for 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsComedy filmsComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Deep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraud | Vinyl | The Guardian
description: Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings
Author: John Harris
Headline: Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings
Content: The lucrative trade in vintage and new vinyl LPs online has spawned a shadow market of bootleggers trying to cash in.Photograph: MarekUsz/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe lucrative trade in vintage and new vinyl LPs online has spawned a shadow market of bootleggers trying to cash in.Photograph: MarekUsz/Getty Images/iStockphotoVinylDeep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraudThousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stingsJohn HarrisSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom 2017 onwards, Rehan Ahmed styled himself as a savvy business owner. But behind the facade of a successful entrepreneur lurked one stark fact: his empire was built on fakery.On Friday, the man behind the biggest-ever UK case of producing fraudulent vinyl, who sold counterfeit copies of records by some of the world’s biggest artists including Taylor Swift, Coldplay andKendrick Lamar, was jailed.Ahmed, a 40-year-old father of three from Southall, westLondon, pleaded guilty to two charges of breach of artists’ copyright, and acquiring and using criminal property. On the first count, Judge Darren Reed sentenced him to two years and eight months in prison, while the more serious second charge led to a custodial penalty of three and a half years. The sentences will be served concurrently, meaning that the second will dictate the time Ahmed spends in prison.In a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Friday, the judge highlighted the “sophisticated and planned nature of the enterprise”, and the fact that Ahmed had caused “wider harm to the music industry”.Operating under the company names Phoenix ofVinyland Paragon Music, Ahmed produced counterfeit vinyl albums that he supplied to record shops or sold directly to consumers through online platforms such as Discogs and eBay. In 2025, eBay removed about 7.9m potentially counterfeit or prohibited items from the platform.A spokesperson said: “Counterfeits are strictly prohibited on eBay. Where listings violate eBay policies, we act swiftly to remove them and may take action against the seller’s account.” Discogs did not respond to a request for comment.Phoenix of Vinyl was no minor operation. When police raided Ahmed’s factory, they found 15,000 records. His previous business endeavours, around which there is no suggestion of criminality, had focused on takeaway food and bodybuilding supplements. But the booming vinyl industry appears to have lured him into the illicit market.3:04Police uncover warehouse involved in the biggest counterfeit vinyl records business – videoIn 2025, UK vinyl sales increased by 13.3% to 7.6m units, maintaining 18 years of constant growth. Led by Swift’s 2025 release of The Life of a Showgirl, the total retail value of vinyl in the US that yearreached over $1bn for the first time in four decades.Rising prices of records inevitably followed this increased demand: some high-profile albums, particularly in “limited edition” versions, are now regularly priced at about £40.View image in fullscreenIllicitly produced vinyl at Ahmed’s factory including albums by Kanye West and De La Soul.Photograph: BPIWhile “bootlegs” of rare and unreleased material have long been part of the music landscape – originally on vinyl and now largely eclipsed by the internet – Ahmed was part of a growing underground industry making counterfeit copies of officially released albums. Over the last two years, the music business umbrella organisation the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) says it has been involved in the execution of 43 search warrants centred on illegal counterfeit vinyl and CDs, and seized about 600,000 items estimated to have a street value of up to £8m.View image in fullscreenPolice officers inspecting piles of counterfeit vinyl.Photograph: BPIThe fakes can be easily spotted when it comes to particular artists. The American star Frank Ocean, for example, digitally released his Grammy-winning debut Channel Orange in 2012, but only put out a vinyl edition in 2025, leaving a huge gap for the counterfeiters to fill. In my experience reporting on counterfeit vinyl, Ocean’s work is ubiquitous in impounded batches and the stash found at Ahmed’s HQ was no exception.Ahmed employed “three or four” people at his factory, which operated exclusively at night. When officers from the Police Intellectual PropertyCrimeUnit (Pipcu), a national taskforce based within the City of London force, raided the premises, they found a squalid mess, with chemicals stored in fridges next to cans of lager. Machinery, some of which was believed to be at least 70 years old, and stock were haphazardly arranged over three floors, suggesting little quality control. Receipts and order documents were found randomly scattered around.In footage of the raid viewed by the Guardian, a framed silver disc apparently presented to Ahmed by “the God of Vinyl” is visible. A representative from the BPI can be heard expressing surprise at the absence of a cutting lathe, the very expensive piece of machinery that commences record manufacturing by producing the “master” disc, from which everything else is copied, which indicated Ahmed’s “masters” were existing records.View image in fullscreenVinyl press moulds used in the knock-off factory.Photograph: BPIAmid the chaos, officers, assisted by vinyl experts from the BPI, found albums with a street value of about £1m alongside production equipment that is considered a relative rarity among illegal British record specialists, who tend to outsource manufacturing. The only things Ahmed did not produce himself were labels and sleeves, which he had printed by a factory in Gravesend, Kent.Iwas led to Ahmed while reporting on what appeared to be a sprawling counterfeit vinyl trade across the UK. In summer 2024, I was writing a feature about the case of Richard Hutter, a Hampshire-based rogue trader who avoided a spell in prison, despite having been found to have made £1.2m from selling illicit records by artists including Amy Winehouse and the US metal band Tool under the company name Vinyl Groove UK.While researching his case, I was told about a Midlands-based inquiry called Operation Typhoon, which had come to life with the seizure of 529 counterfeit vinyl records from a shop in Stoke-on-Trent.Then there was an enticing new development. The Stoke discovery was followed by a new police inquiry called Operation Imatra, which had started with forced entry into “a three-storey industrial unit in west London”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTen days before Ahmed was sentenced, I met DC Daryl Fryatt, who led the investigation. A relative newcomer to the byzantine world of vinyl, he was clearly fascinated by his new line of work. Midway through the investigation, he bought his first turntable, which he used to indulge his love of modern country music.Phoenix of Vinyl, he explained, had already been issued with a legal cease and desist order in 2017, but blithely carried on its activities for another seven years – something Fryatt put down to the fact that systems designed to detect counterfeits were new, allowing Ahmed’s records to slip through the net.By the time raids took place on Ahmed’s business and family home – a pebble-dashed semi in nearby Southall – at 6am on 20 February 2024, Fryatt and his team still hadn’t grasped the scale of his operation. “Then we searched the premises and we seized a huge amount of records. We found all the production equipment there. And clearly, the factory did the whole lot: made the vinyl, distributed it. Everything,” Fryatt said.View image in fullscreenSome of the extensive equipment used in Ahmed’s factory to produce the records.Photograph: BPIPolice and BPI experts faced an arduous task before they were able to bring charges. They needed to contact 108 record labels or artists’ legal representatives to formally confirm that copyright had been breached.It took until 5 February this year for Ahmed, along with his brother and sister, to be charged with copyright infringement and acquiring, using or possessing criminal property. At a hearing a month later at Westminster magistrates’ court, Ahmed’s siblings pleaded not guilty and the charges against them were later dropped.When Ahmed was first interviewed under caution by the police in May 2024, he painted an illusory picture of his operation, identifying a number of supposed business partners and presenting the police with packs of their supposed ID documents.“One of them didn’t exist,” said Fryatt. “One was a heroin addict who struggled with life and the other one was a guy in America that may or may not have been involved, but there were no records on any phone to show he was. So we discredited his account, basically.”‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool againRead moreIn a second police interview, Fryatt recalled that Ahmed “decided to give us another version: ‘Forget all that: it’s my business, I’m the mastermind behind it all and I’ll take the punishment.’”Between the first and second interview, Fryatt said, “his demeanour was completely different: he started out confident and cocky, but in interview two he was kind of crushed.”He said he would now plead guilty.Fryatt believes Ahmed’s motivation for his crime was simple: “Money, getting rich quick … There was no kind of siphoning it off and investing it. It was all just spent.”Peter Ratcliffe, the BPI’s new director of content protection, appointed nine months after Ahmed’s operation was raided, said there were “absolute shockers” among the seized stock. “They were warped: there were bumps in them. The sound was dreadful. The printing quality was awful.”The ex-Pipcu officer, himself a vinyl enthusiast – the last album he bought was The Cure’s Songs of a Lost World – is ambivalent about the soaring cost of records, viewing his role as more about protecting quality and ensuring money made from counterfeit records isn’t used to fund other serious crime.On 22 April, thanks to information provided by BPI vinyl specialists who were present at the subsequent raid, officers from Pipcu forced their way into a warehouse in Luton, where they found counterfeit albums estimated to be worth £260,000, by artists including The Beatles, Queen and David Bowie.Ratcliffe said that at least 10 other counterfeit vinyl investigations are also taking place. “We’re going to find more,” he said, “and I think we’re going to have bigger finds as well. Just the industrial scale now and the increased popularity of vinyl … It’s all going to lead to very big seizures.”Explore more on these topicsVinylCrimeTaylor SwiftKendrick LamarLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Revel review – broken Barbies and a splash of Swan Lake as older dancers limber up | Dance | The Guardian
description: Warm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated show
Author: Róisín O'Brien
Headline: Warm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated show
Content: Stage bright … Kally Lloyd-Jones and Steinvör Palsson in Revel.Photograph: Brian HartleyView image in fullscreenStage bright … Kally Lloyd-Jones and Steinvör Palsson in Revel.Photograph: Brian HartleyDanceReviewRevel review – broken Barbies and a splash of Swan Lake as older dancers limber upByre theatre, St AndrewsWarm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated showRóisín O'BrienSat 19 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe inevitable aches and sprains of an ageing body take on heightened significance for a seasoned dancer turning up to work each day. Revel by Company Chordelia is a whimsical rumination on these changes, and a personal riposte to the fear that you might “make a spectacle of yourself” if you don’t stop at the “right” moment.It is conceived and staged by the artistic director Kally Lloyd-Jones, who performs with the co-creator Steinvör Palsson, a well-known teacher and choreographer in the Scottish dance community.Revel opens on an apparently empty dressing room, until Lloyd-Jones suddenly appears from underneath a discarded puffy dress, and Palsson creeps out of a storage crate. The backstage PA system delivers a message: they have – only! – nine hours to get ready.View image in fullscreenLong stretch … the pair must prepare properly for their performance.Photograph: Brian HartleyEach dancer’s warm-up manifests differently: Palsson serenely wafts through her qigong routine, while Lloyd-Jones prefers a strenuous running, lunging, shaking approach. They must do their checklist (but first get their reading glasses). Multivitamins? Check. Alternate nostril breathing? Check. HRT patch? Check.‘How incredibly stimulating!’ Retirees on discovering a new world through danceRead moreAs the clock counts down, they get lost in dreamlike dance recollections, ranging fromSwan Laketo marching gestural sequences, before resuming the crossword with a banana and two chocolate digestives.Highlights in this stately procession to their curtain call include Palsson’s juicy rendition of Whatever Lola Wants, indulged while Lloyd-Jones runs to the bathroom. They bring out Barbies to demonstrate their former abilities (“I don’t think you could ever do that, Kally”) before smashing the dolls to bits. No amount of exaggerated hunching, however, can hide the dancing histories in their bodies; Lloyd-Jones bounds around the stage with clarity, Palsson hovers delicately on her toes. They have a great comic rapport, every word and beat finely calibrated.Time runs out, costumes are donned for one last practice; there’s no resisting these performers, aches and all.Touring until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceOlder peopleSwan LakeBalletreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky review – the bell tolls for Patrick Hamilton’s lost Londoners | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettling
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettling
Content: Deftly suggesting turmoil … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Jordan Scowen as Bob in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky at Southwark Playhouse Borough.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDeftly suggesting turmoil … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Jordan Scowen as Bob in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky at Southwark Playhouse Borough.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewTwenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky review – the bell tolls for Patrick Hamilton’s lost LondonersSouthwark Playhouse Borough, LondonThe sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettlingChris WiegandSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Hamilton’s 1929 novel The Midnight Bell unfolds over a series of weeks but has the air of one winding night on the tiles in London. The waiter Bob starts out flush, with £80 to his name, as he opens up the eponymous Euston Road pub for business alongside barmaid Ella. At the end of the novel, he wakes with a brutal hangover and loose change, thoroughly undone by his obsession with a sex worker, Jenny. In two later novels, Hamilton reframed each of these women’s stories in turn. His trilogy, Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky, gains great power through separating out their lives, giving each a concentrated interior monologue.Simon Reade’s adaptation instead interweaves them throughout and opens in medias res, diluting the elements of surprise and downward spiral yet drawing out parallels between the relationships. When Ella muddles into a union with a better-off older suitor, Ernest, it raises not dissimilar issues of class, shame and control to Jenny and Bob’s own stumbling, equally imbalanced affair. Each couple is formed by the lonely seeking out the lonely.View image in fullscreenDisquiet … Rosalind Lailey as Ella and Michael Maloney as Ernest in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHamilton’s set of characters is pruned and Matthew Iliffe’s well-blocked, in-the-round production forTroupeemphasises the isolation, heightened by Ellie Wintour’s sparse set design with a bar counter lowered by a pulley system and stools rearranged into a bed. Elizabeth Purnell’s soundscape captures what Hamilton described as the “grim, yet burdened and plaintive” noise of a busy city that is here impervious to these personal crises. Alex Musgrave’s lighting gives us an interwar London of fog, smoke and gas lamps as the cast swirl around each other.The central young characters are each shown to seem old before their time. It’s there in the way Yanexi Enriquez’s Jenny uses a world-weary “dear” and how Rosalind Lailey’s Ella must dig deep not to make do with the fastidious and appropriately named Ernest, whom Michael Maloney turns into a study of later-life disquiet. Maloney excels at a nice bit of comic business with a hat and there is a vein of uneasy humour but more menace is needed across the production, which never fully captures the trilogy’s jaundiced prose or more squalid locations. Jordan Scowen’s Bob switches well between being intoxicated, crestfallen and disgusted with Jenny but should plumb greater depths of despair.View image in fullscreenSadistic encounter … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Alex Bhat as George in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAs a playwright, Hamilton is best known for two thrillers of cruelty – Rope and Gaslight – and Reade draws out Jenny’s formative sadistic encounter with a stranger, George (Alex Bhat), in a flashback heightened by queasy lighting from Alex Musgrave and Sam Spencer-Lane’s sharp movement direction. The physicality is often astute: there are several prolonged embraces that grow uncomfortable for one of those involved.Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaRead moreYou miss the obsessive inner wrangling over social status in the novels, although Enriquez deftly suggests Jenny’s turmoil about what even a choice of drink may signify about her when she meets George through another sex worker, Prunella (Lucy Gray). The minimal setup also denies the chance to pore over a detailed design for the Midnight Bell, whose personal and public atmospheres Hamilton likened to a theatre itself. But this engrossing production mostly gets the measure of the trilogy.AtSouthwark Playhouse Borough, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSouthwark PlayhousereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tristan & Yseult review – Kneehigh’s lovers still soar with giddy glory | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistible
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistible
Content: Aerial shenanigans … Nandi Bhebhe as Yseult and John Leader as Tristan.Photograph: Steve TannerView image in fullscreenAerial shenanigans … Nandi Bhebhe as Yseult and John Leader as Tristan.Photograph: Steve TannerTheatreReviewTristan & Yseult review – Kneehigh’s lovers still soar with giddy gloryTheatre Royal BathThis heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistibleArifa AkbarSat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKneehigh’s take on this medieval legend was first staged in 2003, in the Cornish setting from which the story of knights, love potions and infidelity arose. It earned cult status and a breathless following of balloon-blowing audience participants, returning to just as much acclaim for a10thanniversary outing.Adapted and directed byEmma Rice, here it is again, in all its giddy, fourth-wall trampling glory, with its army of anorak-clad unloved, and its circus-tricked mayhem. We are once again invited to blow up balloons for the wedding between King Mark (Edward Rowe) and Yseult (Nandi Bhebhe) while her lover, Tristan (John Leader), simmers with secret passion in the wings.View image in fullscreenHow can anyone fail to be enraptured? … Tristan & Yseult’s live band.Photograph: Steve TannerWell, I suppose some things just never get old. This is one of the greatest hits of theformer companybut the young crowd at press night is perhaps some proof that it still has sex appeal. But then, how can anyone fail to drink the potent Kneehigh potion as Tristan and Yseult glug back the magic elixir that makes them fall in love and take off for their staggering set-piece of aerial shenanigans? Or fail to become enraptured with the live band on one side of the stage, with compositions by Stu Barker providing accompaniment between a soundtrack of Wagner, Nick Cave and Roy Orbison, all spinning on the record player on the other side? Or not fall in love with the blend of circus, cabaret, comedy and tragedy, which all run ingeniously alongside each other?‘It was like running away with the circus’ – the thrills, shocks and genius of KneehighRead moreThere is wonderful humour from Yseult’s maid Brangian (Tom Fox) and King Mark’s spurned right-hand man, Frocin (Matthew Churcher). The king brings emotional depth; Yseult and Tristan add a physicality that is both comic and sensuous. The love story makes you cry, even if writers Carl Grose and Anna Maria Murphy choose the most benign ending (the myth has several outcomes but there is no brutal kingly command to burn anyone at the stake here).It is a still marvel of theatrical innovation, a blueprint for dealing with an old story in a new way, bringing bathos to romance but without undercutting its power. Yes, it’s a revival of a surefire hit with the whiff of bums-on-seats ambition, and it does not feel as dangerous all these years later. But neither has it sagged with time. The potion still seduces.AtTheatre Royal Bathuntil 19 September. Thentouringuntil 17 AprilExplore more on these topicsTheatreKneehighTheatre Royal BathEmma RiceCircusCabaretImmersive theatrereviewsShareReuse this content
