title: Blind date: ‘We talked about how I don’t like Clapham gays – guess where he lives?’  | Dating | The Guardian
description: David (left), 34, a children’s doctor, meets Dec, 31, a culture and sex writer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: David (left), 34, a children’s doctor, meets Dec, 31, a culture and sex writer
Content:
Composite: Graeme Robertson and Antonio Olmos/The GuardianView image in fullscreenComposite: Graeme Robertson and Antonio Olmos/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘We talked about how I don’t like Clapham gays – guess where he lives?’David (left), 34, a children’s doctor, meets Dec, 31, a culture and sex writerSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenDec on DaveWhat were you hoping for?A sweet-hearted madman who would make me belly laugh.First impressions?Looked like a David. A bit nervous and jittery, but considerate, curious and chatty (all the best C-words).What did you talk about?People in cars shouting “ginge” at him. Us coming from the West Country (but only I sound like it). How I don’t like Clapham gays – guess where he lives?Most awkward moment?I tried on his stethoscope, pretending to listen for a heartbeat from the chicken.Good table manners?Sound as a pound.Best thing about David?His passion for his profession. Also, how he was so keen to ask, listen and hear.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Would you introduce David to your friends?Possibly, so they can give him his second Buzzballz ever!Describe David in three wordsMoustached, kind, grounded.What do you think David made of you?Probably an absolute loony. No, I wonder if he saw through the tarty humour to my kind, smart, caring self.Did you go on somewhere?The kitchen was closing, and he had to work in the morning, saving lives – very inconsiderate.And … didyou kiss?I gave him a polite peck on the cheek when we hugged bye-bye.If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?Nothing: it was the perfect balance of sincere connection and nonsense.Marks out of 10?A solid 6. He’s a cracking bloke and rocks a floral shirt better than anyone I know. It’s a 6 not a 7 because I don’t like fish or salad; he kindly ordered me both.Would you meet again?We swapped numbers. We’re not each other’s “spark”, but had a good evening.View image in fullscreenDec, left, and David on their date.View image in fullscreenDavid on DecWhat were you hoping for?Someone who put me at ease, asked me questions and made me want to text my friends about him in the toilet.First impressions?Definitely a main character. Handsome, potty-mouthed, charming and equally clueless about tapas.What did you talk about?Dec’s love of swearing. Coming out.Most awkward moment?Possibly when I realised I had a child’s blood on my trousers.Good table manners?Impeccable.Best thing about Dec?He’s very free and at ease in himself, and made me feel I could be too. And his autobiography will be a bestseller.Would you introduce Dec to your friends?I would. But I didn’t toilet-text them.Describe Dec in three wordsCurious, beautiful, free.What do you think Dec made of you?Hopefully good company! “Doctor” brings a whole set of expectations, but it felt like he was able to see past all that.Blind date: ‘Would we meet again? Stay tuned, divas’Read moreDid you go on somewhere?We didn’t – but we stayed until closing.And … did you kiss?A quick peck at the station.If you could change one thing about theevening, what would it be?We were side-by-side at the bar, which is weird for a first date. And he got my right side, which is definitely less good.Marks out of 10?8.Would you meet again?We agreed the chemistry felt more friendly than romantic, but I’d love to stay in touch.Dec and David ate atBarrafina Drury Lane, London WC2. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Black women who choose to have children on their own: ‘We’re going in eyes open’ | Parents and parenting | The Guardian
description: With growing support networks online and in person, these moms say they’re changing the narrative around Black single motherhood
Author: Melissa Hellmann
Headline: With growing support networks online and in person, these moms say they’re changing the narrative around Black single motherhood
Content: Black single mothers by choice work to assemble a strong familial and social village of support.Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBlack single mothers by choice work to assemble a strong familial and social village of support.Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe great fertility divideParents and parentingThe Black women who choose to have children on their own: ‘We’re going in eyes open’With growing support networks online and in person, these moms say they’re changing the narrative around Black single motherhoodMelissa HellmannSat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareWhen Chamise Alston was ready to have a child, she connected her computer to her TV and scrolled through profiles with her best friend, dismissing people who seemed like the wrong fit. Unlike the average millennial on a dating app, Alston was scanning a sperm bank catalogue for potential donors. The Maryland-based therapist hoped to conceive a child through the assisted reproductive technology in vitro-fertilization (IVF).That winter day in 2023, Alston and her friend chose a donor who would help her become pregnant with her now 16-month-old daughter. As a Black woman, she felt empowered taking control of her reproductive destiny.“I always wanted to be a mom,” said 40-year-old Alston. “Once I realized that there was a route for me to be a mom, sans a relationship, that’s always been my mission.”Alston is part of a growing number of Black women opting to be single moms by choice (SMBC) through IVF, intrauterine insemination and adoption.Studies showthat SMBCs are most likely to be financially stable, educated women in their late 30s. While Black women who choose solo parenting fit a similar profile as their white peers, they face unique challenges. Along with navigating stigmas around Black single motherhood, they also contend with a limited number of Black and brown sperm donors, and sometimes face discriminatory experiences from hospital staff during labor and delivery.Considering these hardships, many Black SMBCs work to assemble a strong familial and social village of support. The Guardian spoke to several women who said that they rely on a community of family, friends, neighbors and other moms who assist them in raising their children. In-person and virtual networks such asMocha Moms IncandSingle Mothers by Choicealso provide them with tips and camaraderie with other parents.“I think we’re changing the narrative. We’re going in eyes open, understanding what the expectations are of us, versus going in with a partnership and then being left to fend for [ourselves],” Alston said. “It’s showing for me that you don’t necessarily need a man to fill that void and help create your family. It’s the family you make.”‘Safe haven’Support from a virtual and in-person community has helped Jennifer Cruz throughout every step of her parenthood journey. She’s a board member of Single Mothers by Choice, a national network for SMBCs founded in 1981. The organization’s Facebook has15,000 followers, and local chapters offer virtual and in-person meetups where single moms share tips and experiences.Cruz, an Afro-Latina based in New York City, originally joined the group when she was first considering single motherhood at 29 years old in 2014. Seeing other moms breastfeeding their children and attending doctor’s visits alone showed her that it was possible. When Cruz first joined the meetings, held at a performance art center in Manhattan, she was the only woman of color in attendance. But it became increasingly diverse when she led the New York City chapter from 2015 to 2020.She’s shared with members everything from experiencing her baby’s first kick in utero, to raising a child with special needs. The special education teacher has an 11-year-old son conceived through IVF with a donor’s sperm, and a four-year-old daughter with her ex-husband. Cruz hopes to inspire other women who look like her to become single mothers by choice and to know that they won’t be alone.“Hispanic women can do this too. Black women can do this too, and it may not be the easiest path, but it is doable,” 41-year-old Cruz said. “You don’t have to make choices of putting your career on hold or not being able to have kids because you can’t find someone. If this is something you truly feel is right for you, everyone should have that support to be able to do that.”Jamila Galloway, a 44-year-old marketing executive based in Washington DC, is proud to call herself a single mom by choice. She decided to pursue solo motherhood while living alone in March 2020. Over the course of several years, Galloway completed nine intrauterine inseminations and eight IVF cycles that were covered by health insurance and a fertility fund through her job. After a long and complex journey, she welcomed her daughter through IVF six months ago. Alston and Galloway, who are cousins, have communed with each other through the joys and trials of solo parenting.Galloway also finds camaraderie as a member of Mocha Moms Inc, a virtual and in-person national network for moms of color. She’s used the group’sFacebook pagewith 75,000 followers to research questions that she had during pregnancy and after delivery. Some of the members were acquaintances she reconnected with after seeing their profiles on the page. The group’s single-moms network with about 100 members nationwide meets twice a month on Zoom, and also hosts regional meetups once a year. Members discuss a range of topics including dating as a single parent.“I call it a safe haven for you to be vulnerable,” said Clarice Doctor, the Mocha Moms singles network director, “and have the opportunity to talk without judgment.”‘We always will find a way’For Black women pursuing solo motherhood, their journey is sometimes filled with hurdles from conception to delivery. Since Black men make upless than 3% of donorsat sperm banks, Galloway conceived her child with sperm from a white donor. “When it comes to other ethnicities, I don’t think they have the same struggles in continuing to build the family that they envision for themselves,” Galloway said. “Black women don’t always have agency over the options that we have available, but we always will find a way.”Over the past few years, Galloway has developed a passion for increasing the supply and access to Black and brown donors. She helps market her friend’s cryobank,Reproductive Village Cryobank, which specializes in Black donors.Cruz found only three donors who matched her Puerto Rican heritage when conceiving her son. Her family, adhering to traditional expectations in Hispanic culture, also opposed her pursuit of motherhood without a husband. Her father stopped speaking to her when he found out about her plan. When Cruz gave birth to her son, hospital staff insisted that she fill out an application for Wic, a federal nutrition program for low-income families, even though she made too much money to qualify. A social worker also came into Cruz’s hospital room to ask her if she wanted to put her child up for adoption. “If I had been white coming into the hospital, would they have done this?” Cruz said. “Especially here in the Bronx, going into these hospitals, when you hear ‘single mom’, there’s just this preconception that that means you don’t have money, you don’t know what you’re doing or that this was unplanned.”Black single mothers in the US have long been negatively portrayed in the media and in government policy. In the 1965 federal reportThe Negro Family: The Case for National Action, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, the former US assistant secretary of labor, wrote that the rise of single mothers helped drive poverty in Black communities. And in the years since, the trope has continued in countless TV shows and films, such as the charactersMaryin Precious,Lytiain The Single Moms Club andWilhelminain Ugly Betty.In her recent bookBlack. Single. Mother.: Real Life Tales of Longing and Belonging, the writer and cultural critic Jamilah Lemieux spoke to 21 moms to push back against some of the harmful narratives. Lemieux, a Los Angeles-based single mother who co-parents her teenage daughter with her former partner, said that “single mom by choice” is a complicated term, because it creates a hierarchy that places moms who chose to be solo parents on top.“It implies something that’s not necessarily true, that the vast majority of single mothers had no agency in their position,” Lemieux said. “So many mothers are single mothers because they left an unhappy, unhealthy or unsafe relationship. They don’t get the same credit or respect that we would give to somebody who conceived via IVF or adopted a child.”‘No hood like motherhood’Despite their negative portrayal in the media, Black single mothers have long banded together to help each other. It’s taken Galloway by surprise to see how enthusiastic her community has been to offer companionship, advice and meals. “If my daughter could really understand what’s going on, she’d probably be like: ‘How many aunties do I have?” Galloway said.Alston has also connected with other single Black moms who exchange hand-me-down clothes with each other. She recently hosted a water play-date for several of her friends’ and relatives’ children, including Galloway’s daughter.“Until I became a mother, shortly after giving birth, I just didn’t realize how beautiful the motherhood community was. People were checking in, giving tips on breastfeeding, sleeping,” Galloway said. “Someone has said there’s no hood like motherhood, and I couldn’t agree more.”

title: Domestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your home | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Energy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save money
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Energy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save money
Content: More companies are working on ways people can heat their homes in different and cheaper ways.Photograph: Jamie Grill/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreenMore companies are working on ways people can heat their homes in different and cheaper ways.Photograph: Jamie Grill/Getty Images/Tetra images RFEnergy billsDomestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your homeEnergy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save moneyShane HickeySat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Giles Gibson turns on the hot tap in his home, the water that comes out of it is not heated by gas but by the tiny datacentre strapped to the tank.Attached to the hot water cylinder in his London home is a compact computer server that generates heat and then transfers it as it operates.Gibson gets the benefit of hot water when he needs it at a reduced cost, while the heat that is generated by the server is not lost into the air, a big environmental problem with large datacentres around the world.“As soon as I read about it, I thought: ‘This is obvious – why wouldn’t you do this?’”he says. “It just makes sense to take a computer out of a datacentre and to strap it next to your water tank and get free heat.”View image in fullscreenGiles Gibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom home have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the datacentre system installed last year.Photograph: Giles GibsonGibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom house in south-east London have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the system installed last year.“So over a year, it adds up, and it’s just another little extra that helps,” Gibson says. “Having one of these units is a no-brainer.”Saving waste heatWithdomestic energy bills set to rise again next month, and growing disquiet about the impact of large-scale datacentres on the environment, there are lots of projects looking at how to harness the heat being thrown out by computers.Gibson’s system, supplied by the Surrey-based companyheata, is one of a number of innovative ideas on the market that aim to tackle the problem of waste heat on a domestic scale.Heata operates a sustainable cloud computing business that sends processing jobs from its clients to the servers in people’s homes. The devices have the combined power of about eight laptops.“What the home gives us is effectively somewhere to put a server that has a power connection, and a fibre connection, and a place for heat to go,” says Charlie Beharrell, commercial director of heata.View image in fullscreenThe heata unit in Giles Gibson’s home.Photograph: HeataHe says the company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water. “The water in their hot water cylinder will effectively be heated by our server, and they might have to use the gas boiler for the peakier moments in the day, like when they have a bath,” Beharrell says.“The idea is that the primary heating system is working a lot less hard to heat the water than it would normally have to do if our system wasn’t in place.”How it worksIt can only work in homes with vented, unpressurised water cylinders, typically recognisable by the blue insulation around the outside.A container with the server in is attached to the front of the cylinder after engineers cut a hole in the insulation.It is glued to the boiler with a thermal paste so the unit can conduct heat to the cylinder with no plumbing involved. There is no cost for the installation.View image in fullscreenA heata unit being installed in a home.Photograph: Heata“It takes a couple of hours and we retrofit it to the domestic water system,” Beharrell says.Heata pays for the electricity that is used to keep the server running, while the homeowner pays for the fibre broadband connection that is necessary.Beharrell says that millions of homes are fitted with vented water cylinders, while the units can also work with heat pumps.However, the system is not suitable for homes with combi boilers. A version for unvented cylinders is in development.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHeata’s units are now in 100 homes and there are 3,000 people on the waiting list for installation.Anyone interested in having one can sign up on the company’s website, heata.co.The company says hundreds more are expected to be installed next year.Easy as Raspberry Pi?In aseparate project in Essex, two households are testing a concept where almost 500 matchbox-sized computers are stored together to form a mini datacentre, and the heat generated from them is converted into energy.The freezer-sized HeatHub units are made by the Wales-based companythermifyand, like heata’s, also recycle the energy created when computers process tasks.They work differently from the heata system and the makers say they could one day replace domestic boilers.The heat created by the rows of Raspberry Pi computers warms a mineral oil that surrounds them.“The computers get the mineral oil hot,” says thermify’s chief executive, Travis Theune. “We send that through a heat exchanger. The heat exchanger heats up the water that’s going through a radiator, and the radiator delivers heat to the room. It’s the same basic concept as an induction heater.”View image in fullscreenHeata company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water.Photograph: Soho Studio/AlamyThe existing units have 480 computers in them, which carry out tasks for companies that buy time to process the work they want done.Theune says that the company plans to make a range of units to cater for different-sized homes. For example, a three- to four-bedroom house will have a unit which is about the size of a washing machine, while a flat could have one the size of a microwave.He says that the thermify systems will cost homeowners £90 a month, based on an average-sized home. A bigger house, that requires more energy, will cost more, and a flat less, he says.The planned cost includes installation, leasing the unit, repairs, and will have a minimum 10-year contract.The company claims that the device will lead to a 14% reduction in bill costs compared with homes with a gas boiler, and 34% for those households with a heat pump, over a 15-year period.The savings come from not having to pay for the installation of a boiler or the heat pump.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHome improvementsSaving moneyConsumer affairsHousehold billsEnergy industryDatacentres - UKfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We lost £14,000’: can a new clampdown stamp out cowboy builders? | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: An app and a register of trusted traders may give greater protection to consumers but it is too late for some
Author: Sarah Marsh
Headline: An app and a register of trusted traders may give greater protection to consumers but it is too late for some
Content: Sheri Ingram faced problems with a builder hired to renovate her boyfriend’s home.View image in fullscreenSheri Ingram faced problems with a builder hired to renovate her boyfriend’s home.Consumer affairs‘We lost £14,000’: can a new clampdown stamp out cowboy builders?An app and a register of trusted traders may give greater protection to consumers but it is too late for someSarah Marsh, Consumer Affairs CorrespondentSat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn hindsight,Sheri Ingram, 35, can see the red flags. Lee Slocombe, a builder hired to renovate her ex-boyfriend’s home in the south Wales valleys, offered to do the work cheaply because he had materials left over from another job, then asked for money upfront to buy additional supplies.“At the time, we believed him,” says Sheri, who was in her early 20s when it happened, and had just left university. The couple budgeted about £8,000 for work that included removing a supporting wall and building an extension with a balcony.Does Checkatrade’s vetting really check out?Read moreWithin weeks, the house had been ripped apart. “He pulled up the floorboards and removed the floor joists – he said they had wood rot and needed to come out – took out the staircase, took down the walls, and removed the ceiling,” Ingram says. “The first floor was pinned up using metal poles, and he threw the rubble out the back.”Slocombe kept finding problems and asking for more money, so Ingram’s then boyfriend borrowed another £6,000 from family. By the end, the couple had handed over about £14,000. The builder gave various excuses about where the money had gone and said he was expecting a medical payout for an injury suffered on another job, which he would use to repay them. He even turned up one day in a sling and said he needed a few weeks off. Then, after about six weeks, he disappeared.View image in fullscreenSheri Ingram says her then-boyfriend’s home refurbishment cost them nearly double the original quote, with the builder disappearing after just six weeks of work.Photograph: Sheri IngramSlocombe, from Swansea, was jailed for six years in February after defrauding nine victims of £400,000– his latest conviction in a decade of offending. Ingram’s case was part of a previous trial.Ingram is one of many customers who have lost money to cowboy builders. In July, Citizens Advice said4.8 million homeowners had a problem with a home repair job in the previous 18 months, from unfinished or unsafe work, to disputes with traders. About 1.7 million had to pay more to fix earlier work, or had been overcharged, losing an average of £750 each. For one in 10, the extra cost topped £5,000.AmongAndy Burnham’s first promises as prime minister was a crackdown on rogue builders, with a register of trusted traders scheduled to go live this month.double quotation markThe government is also backing a Trusted Payment app, endorsed by the Chartered Trading Standards InstituteThe government is also backing a Trusted Payment app, endorsed by the Chartered Trading Standards Institute. It will create a “fair contract between trade and consumer”, says its director, James Walker.Under the system, milestone payments are delayed by 24 hours, giving time to cancel if consumers feel under pressure, with payments for completed work held in escrow by the Dispute Resolution Ombudsman until the job is finished to both parties’ satisfaction. Projects costing more than £2,500 are covered by a two-year warranty. Traders who fail to follow ombudsman decisions can be banned from the app.View image in fullscreenSheri Ingram.Photograph: suppliedWalker says the aim is to create a “trusted network for consumers” while helping reputable tradespeople win more business.“We are not going to stop a rogue trader going out … but we are providing a trusted mechanism so you know if you use this process you are protected,” he says.With the promise of greater protection, Paul Boielle, 82, hopes others will be spared his experience. He had noticed a problem with a corner of his roof when three men knocked on his door. It was soon after his wife’s funeral, and he was caught off-guard and “vulnerable”.“They said they were doing work in the area and asked if I needed any roofing work,” Boielle says. He showed them the problem. “Before I knew it, they’d taken the tiles off.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham has vowed to crack down on rogue builders.Photograph: Leon Neal/PAAmong the men was the roofer David Vincent, from Orpington, London, who was later sentenced to 28 months in prison. He pleaded guilty to fraud by false representation and engaging in unfair commercial practices.The men told Boielle the problem was more serious than he realised, and advised replacing the entire roof, quoting £30,000 – about twice what he says it should have cost. He paid a £5,000 deposit.Roofers arrived soon afterwards, removed the solar panels and tiles, re-felted the roof and replaced everything. The job was finished in 48 hours. Boielle’s son and neighbours were concerned by how quickly it was done, and contacted Trading Standards. An investigation by Hertfordshire council’s Trading Standards service found that Vincent had grossly overcharged Boielle for the work, carried it out to a poor standard, and failed to provide information about the right to cancel.View image in fullscreenThe National Federation of Builders says many reputable builders may simply choose not to join Trusted Payments because they are busy and do good work.Photograph: Mediablitzimages/AlamyFor Boielle, the ordeal continued after the roofing team left. Tiles were crooked and the wrong capping tiles had been fitted. The work had to be redone andit took most of the next year to sort it out.The head of policy and market insight at the National Federation of Builders, Rico Wojtulewicz, says many reputable builders may simply choose not to join Trusted Payments because they are busy and do good work. “We don’t think this is the best approach,” he says.“We believe every building should have a digital building passport – effectively a logbook recording all significant work, and who did it. If it subsequently fails, or is found to be substandard, that should be recorded against the builder responsible. It would shine a light on companies that consistently do poor-quality work.”Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsPropertyConstruction industryHome improvementsScamsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closely | Plants | The Guardian
description: Stanhope, Weardale: I’ve realised in that time that beauty and fascination can lie in the most mundane of plants – in this case, broad-leaved dock
Author: Phil Gates
Headline: Stanhope, Weardale: I’ve realised in that time that beauty and fascination can lie in the most mundane of plants – in this case, broad-leaved dock
Content: Dock seeds are important items in bullfinches’ diet.Photograph: Phil GatesView image in fullscreenDock seeds are important items in bullfinches’ diet.Photograph: Phil GatesCountry diaryPlantsCountry diary: A lesson from my final diary after nearly 40 years – keep looking closelyStanhope, Weardale:I’ve realised in that time that beauty and fascination can lie in the most mundane of plants – in this case, broad-leaved dockPhil GatesSat 19 Sep 2026 00.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter another exceptionally dry summer, there’s a nagging question lurking at the back of naturalists’ minds: which species will be the winners and losers in our evolving climate?Throughout summer’s heatwaves and drought, I watched a dense stand of broad-leaved docks,Rumex obtusifolius,thrive while surrounding fields turned the colour of bleached straw. They have promising credentials as drought survivors, thanks to a deep taproot, fast, early spring growth and a long-lasting dormant seed bank in the soil.“One year’s seeding, seven years weeding” goes the old adage, warning of the consequences of allowing weed seeds to ripen and disperse on cultivated ground. That’s an over-optimistic outlook in the case of docks, whose buried seeds can remain viable for up to 80 years. They need light to germinate, but some of today’s bumper seed crop, brought to the surface by burrowing animals eight decades hence, could conceivably grow, flower and set seeds in the early years of the 22nd century.View image in fullscreenA male bullfinch.Photograph: Phil GatesBroad-leaved dock, growing as a weed, has colonised cultivated land since the earliest days of British agriculture. As a wildflower, it’s a rather coarse, unattractive but medicinally useful ruderal (early coloniser). Country children of my generation learned to identify and crush dock for the sap that soothes nettle stings – perhaps the most widely used of all folk remedies. This morning, it was the flash of cerise breast feathers of a male bullfinch, feeding on the docks’ forest of russet seed heads, that caught my attention. There is enough food here to feed a bullfinch family for months.After 39 years andmore than 500 country diaries, this is my last. During that time, I’ve realised that there is often hidden beauty in commonplace and superficially mundane plants, if you look closely enough with a hand lens. So it was with the dock seed that the bullfinch had been eating. Each was oblong, reminiscent of the head and body of a miniature mouse sitting on a papery bract, whose spiky, dry veins extended beyond its margins like claws: exquisite, natural Gothic architecture.Later, at home, I found some of those clawed seeds hooked into my coat sleeves. In autumn, wherever we go, plants often travel with us.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsPlantsCountry diaryBirdsRural affairsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: could the new dog’s tricks make her into a star? | Family | The Guardian
description: Two women I meet on our walk are way more interested in Jean than me – and insist she’ll clean up if we enter her in the local dog show
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: Two women I meet on our walk are way more interested in Jean than me – and insist she’ll clean up if we enter her in the local dog show
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: could the new dog’s tricks make her into a star?Two women I meet on our walk are way more interested in Jean than me – and insist she’ll clean up if we enter her in the local dog showTim DowlingSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a Saturday morning and I’m walking the dog on a vast bit of scrubland. The path in front of me is parched and deserted. Up ahead, the dog turns the corner at a patch of brambles, and I hear the excited voices of two women. My immediate reaction is one of alarm; I whistle, but the dog doesn’t reappear. The voices rise.Only when I turn the corner myself do I see that everything is fine: the dog is dashing from one woman to the other, tail wagging, and the women are both delighted. Meanwhile, their own dogs stand to one side, staring balefully at the ground, leads trailing.“I think we know this one!” says the first woman.“Isn’t she lovely!” says the second. “What’s her name again?”“Um, it’s Jean,” I say.“Hello, Jean!” she says. “We’ve met Jean before! Haven’t we, Jean?”I think: I also have a name.“Let me give you one of these,” says the first woman, handing me a bit of paper from a stack. It’s advertising a dog show, taking place on the same scrubland the next afternoon.“It’s for charity,” says the second woman.“We’ve got a celebrity compere,” says the first, mentioning a name I’ve never heard.“Really?” I say. “Well that sounds … ”“Anyway, you can register online, and Jean would be most welcome,” says the second woman.“I think she’d do very well!” says the first.double quotation markHer best trick is the one where the middle one pretends to shoot her and she falls down deadWe chat for a little while longer, and then the dog and I continue on our way without seeing another soul for the rest of the walk.“It was like we were being headhunted,” I tell my wife later. “They made it sound like we’d clean up. Like it was in the bag.”“She is very well trained now,” my wife says. The dog does have a dog school level 1 certificate, although she dropped out halfway through level 2 to pursue other interests.“I don’t think it’s really a discipline thing,” I say. “It’s more like, waggiest tail, best trick … ”“She does tricks,” my wife says. It’s true – the middle one has taught the dog a few tricks. Unfortunately, her best trick is the one where he pretends to shoot her with a gun and she pretends to fall down dead.“Maybe not for export, that one,” I say.That evening, I think about other dog shows we’ve been to – three, possibly four. They are charming events, but with a bit of an edge. So many excited dogs in close proximity, along with children and a tense air of competition.The last time we attended one, more than 10 years ago, my wife and the old dog were beaten into second place by a six-year-old girl, whose spaniel sat down at her command. My wife spent the rest of the weekend saying she’d been robbed.“What can you do?” I said at the time. “It was cute.”“It’s not supposed to be about cute,” she said. I didn’t say: I think it is.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe next morning, my wife is uncharacteristically despondent.“I don’t think I can face the dog show,” she says.“No?” I say.“We don’t even have teenagers to bring,” she says. “If we show up, just a dog and two old people, and start taking prizes off toddlers … ”“You seem very confident,” I say.“It would just look so desperate,” she says. “Like, what am I trying to prove?”Tim Dowling: my TV contract has run out – and so has my patienceRead moreWe take the dog to a different park in the morning. In the afternoon, we avoid the scrubland until 4pm, and even then proceed across it with caution.“If the dog thing is still going on, we’ll have to turn around,” I say. “Because if those two women see Jean we’ll be forcibly registered, and they’ll probably rerun the whole contest for us.”“There’s nothing here,” my wife says, looking over the empty expanse. “Are you sure you didn’t dream these women?”“I showed you the leaflet,” I say.Back at home, my wife explains her decision to the middle one.“It’s sad,” she says. “I remember when you were little and we went to that dog show in Wiltshire and won all those rosettes. It was all so sweet.”“I don’t remember that,” he says.“All gone, for ever,” my wife says.The middle one straightens his forefinger, cocks his thumb and pretends to shoot the dog. Charmingly, the dog drops dead.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture war | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Moment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaire
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Moment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaire
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend in Liverpool last year.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/Zuma/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend in Liverpool last year.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/Zuma/ShutterstockThe Saturday readEd Sheeran‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture warMoment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaireNadia KhomamiSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.02 EDTShareEd Sheeran has long been known as the “Mr Nice Guy” of music. His is an unthreatening kind of pop stardom; he looks and talks like the bloke who might be standing behind you in a pub, rather than someone selling out stadiums. He champions other artists, he celebrates different cultures. His songs are about love, heartbreak and friendship. People get engaged at his concerts.But this week, one of the most successful musicians in the world faced the biggest controversy of his career, and found himself dragged into exactly the kind of political row he has spent his career avoiding.It began whenMacklemore, the Grammy-winning rapper supporting Sheeran on the US leg of his Loop tour, used his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to call for a “free Palestine”. He performed Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song for a five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces, while footage of pro-Palestine student demonstrations and destruction in Gaza played behind him.The backlash was immediate. The StopAntisemitism group accused Macklemore of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”, a post amplified by the singer Pink. The Israeli-American Council called for him to be pulled from the tour, asking where the line should be drawn “when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”. There was extra heat given Macklemore’s history: in 2014 he performed in a fake beard, wig and prosthetic nose widely read as a Jewish caricature. He was soon dropped from the remaining tour dates.But then Macklemore turned the story on Sheeran, accusing his friend of a “determination not to take sides publicly”, and claiming Robert Kraft – owner of the New England Patriots – had pressured Sheeran by threatening to pull his stadium from the tour dates and urging other venues to do the same. Sheeran’s team confirmed multiple venues had objected to Macklemore staying on the bill. Kraft, a prominent supporter of Israel and founder of the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, has a personal relationship with Sheeran, who sang at his 2022 wedding. In a phone call with Sheeran, the billionaire reportedly acknowledged the sensitivity ofGazabut argued Macklemore’s remarks crossed into hate speech.“Taking a side can cost you,” Macklemore said. “Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed.”View image in fullscreenSheeran and Macklemore pictured in 2014. The US rapper claimed the British singer was pressured by the billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesSheeran’s own statement, published a day later, did little to calm things. He said dropping Macklemore was not his decision and he was “deeply disappointed” by it, but made clear he was not using the moment to declare a position on Israel andPalestine.He was “appalled by the conflict”, he wrote, adding that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides” was “a human tragedy”. “I am not complicit. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have [personal views], and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care.” He wanted his concerts to stay places of “safety and sanctuary”, where people could gather regardless of politics.View image in fullscreenPalestinian artists put the finishing touches on a mural depicting Macklemore on the ruins of homes in Gaza City – the rapper has been vocal in his support for Palestinians.Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) was unconvinced: Sheeran’s statement, it said, “attempts to ‘both-sides’ Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza” and its appeal to “peace” left out “its crucial condition – justice”.“The stakes for him would have been very, very high,” said Dorian Lynskey, the author of 33 Revolutions Per Minute: A History ofProtestSongs. “Taking a stand meant potentially cancelling the rest of your tour, with all the refunds, people who work on the tour losing their work. It’s an enormous thing.”View image in fullscreenThe far-right activist Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersLynskey, who has interviewed Sheeran several times, has “a lot of sympathy” for him, but he thinks the attempt to frame the decision as something that simply happened around him, rather than a choice he made, has backfired. “He may end up being put in another position which is further away from where his sympathies lie. He’s now being seen as a supporter of genocide, when he obviously isn’t.”Within days, every other support act on the US tour pulled out, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, the Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe. Sheeran’s Instagram following dropped by almost 150,000 in 24 hours; Macklemore gained more than 750,000. The actor Hannah Einbinder, Irish musician CMAT and Zara Larsson spoke up for Macklemore. Then Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran, yanking the singer into a political camp about as far as possible from where he would want to be.Suddenly, one rapper’s decision to speak from a concert stage had ballooned into a full-blown culture war. Many were asking: how does a man who has built a fortune on being liked by everyone end up here?Subtly progressiveThe answer partly lies in the distinction Sheeran has always drawn between having political views and making them part of his public identity. He has never been entirely apolitical. In 2017, he said he was supporting Jeremy Corbyn at the general election, while also saying he did not want to tell other people how to vote. He has campaigned on music education and copyright and supported charities including Crisis. In 2022, he performed at the Concert for Ukraine alongside other artists, raising more than £13.4m for humanitarian relief after Russia’s invasion.Paloma Faith, who also played at the Concert for Ukraine, highlighted what she perceived as a hypocrisy. “He wasn’t apolitical by doing that and I don’t really understand why one felt more political than the other,” she told Channel 4 News.View image in fullscreenThe songwriter and actor Paloma Faith, pictured here at a pro-Palestine protest in 2025, notes that Sheeran took a stand over Ukraine.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAThe difference, said Lynskey, is that Ukraine reads in the west as a “consensus position” – “like Chris Martin wearing the pride flag, subtly progressive without risk of a massive backlash. That’s the realm Sheeran exists in: generally on the right side of things without talking about them too much. This time he’ll have had people around him going ‘this is how much money you lose’ or ‘this is how you could be tarred as antisemitic’.”Musicians speaking out is nothing new, from Dylan and civil rights to punk and anti-apartheid – and neither is the price of doing so.In 2003, the Dixie Chicks faced boycotts, radio bans and death threatsafter Natalie Maines criticised George W Bush over Iraq. What sets Sheeran apart is that he did not say the controversial thing himself – someone he chose to put on his stage did. Choosing Macklemore was not the same as endorsing everything he says. But Macklemore’s politics are not incidental to who he is.View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran’s people knew that Macklemore’s music was ‘explicitly political’, says Billy Bragg.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters“He can’t say: ‘I didn’t know Macklemore was going to do that’,” said Billy Bragg, who has spent decades making explicitly political music. “Macklemore has been speaking out about Palestine and the war in Gaza for quite some time now. His song Hind’s Hall and its accompanying video are a central aspect of his set. Ed’s people must have seen that on every other night of the tour.”Stephen Millar, the author of Sounding Dissent, calls it “a maelstrom partly of Sheeran’s own making”. Sheeran had chosen an artist whose politics were well established, he said. “By doing that you could say that was his effort to the cause. But to pull that back is almost like wanting your cake and eating it.”David Hesmondhalgh, a professor of media, music and culture at the University of Leeds, said while artists should not be compelled to take a position on everything, “Sheeran arguably gains credibility from associating himself with an act like Macklemore whose star persona is based on strong political commitments … So his declarations of neutrality look a bit spineless”.‘A real S-storm’The episode also points to a broader shift in what people expect of celebrities. Social media and the sheer weight of feeling over Gaza have made the old split between public image and private politics much harder to hold. “If you’re not using your platform, you’re seen as doing something wrong,” Millar said.At the same time, artists have become proxies for arguments much bigger than themselves. Lynskey pointed to figures such as Gal Gadot and Mark Ruffalo, who have become stand-ins for opposing sides of the Israel-Palestine debate. “There is this sort of proxy war fought out with celebrities. People have been protesting for almost three years and it doesn’t seem to have made any difference, so I think they’re getting more and more angry and frustrated.”The journalist Lulu Garcia-Navarro made a similar point to CNN: “There’s an increasing antipathy towards Israel, regardless of left or right, and popular culture gives people a way in – they’re not talking about what’s happening in Congress, but this they can understand.” She pointed to a second layer, too: “Both the left and right feel like they don’t have control over their free speech … today there’s a perception that pro-Palestinian voices get censored. So it’s become a real S-storm.”View image in fullscreenCelebrities like the actor Gal Gadot, pictured, and Mark Ruffalo have become proxies in the Israel-Palestine debate.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosLisa Nandy, the UK culture secretary, said she had “enormous sympathy” for Sheeran, calling his position “really difficult and impossible” – he wanted to platform his support acts, she said, while promoters were warning himthey would cancel shows over politics on stage.Bragg also acknowledged the practical realities. “Undoubtedly Ed has contractual obligations, and he’d get sued and it would cost him money,” he said. “I can understand it.” But he believes Sheeran could have drawn a cleaner line between defending Macklemore’s right to speak and endorsing every word of it.“He doesn’t have to come out and say ‘free Palestine’. Put purely on the grounds of free speech, he can say an artist must be able to express their view. He needs to let people know how he feels about billionaires deciding what can and can’t be said from a stage,” he said.“Of course, someone like Kanye West should be banned because of the antisemitic things he’s said. But drawing attention to the suffering of civilians in Gaza is not a reason to lose your gig. Culture has to entertain, but it can also challenge.”The point found an echo on the American left. “When you see what Robert Kraft did, to line up all of the stadiums to censor speech in that one specific way, it’s become clear this isn’t about one or two music artists – it’s about how a handful of stadium owners and the elite can bury an entire massive issue. In this case, the genocide in Gaza,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told TMZ. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is.”Lynskey worries about the wider lesson. “Are you just going to vet your support act for politics? Is the lesson that big artists learn that you don’t book anybody who might be a bit spicy? That would be terrible.”Taking a standSheeran is due back onstage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday – with no support acts and no band. “I can’t think of a clear precedent where a star of that size has been put in that kind of situation because of support acts,” Lynskey said. It’s a sharp contrast to his last tour, one of the best-attended of all time; this time thousands of tickets sit unsold, some going for $65 online. Classic Hits Radio in Ireland has dropped him from its playlist “for the foreseeable future”, citing listener reaction.View image in fullscreenFinneas is among the musicians who have pulled out from the Loop tour, leaving Sheeran to perform alone.Photograph: Jerod Harris/Getty Images“In Ireland, rebel songs were used to resist against British occupation for centuries, so the fact that Sheeran makes so much of his Irishness makes his stance all the more jarring,” Millar said.Sheeran has tried to answer the controversy on his own terms: through money instead of words. Macklemore has pledged $1m of his Loop tour earnings to humanitarian organisations in Gaza; Sheeran and Kraft have each promised $2m for “aid in the region”. It is a way of showing he cares about the human cost without making any overt political statements – but whether it satisfies the people who wanted him to speak is another matter.Paul Rieckhoff, the founder of Independent Veterans of America, who was inside MetLife Stadium with his two young children on the night of Macklemore’s statement, told CNN Sheeran might be better placed than most to do some good here: “Maybe Ed Sheeran is the person who can actually bring people together around this. But it’s not going to be by throwing Macklemore under the bus or by appeasing Bob Kraft.”Bragg said: “By trying to be Mr Nice Guy and not take sides, he’s in danger of becoming a pariah himself. And that would be a shame, because it’s not his fault. He does need to make a choice here, and it’s one I think that will define him in the eyes of the public for a long time.”

title: As tobacconist firebombings intensify in Melbourne, nearby stores are being denied insurance | Business | The Guardian
description: Arson attacks related to illegal tobacco trade are also causing revenue and reputation problems for neighbouring businesses
Author: Jonathan Barrett
Headline: Arson attacks related to illegal tobacco trade are also causing revenue and reputation problems for neighbouring businesses
Content: A fire-damaged tobacco store in Coburg in Melbourne’s north in 2024.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenA fire-damaged tobacco store in Coburg in Melbourne’s north in 2024.Photograph: James Ross/AAPBusinessAs tobacconist firebombings intensify in Melbourne, nearby stores are being denied insuranceArson attacks related to illegal tobacco trade are also causing revenue and reputation problems for neighbouring businessesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastJonathan BarrettBusiness editorSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 20.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSmall businesses located near tobacconists are being denied insurance or priced out of coverage as rising arson attacks turn neighbouring shops into collateral damage.The problem has intensified after a spate of firebombings, whichincludes a recent Melbourne blazethat destroyed a Richmond tobacco retailer and nearly a dozen neighbouring shops, requiring 80 firefighters to contain.Crime syndicates have been implicated in more than 200 firebombings of commercial and residential premises in Australia since 2023, according to government data, as rival groups vie for control of the illicit tobacco market.AMelbourneretailer, who asked not to be identified, told Guardian Australia their insurer refused to renew a policy because they were a “few doors down” from a tobacconist.“Even if we re-located, which is not really an option for us, who’s to say a tobacconist doesn’t move in next door?” the retailer said.The retailer said they’d received quotes from other insurers that don’t include fire cover.Big tobacco is back in town as cigarette tax fight lights up Australian politicsRead moreLegitimate tobacconists have also reportedly beentargeted by syndicates expanding their revenue base, making it difficult for them to secure coverage as well.Skye Cappuccio, the chief executive of the Council of SmallBusinessOrganisations Australia, said accessing or affording insurance for businesses located near tobacconists was becoming problematic.“Small businesses should not be left carrying the financial consequences of criminal activity that is beyond their control,” Cappuccio said.“We need a comprehensive effort from governments, law enforcement and regulators to address the illicit tobacco market, alongside broader action to address rising insurance costs and access to affordable cover for small businesses.”Small businesses close to tobacco market-related firebombings are also affected by loss of foot traffic, revenue and reputation, according to the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission.While insurers have not disclosed what constitutes “close proximity”, brokers generally consider it to be within about 20 metres of a tobacconist. Tobacco retailers within shopping complexes are seen as a lower risk.Illicit tobaccoaccounted for 80% of the cigarettes smoked by Australians in 2025, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, with untaxed packets costing as little as $10 compared with more than $40 for a legal packet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe surge in demand has sparked a political debate overwhether Australia should reduce the tobacco exciseto make legal cigarettes cheaper in order to curb illegal sales. Health experts have called for a focus on enforcement, which includes intercepting illegal products that enter the country through Australia’s ports.A spokesperson at Suncorp said the insurer no longer offered insurance cover for tobacconist retailers, including renewals for existing customers.The representative said businesses located near tobacconists may still be eligible, with underwriting decisions based on a range of factors, including the nature of the business and location-specific risks.“As with all commercial insurance, applications are considered on a case-by-case basis,” the spokesperson said.A QBE spokesperson said decisions were assessed individually.“Where risk profiles change, this can influence the price, terms or availability of cover,” the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsBusinessInsurance (Australia)Tobacco industryMelbournenewsShareReuse this content

title: Victorian Labor vows to close loopholes that allow domestic violence perpetrators to ‘slip through the cracks and walk free’  | Victorian politics | The Guardian
description: Premier Ben Carroll says a re-elected Labor government will legislate a new form of manslaughter and increase maximum penalty for rape to life imprisonment
Author: Benita Kolovos
Headline: Premier Ben Carroll says a re-elected Labor government will legislate a new form of manslaughter and increase maximum penalty for rape to life imprisonment
Content: Premier Ben Carroll (right) says the government ‘must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks’.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenPremier Ben Carroll (right) says the government ‘must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks’.Photograph: James Ross/AAPVictorian politicsVictorian Labor vows to close loopholes that allow domestic violence perpetrators to ‘slip through the cracks and walk free’Premier Ben Carroll says a re-elected Labor government will legislate a new form of manslaughter and increase maximum penalty for rape to life imprisonmentFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastBenita KolovosVictorian state correspondentSat 19 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA re-elected Victorian Labor government will create two new Australian-first offences aimed at closing “loopholes” it says have allowed perpetrators of family violence to escape punishment.On Sunday, the premier,Ben Carroll, will announce an election commitment to legislate a new form of manslaughter covering cases in which a person takes their own life as a result of family violence, as well as a new offence covering perpetrators abandoning a victim in need of medical care.The latter responds to recommendations made by the coroner after the deaths of Belinda Jones and Narelle Simmons.Jones, 40, died on the floor of her Maryborough home in July 2023 after her partner left her there overnight and then waited two hours to call an ambulance after waking to find her cold and not breathing.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereJones had succumbed to treatable bacterial infections and sepsis, which a hospital failed to diagnose during an emergency presentation days earlier. Her partner was not charged with any offence in relation to her death.In herfindings published last month, the state coroner, Liberty Sanger, said: “In my view, the act of abandoning a victim of family violence requiring medical attention is an act of family violence, that instils fear in the victim and affirms a perpetrator’s control over the victim.”Molly Ticehurst’s parents fought for 870 days to see her killer jailed. Their courage may help save other womenRead moreSimmons, 42, died in October 2021 after her partner admitted to punching her twice in the face and elbowing her once in the back of the head before leaving her Cranbourne home.Her body was found nine days later after her daughter requested a welfare check. Sanger was unable to determine whether she died immediately after the assault or hours or days later.Her partner – whom the coroner said had 18 previous family violence victims – pleaded guilty to common assault and failing to report a reportable death. He was sentenced to five months’ imprisonment and a 12-month community corrections order.The government’s media release said the two new offences would close “loopholes” that allow perpetrators to “slip through the cracks in the justice system and walk free”.The government has also committed to increasing the maximum penalty for rape from 25 years to life imprisonment and upping the maximum penalty for every other serious sexual offence by five years. The maximum penalty for persistent breaches of family violence intervention orders would also double from five years’ imprisonment to 10.It will also make the standard sentence for the murder of a current or former partner 30 years – up from 25.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLabor will amend the Evidence Act to prevent barristers from using humiliating and invasive questioning techniques on victim-survivors in court. Courts would also be able to consider patterns of sexual abuse as evidence at trial.The announcement comes after a week of crime-focused election commitments from Carroll, including creating a new police training facility in Melbourne’s western suburbs and the introduction ofJack’s Law, which would give police and protective services officers the power to stop and search people for knives using handheld metal detectors.“I’m a tough-on-crime premier – and that means being tough on family and sexual violence,” Carroll said in a statement before Sunday’s announcement.“We must act on the violence that is killing a Victorian woman every two weeks.”The Coalition last year committed to Jack’s Law and also have plans to expand adult sentencing for youth offenders, increase police numbers andsplit the existing court of appealinto two separate entities, if elected in November.In Australia,domestic and family violence counsellingis available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsVictorian politicsVictoriaBen CarrollMelbourneLabor partyDomestic violencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Shark catch-and-kill order issued after swimmer dies off popular Perth beach  | Western Australia | The Guardian
description: Man, 63, fatally bitten by shark at Sorrento beach on Friday morning
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: Man, 63, fatally bitten by shark at Sorrento beach on Friday morning
Content: Emergency services, including water and air personnel conducted an extensive search of the area off Sorrento Beach in Perth on Friday.Photograph: Andrew O’Connor/Australian Broadcasting Corp/APView image in fullscreenEmergency services, including water and air personnel conducted an extensive search of the area off Sorrento Beach in Perth on Friday.Photograph: Andrew O’Connor/Australian Broadcasting Corp/APWestern AustraliaShark catch-and-kill order issued after swimmer dies off popular Perth beachMan, 63, fatally bitten by shark at Sorrento beach on Friday morningGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAchol ArokandKat WongSat 19 Sep 2026 02.43 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 03.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA shark that fatally attacked a man on a beach in Perth’s north will be “destroyed” if it is captured, after an order was issued by the Western Australian government.As the hunt for the animal remained under way on Saturday, the WA fisheries minister, Jackie Jarvis, revealed she had greenlit the order.“Given the shark had been positively identified, remained in the vicinity following a fatal attack and was considered to pose an ongoing threat, I authorised fisheries officers to destroy the shark if captured,” she said in a social media post.Rabbits are the biggest threat to Australia’s native species. Why are their numbers booming again?Read moreEmergency services were called to the popular Sorrento beach at about 10.30am on Friday after reports of a shark-related incident.Western Australia police said a 63-year-old man had been bitten by a shark while swimming along the coast. He died as a result of his injuries, police said.Emergency services, including water and air personnel, conducted an extensive search of the area. The swimmer’s body had not been found.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWater police requested the shark be captured to assist with the recovery of potential coronial evidence.Police and fisheries officials remained in the area and nearby beaches were closed.“My deepest condolences are with the family and loved ones of the 63-year-old man who tragically lost his life at Sorrento Beach yesterday,” Jarvis said.“This is an incredibly sad and distressing incident and my thoughts are with everyone involved.”Locals were urged to stay out of the water until the beach was declared safe for swimming.The local state MP, Liam Staltari, extended his condolences to the man’s family, friends and loved ones.“Like all locals and people from across WA, I’m deeply saddened by the tragic death of a man following today’s shark attack at Sorrento beach,” he said.“Our entire community is thinking of you at this incredibly difficult time.”A witness, Darrel Haythornthwaite,told 7Newsthat he could not believe the incident had occurred, “especially in a place like this”. He said the man’s friend, who was swimming with him, made it back to shore but was inconsolable.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“He felt bad because he didn’t go back to save his mate and I said, ‘Nah you couldn’t have done that’,” he told the outlet. “There’s nothing that anyone could have done.”Another witness, Ingrid Mitchell,told 9Newsshe swam at the beach every day and did not expect sharks to attack outside dawn and dusk.“There was other swimmers in there … just near the seaweed, and there was one poor girl there who was sunbaking, and she saw the whole lot as well,” she said.A third witness, Jacqui Rapaic,told the ABCshe was walking along the beach with a friend when the incident occurred.“My friend said, ‘Jac, I think there’s been a shark attack,’ and I looked out to the ocean and I could see a pool of blood,” she said.“I hugged on to my friend … [we] felt rather traumatised at that point. It happened so quickly.”The fatality followed a shark attack on Monday at the remote Glenfield beach, north of Geraldton on WA’s mid-west coast, which left a surfer with serious injuries.He was taken to the nearby Geraldton health campus and was in a stable condition.– with AAPExplore more on these topicsWestern AustraliaSharksMarine lifePerthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Dutch riot police break up violent far-right protest in The Hague  | Netherlands | The Guardian
description: Authorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre park
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Authorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre park
Content: Police made several arrests as they dispersed hundreds of activists.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice made several arrests as they dispersed hundreds of activists.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press/ShutterstockNetherlandsDutch riot police break up violent far-right protest in The HagueAuthorities ban anti-immigration march after fireworks and other projectiles thrown at officers in city centre parkAssociated Press in The HagueSat 19 Sep 2026 15.43 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDutch riot police dispersed several hundredfar-rightprotesters in The Hague on Saturday after violence erupted and local authorities banned a planned march in the city against immigration and asylum policies.The Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that 24 people had been arrested, after some protesters threw fireworks and other projectiles at police.Justice minister David van Weel called on X for an “extremely firm” response to what he described as “disgusting scenes” at the protest, organised by the far-right We Are the People organisation.He said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, and attacked and threw fireworks at police.“Thanks to all the police officers who are once again standing up for our democratic rule of law,” he wrote.View image in fullscreenThe march was organised to protest about immigration and asylum policies in the Netherlands.Photograph: James Petermeier/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockThe Hague municipality banned the march after violence broke out among demonstrators gathered at the Malieveld, a park in the city centre, and later ordered the crowd to disperse.Those arrested were detained for various offences, including failing to comply with the order and illegally possessing weapons.Police reportedly used pepper spray and a water cannon on the rioters.Saturday’s unrest came a year afterrioting erupted during a rightwing demonstrationin The Hague.A police car was set on fire during the clashes between black-clad protesters and police. The headquarters of the centrist D66 party – whose leader, Rob Jetten,is now prime minister– was also attacked.Jetten said on X that the demonstrators deliberately sought confrontation with the police and chanted “abhorrent” far-right and antisemitic slogans.Explore more on these topicsNetherlandsThe far rightProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims sue California museum over Nazi-looted art | Holocaust | The Guardian
description: Pasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world war
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world war
Content: Adam and Eve, painted in 1530 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, on display in the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.Photograph: Gerard Vuilleumier/Norton Simon Art Foundation/APView image in fullscreenAdam and Eve, painted in 1530 by Lucas Cranach the Elder, on display in the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena, California.Photograph: Gerard Vuilleumier/Norton Simon Art Foundation/APHolocaustJewish heirs of Holocaust victims sue California museum over Nazi-looted artPasadena’s Norton Simon Museum holds 16th-century paintings stolen by the Nazis during the second world warAssociated PressSat 19 Sep 2026 10.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJewish heirs ofHolocaustvictims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits inCaliforniastaking their claims toNazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums inLos Angelesand Auschwitz.This pair of lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws byCaliforniaand the US Congress, which strengthen US-based claims to artwork that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during the second world war.One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles superior court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair, Daniel Gryczman, against the Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of painting Adam and Eve. These are two lifesize oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.Nazi-looted painting must be returned to Jewish art dealer’s heir, Argentina court rulesRead moreThe other lawsuit was filed in federal court in Los Angeles the same day by the daughters of the late Dina Gottliebova Babbitt, aHolocaustsurvivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the “Angel of Death”, from the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum in Poland.Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works, and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don’t specify the monetary value of the paintings.The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotionally, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered intergenerational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history.Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing more than 600,000 works of art acrossEuropefrom Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker’s collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler’s second-in-command, and changed a number of hands before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of ModernArt, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the approximately 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the Los Angeles area.Von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family’s cause.“This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi-era atrocities,” she said.The Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the US supreme court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin, where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.“For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come,” the statement said.Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz-Birkenau museum, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research “must remain in the memorial” to document the man’s crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as “Nazi-looted art” because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn’t have ownership of the watercolors.While he understands the family’s sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele’s criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.“While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the memorial will constitute irreparable harm,” he said. “The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz.”Explore more on these topicsHolocaustPaintingNazismArtSecond world warPolandCalifornianewsShareReuse this content

title: Record fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firms | European Union | The Guardian
description: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: German minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leaders
Content: A display board shows prices at a fuel station in Leezen, Germany. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% up on a year ago, while diesel is up 38%.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersView image in fullscreenA display board shows prices at a fuel station in Leezen, Germany. Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% up on a year ago, while diesel is up 38%.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersEuropean UnionRecord fuel prices across EU prompt calls for bloc-wide windfall tax on firmsGerman minister says companies are ‘exploiting situation’ in Middle East, as sky-high prices become major domestic issue for leadersJon HenleyEurope correspondent andJillian AmbroseEnergy correspondentSat 19 Sep 2026 02.46 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean governments have discussed imposing a bloc-wide windfall tax on energy companies, as near-record fuel and gas prices pile pressure on leaders desperate to contain mounting public discontent and the challenge of the far right.With elections due next year in eight EU countries includingFrance, Italy, Spain and Poland, leaders are scrambling to head off the potential fallout from what analysts have warned could be one of the continent’s biggest energy shocks in decades.Germany’s finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, called on ‌the European Commission at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday to propose possible ways to tax what he described as the excessive profits of oil companies.“Several member states have been calling for models for a long time,” Klingbeil said, demanding proposals by next month. “People can see how oil companies are exploiting the situation, overcharging and significantly increasing their profits.”Oil futures have climbed back above $100 a ⁠barrel, about 50% higher than before the Iran war, as escalating attacks across the Middle East threaten more ​supply routes. Derivatives markets suggest traders do not ‌expect a near-term drop in ‌prices.Pump prices have already reached all-time highs across Europe.
