In Germany, diesel prices surged to a record average of €2.45 a litre on Wednesday, while petrol hit a fresh high of €2.31 a litre, according to Europe’s largest motoring association, ADAC.Prices are even higher in the Netherlands, where petrol eclipsed last week’s record high to reach €2.73 a litre on Wednesday, with diesel at an average €2.78 a litre. Prices have risen higher still for petrol in Denmark and for diesel in Finland.Across the EU, petrol prices are 24% higher than a year earlier, while diesel is up 38% and jet fuel costs more than 100% more. Benchmark gas is trading at €81 a megawatt hour, up 150% on a year earlier, with analysts suggesting it could hit €100.The EU’s economic commissioner, Valdis Dombrovskis, has said the commission has no plans “at this stage” for an ⁠EU-wide taxing mechanism, but stressed it was “ready to engage in discussion” and member states were free ​to impose their own taxes.Sky-high fuel prices are already a major domestic political issue in France andItaly, both of which next year face crunch elections in which voters’ concerns are likely to be dominated by the soaring cost of living, driven largely by high energy prices.In Italy, Giorgia Meloni’s ruling rightwing coalition, trailing rivals in the polls, said this weekit would scrap road taxfor 14.5m cars and motorbikes from next year at a cost of over €2bn, on top of a cut to diesel duty that has already cost €2.8bn.“We have chosen to redirect a portion of the resources used to address rising fuel prices into a simple, structural measure designed especially for those who use cars and motorcycles every day to work, take their children, or get around,” Meloni said.France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, told ministers he wanted the government’s “full mobilisation” on fuel supply and prices, including efforts to secure supplies internationally by working toward the “peaceful reopening” of the strait of Hormuz.In the latest of a wave of protests, French fishers blocked access to two ports and a fuel depot in southern France on Thursday over soaring diesel prices that this week rose to €2.37 a litre, just below their record of €2.38.The fisheries minister, Catherine Chabaud, said the fishers had agreed after six hours of talks to lift the blockades after a promise that those with ​cashflow issues would be granted zero-interest ⁠loans and support measures ​would ​to be ​tied ‌to ​fuel price changes.The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, this week extended emergency fuel subsidies until the end of the year for the agriculture, fishing and construction sectors. But the government is reluctant to step in to cut fuel prices for all.“Blanket measures that affect everyone – including those who don’t need them – are a false economy,” the country’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, told journalists earlier in the week. “Why? Because ultimately, we’ll have to fund them.”In August, Spaindoubled its diesel tax discountto €0.20 a litre from 1 September after diesel prices jumped by 15.7% in July, while in Germany, the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced a fuel tax cut late on Friday.Taxes on petrol and diesel ⁠would be cut by by €0.17 from 1 October until the end of the year, the government said, as well as holding talks with the oil industry with the aim of ​introducing a cap on fuel prices by 1 January 2027 ‌at the latest.“Anyone who relies on their car every day is reaching breaking point,” Merz said in a statement. “We are ‌showing that we are resilient in the face of the crisis and are helping our citizens,” he added.Merz’s centre-right CDU was this monthheavily defeated in state electionsin Saxony-Anhalt by the far-right AfD, and two more state elections this weekend are likely to bring further gains for the far-right party, which has campaigned on a platform of a return to the cheap Russian gas imports Europe largely abandoned after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionOil and gas companiesEnergy industryFranceGermanyEuropeFossil fuelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activists  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Exclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSB
Content: Rita Flores claims that after her recruitment she instigated fights with fellow artists to push them away, and prevent them sharing information with her.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresView image in fullscreenRita Flores claims that after her recruitment she instigated fights with fellow artists to push them away, and prevent them sharing information with her.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresRussia‘My fear was too great’: the Pussy Riot member recruited by Russian spies to inform on fellow activistsExclusive: In her first media interview since fleeing Russia, Rita Flores describes her three years of being run by the FSBShaun WalkerSat 19 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst came the blackmail and death threats to secure cooperation, then came a series of tasks, each more sinister than the last: to inform on fellow activists, to elicit personal information from protest-minded artists and – eventually – to help with a plot to kidnap and murder a Kremlin enemy.That is how Rita Flores, a 29-year-old Russian artist, activist and former member ofthe Pussy Riot collective, described her recruitment and three-year handling by officers from Russia’s FSB security service, a cooperation she only broke when she fled the country last month.Flores made details of her collaboration public in avideo discussionwith her lawyer, Dmitry Zakhvatov, published just days after she left Russia at the end of August. She explained she was coming clean in the hope that others in a similar situation might feel emboldened to break their ties with the FSB.Revealed: how Russia uses mobile ‘super-app’ Max to spy on its citizensRead moreNow, in her first media interview since leavingRussia, she gave further detail on how she was recruited and run by the FSB. “For the first time in years, I feel calm. All this time I was dreaming about getting out and being able to talk about it all,” she said. The Guardian could not corroborate the details of Flores’s account, but there have been numerous cases of the FSB infiltrating opposition groups over the past few years.View image in fullscreenRita Flores was arrested multiple times for provocative art performances as part of Pussy Riot.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresFlores, also known as Margarita Konovalova, has been associated with Pussy Riot since 2020, when she was detained after a performance near the Kremlin. She had served several short stints in jail and been subjected to surveillance and house searches on numerous occasions, which intensified after the domestic crackdown that followed the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.She was recruited after one of these police searches in February 2023, when two men stayed behind and introduced themselves as FSB officers, she said. They threatened to open a criminal case, under wartime censorship laws, over an Instagram post she had made criticising Russian killings in Ukraine. They also suggested they could arrange for her mother to be killed if she did not sign cooperation papers.“I believed them. I believed they could do everything they said they would … My fear was too great. I was so worried for my family and also for myself,” she said. As a reward for signing, she was given a one-off cash payment of 30,000 or 40,000 roubles (£266 or £355), she said.Her first tasks were to gather information about other opposition-minded artists in the same circles as her and report back to the FSB. The two FSB officers who recruited her became her regular handlers, she said, organising frequent meetings and largely sticking to a classic good-cop, bad-cop routine. She saw the senior officer only occasionally, a crude man in his late forties who introduced himself by a series of different names. In the end, Flores began calling him “the Jacket”, based on the shiny black suit he liked to wear. The junior officer, named Ivan, became her primary handler, and he often tried to be friendly and helpful, leaving direct threats to the Jacket.View image in fullscreenOne of Flores’s handlers promised to ‘re-educate’ her until she became an ‘obedient wife’.Photograph: courtesy Rita Flores“Whenever I met with Ivan and the Jacket together, Ivan was silent. The Jacket would be rude, threatening; he’d insult me as a woman. He was the devil incarnate. Then just me and Ivan would meet, and Ivan would be nice, friendly,” she recalled. “He liked to say, ‘The FSB will re-educate you, I will re-educate you, you’ll have a nice and calm life, and you’ll love Russia, have children and be an obedient wife,’” she said.Flores said she was not supposed to tell anyone about her recruitment, but immediately told “about 20 people”, putting it down to the fact she is a “massive gossip”.Still, she stopped short of telling the people from the art world she was meant to report on, instead claiming that she initiated conflicts with them on pretexts, designed to push them away from her and prevent them sharing sensitive information. Her two handlers kept up the psychological pressure by repeating their threats, and even the friendlier Ivan on occasion made it clear that the consequences for crossing him would be severe, she claimed.“He tried to befriend me, but he could also be threatening. He’d calmly say, ‘they’ll kill your mother and you won’t be able to prove anything’ or ‘if you go abroad they’ll find you immediately and kill you,’ and then he would giggle, like it was all a joke. The Jacket, on the other hand, never joked. His threats were more direct.”In time, there were fewer targets to inform on, as most of the protest-minded artists left the country. She described life in wartime Moscow as an exercise in cognitive dissonance. “Moscow is booming; restaurants, bars and clubs are opening and there are a huge number of events. But those people who understand things have empty eyes and speak empty words,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenFlores claims most of the provocative, protest-minded artists have left Russia under Putin’s regime.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresArtists who stayed are careful not to produce any work that could be considered even tangentially political, she said. “People who have stayed in Russia have accepted the rules of a game. You go to a gallery and every artwork may as well come with a sign saying ‘we were forbidden from saying anything’ … there are artists who used to make strong statements, and in 2026 they are drawing flowers in a vase.”Last May, Ivan and the Jacket first started asking her questions about Pyotr Verzilov, an activist previously linked to Pussy Riot who now lives in Ukraine and fights with the Ukrainian army against Russia. A longtime irritant to the Russian authorities, in 2018German doctors saidthey believed Verzilov had been poisoned in Russia.Flores said her handlers wanted her to get information from Verzilov, including his address in Ukraine. Then, they suggested she use her old friendship with him to arrange a meeting in Serbia. There, he would be kidnapped and killed by a waiting FSB squad, they claimed. Ivan began to pay her 50,000 roubles a month as an additional incentive to help with the Verzilov case.Meanwhile, Flores said, she was plotting a way out. She married her partner last September, which she said was partly a way of worming out of the Serbia task, so she could claim to Ivan that her husband would never let her go on a trip to meet another man. Previously, her handlers had banned her from leaving the country, she claimed, and it was only when she contacted the lawyer, Zakhvatov, that she realised there could be a way for her to leave. The pair began scheming in secret over the details.“They created a reality where she felt like they controlled everything, but actually it is not that hard to leave,” said Zakhvatov. In 2022, fellow Pussy Riot activists Lucy Shtein and Masha Alekhina fled house arrest in Moscow bydressing up as food delivery couriersto evade police and eventually leave Russia. Flores’s escape was less dramatic, but both Zakhvatov and Flores declined to give details, citing the need to protect methods for future cases.View image in fullscreenHaving escaped Russia, Flores is now keen to help those in similar situations flee the country.Photograph: courtesy Rita FloresAfter Flores’s escape, Zakhvatov announced a secure line for people in similar positions to contact him if they need help. Flores said she would also like to work to help others, and added that she was certain that recruitments in activist circles are a “mass phenomenon”. She said there was at least one person in her own surroundings who had informed on her before she agreed to cooperate, a fact she discovered when it turned out that the FSB had possession of a sex tape featuring her, covertly filmed by the person. Earlier this year, Polandjailed an exiled Russian activistfor seven years, after it emerged he had passed information about fellow exiles to an FSB handler who had recruited him back in Russia.Flores’s video confession at the end of last month was met with praise from some parts of the exiled Russian opposition, who commended her bravery for speaking out and explaining how the FSB operates, but also some scepticism from those who criticised her decision to cooperate for so long. Since then, Flores has been making calls to people she informed on as well as other old friends to explain herself, and said everyone had been supportive in these conversations.“It’s not a big secret that it’s not great to work for the FSB, but fear can change a person,” saidAlekhina. “It’s important that she’s now out of the country and that she said what happened to her out loud. Nobody was killed and nobody went to prison [because of her], so that is good news.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over Greenland | World news | The Guardian
description: The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: The agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determination
Content: Trump called the new security pack ‘very important, historic, and special’ on his Truth Social.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTrump called the new security pack ‘very important, historic, and special’ on his Truth Social.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesWorld newsUS and Denmark reach security deal after Trump’s threats to take over GreenlandThe agreement would allow the US to expand its military presence, while Denmark and Greenland say it preserves their sovereignty and right to self-determinationRobert MackeyFri 18 Sep 2026 21.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 18 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump announced on Friday that the US had struck an Arctic security pact with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland, after threatening for much of his second term to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory by force.The full scope of the deal Trump described as “very important, historic, and special” was not immediately clear. But soon after his announcement in a post on Truth Social, the leaders of Denmark andGreenlandissued statements indicating the deal would be signed by the three governments on the sidelines of the United Nations general assembly in New York City next week.Trump renews call for US to take over Greenland as he arrives for Nato summitRead moreIn his social media post, Trump cast the deal as a personal triumph,claimingthat the agreement “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns”.“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large Military presence in the appropriate part of Greenland,” Trump added. The US already has a presence on the island, and the right to expand bases, throughNato.The announcement comes just weeks before November’s midterms, giving the president a foreign policy accomplishment he can tout to voters as the deeply unpopular war with Iran becomes an increasingpolitical liabilityfor Republicans vying to hang on to their narrow majorities in the House and Senate.The US has long had a military presence inGreenland– a self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, a fellow Nato member – and has had a military base at Pituffik since the cold war.In his post, Trump said that the agreement means “no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval”.Statements from Denmark’s prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, and the leader of Greenland’s government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, posted online late on Friday, emphasized that the agreement would fall far short of Trump’spreviously stated desirefor “the acquisition of Greenland by the United States”.Frederiksen saidthat what she called “a great agreement” for all three parties “recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination”.Nielsen saidit was “joyous” that the agreement “ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western Alliance”, suggesting that the deal might possibly just reiterate the existing US rights through Nato to use the island as a security base.Once agreed to, the pact would need to go through parliamentary procedures to be enacted, the Danish and Greenlandic statements said.Earlier in his term, Trump argued that the US needed control of Greenland for“economic security”, and has described ownership and control of the territory as an “absolute necessity”. The island had long been on the president’s radar as a target for purchase, and during his first term,in 2019, Trump confirmed reportshe had been urging aides to find out how the US could buy Greenland, describing any sale as “essentially a large real estate deal”.Trump’s claims deepened divisions among the western alliance, with the Danish government repeatedly stating that Greenland was “not for sale”. When concerns over Trump’s annexation threats reached a fever pitch last year, the Guardianreportedthat the Danish government set up a “night watch” in the foreign ministry to monitor the US president’s pronouncements while Copenhagen sleeps.At a Nato summit in Ankara earlier this year, Trump renewed his bid for the US to acquire Greenland. He threatened to pull all American armed forces out ofEuropeafter the continent repeatedly pushed back.Strategically positioned between the US and Russia, Greenland is viewed as increasingly important for defense and is emerging as a geopolitical battleground as Arctic ice melts.The US vice-president, JD Vance, and his wife Usha, received afrosty receptionwhen they visited US troops stationed at Pituffik space base last year, amid the White House’s aggressive campaign to take the mineral-rich island with roughly 56,000 inhabitants.Polling has found Greenlandersstrongly opposeany effort to make Greenland a part of the US.Even so, a Trump administration insider dropped a hint online that the US side intends to present whatever the deal actually is as an American triumph. Katie Miller, a former White House aide whose husband is Trump’s closest adviser,posteda map of Greenland covered in the American flag, with the caption: “ITS [sic] HAPPENING”.Miranda Bryant contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWorld newsDonald TrumpTrump administrationGreenlandDenmarkNatoEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attacker | Israel | The Guardian
description: Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Elor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide country
Content: Elor Azaria, pictured in an Israeli military court in April 2016, was 20 when he was sentenced.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APView image in fullscreenElor Azaria, pictured in an Israeli military court in April 2016, was 20 when he was sentenced.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APIsraelIsraeli president pardons combat medic who shot dead wounded Palestinian attackerElor Azaria’s conviction in 2017 for manslaughter of man who stabbed soldier continues to divide countryAssociated Press in JerusalemSat 19 Sep 2026 16.32 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s president has pardoned a combat medic who shot dead a badly wounded Palestinian attacker who had stabbed a soldier in the occupied West Bank, in a case thatdivided the countrya decade ago.Elor Azaria’sconviction in 2017 for manslaughterand his release after serving two-thirds of his 18-month sentence drew enormous attention in Israel, where military service is compulsory for most Jewish men.In his first interview after his release, Azaria said he would “act exactly the same, because that’s how I needed to act”.Azaria had approached Abdel Fattah al-Sharif as he lay on the ground, unarmed and badly hurt, after stabbing a soldier in the city of Hebron. Amobile phone videocaptured Azaria shooting al-Sharif in the head.The office of president Isaac Herzog said in a statement on Saturday that he acted on the recommendation of defence ministerIsraelKatz. The statement cited the time that had passed, and the spirit of the approaching Yom Kippur, or Day of Atonement, holiday as among the factors in the decision.This Israeli election could be the country’s last – this week I saw that for myself | Jonathan FreedlandRead moreHerzog’s office also said that Azaria, who was 20 when he was sentenced, had “expressed his sorrow” in his request. The statement noted that in an earlier request, he called his gunshot an “operational error”.In a separate statement, Katz called it a “right, humane and fitting decision” and said Azaria had been in a “complex operational mission”.But the military’s chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, had said in a letter to the defence minister that the pardon should not be granted, Israeli media reported.The conviction was a rare case of a military court ruling against a soldier for deadly action taken in the field. Top generals had pressed for his prosecution, while many in the Israeli public supported Azaria at a time when there had been a series of stabbings and car-ramming attacks by Palestinians or Israeli Arabs. Some supporters protested outside his trial.On Saturday, Israel’s hard-line national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said in a statement that “cancelling the criminal record of someone who killed a terrorist makes me emotional and very happy”.Some Palestinians and human rights groups had described Azaria’s sentence as far too lenient. Prosecutors had sought a sentence of three to five years.The statement by Herzog’s office on Saturday said that his decision “does not constitute a reassessment of the case”.The divisions over Azaria’s case led to public polling and political pressure that led the defence minister at the time, Moshe Ya’alon,to resign.After the verdict, Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahucalled for Azaria to be pardoned.After the sentencing, the Palestinian government minister in charge of prisoner affairs, Issa Karaka, called it a “joke”.Explore more on these topicsIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaWest BanknewsShareReuse this content

title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Content: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesNAZAFrom ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryAs Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaignPeter BeaumontSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was theGazadocumentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers –describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.Rightwingpolitical figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he wouldseek new laws to strip citizenshipfrom people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretzwarnedthat their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as didinternational press freedom organisations.The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”View image in fullscreenA protest against the NAZA film-makers in Savyon, Israel.Photograph: Sharon Eilon/Sopa Images/ShutterstockThe rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”At points, the threats of violence have been realised.On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.“The discussion aboutNAZAhas been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towardsdissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry foundIsrael continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreIsrael’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz,wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” hewrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Kemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’ | Kemi Badenoch | The Guardian
description: Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spending
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spending
Content: Kemi Badenoch said the prime minister had to ‘stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said the prime minister had to ‘stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history’.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAKemi BadenochKemi Badenoch accuses Andy Burnham of ‘fiddling while Europe risks burning’Tory leader claims prime minister is avoiding difficult decisions as she urges him to increase defence spendingYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 19.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of “fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning”, as she repeated her call for the prime minister to cut the welfare budget to fund increase spending on defence.Speakingto the Telegraph, the Tory leader said that “Burnham may be a people pleaser but difficult choices cannot be avoided through dither and delay”.She said the government had to “fund our defence properly” at a time when former military chiefs have raised questions about Britain’s preparedness for war.Badenoch said: “Our government is fiddling while Europe is at risk of burning. In France and Poland, leaders are taking action now against the growing Russian threat. What is our government doing? Has anyone heard from Wes Streeting, the former head of the National Union of Students, who has rocked up as defence secretary?”Discourse on the “welfare v warfare” debate has grown louder in recent days since Burnham’s comments during prime minister’s questions on 9 September that national security could not “come at the expense of social security”.John Healey in talks with Canada about UK joining new global defence bankRead moreTheTory leadersaid Burnham was sending a “dangerous” message that he would not cut welfare to fund the military, which was “heard loud and clear in Moscow as well as Manchester”.She added: “We have to stop pretending that we are living in a carefree end of history when Russia is testing our resolve week after week. It’s time to get serious.”The UK has promised to commit 3.5% of national income to defence by 2035, in line with a pledge by Nato members, but there isgrowing pressureon the chancellor, John Healey, to outline how further increases will be achieved before next month’s budget.Adm Lord West, a former security minister under Gordon Brown, said Britain’s military was in “quite a parlous state”.“In many ways, one could argue we are already at war. We are certainly in the grey zone – whether it’s cyber-attacks, drones getting near the edge of somewhere or threats to underwater cables,” he added.Lord Dannatt, a former chief of the general staff, said: “My bottom line is thatAndy Burnham, and regretfully I would now add John Healey, are playing fast and loose with the nation’s security.”The Conservatives have proposed capping housing benefit to raise £4bn to spend on defence. The party has rejected suggestions that the policy would make people homeless but suggested some would have to “move somewhere cheaper.”The Tories will hold their annual conference in Birmingham in two weeks.Explore more on these topicsKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamDefence policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Footballers and fans pay tribute to Noah Woods after toddler’s death in Suffolk | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Players in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applause
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Players in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applause
Content: Ipswich Town's Leif Davis joined a search party to look for the toddler before his body was found. He later donated £2,000 to the boy’s family.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenIpswich Town's Leif Davis joined a search party to look for the toddler before his body was found. He later donated £2,000 to the boy’s family.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/ReutersSuffolkFootballers and fans pay tribute to Noah Woods after toddler’s death in SuffolkPlayers in Everton v Ipswich Town match wear black armbands as supporters join in minute’s applauseYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 18.13 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlayers wore black armbands duringEverton’s home match against Ipswich Townon Saturday, as part of a tribute to three-year-old Noah Woods, whose body was found after he went missing in Suffolk this week.A photograph of the boy was shown on the big screen before the Premier League game in Liverpool, and three minutes after kick-off both sets of supporters stood to applaudin memory of Noah.The toddler, who was non-verbal, partially deaf and had been undergoing an assessment for autism, became separated from a relative after visiting a playground in Brantham on Tuesday afternoon,Suffolkpolice said.About 1,300 members of the public joined a search which ended on Wednesday whenpolice divers recovered a body from a nearby lake.On Thursday, Noah’s father Rhys Woodspaid tribute to his sonin a message shared on a community Facebook group.He wrote: “There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.”View image in fullscreenA photograph of Noah Woods was displayed on the big screen at Everton’s Hill Dickinson stadium on Saturday afternoon.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersIpswich Town’s captain Dara O’Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton were among a delegation from the Suffolk club who laid flowers at the playground where he went missing.Town defender Leif Davis donated £2,000 toa fundraising appealset up by Good Dads Club, a group of fathers in Colchester, Essex, to support Noah’s family. It had already received more than £100,000 in donations from more than 6,000 supporters by Saturday evening.Suffolk constabulary said the child’s death was not being treated as suspicious but that the force still has a number of inquiries to complete before submitting a file to the coroner.Explore more on these topicsSuffolkIpswich TownEvertonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ed Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference begins | Liberal Democrat conference | The Guardian
description: Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton
Author: Yassin El-Moudden
Headline: Leader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in Brighton
Content: Ed Davey urged delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope ‘that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down’.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenEd Davey urged delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope ‘that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down’.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PALiberal Democrat conferenceEd Davey takes aim at Reform and Elon Musk as Lib Dem conference beginsLeader says party ‘won’t give up the fight’ to defeat ‘nasty populism’ in first-day speech to delegates in BrightonYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 17.37 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Liberal Democrats’ leader, Sir Ed Davey, took aim at Nigel Farage and Elon Musk on the first day of his party’s annual conference, saying Lib Dems would not give up the fight to defeat “nasty populism” and Reform UK’s “£72m arsenal of hate and lies”.On stage at Brighton Centre, Davey called on the assembled delegates not to be deterred in the face of Reform’s hope “that the anger and the hatred and the lies will grind us down until eventually we just give up”.He also praised earlier speakers for showing “why we care and why we fight” and contrasted this with Reform, which, he said, “care about their own bank balance and they fight because two crypto billionaires gave them 72 million quid”.Davey,who entered conference season having to address frustrations over his leadership expressed by some Lib Dem MPs, also used the speech to recall his early political life as a student campaigning successfully for his university college to boycott Barclays, due to its investments in apartheid-era South Africa.He spoke of his “visceral shock [and] overwhelming anger at seeing human beings treating other human beings with total contempt” and drew parallels between that experience and the need to not look away “when we see human dignity under attack”.Lib Dems have ‘moral responsibility’ to block Reform, says Ed Davey as party gears up for snap electionRead moreDavey said: “Today – we are back. Fighting again the fight that fired me up at university. The fight to end injustices. In our country and around the world. The fight to defeat the nasty populism of Trump, Le Pen, the AfD and the rest.“The fight to stop the world’s richest man who learned racism in apartheid South Africa from funding racism around the world.”He also referred to the “fight to defend the Royal National Lifeboat Institution after volunteers for the coastal rescue charitywere recently targeted online amid anti-migrant protests”.He said “Reform know they don’t speak for the real United Kingdom” – and what Farage was “counting on to get him to No 10” was that people would get “tired, depressed, fed up with seeing Zia Yusuf on BBC Question Time week after week”.But Davey said he hoped Reform were watching and would see “a party that won’t be ground down. That won’t be deterred. That won’t give up the fight.”Also during the first day of the conference, Lib Dem health spokesperson Helen Morgan set out a £600m plan to improve maternity care, including proposals to bring in one-to-one midwifery for every woman in labour backed by a round-the-clock senior consultant.The party said the measures will pay for themselves by reducing how much the NHS has to spend on compensation for maternity negligence claims every year – totalling £1.3bn in 2024-25.Munira Wilson, the Lib Dem education spokesperson, said the party would introduce a guarantee to provide 100 hours of work experience for students from GCSE age to 18 to tackle the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training.Explore more on these topicsLiberal Democrat conferenceLiberal DemocratsEd DaveyReform UKThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quit | Jim Ratcliffe | The Guardian
description: Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
Author: Daniel Lavelle
Headline: Supporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empire
Content: ‘At the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it,’ Ratcliffe said.Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAView image in fullscreen‘At the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it,’ Ratcliffe said.Photograph: Bo Amstrup/EPAJim RatcliffeManchester United Muslim fans group calls on co-owner Jim Ratcliffe to quitSupporters’ club says billionaire should stand down after ‘completely unacceptable’ comments on the UK and empireYassin El-MouddenandDaniel LavelleSat 19 Sep 2026 13.44 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s Muslim supporters’ Club (MUMSC) has called for the Premier League side’s co-owner to step down after he made “completely unacceptable” comments during a BBC interview.SirJim Ratcliffedescribed the UK as being a country “on the slide” from the days when it had “the greatest empire in the world”.In what was described as a “statement of no confidence” posted on X, MUMSC said: “Our players, staff, stewards, security teams and supporters come from different countries, cultures, ethnicities, religions and backgrounds. Manchester United would not be Manchester United without them.“Manchester United does not belong emotionally to investment funds, shareholders or billionaires.“After years of decline, broken promises and repeated failure, Manchester United Muslim Supporters’ Club has lost confidence in the current ownership structure of Manchester United Football Club.“Enough is enough. It is time for change. The Glazers [co-owners] and Sir Jim Ratcliffe must go.”Ratcliffe, who founded petrochemicals giantIneos, and has resided in Monaco, which has a relaxed tax regime, since 2020, said Britain was in decline because of high taxes and immigration.His latest attack on the UK comes seven months after he told Sky News that the country wasbeing “colonised by immigrants”. He subsequently said he was sorry if those remarks had “offended some people”.MUMSC said it had challenged those remarks earlier this year, adding: “We hoped a lesson had been learned. Clearly, it has not.“This week, Sir Jim has again placed immigration and people receiving benefits at the centre of his explanation for Britain’s problems, arguing that nobody is ‘tough enough’ to deal with either.“We find these latest comments deeply disappointing and completely unacceptable.”The billionaire told BBC News’s Big Boss Interview he believed the UK was in decline.He said: “We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars. We’re good, honest folk.“But unfortunately, at the moment, I think the UK is on the slide. It’s quite difficult to see how we arrest it.”Ratcliffe also said the UK had “a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment”, “encouraging” the wealthiest to relocate.He told the podcast: “In America, they applaud people who create wealth.“And the good thing about those people who create wealth is that they then spend that wealth in the economy in which they’re resident.“And, unfortunately, with the things that they’ve been doing, they’ve been encouraging the people who have created wealth to leave the UK because it’s just become uncomfortable for them for tax reasons or whatever.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGuardian view on Sir Jim Ratcliffe: Britain does not need political lectures from a billionaire tax exile | EditorialRead moreWhile the UK’s tax burden has risen to its highest level since the second world war at about 35.3% of GDP, theOffice for Budget Responsibilitysays it remains well below the average of 14 western European economies.Ratcliffe has also been at odds with Manchester United fans over the summer after the club embarked on a major ticket-touting crackdown that ultimately revoked 685 season tickets, prompting protests from United supporter groups such asthe 1958.The businessman was already fiercely unpopular among the Old Trafford faithful, ever since he decided to increase ticket prices and sack 450 club employees.Ratcliffe also took aim at the government’s decision not to invest further in North Sea resources by granting licences for the Jackdaw and Rosebank oil and gasfields, which he said amounted to “insanity”, and warned the UK’s reliance on energy imports meant the country could “run out of gas” if there was a cold spell this winter.He said: “The risk you’ve got this winter is that we run out of gas. If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we’ll run out of gas and have to switch the industry off.”In response to the criticisms, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.A spokesperson told the BBC they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: “We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply.”Asked if he was planning on returning to the UK, Ratcliffe said: “Not at the moment, no. I don’t see growth being tackled.“Two things: we need politicians who are tough enough to deal with some very difficult problems, and we know what the problems are.“And we need politicians who will make decisions which are good for the country, not good for themselves and their party. And we haven’t had one of those for a long time.”Explore more on these topicsJim RatcliffeManchester UnitedIneosIslamBritish empirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Kent hotel fire that forced hundreds to evacuate being treated as suspicious | Kent | The Guardian
description: No injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blaze
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: No injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blaze
Content: Inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenInquiries into the cause of the fire are under way.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesKentKent hotel fire that forced hundreds to evacuate being treated as suspiciousNo injuries reported after about 280 people taken to safety from the Grand Burstin in Folkestone after blazeSammy GecsoylerandYassin El-MouddenSat 19 Sep 2026 13.21 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA large fire that broke out overnight at a seaside hotel and forced hundreds of people to evacuate is being treated by police as suspicious.Emergency services were called just after 1am on Saturday to the Grand Burstin hotel in Folkestone, where a fire is believed to have started in the basement,Kentfire and rescue service said.About 280 people were taken to safety and Folkestone and Hythe district council set up a welfare centre.No injuries have been reported and inquiries into the cause of the fire are under way. Detectives from Kent police are also seeking dashcam footage and asking witnesses to come forward.View image in fullscreenFire damage at the hotel.Photograph: Andrew Aitchison/In Pictures/Getty ImagesTwenty-six fire engines were dispatched to the seafront hotel, the fire service said. According to the BritanniaHotelswebsite, the Grand Burstin overlooks Folkestone’s harbour and has 550 rooms.Folkestone and Hythe district council posted on X: “A fire is currently ongoing at the Folkestone Grand Burstin hotel.“We are operating a welfare centre at Three Hills Sports Park for people being evacuated from the site, where we are providing support to those affected.“We are supporting all emergency services involved in the response and their efforts to get people to safety.“Our advice to residents living nearby is to: close all windows and doors; avoid the area and do not attempt to approach the hotel; follow the instructions of emergency services; keep roads clear to allow emergency vehicles to access the area.”Kent fire and rescue service said in an update: “Ten fire engines remain at the scene of a fire at the Grand Burstin hotel in The Harbour, Folkestone.“Crews wearing breathing apparatus have worked hard to bring the fire under control and are now dampening down any remaining hotspots.“It’s believed the fire started in the basement of the property, but the cause is not yet known.“Around 280 people evacuated the building, and a welfare centre has been organised by Folkestone and Hythe district council. No fire-related injuries have been reported.”A spokesperson for Kent police said: “Kent police was called at around 1.20am on Saturday 19 September 2026 to reports of a fire at a hotel on Marine Parade, Folkestone.“Officers remain in attendance to assist traffic flow while our Kent fire and rescue service colleagues work to tackle the fire.”Explore more on these topicsKentHospitality industryHotelsFirefightersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Baby born via surrogate can leave Texas for treatment in California, court rules | Texas | The Guardian
description: Ruling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate rejected couple’s request for abortion
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Ruling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate rejected couple’s request for abortion
Content: McKenna West, left, arrivers with her legal team for a court hearing in Dallas in August.Photograph: LM Otero/APView image in fullscreenMcKenna West, left, arrivers with her legal team for a court hearing in Dallas in August.Photograph: LM Otero/APTexasBaby born via surrogate can leave Texas for treatment in California, court rulesRuling latest step in legal fight over medically fragile child born after surrogate rejected couple’s request for abortionUwa Ede-OsifoSat 19 Sep 2026 18.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 18.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Texas supreme court has decided that the month-old infant that surrogate McKenna West gave birth to can be relocated to Los Angeles, a Thursday ruling that came weeks after aCaliforniacourt had recognized the biological parents’ custody rights.“Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the courtwrotein a Thursday order, referring to the baby’s rare severe heart defect. West had attempted to block the biological parents from removing the child from Texas and taking him to a hospital in Los Angeles where the couple live.The court cited testimony from the infant’sTexasphysician, who described the window for an ICU-to-ICU transfer as short and “ripe now”.West’s attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment about the Thursday ruling.The infant, named Rumi by his biological parents, has hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a condition that impedes blood flow and requires extensive surgery. Without treatment, the defect can be fatal.The condition was detected when the baby was a fetus, prompting California couple Nausheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed to ask that West terminate the pregnancy. West, who resides in Alaska, traveled to Texas, where abortion is illegal, to deliver the child.West and her legal team maintain that the couple attempted to force her into having the procedure, while lawyers for Gilkar and Ahmed say that West initially agreed to the abortion, before blindsiding them with the legal battle for custody.The case has stoked enormous debate around abortion and parental rights, particularly in conservative mediasphere.Texas attorney general Ken Paxton elevated the dispute’s national profile, when he intervened to ensure the baby would receive medical care after his birth.West had appealed to the US supreme court, suggesting Gilkar and Ahmed would put the baby into end-of-life care at a hospice rather than continue treatment for the heart defect.West was seeking to be informed about the baby’s medical status and to “advocate for her rights,” according to court documents.“Ordinarily, MW would have been deemed [the baby’s] mother under Texas law by virtue of giving birth to him. But because of the unlawful California judgment, she has been dismissed with prejudice from the Texas proceedings and denied any information,” West’s lawyerswrotein a court filing, using West’s initials.The couple’s attorneys responded in a court filing saying “there is simply no truth whatsoever” to the hospice claim. They argued that if the court sided with West it would sow confusion over who had authority to dictate and consent to medical decisions for the child.Gilkar told a Dallas court in August that Rumi was “the most beautiful person”.“He’s the love of our lives. He’s suffering a lot,” she said.Explore more on these topicsTexasReproductive rightsCaliforniaWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: President had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled caution
Content: In the past, Trump has said that only he was necessary to prevent AI disaster.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreenIn the past, Trump has said that only he was necessary to prevent AI disaster.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APDonald TrumpTrump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents growPresident had brushed away suggestions to slow down AI technology, even as his own party counseled cautionEdward Helmorein New YorkSat 19 Sep 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpon Saturday said he would appoint anartificial intelligenceczar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan.As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry.The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear thatChinawill best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even manyRepublicanshave been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety.Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companiesRead more“I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post.But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned.Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”.“Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”.The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”.The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”.The post cameafter an earlier missivein which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way.Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”.Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector.The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs recently as Monday,Trump argued on social mediathat his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China.“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote.Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change.The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collectiveconducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”.Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after manyRepublicanshave rejected his hands-off approach.Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpAI (artificial intelligence)Trump administrationRepublicansUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: California warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passenger | California | The Guardian
description: Health authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six counties
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Health authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six counties
Content: Pennsylvania has seen four measles-related deaths as the US grapples with the fallout from increasing vaccine hesitancy.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPennsylvania has seen four measles-related deaths as the US grapples with the fallout from increasing vaccine hesitancy.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesCaliforniaCalifornia warns of measles exposure in six counties from unvaccinated train passengerHealth authorities work to notify people who were exposed to person who traveled through at least six countiesMarina DunbarSat 19 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCaliforniapublic health officials are warning of a possible measles exposure spanning multiple counties after an infected and unvaccinated passenger traveled through the state viaAmtraktrains and thruway buses.The warning comes as the US faces its largest measles resurgence inmore than three decades, fueled largely by growing vaccine hesitancy.TheCaliforniadepartment of public health said the traveler passed through at least six counties – Alameda, Butte, Kern, Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Joaquin – while making multiple transfers.RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreakRead moreOfficials said the passenger entered California on an Amtrak train that arrived in Los Angeles on 10 September. From there, the traveler continued to Bakersfield before heading through Stockton, Oroville, Sacramento and Emeryville, eventually leaving California for Denver.Health officials said passengers who were onboard thesame trains or buses, as well as people who were inside the stations along the route on the dates involved, have been exposed to measles.The state said it is working with federal partners and local health departments to identify and notify people who may have been exposed.“This case, along with previous measles outbreaks in California this year, serve as reminders of the importance of vaccination against measles,” assistant state public health officer Rita Nguyen said in a statement. “The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is safe and provides long-lasting protection against measles. Vaccination protects both our own families and those who are too young to be fully vaccinated.”Pennsylvania is currently dealing with the country’s worst active measles outbreak. The Pennsylvania health department announced on Wednesday that 731 cases have been confirmed across 38 counties so far this year. At leastfour peoplein the state have died from measles-related illness.Pennsylvania is now seekingemergency assistancefrom the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as the outbreak continues to spread. State officials have warned, however, that the request could be withdrawn unless the CDC publicly recognizes the four measles-associated deaths, something the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, previously instructed the CDCnot to do.And as the death toll from the outbreak continues to rise, Kennedyheadlinedthe Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense earlier this week, an group he led for nearly a decade.He only addressed the measles outbreak in Pennsylvania once during his speech, instead peddling unfounded fears about vaccines at a time when health experts are urgently encouraging people to vaccinate against measles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.”The California warning also follows another recent mass-exposure incident involving Amtrak.Earlier this week, it was reported that a person infected with measles traveled onboard an Amtrak train from Sedalia, Missouri, to Chicago, Illinois, resulting inmore than 250 peoplebeing exposed to the virus in Jackson county alone.This month, it was also revealed that the Trump administration changed howmeasles deaths are countedduring the outbreak. The CDC is now relying on data from the National Center for Health Statistics, which is used to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaMMRInfectious diseasesRobert F Kennedy JrTrump administrationHealthWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lindsay Clancy ex-husband says ‘I think I did the best I could’ | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trial
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trial
Content: Lindsay Clancy in court earlier this month.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersView image in fullscreenLindsay Clancy in court earlier this month.Photograph: Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger/ReutersMassachusettsLindsay Clancy ex-husband says ‘I think I did the best I could’Patrick Clancy and wife Rachel Danis to speak publicly on 60 Minutes on Sunday about Massachusetts murder trialEdward HelmoreSat 19 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Clancy and his wife Rachel Danis are set to describe their experiences of theMassachusettstriple-murder trial of his former wife Lindsay Clancy, with Clancy telling 60 Minutes: “I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.”The couple will on Sunday night make their first public comments on the case. CBS has been trailing excerpts of the broadcast.The interviews with the pair marks a second significant media “get” for 60 Minutes since it came under new leadership earlier this year. Last week, it secured an interview with a pilot who was rescued by special forces after being shot down over Iran.The Clancy interviews come as Massachusetts prosecutors are set to decide later this month whether to retry Lindsay Clancy over the killings of the couple’s three children – Cora, five; Dawson, three; and Callan, eight months old – in January 2023. A hearing is slated for 29 September at Plymouth superior court.A trial over the summer riveted public attention and ended in a mistrial when a single juror rejected the Clancy’s defense position that she had carried out the killings because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis that meant she could not be found criminally responsible for her actions.The trial shed light on the little-understood mental health condition, and the resulting mistrial sharply divided public opinion. The single holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, came forward last week to say he thought enough physical evidence and key witness testimony presented at trial proved Clancy “knew exactly what she was doing and planned [it]”.Patrick Clancy, who testified in the prosecution phase of the trial but has supported his former wife, has been subject to intense speculation outside the courtroom from online content creators and conspiracists.Earlier this month, an attorney for Clancy threatened legal “consequences” over what he called a “relentless, escalating and destructive defamation campaign” targeting his client.“Enough is enough – this spread of blatant and baseless falsehoods must stop,” attorney Howard Cooper said. “Those responsible should understand that there will be consequences, and every appropriate measure will be pursued to hold them accountable, including legally.”According to excerpts of the 60 Minutes interviews released ahead of airtime, Patrick Clancy talks about his grief, his memories of his children, and conspiracy theories.Clancy tells correspondent Ross Douthat he still talks to his kids “all the time” and asked them for help. Asked if they do, Clancy responds: “I like to believe they do. It’s a way I stay connected to them.”Clancy, who discovered his three children after finding his injured wife lying in snow below a second floor window and is now paralyzed from the waist down, also told the news program: “I think I did the best I could with what I had at the time, and I live with the outcome. I live with it every day, but I think I did the best I could.”The Clancys repeatedly sought psychiatric and mental care for the young mother in the months before the incident, and have since filed a civil lawsuit alleging negligence and over-prescription of medications on the the part of two health professionals and healthcare providers.In the released interview excerpts, Danis, 37, discusses how she met Patrick, their marriage, and defends her husband against the theories that have appeared online.“I don’t understand how the story’s been so twisted, but I would hope people know that Pat is, as I said before, the most selfless father and supportive partner,” Danis, an infertility specialist, tells the program.The couple met while jogging and Patrick moved to New York and married earlier this year, she says. “I was just a girl that met a guy running in Central Park on a really cold Saturday, and I don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.”Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy? | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Fed chair presided over unanimous decision to raise interest rates despite intense campaign from White House
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Fed chair presided over unanimous decision to raise interest rates despite intense campaign from White House
Content: Kevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in Washington DC on 16 September.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in Washington DC on 16 September.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAFederal ReserveAnalysisKevin Warsh may be the adult in the room. But can he calm the US economy?Eduardo PorterFed chair presided over unanimous decision to raise interest rates despite intense campaign from White HouseSat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareIn the end, Kevin Warsh’s Federal Reserve acquitted itself well. For all the uncertainty he had sparked at the previous meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee, when he refused to provide any indication of what he was prepared to do to tame stubborn inflation, the chair on Wednesday presided over a unanimous decision toraise interest ratesfor the first time in three years.“Today’s action starts to show that we’re serious about this,” he said at the press conference after the meeting, with “this” meaning inflation in excess of the Fed’s 2% target for over five years. Welcome though it was, his embrace of economic orthodoxy nonetheless did little to dispel the Keystone Cops quality of governance in Donald Trump’s US.Warsh’s resolve – raising rates just a few weeks before elections that will determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress – appeared even more resolute in the face of a veiled threat from White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett, who pointed out to his chums on Fox that “if you want an independent Fed, then one thing the Fed does is it stays out of the way of elections”.The central bankers’ parsimonious comments in the press conference following the meeting made a sharp contrast with the more unhinged commentary from other members of the administration, including the president himself, who earlier this month celebrated the resilience of the labor market with a mind-boggling threat to “STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT” unless the Fed cut interest rates.Trump has yet to turn on Warsh in the way he did on his predecessor, Jerome “numbskull” Powell. But the signs are ominous. After the rate hike, Trump went ballistic – spewing more of the random, incoherent thoughts that have become his trademark. “Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World,” he wrote on social media, despite recalcitrant inflation and a budget deficit that is likely to exceed $2tn this year. He again demanded the powers that be to “LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!”Yet more significant than the contrast between Warsh’s words and the incongruent economic rhetoric from the White House is the tension between the Fed’s decision on Wednesday and pretty much every other initiative from the administration, from the volley of tariffs against imports from everywhere to the war in Iran to Trump’s “promise” of $5,000 a head if he wins the midterms to treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s desperate efforts to pull interest rates down even as the Fed is raising them.All things considered, financial markets reacted relatively calmly to the day’s events. For sure, the S&P 500 index took a nosedive on Wednesday afternoon, closing some 0.4% lower at the thought that the Fed would likely now raise rates again in December and twice in 2027. The yield on the 10-year bond rose sharply, again surpassing 5%. But investors appear to have bought – for now at least – that whatever deranged policies may emerge from the rest of the administration, monetary policy will remain comparatively sane.Investors should probably remain on their toes, though. A rational Trump would probably thank Warsh for his hawkishness. There might be a plausible argument to keep rates where they were because inflation is driven by temporary forces, like a war. Yet had the Fed staid its hand, or – goodness forbid – cut rates as the president has demanded, the bloodbath in the treasury market would have been gruesome, as investors were forced to accept that the chair of the central bank would not stand up to the nut who appointed him.By contrast, by raising rates and demonstrating he is serious about curbing inflation, the Fed is likely to calm market jitters and reduce long-term inflation expectations, which will ultimately redound in lower yields on treasury bonds, allowing for lower interest rates on mortgages and other long-term loans that matter to businesses and consumers.More clown cars are likely on the way. In his fury on Wednesday, Trump again threatened to stop trading with countries that have a surplus with the US – a proposition so devoid of sense that it is hard to comprehend, let alone critique. The war in Iran is likely to continue throughout the administration, bringing more volatility to energy markets.Even Bessent seems to be losing his hold on reality. Vexed overrising treasury yields– which are raising the cost of servicing the government’s Brobdingnagian debts – the man whom markets believed would play the role of adult in the Oval Office on matters of economic policy has started to emulate the desperate government officials he once pummelled into submission.Bessentbuilt a reputationin financial circles in 1996 as part of the team built by George Soros and Stanley Druckenmiller that pushed the British pound out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism. They made a tidy profit by teaching hapless British ministers that however many pounds they bought to defend the exchange rate, they could never overcome a market determined to sell. Today, Bessent has taken the losing side of that trade, betting that he can buy enough treasuries to bring long-term interest rates down.The Fed on Wednesday likely helped Bessent’s cause. Still, the peculiar image of a central bank raising interest rates while the treasury secretary resorts to gunslinger tactics to lower them won’t restore trust in the creditworthiness of the United States. (“I am the house,” he proclaimed, hoping to achieve a steely gaze, rhetorically twirling and reholstering his revolver. “You can bet against me if you want.”)Can an unexpectedly solid Fed chair stabilize the ship of an American economy discombobulated by slapstick policymaking? Here’s hoping. But holding one’s breath may be a bad idea.Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletterBeing Thereon SubstackExplore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS economyDonald TrumpUS politicsTrump administrationanalysisShareReuse this content
