title: Brighton demolish champions Arsenal 3-0 to mark anniversary in style | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Brighton produced a superb performance in a 3-0 home win over the champions Arsenal, with goals from Gross, Kostoulas and Andrés
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Brighton produced a superb performance in a 3-0 home win over the champions Arsenal, with goals from Gross, Kostoulas and Andrés
Content: Brighton's Chema Andrés celebrates scoring their third goal with Luka Vuskovic.Photograph: Tony O'Brien/ReutersView image in fullscreenBrighton's Chema Andrés celebrates scoring their third goal with Luka Vuskovic.Photograph: Tony O'Brien/ReutersPremier LeagueBrighton demolish champions Arsenal 3-0 to mark anniversary in styleEd Aaronsat the Amex StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 12.06 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo much for the new Invincibles.Arsenalwere brought back down to earth with a shuddering bump by a scintillating display from Brighton as Fabian Hürzeler’s vibrant side celebrated the club’s 125th anniversary in style.The special edition shirts they wore to mark the occasion will end up being collector’s items after thePremier Leaguechampions were ripped apart. Arsenal were attempting to record an eighth successive victory in all competitions to start the new campaign for the first time since 1903 when they were still known as Woolwich Arsenal.‘They deserved to win’: Mikel Arteta left humbled by Brighton defeatRead moreInstead, it is Brighton – inspired by first-half goals from the veteran stand-in captain, Pascal Gross, and the exciting teenager Charalampos Kostoulas – who find themselves in third place, two points behind Arsenal. New signing Chema Andrés made the points safe from a corner 12 minutes into the second half. That meant Arsenal conceded three goals for the first time since December 2023 in all competitions and Mikel Arteta will be most concerned that it could easily have been more against the division’s top scorers, 16 in five games.The home supporters waved blue and white flags before kick-off as the players swapped their usual kits for a deep blue limited edition shirt that was inspired by their first season in Southern League Division Two in 1901. That has caused controversy among fans after originally being listed on sale for £150 in a package that included a letter of authenticity from the club owner, Tony Bloom, and a keyring. Given this is the only time they will wear it, those who shelled out will be pleased they did now.What has made Brighton’s goalscoring exploits so impressive is that they have managed it almost completely without their first-choice attack due to injury, while last year’s top scorer, Danny Welbeck, was sold to Chelsea in the summer. Georginio Rutter returned as a late substitute, but the damage had already been inflicted by then thanks to Gross and Kostoulas.Jurriën Timber looked leggy on his first start since March and Bruno Guimarães was disappointing on his first Premier League start for Arsenal. Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy and drive in midfield was sorely missed in the week he was recalled to the England squad.View image in fullscreenPascal Gross fires home Brighton’s first goal against Arsenal.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersFrom the first whistle, Kostoulas – signed last summer for £30m – led Brighton’s fearsome press that provoked Arsenal into a number of uncharacteristic errors, including a misplaced pass from Guimarães that forced David Raya to tip a deflected effort from the 19-year-old around the post. Raya was also guilty of donating possession to the lively Yasin Ayari in a dangerous position. Arsenal and Arteta looked rattled for the first time this season.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAston Villa grab victory despite late Spurs goals as De Zerbi’s side are booed offRead moreChristos Tzolis could not take a rare opportunity on the break after being picked out by Bukayo Saka and they were made to pay for it just after the half-hour mark. Perhaps wary of the unmarked Ayari to their left, Gabriel Magalhães and Riccardo Calafiori were slow to challenge Gross when he received the ball on the edge of Arsenal’s area from Kostoulas and the veteran picked his spot perfectly off the inside of the post.Ayari came close to doubling the lead five minutes before half-time when he fired into the side-netting before Kostoulas did. Saka had just spurned a great chance to equalise after being set up by Martin Ødegaard and once again Gabriel was guilty of ball watching as the Greek striker thumped the ball past Raya from 25 yards.Arteta immediately sent out Max Dowman, who scoredtwo goals against Ipswichin midweek, to warm up. He must have been tempted to throw the 16-year-old on at the start of the second half as Kostoulas went close again for Brighton.It was too late once Andrés nodded in at the far post from a pinpoint Gross corner. “Are you Tottenham in disguise?” sang the delighted Brighton fans.Arteta introduced Dowman with 10 minutes remaining as he emptied his bench. But having been knocked off the top of the Premier League on goal difference courtesy of this heavy loss, there will be plenty of soul-searching during the three-week international break for the Arsenal manager.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBrighton & Hove AlbionArsenalmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Belmont Park is back: inside New York’s $555m bet on horse racing | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: The storied Long Island racetrack, rebuilt with a $455m state loan, is smaller, sleeker and designed for a changing audience. Can it create the public needed to sustain it?
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The storied Long Island racetrack, rebuilt with a $455m state loan, is smaller, sleeker and designed for a changing audience. Can it create the public needed to sustain it?
Content: Horses compete in the third race on the opening day of the rebuilt Belmont Park in Elmont, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHorses compete in the third race on the opening day of the rebuilt Belmont Park in Elmont, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianHorse racingBelmont Park is back: inside New York’s $555m bet on horse racingThe storied Long Island racetrack, rebuilt with a $455m state loan, is smaller, sleeker and designed for a changing audience. Can it create the public needed to sustain it?Bryan Armen Grahamat Belmont Park in Elmont, New YorkSat 19 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHenry Miller stood on the trackside apron of the new Belmont Park on Friday trying to decide what he thought of the place.“It has to grow on me,” said Miller, a 59-year-old retired sanitation worker from Brooklyn’s Bedford-Stuyvesant neighborhood who has been coming toNew Yorkracetracks for 47 years. “For me, it’s too much concrete. I don’t think it’s as friendly as the old Belmont.”He missed the familiar trees and the ivy-covered brick facades. He missed the old bar and grandstand. Most of all, he was still mourning Aqueduct, the ramshackle Queens racetrackthat shuttered in Juneas part of the $555m experiment that has made the reimagined Belmont possible.“That broke my heart,” Miller said.For the first time in more than three years, horses were racing at Belmont Park on Friday. But almost everything else about the 121-year-old race course just outside New York city limits had changed.‘I’m going to miss this place’: Aqueduct bids farewell after 132 years as New York City’s racetrackRead moreThe cavernous grandstand that once loomed over the home straight is gone, replaced by a smaller, glass-fronted building designed for a sport that no longer expects tens of thousands of people to turn up on an ordinary afternoon. The old Belmont had a footprint of roughly 1.25m sq ft; its five-storey replacement is less than a quarter of the size, at about 300,000 sq ft. EvenBig Sandy, the famously deep mile-and-a-half dirt track that became synonymous withthe grueling final leg of US horse racing’s Triple Crown, has been relegated to the past, recreated with the same soil composition used at Saratoga with the finish line repositioned for a longer stretch run. There are four rebuilt racing surfaces in all, a paddock 50% larger than its predecessor and roughly 20 acres of newly accessible green space.Inside, the aesthetic is almost aggressively modern: bright white walls, gleaming floors and long, clean expanses that feel more THX 1138 than old-school racetrack. As one Fox Sports production assistant could be overheard describing it: “It looks kind of like an airport, but it’s beautiful.”It is a dramatic break with the Belmont that has stood on this corner of suburban Long Island in some form since 1905, a piece of New York cultural furniture along the Queens-Nassau County line whose hulking structure and sweeping turns were recognizable even to people who never studied a racing form. Secretariatsurged into history by 31 lengthshere, generations before American Pharoahended a 37-year Triple Crown hoodoo. The track appeared on screen everywhere frommultiple Woody Allen filmsto aFrederick Wiseman documentarytoGodfrey Reggio’s Koyaanisqatsi.What opened on Friday was not simply a renovated sports venue, but New York’s half-billion dollar wager that horse racing can shrink its physical footprint, upgrade the experience and find enough new customers to survive a gambling landscape that has largely moved beyond it.The $455m state loan that financed the reconstruction was accompanied by another $100m from the New York Racing Association, the nonprofit that operates Belmont, Saratoga and, until recently, Aqueduct. The state money is to be repaid from NYRA’s cut of slot-machine revenue from the Resorts World casino, which sits alongside the now-closed Aqueduct property, only nine miles from Belmont.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Belmont ParkBottom: Horses are led out for the fourth race.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianAt a ribbon-cutting on Friday morning, New York governorKathy Hochulcalled the loan a calculated investment in the future of the industry.“Three and a half years ago, we made a big bet on Belmont,” Hochul said. “We made the bet because we saw the enormous economic potential.”She described the goal as an “international racing hub” that could double as a concert and entertainment space – “a versatile venue” intended not only for racing fans but “the entire community”.The bargain came with significant consequences. NYRA consolidated its downstate operation at Belmont, bringing an end to 132 years of racing at Aqueduct and leaving New York City without a thoroughbred racetrack for the first time since the 1821 opening of Union Course in what is now Woodhaven, Queens. The roughly 100-acre Aqueduct site is being returned to the state for redevelopment, with Hochul’s administration planning for a mixed-use redevelopment of housing, retail, community facilities and open space.Belmont itself has been reconceived around a blunt reality. The old structure, which re-opened in 1968 after a five-year rebuild, was engineered for crowds of a scale that rarely materialized outside the biggest racing days – like the 120,139 who turned out forSmarty Jones’ doomed Triple Crown bidin 2004. Its replacement will hold roughly 10,000 people inside, while access to the infield and temporary seating will allow the property to accommodate around 50,000 for the Belmont Stakes.The new facility will stage a 46-day fall meet featuring 72 stakes worth $17.7m, before theBelmont Stakesreturns next year and the Breeders’ Cup comes back to New York for the first time since 2005.Fittingly for a venue being pitched as an international racing destination, the first winner at the new Belmont on Friday afternoon was a UK product. Lisa Joy, a British homebred owned by Andrew Rosen, won the opening mile-and-a-quarter maiden on the inner turf for Hall of Fame trainer Shug McGaughey and jockey Antonio Fresu.McGaughey, a stalwart of New York racing who denied Sunday Silence the Triple Crownwhen Easy Goer won the Belmont in 1989, was enthusiastic about the rebuilt track even as he acknowledged the place was still finding its feet.“I think it’s a beautiful place,” he said. “It’s different than what I expected. We just need to get the kinks out and get the people in it and it’ll be really special. I think it’s going to be great when everything gets settled in.”For longtime patrons, getting used to the new Belmont may take a little longer.Kathie Riccobono, a 74-year-old from nearby Garden City who has been coming to Belmont for half a century, was impressed by what she saw but immediately identified what she missed about the old place.“The crowds,” she said.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Fans attend opening day.Bottom: Racehorse Osmosis is walked before the first race.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The Guardian“It’s a big change,” Riccobono said. “Change is good, but you’re not going to have the old Belmont like we used to. The old people, there’s not many of us left. And the new group don’t know nothing about horses.”Attendance was capped at 6,000 during opening weekend and will drop to 4,000 beginning next week while construction continues. Right now only the first two floors are open, while the remaining three are expected to be finished early next year.The transformation is perhaps most obvious in the way spectators are distributed. General-admission customers occupy the first floor, apron and backyard, with bars and food concessions including Big Red’s, Silks, Homestretch Market and the Trackside Lounge accessible without reservations or cover charges. One floor up, the Turf Club, Overlook and Stretch View require reservations. Above them, still under construction, will be the suites and boxes.The prices rise accordingly. A box seat runs between $55 and $75, while the Overlook and Stretch View can cost $100 to $150 more per person and the Turf Club charges $75 per person, climbing to $150 for its premium menu.General admission, at least, remains cheap. After opening weekend, tickets will cost $7 in advance or $10 at the gate, the same price NYRA charges at Saratoga. Yet some regulars say the cost of admission tells only part of the story.The Fair Hill Five: horse racing’s bizarre transatlantic betting coup – explainedRead moreMiller was among them. Parking, he noted, costs $20. Factor in other costs like admission and a program and the economics begin to look different.“You’re spending $35 or $45 before you even make a wager. It’s not going to get people in the doors when you have the other option to stay home and gamble or bet on the app,” Miller said. “That $45 is going on a parlay.”The same tension can be found in the new backyard. NYRA has promoted a space roughly five times larger than its predecessor as a communal gathering place, but coolers and outside beverages are prohibited, eliminating a longstanding way for families and groups to keep the cost of a day at the races down.For anyone who spent time at Aqueduct, the distinction is significant. Miller called it “the poor man’s track”.“I don’t know if there’s another racetrack that you could take public transportation to, directly to the track,” he said. “Everybody knows everyone. The jockeys are even closer with the guys. It’s more interaction.”Belmont, he said, had always been “more prestige or boutique”. And he had noticed the same trends surfacing elsewhere.“I was down at Gulfstream, I was at Churchill [Downs]. They’re all gearing towards this boutique kind of thing,” Miller said. “The average horseplayer, the nickel-and-dime guy who keeps the industry going is going to get squeezed out.”Aqueduct was nobody’s idea of luxury. By its final years it was dim, dilapidated and increasingly swallowed by the casino next door. But entrance was free, the A train stopped outside and patrons could bring their own food. Regulars carved out territories around particular tables, simulcast monitors and betting windows.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Miss Snaffles is led by a staff member before the first race.Bottom: A fan wears a horse racing themed bowtie.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianThat accessibility helped make Aqueduct an increasingly rare thing in American sport: athird placewhere anyone could walk in off the street and stay the whole day without spending very much. Its democratic crowd reflected the borough that surrounded it: a racially and economically mixed collection of horseplayers, families, retirees and obsessive handicappers. Belmont remains accessible by public transport, with the Long Island Rail Road stopping at the neighboring Elmont-UBS Arena station. But Aqueduct’s location directly on a major subway line gave it a different relationship with the city.On Aqueduct’s final day in June, 6,866 people came for what felt alternately like a celebration and a wake. Many posed for photographs in front of the Secretariat mural or pocketed small keepsakes. Others wondered aloud whether they would make the trip east to Belmont at all.“Probably not,” one retired horseman turned Aqueduct regular, Robert Bourget, said that afternoon when asked whether he would go. “They’ll charge too much to get in.”Not everyone on Friday regarded the transformation with suspicion. Joseph Gillespie, a 60-year-old retiree from Levittown who was at the track with his wife, Eileen, has been coming to Belmont for 35 years and said he expects to visit even more often now that he is retired. He called the new building “very nice” and was unbothered by what he had seen of the prices: even a $12 beer, he reckoned, “is not so bad these days”.Gillespie also understood immediately what NYRA appeared to be aiming for.“I think they’re trying to make this like a Keeneland destination type of thing,” he said. “People get fancied up. Hopefully you don’t get the riff-raff. Not that there’s anything wrong with that. Hopefully it thrives.”The question extends well beyond New York. More than 40 American racetracks have closed since 2000 as the sport has contended with an aging fanbase, declining attendance and a gambling marketplace that bears little resemblance to the one that made horse racing a mass spectator sport.Another signpost of the contraction arrived this year when FanDuel TV, the former TVG and for more than two decades a central hub of American racing coverage, announced plansto wind down its television operation. The network, which reaches about 30m households, is cutting its workforce by roughly 60% and plans to eliminate studio production by the end of the year before ceasing linear racing broadcasts altogether in 2027. FanDuel’s wagering platforms, meanwhile, will continue operating.For much of the 20th century, the racetrack possessed an enormous house edge: in many places it was one of the only legal ways to gamble. That monopoly began disappearing with the spread of lotteries, casinos and off-track betting and has been obliterated in the mobile sports-betting era. Americans wagered nearly $167bn on sports in 2025, compared with roughly $11bn on US horse racing.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Fans wait for the fourth race.Bottom: A racehorse is washed after the third race.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianThe irony is that Belmont’s rebirth comes as horse racing itself loses ground, but that may be precisely the point. Across American sports, venues have increasinglybecome anchors for year-round economiesof restaurants, shops, hotels and entertainment rather than self-contained destinations. Belmont now has its own version: a $455m racetrack only footsteps froman expanding luxury shopping villageand UBS Arena, the 17,255-seat home of the NHL’s New York Islanders.Miller didn’t need the statistics to understand racing’s demographic problem.“I’m 59 now, so like my cousins say, ‘I’m in the departure lounge now. I’m not in arrivals,’” he said. “So you got to get the younger people to get more involved.”He could remember when Aqueduct on an otherwise unremarkable Wednesday or Thursday might attract 15,000 or 20,000 people. The Meadowlands on a Friday or Saturday night could be the place to be even for people who had little interest in gambling. That, he believed, was the challenge facing the new Belmont in an age when the casino is already sitting in everyone’s pocket.“You got to give a person a reason to come,” he said.Some of the arrivals Miller was talking about were plainly visible on Friday for a re-opening that was intended as a showcase. On a sun-splashed 83F (28C) afternoon beneath a cloudless sky, a sold-out crowd of about 6,000 filled the partially completed grounds, country singer Dierks Bentley performed an abbreviated set and the nine-race card was built around the $1m Jockey Club Gold Cup and one of world’s most famous equine athletes today.Forever Young arrived at Belmont as a bonafide globetrotting star. Friday marked the five-year-old Japanese horse’s 16th career start at his 10th different track. The strapping bay stallion had won 11 of his first 15 races, including the 2025 Breeders’ Cup Classic, never finishing outside the top three.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHis following had traveled too. Hordes of younger fans crowded the paddock and apron for a glimpse of him, includingmany groups dressedin elaborate anime-inspired cosplay – a strikingly different image of the racing enthusiast from the aging horseplayers the sport has spent years of hand-wringing about losing. They were not the traditional railbirds Miller remembered from Aqueduct, but neither were they indifferent newcomers being coaxed into caring about the sport with trackside concerts and food vouchers.Forever Young duly supplied the reborn Belmont with its first marquee moment, sitting comfortably behind the early pace before sweeping to the lead around the far turn, winning by three and a quarter lengths and pushing his career earnings beyond $32m. Even that was apparently not enough to satisfy his famously demanding trainer. Yoshito Yahagi pronounced himself only “50% satisfied”, estimating Forever Young at about 80% fitness before his attempt next month to become only the second horse after Tiznow to win back-to-back Breeders’ Cup Classics.“I think I will never see again a horse like this in my life and my career,” Yahagi said through a translator.The mania around Forever Young offered one glimpse of the audience NYRA hopes to cultivate, but attracting a new generation of fans is only one part of its attempt to remake Belmont for a changing sport. The physical plant itself has been designed around year-round use. Alongside the traditional mile-and-a-half dirt track and two rebuilt turf courses is a new one-mile Tapeta oval that will become the exclusive racing surface during the winter, allowing NYRA to consolidate a calendar once divided between Belmont and Aqueduct onto a single property.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: Racehorse Cream of the Crop and jockey Antonio Fresu exit the track after the second raceBottom: Racehorses compete in the fourth race.Photograph: Pamela Smith/The GuardianEven the Belmont Stakes itself may not return unchanged. NYRA isconsidering shortening its signature racefrom its traditional mile-and-a-half distance to a mile and a quarter, with NYRA CEO Dave O’Rourke arguing that the historic distance no longer reflects what modern breeders are producing.Taken together, the changes make Belmont an unusually literal experiment in the future of American horse racing. The old model was a gigantic betting hall that happened to surround a racetrack. The new one is smaller, brighter and more flexible: part racetrack, part entertainment complex, with the biggest crowds concentrated into a handful of destination events and premium spaces available for customers willing to pay for them.There were signs Friday that the experiment might work. Riccobono, for all her nostalgia for the old Belmont, was struck by the mood around her.“Everybody is cheerful,” she said. “And that’s how it always is at Belmont.”After 50 years of coming here, she was less interested in delivering a verdict than appreciating the fact that she had made it to another incarnation of the place.“I feel lucky to be alive,” she said. “I feel lucky I’m here.”For one afternoon, at least, the formula clicked. Six thousand people filled the grounds. Families spread across the new backyard, old horseplayers filled the tables and benches at trackside and toiled over their forms (or tablets), while younger fans celebrated the Japanese stallion who had made his name around the world. Whether the same energy can be reproduced on an ordinary Thursday in November – without a $32m global superstar, a concert or the novelty of seeing the place for the first time – will be the more consequential test.Explore more on these topicsHorse racingBelmont StakesBreeders' CupKathy HochulNew YorkNew York IslandersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Union Jack Classic fails to spark on the pitch but electric atmosphere fires up Wembley | College football | The Guardian
description: Arizona State beat Kansas 24-17 at Wembley in a humdrum game that will be better remembered for the noise and colour that surrounded it
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Arizona State beat Kansas 24-17 at Wembley in a humdrum game that will be better remembered for the noise and colour that surrounded it
Content: Arizona State’s Jaren Hamilton scores a touchdown during the Union Jack Classic at Wembley.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAView image in fullscreenArizona State’s Jaren Hamilton scores a touchdown during the Union Jack Classic at Wembley.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PACollege footballUnion Jack Classic fails to spark on the pitch but electric atmosphere fires up WembleyThe Arizona State Sun Devils cantered to victory in the first ever Union Jack Classic in front of a noisy crowd – despite thousands of empty seatsSean Ingleat WembleySat 19 Sep 2026 18.36 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 19.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou sensed that Britain’s first US college football game in nearly 40 years was going to be a very different experience when Wembley Way began to reverberate to the sound of steel, muscle and a few whoops long before kick-off.The noise came from the Arizona State Sun Devils’ marching band, who were so energetic their horns and trombones swished from left to right like air raid lights hunting a target as they played.Soon afterwards there came a risposte from the Kansas Jayhawks’ marching band, along with more cheers from the large crowd outside the stadium.Watching on, two relaxed police officers were taking it all in when they were approached by a fan, Ian Taplin, from Milton Keynes. “I bet you’re glad you are not at Millwall,” he told them, leading them both to smile.View image in fullscreenThe Kansas University marching band in action before the Union Jack Classic at Wembley.Photograph: Josh Smith/PPAUK/ShutterstockIt was a scene that lingered during a humdrum match, played out over a long three hours and 37 minutes. Because, even in the lulls, those marching bands never let the atmosphere drop. The Jayhawks’ band played the Beatles Twist and Shout and Cameo’s Word Up. The Sun Devils’ band responded with Salt-N-Pepa’s Push It. It made for a great – and unique – atmosphere.NC State’s unfathomable last-second blunder gifts Vanderbilt miracle winRead moreAnd the game itself? Well, let’s just say the Union Jack Classic did not live up to its billing. It was not a classic. The Arizona State Sun Devils won 24-17, a scoreline that was nowhere near as close as it sounds. Especially as, until the final minutes, the Jayhawks’ offense was as stodgy and uninspiring as suet pudding.Before the game, the Fox Sports analyst Chris Fallica suggested to the Guardian that this match was the equivalent of a lower-tier Premier League or upper-tier Championship match. Think Nottingham Forest versus Coventry. He was soon proved correct.Little happened until the game turned decisively in the space of a minute either side of half-time. At that point Kansas were leading a dull game 7-3, following a 72-yard punt return from Taty Nagy. But then everything changed.View image in fullscreenKeaton Kubecka of Kansas and Arizona State’s Jessiah McGrew take a tumble.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAFirst the Jayhawks’ punter Matthew Gill sliced a kick 17 yards. Then, on the following play, ASU quarterback Cutter Boley found Reed Harris for a 25-yard touchdown to make it 10-7.Then, to rub vinegar into the wound, Jaren Hamilton dropped a shoulder, evaded a tackle, and ran in a 100-yard kick-off return to increase the lead to 17-7. “I had a feeling deep in my soul,” said the man they call Turbo. “I knew something was going to happen.”The game was in effect over when 305lb defensive lineman Hyrum Vaeono recovered a fumble and ran 77 yards to set up a score that made it 24-7. There was a late comeback attempt from Kansas. But it was largely window dressing.Meanwhile as the casual observers left Wembley they had more questions than answers. Was the 46,532 attendance a decent first effort, given the posh seats and executive boxes were full? Or was it a forced fumble, given that organisers had promised a 60,000 crowd?It also seemed strange not to stage the game next weekend, during the three-week Premier League international break. Either way, it wasn’t the greatest of looks to see Wembley’s upper tier empty.View image in fullscreenThe 46,532 attendance at Wembley fell short of the 60,000 crowd promised by organisers.Photograph: Josh Smith/PPAUK/ShutterstockThen again, the atmosphere was good. And this was the start of what the Big 12 conference hopes will be a significant piece of brand-building in Europe.“These schools are obviously getting rewarded financially to come over,” Fallica told the Guardian. “But it’s also about exposure. All these schools have international branches. They want international students to come over. So they are getting their brand out there.”That much was clear as early as the game’s first timeout, with adverts telling the crowd that ASU has launched a London Campus and provides an “education unlike anything in the UK”, pumped on the big screens.Brett Yormack, the commissioner of the Big 12, said that they wanted to follow the NFL by having more games in Europe – and said he hoped to announce next year’s Wembley game soon. “We’re not there yet, but I’m confident we’ll be back,” he said. “It’s been fantastic.”View image in fullscreenArizona State Sun Devils’ marching band at Wembley.Photograph: Malcolm Fell/Focus Images Ltd/ShutterstockThat message was echoed by ASU coach Kenny Dillingham, who described the experience of coming to London as life changing,“We’ve had multiple players saying: ‘Man, I want to come back now. I love this place. London is awesome. I want to come back and spend summer or Christmas out here’.“When they asked me to do this game I said there’s a few things that are just mandatory for me. We’re bringing all 105 players. And our families are going to have a once in a lifetime experience. And our team didn’t flinch. They stepped up, they covered the cost, and they made it an experience that I think everybody and every family member, every player will remember for the rest of their life.”His team clearly bought into the London experience. But whether the feeling is reciprocated between college football and Britain’s capital is likely to remain an open question.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: NC State’s unfathomable last-second blunder gifts Vanderbilt miracle win | College football | The Guardian
description: NC State had the ball, the lead and only six seconds to kill. One extraordinary fumble later, Vanderbilt had completed a 35-31 comeback
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: NC State had the ball, the lead and only six seconds to kill. One extraordinary fumble later, Vanderbilt had completed a 35-31 comeback
Content: Vanderbilt’s Cayden Daniels recovers a fumble in the end zone during the second half against NC State at FirstBank Stadium in Nashville.Photograph: Vanderbilt Athletics/University Images/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVanderbilt’s Cayden Daniels recovers a fumble in the end zone during the second half against NC State at FirstBank Stadium in Nashville.Photograph: Vanderbilt Athletics/University Images/Getty ImagesCollege footballNC State’s unfathomable last-second blunder gifts Vanderbilt miracle winWolfpack fumble with six seconds left proves decisiveVanderbilt recover in end zone for stunning 35-31 winCommodores complete comeback from 17 points downAssociated PressSat 19 Sep 2026 19.02 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 20.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCall this one the Music City Miscue.NC State quarterback CJ Bailey fumbled in the end zone while trying to take an intentional safety in the final seconds and essentially handed Vanderbilt a 35-31 victory no one saw coming in Nashville.Union Jack Classic fails to spark on the pitch but electric atmosphere fires up WembleyRead moreIt was as improbable a finish as theMusic City Miracle, the famous last-second kickoff return in January 2000 that gave the NFL’s Tennessee Titans a 22–16 playoff win over the Buffalo Bills.“I can’t put into words what I felt. ... You get one of those in a lifetime,” Vanderbilt coach Clark Lea said. “We cheated the football gods today and got away with it.”According to ESPN, college football teams were 1,046-1 over the last 20 seasons when having the ball and the lead with 10 seconds to go in a game. The lone loss: Michigan falling to rival Michigan State in 2015.Leading 31-28, Bailey and the Wolfpack (1-2) were attempting to milk the clock on the final snap. They faced a fourth-and-3 play from their five-yard line with six seconds remaining. Bailey could have taken a knee, scrambled out of the end zone or even tossed the ball high into the air as the clock expired.Instead, he paused and then did the unthinkable – coughed it up.Miles Capers knocked the ball out of Bailey’s hands, and Cayden Van Daniels recovered it in the end zone for a touchdown. It capped Vanderbilt’s rally from a 17-0 deficit in the first half.“It’s having true brotherhood,” Capers said. “We trust each other, we’re going to play for each other, and we know that we not out of the fight no matter what.”The ending was reminiscent of Miami’s debacle against Georgia Tech in October 2023, when Hurricanes coach Mario Cristobal chose to run the ball instead of taking a knee with 26 seconds left and no timeouts remaining for Georgia Tech. Miami’s Donald Chaney Jr fumbled, Georgia Tech’s Kyle Canard recovered and the Yellow Jackets won on a 44-yard touchdown pass from Haynes King to Christian Leary.NC State coach Dave Doeren surely will lament his decision. The Wolfpack could have simply punted and played defense for a play or had Bailey do anything else.“It’s just a play where you roll out, and you don’t get tackled,” Doeren said. “You try to burn as much time as you can and then fall to the ground and protect the football. He got hit and didn’t protect the football. The plan was to take a safety, and you’re trying to run out the clock if you can.”NC State, still reeling from a 34-8 loss at Virginia to open the season, was looking for their first road win against a Southeastern Conference opponent since 1977. Vanderbilt (3-0) matched their largest comeback victory since beating Ole Miss in 2012. Vandy’s fumble recovery in the end zone ended up being the team’s only lead of the game.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa grab victory despite late Spurs goals as De Zerbi’s side are booed off | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Tottenham finally scored in the league, twice, but it was too little too late as Aston Villa picked up a first win, 3-2, with Emi Buendía’s the best of the goals
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Tottenham finally scored in the league, twice, but it was too little too late as Aston Villa picked up a first win, 3-2, with Emi Buendía’s the best of the goals
Content: Emi Buendía shoots past James Maddison to score Aston Villa’s clinching third goal.Photograph: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEmi Buendía shoots past James Maddison to score Aston Villa’s clinching third goal.Photograph: ShutterstockPremier LeagueAston Villa grab victory despite late Spurs goals as De Zerbi’s side are booed offPaul MacInnesat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpurs have a remarkable ability to find new ways of inflicting pain on their fanbase and they did it again here, petering out from a strong start into humiliating defeat to confirm their worst ever start to aPremier Leaguecampaign. On the upside, they did get two goals. They were both late consolations, but beggars can’t be choosers.Aston Villa were meanwhile ruthless in claiming their first victory of the season. They capitalised in first-half added time to take the lead while Spurs were temporarily down to 10 men. In the second, Unai Emery’s side were robust in defence and clinical on the counter, and supreme strikes from both Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendía decided the contest. With Johan Manzambi the other goalscorer, there were pleasing signs for the Spaniard’s turbo-charged refit of his team.De Zerbi rips into Spurs players after Villa defeat: ‘Disappointed, sad and frustrated’Read moreZion Suzuki was probably the man of the match and certainly the star of the first half hour. He made a series of saves in the opening phase of the game to deny Spurs the goal they so desperately craved. The highlight perhaps was a double stop from Sávio in the 11th minute, but also worth a mention is the save that denied Archie Gray from a tight angle with his heel. Suzuki made more passes into the final third than any other player on the pitch too, his 14 double the tally of Spurs’ £100m signing Sandro Tonali.All the Japan international’s saves added up to frustration in the ground and that frustration began to affect the tone of the match. Spurs’ supporters were getting a sense that it might be (another) one of those days, and Villa’s players began to relax a little knowing they had a barrier behind them. With direct passes to Jackson regularly troubling the Spurs defence, a chance would surely fall their way eventually.That moment ultimately arrived in first half added time and with one half of Spurs’ central defensive pairing – Micky van de Ven – receiving treatment on the touchline. The captain was being mopped up for a cut cheek as Buendía dinked yet another pass over the Spurs defensive line. It was partially dealt with, but Andy Robertson overplayed and in trying to activate a counterattack, slid the ball blind to John McGinn. The Villa captain whipped the ball back into the box, Boubacar Kamara’s shot was deflected and Manzambi was on hand to scoop a shot into the net from six yards out.View image in fullscreenTottenham fans leave the stadium with their side three goals behind.Photograph: ShutterstockRoberto De Zerbi brought on Mohammed Kudus for the wishy-washy Mateus Fernandes at half-time and the mercurial Ghanaian lifted the roof off the stadium within 15 minutes of his arrival as he poked home from six yards out after a Robertson cross, only for the video assistant referee to pull it back for an offside on the Scotsman.It felt in the moment that that was game over, so fragile was the Spurs sense of confidence. But there was time for Villa to turn the screw, Jackson next to strike with a piece of predatory magic. Latching on to a long kick from Suzuki, Jackson laid the ball off to Manzambi, who quickly returned the pass. The Senegal forward took the ball on his chest, lifted it Gazza-like over the head of Van de Ven and ruthlessly finished right-footed into the bottom corner. Antonin Kinsky got a touch but it wasn’t nearly enough and Jackson celebrated by playing the Roman emperor and turning his thumb down to the camera.With 10 minutes remaining, and Villa camped out on the edge of the Spurs box, Buendía joined the fun with a perfect long-range effort. With minimal backlift it swept round his marker, out beyond the goal and then back in to smash into the top corner of Kinsky’s net.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideTottenham 2-3 Aston Villa key statsShow• Tottenhamhave failed to winany of their previous 48 games in all competitionsin which they’ve conceded the opening goal(D11 L37), with 37 of those games coming in the Premier League (D8 L29).• This is Spurs’worst start to a Premier League seasonafter five games, with two points and a goal difference of -6, eclipsing their 2008-09 start (2 points, -3 goal difference).•Conor Gallagher’s goal(pictuted) ended a run of 492 Premier League minutes without scoring for Tottenham Hotspur, while their first league goal of 2026-27 came with their 67th shot.OptaPhotograph: Andrew Matthews/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Conor Gallagher, coming off the bench with six minutes of normal time remaining, scored within three minutes of his arrival, while Jan Paul van Hecke reduced the deficit to just one with the last touch of the match. But the boos still rose up as fans contemplated the increasing likelihood of another tormented season. This had been billed as a match between two teams with poor form but high hopes. Villa look to have shed the former, can Tottenham still lay claim to the latter?Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTottenham HotspurAston Villamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Alex de Minaur roars back to life as Australia and Poland share spoils in Davis Cup | Tennis | The Guardian
description: World No 9 beats Maks Kasnikowski 6-3, 6-0 in World Group I match before James Duckworth loses to Kamil Majchrzak in Brisbane
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: World No 9 beats Maks Kasnikowski 6-3, 6-0 in World Group I match before James Duckworth loses to Kamil Majchrzak in Brisbane
Content: Alex de Minaur defeats Maks Kaśnikowski as Australia and Poland end day one of Davis Cup World Group I tie all square at Pat Rafter Arena in Brisbane.Photograph: Bradley Kanaris/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex de Minaur defeats Maks Kaśnikowski as Australia and Poland end day one of Davis Cup World Group I tie all square at Pat Rafter Arena in Brisbane.Photograph: Bradley Kanaris/Getty ImagesTennisAlex de Minaur roars back to life as Australia and Poland share spoils in Davis CupWorld No 9 beats Maks Kasnikowski 6-3, 6-0 in World Group I tieJames Duckworth loses to Kamil Majchrzak 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in BrisbaneAustralian Associated PressSat 19 Sep 2026 01.56 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex de Minaur has taken his frustrations out in a Davis Cup thumping to put Australia up 1-0 in their must-win Brisbane tie against Poland, before Kamil Majchrzak edged James Duckworth in a tense two-hour affair.The world No 9, keen to rediscover his mojo after a disappointingsecond-round US Open loss, lit up Pat Rafter Arena on Saturday afternoon with a dominant 6-3 6-0 defeat of world No 231 Maks Kasnikowski.But the tie is all square after Brisbane home town hero Duckworth was defeated by Majchrzak 2-6, 6-3, 6-3 in the second singles match, beforeSunday’s doublesand reverse singles.Australia’s Max Purcell straight back in Davis Cup fold after 18-month anti-doping banRead moreThe first singles match lasted 56 minutes and de Minaur lost just six points in the second set as the Australian No 1 found range on his serve, angles from the baseline and got to the net to finish points with authority.De Minaur roared after breaking for the first time in the fourth game and then, after a tight call went against him with his tail up at 4-1, steadied with back-to-back aces.Kasnikowski saved two set points on serve and forced de Minaur to serve out the first set, which he did with ease before breaking instantly to set the tone for a one-sided second set.View image in fullscreenAlex de Minaur celebrates during the Davis Cup match between Australia and Poland in Brisbane.Photograph: Russell Freeman/AAP“That’s what these ties are all about; get fired up, get the crowd involved and there’s no better feeling,” de Minaur said of his theatrics.“We play outside of Australia for 10 months a year … so being here, in front of a packed crowd, great atmosphere it’s one I’ve missed.“The serve felt great … I had some nice words to it and it’s coming out to play.”Kasnikowski admits he was blown away in his first meeting with a member of the world’s top 10.“It was a unique experience. A really, really tough challenge and happy I put up a little bit of a fight in the first set,” he said.“In the second, Alex increased the level a lot and it was too much for me today.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“He started playing way faster and was making no mistakes.”The hosts looked set to surge ahead 2-0 when Duckworth peeled off five straight games to take the first set and then break early in the third.But Majchrzak broke straight back, then saved two more break points at 3-3, before a string of unforced errors cost Duckworth in his next service game.Sunday’s doubles will be pivotal before de Minaur and Majchrzak meet, just months after the Polish talent beat the Australian in a tight, three-set final in ‘s-Hertogenbosch.If the tie is split 2-2, Duckworth and Kasnikowski are slated to play the decisive fifth rubber, with the winners progressing to next year’s qualifying round and the losers eliminated altogether from the 2027 Cup race that culminates in Italy next November.Australia were upset in Ecuador earlier this year and must win this clash to progress to next year’s qualifying round, where they can then book a place in the eight-team finals in Italy in November.Explore more on these topicsTennisAlex de MinaurDavis CupAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: De Zerbi rips into Spurs players after Villa defeat: ‘Disappointed, sad and frustrated’ | Tottenham Hotspur | The Guardian
description: Roberto De Zerbi tore into his failing Tottenham team after their 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa, saying ‘we can’t lose the game in this way’
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Roberto De Zerbi tore into his failing Tottenham team after their 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa, saying ‘we can’t lose the game in this way’
Content: Roberto De Zerbi looks away after Aston Villa’s second goal.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi looks away after Aston Villa’s second goal.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersTottenham HotspurDe Zerbi rips into Spurs players after Villa defeat: ‘Disappointed, sad and frustrated’Tottenham lose 3-2 at home with two late goals‘We can’t lose the game in this way,’ says managerPaul MacInnesat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 14.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRoberto De Zerbi tore into his failing Tottenham team after their 3-2 defeat by Aston Villa, saying “we can’t lose the game in this way”. The Italian headed straight down the tunnel at full time, but was once again forced to endure boos as Tottenham went into the three-week international break without a Premier League victory to their name and just two points on the board.De Zerbi criticised his team’s mentality, but also the physical condition of his players, and said the substitute Mohammed Kudus had disrupted the balance of his team.Aston Villa grab victory despite late Spurs goals as De Zerbi’s side are booed offRead more“I am very disappointed, sad and frustrated for the performance,” De Zerbi said. “We can’t lose the game in this way, we can’t concede the second goal, we can’t lose balance just because we are losing. I spoke with our four attackers in minute 51, I asked them to use their head, all second half I was telling people to be calm. But the second goal was incredible.”Jackson scored in the 67th minute after latching on to a long kick by the impressive Zion Suzuki. De Zerbi said his players had been prepped to deal with the Villa goalkeeper’s clearances, but had switched off.“We knew this season Aston Villa are playing 86% more long balls than last season and we spoke in many meetings about it,” De Zerbi said. “Now we have to explain another game like [the home defeat against] Newcastlewhere we played the first half well, got to 60 minutes OK, and then we lose.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.With players now heading out to play for their national sides, De Zerbi said he had left them with no parting message. “I didn’t speak with the players because I didn’t want to say anything. The players who go with the national team have to play and work. For sure we have to work more because I didn’t like the finish to this game. We can’t say everything is bad, but it is not enough.”ForUnai Emery, a first Premier League victory of the season a reminder to his players of the style of play that has resulted in success for Villa in recent seasons. “The players did well because they believed,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We needed to build a team that could play in this way, could defend with resilience and playing with passion when our opponents were attacking. We needed defenders, we needed the keeper, we needed everyone committed in that direction. We needed to feel strong first, then we could try to play with our structure and our ability. This is the competitive way.”Explore more on these topicsTottenham HotspurAston VillaRoberto De ZerbiUnai EmerynewsShareReuse this content

title: Holmberg rescues point for Arsenal but Manchester United off the mark in WSL | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Arsenal needed a stoppage-time equaliser to draw 1-1 with Manchester United who won their first point under new head coach, Eva Olid
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Arsenal needed a stoppage-time equaliser to draw 1-1 with Manchester United who won their first point under new head coach, Eva Olid
Content: Smilla Holmberg scores Arsenal’s late equaliser against Manchester United.Photograph: David Price/AFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSmilla Holmberg scores Arsenal’s late equaliser against Manchester United.Photograph: David Price/AFC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueHolmberg rescues point for Arsenal but Manchester United off the mark in WSLTom Garryat the Emirates StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal were mightily relieved as a 95th-minute Smilla Holmberg volley rescued a point at home to a much-improved Manchester United side, but the draw will not be enough to eradicate concerns about how far behind the leaders Manchester City Renée Slegers’ team are slipping already and how frequently they seem to struggle to break down a low block.Manchester City scramble to dramatic WSL win over Liverpool with two goals in added timeRead moreA defiant Manchester United stunned the north Londoners as Eva Olid’s side claimed the first point of her tenure with a performance that defied all of the pre-match scripts, but it was very nearly a victory, had it not been for Holmberg’s last-gasp back-post finish from Leah Williamson’s deep, diagonal ball into the box, which finally broke the visitors’ stubborn resistance.Widely criticised for their dismal displays in their opening two defeats against London City Lionesses and Chelsea, Manchester United were heavily tipped to struggle again at the Emirates but an encouraging defensive effort and an against-the-run-of-play Julia Zigiotti Olme strike gave them a precious lead in a display that will buy the former Hearts manager Olid plenty of time to continue working on her style on the training ground and quieten those doubting her.Instead it will be Arsenal now facing scrutiny as they failed to win at home for a second straight game and slipped four points behind the defending champions, Manchester City, after just three rounds of fixtures. Last term, Manchester City dropped points in only four games and the early-season leaders have a 100% record so far. Arsenal’s next two WSL games are away to Chelsea and Manchester City.“It’s not ideal, it’s not what we wanted at all, four lost points,” Slegers admitted, reflected on consecutive home draws, but she added: “It’s round three in the WSL, there are a lot of games left to play. Let’s see in May, how it ends. Not converting dominance into wins, that’s something we have to look at. We believe in the quality of the squad. When that starts clicking, it’s going to be really good.”View image in fullscreenManchester United’s Julia Zigiotti Olme celebrates scoring against Arsenal.Photograph: Paul Harding/WSL/WSL Football/Getty ImagesIn truth, this was a result that Arsenal could ill-afford, especially after last weekend’s goalless draw at home to the newly promoted side Crystal Palace, where the north Londoners were surprisingly wasteful in the final third. Slegers’ team had scored just one goal from 43 shots across their opening two league fixtures. Surely, therefore, a home match against a side who conceded five goals last time out was the perfect opportunity to banish any concerns of a lack of clinical quality in the final third? Think again.The hosts did create good openings and looked to have control of the midfield. Their winger Lisa Baum shot straight at Phallon Tullis-Joyce early on and was providing dangerous crosses from the left. Mariona Caldentey also went close, curling just wide and Tullis-Joyce made a fine save to keep out Stina Blackstenius’ header. Nevertheless, it had been United’s Elisabeth Terland who went closest in the first half, being thwarted by two excellent Misa Rodríguez saves in quick succession.View image in fullscreenPhallon Tullis-Joyce leaping up to make a crucial save to keep Arsenal at bay.Photograph: Nina Farooqi/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockArsenal stepped up the pressure after half-time but Georgia Stanway – one of Arsenal’s better performers for the rest of the game – made a costly error as she tried to play a simple pass back towards the centre-back Steph Catley that carelessly rolled the ball into the path of Zigiotti Olme instead. The grateful Manchester United midfielder confidently stepped the ball around Catley and slotted through the legs of Rodríguez. The Emirates was astonished. The United bench, jubilant.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom then on, it was ‘backs to the wall’ for the visitors, much like it was during the majority of this fixture last term, which ended goalless. Tullis-Joyce dived low and strong to keep out a Cailtin Foord effort and United battled well to clear the danger from several set pieces as the home side grew increasingly frustrated. The crowd eventually erupted as the substitute Holmberg earned them a point and Manchester United’s players fell to their knees.Quick GuideWSL roundup: Chelsea's Potter and Malard sink BirminghamShowChelseaandLondon City Lionessesclimbed the Women’s Super League table with respective victories overBirminghamandCharlton.After thumping Manchester United 5-0 last weekend, Chelsea won again as Lexi Potter and Melvine Malard secured a 2-0 win. Potter found the roof of the net in the eighth minute (the celebrations pictured above) and in the 71st minute the France star Malard made a quick impact from the bench with her first goal at Stamford Bridge. Chelsea moved up to second and with their goal difference were likely to stay there.London City lost 2-1 to West Ham last time out but impressed in a 4-1 triumph at promoted Charlton. Isobel Goodwin’s double had London City two goals ahead after 15 minutes and, despite Jodie Hutton halving the deficit in the 39th minute with a fine finish, Jana Fernández restored their advantage before half-time. The German forward Nicole Anyomi made sure the outcome was no longer in doubt with the Lionesses’ fourth after 76 minutes. They sit third, a point behind Chelsea.Press AssociationPhotograph: Yaroslav Dunka/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Olid was pleased with their display, though, explaining: “Afterlosing 5-0, the focus this week was the defensive shape, because I think the attack will come. Implementing a new style of play needs time. But the effort, the hard work, the intensity, that can never be missing. It was so important to see that today. That is the minimum. Now, from here, little-by-little, we will improve the attacking style.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueArsenal WomenManchester United WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Coventry delight in Jay Dasilva winner but ruled-out goal riles Nottingham Forest | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Coventry have their first goal and with it a 1-0 win but only after VAR intervened when Igor Jesus thought he had a late Nottingham Forest equaliser
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Coventry have their first goal and with it a 1-0 win but only after VAR intervened when Igor Jesus thought he had a late Nottingham Forest equaliser
Content: Jay Dasilva roars in delight after scoring Coventry’s winner.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJay Dasilva roars in delight after scoring Coventry’s winner.Photograph: Ryan Browne/ShutterstockPremier LeagueCoventry delight in Jay Dasilva winner but ruled-out goal riles Nottingham ForestJohn Brewinat the City GroundSat 19 Sep 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo, but seriously. Maybe Frank Lampard and Coventry can achieve Premier League survival. The club’s first top-division win since April 2001 was celebrated rapturously, victory an object lesson in unsettling opponents for whom confidence can waver. Jay Dasilva’s excellent goal was built on the foundations laid by a battling defensive performance that must be replicated on a weekly basis. Coventry, dogged throughout, blunted Nottingham Forest’s creativity, though could thank a late video assistant referee call that enraged the City Ground crowd.Lampard declared, with his broadest grin: “I feel great, I feel amazing.” Next, as is his way, back to serious business. “The reality in football is you have to fight for it, you have to work for it, you have to have organisation.”Everton hold off Ipswich thanks to Thierno Barry goal despite VAR controversyRead moreCoventry’s troubled start to the season had revived doubts in his capabilities as aPremier Leaguemanager and far too many echoes of a quarter century in the wilderness. Whatever happens, their fans, under the weakening, early-evening sun, were determined to enjoy themselves. Even if it’s for a single season, why not make the most of things? “Something we have to build on and not get too carried away,” said Bobby Thomas, having personified that rearguard effort.“We are a team with a lot of players having their first stint in Premier League football,” said Lampard. “Not everyone is a Wayne Rooney or a superstar that can just own it.”Forest’s home league record in 2026 continues to be wretched: only Burnley, in April, have left in defeat. The previous week’svictory at Aston Villaoffered further confirmation of Morgan Gibbs-White’s importance to Forest, as if it were needed. He remains ignored by Thomas Tuchel despite verifiable claims of being the most in-form English No 10 around, only Pascal Gross creating more chances in the Premier League this season, though like his team as a whole, Gibbs-White is doing his best work away from West Bridgford. Forest hit 26 shots on Coventry’s goal, just three on target.View image in fullscreenJay Dasilva fires home Coventry’s 55th-minute winner.Photograph: David Klein/Reuters“We struggled with scoring,” was Oliver Glasner’s simple diagnosis. “Today was the first time I could feel the heaviness of the past, it was very quiet in the dressing room. When we conceded the goal, everyone was nervous, the entire ground was nervous and I think the reason is last year.”An early deft header to Liam Delap and a cogent flick to James McAtee had suggested Gibbs-White was in the mood but Forest never found the momentum to crack Coventry’s defensive shield. McAtee’s talents have never quite found their position but playing deeper as Gibbs-White’s creative partner has suited him. However, the duo were far less in tune than the previous week. Delap has shown signs of being the player glimpsed at Ipswich but was another lost in heavy traffic, Forest reduced to potshots such as his snapshot wide.Quick GuideNottingham Forest 0-1 Coventry key factsShow• Coventry earned their first Premier League victory of the season – it’stheir 100th winin the competition overall, and first since April 2001 (1-0 v Sunderland).• Jay Dasilva scored Coventry’s first Premier League goal of the season. Assisted by Carl Rushworth, it’s justthe second timea team’s first goal in a campaignhas been assisted by a goalkeeper, after Peter Schmeichel for Manchester United in 1992-93.• Nottingham Foresthave failed to scorein their first three home games in a league campaign for the first time in their history.OptaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Coventry’s kick-off for the second half saw their players line up in a formation resembling that for a rugby union dropout. It achieved little but previewed the long-ball tactics that brought about the breaking of their 25-year duck.Loum Tchaouna, a half-time arrival, cutting inside to shoot, if too weakly to beat Matz Sels, might have served as a further warning to Forest, as within moments, Dasilva, showing admirable strength for someone of such diminutive dimensions and a beautiful first touch to beat Daniel Muñoz, blazed to a diagonal ball from his goalkeeper, Carl Rushworth. The finish was just as adept, the celebrations deafening. Coventry’s previous Premier League scorer had been Mustapha Hadji in a losing effort at Aston Villa that confirmed relegation.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe big screen shows Igor Jesus has been deemed to have fouled Caleb Yirenkyi on review.Photograph: Mike Egerton/PAFor an increasingly ragged Forest, Chris Wood, old reliable, was thrown on, as was Igor Jesus, with Delap pushed to the wings. If anything, that led to Forest losing their shape and poise further, even if chances came. Thomas dashed back to the goalline to clear a chip from Igor Jesus that had Rushworth beaten.Igor Jesus did get the ball in the net, only for the video assistant referee to advise Jarred Gillett that Caleb Yirenkyi had been fouled, and the on-pitch official agreed. It looked harsh: Yirenkyi had fallen readily under minimal contact. “I was worried,” Lampard said.A shrugging Glasner said: “The referee decided and we accept it, that’s it.” Forest fans have had more than their fill of video-assisted officiating. Their seething, guttural rage came by contrast to Coventry fans now able to savour the Premier League ride.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNottingham ForestCoventry CityVideo assistant referees (VARs)match reportsShareReuse this content

title: Zidane’s next move as France coach may reveal the wizard behind the curtain | Zinedine Zidane | The Guardian
description: It is apt that France, the most perplexing football country, will now be guided by Zinedine Zidane, the most enigmatic of leaders
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: It is apt that France, the most perplexing football country, will now be guided by Zinedine Zidane, the most enigmatic of leaders
Content: It is hard to isolate any one moment in Zinedine Zidane’s success at Real Madrid that could definitively be assigned to his coaching genius.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIt is hard to isolate any one moment in Zinedine Zidane’s success at Real Madrid that could definitively be assigned to his coaching genius.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianInside footballZinedine ZidaneZidane’s next move as France coach may reveal the wizard behind the curtainJonathan WilsonIt is apt that the most perplexing football country will now be guided by the most enigmatic of leadersSat 19 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.03 EDTShareEven in his playing days,Zinedine Zidaneseemed unknowable. As a manager, the sense of distance has only grown. He won three Champions Leagues with Real Madrid without ever giving a sense of what his idea of football looked like.France are perhaps the most perplexing football country: a squad that teems with such talent that a B team would be serious contenders at a World Cup, that reached three major finals under Didier Deschamps with a sense of unfulfilment, a team that progressed but rarely entranced, or at least didn’t until this summer’s World Cup, when they attacked with gusto and ended upoverrun in midfield by Spain.On Friday, the two come together as Zidane, for the first time,leads Francein their Nations League fixture against Turkey, an enigmatic coach leading a mercurial squad.‘He’s back’: Zinedine Zidane named France head coach in long-awaited homecomingRead moreZidane is one of five coaches to have won the Champions League on three or more occasions, ranking alongside Bob Paisley, Pep Guardiola and Luis Enrique and behind only Carlo Ancelotti. He is the only manager to win three successive Champions Leagues and yet few would consider him one of the game’s elite coaches. In that spell he won one La Liga title.He left five days after the third of those Champions League successes, vaguely citing the club’s need for change. Like so much else in his career, his motivations were opaque. But he returned the following March after the inglorious reign of Julen Lopetegui and Santi Solari’s attempt to pick up the pieces. He won another La Liga title in the two full seasons that followed.How to assess a coach in the modern world? Two league titles in four full seasons. Three Champions Leagues in his first two and a half seasons. In another age, in another country, that would have marked Zidane as indisputably elite, but in Spain in the past decade? Domestically, his achievements feel about par.View image in fullscreenZinedine Zidane was viewed at Real Madrid as a head coach who let his star players like Ronaldo and Gareth Bale just be.Photograph: Matt West/BPI/ShutterstockMadrid and Barcelona win everything, so for a Madrid coach to win half the league titles available is essentially what would be expected. But he lost eight of his first 100 games, a record. His side scored in a record 73 consecutive games. They won a joint-record 16 La Liga games in a row. They won a record 13 successive away games.They are stats that seem unanswerable, but their accumulation has the opposite effect to that which might be expected. Zidane’s Madrid, in his first spell, were crushingly dominant. But were they dominant because of his genius or did he appear a genius because of their dominance? What comes to matter, then, is not the how many, but the how. Did Madrid win with dashing football of fitting elegance? To which the answer is, again, a shrug: they were fine.Those three Champions League wins in a row, equally, offer surprisingly little evidence for Zidane’s greatness. Madrid have always had a tremendous capacity for achieving European success in the shadows, as though they are the default, the club that wins when nobody else is quite inspired enough to do so. Rarely has that been felt as acutely as in 2016, when they beat Roma and Wolfsburg, then edged by Manchester City on penalties in the semi-final thanks to a Fernando own goal beforebeating Atlético Madrid on penaltiesin an unmemorable final.The following year was more impressive: the extra-time surge against Bayern and Cristiano Ronaldo-inspired demolitions of Napoli, Atlético and Juventus. But 2018 was a return to curiously ordinary success. Yes, Ronaldo and Luka Modrić were often brilliant, but there was also carelessness, notably in the quarter-final win against Juventus when they let a three-goal lead slip before a late penalty rescued them.Victory over Liverpool in the finalcame after a shoulder injury sustained by Mohamed Salah in a challenge with Sergio Ramos, a terrible error by a possibly injured Loris Karius and a Gareth Bale wonder goal.View image in fullscreenDidier Deschamps was successful as head coach of France, but his side rarely captivatedPhotograph: Martin Meissner/APIt was hard to isolate any one moment in the success that could definitively be assigned to Zidane’s coaching genius. He didn’t create the midfield three of Casemiro, Modric and Toni Kroos. He didn’t find some new role for Ronaldo or Bale. Perhaps Zidane was some elite player whisperer, coaxing them to habitual greatness, but it was hard for an outsider to tell. Being Zidane, he was inscrutable, a cipher into which observers could read whatever message they wished.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReal Madrid coaches often run into a similar problem. They have great players. Great players do great things. Philosophies and structures always seem subservient to their talents. Ancelotti, like Zidane, has often been underappreciated, seen as somebody who essentially lets the players be. That is probably unfair and, even if it were not, perhaps that, too, is a skill. After all, plenty of coaches atReal Madridhave not been able to let the players express their innate superiority.At the very least, it can be said that Zidane has an aura. Even those who accused him of being little more than a pair of hands clapping on the touchline must acknowledge that some hands are more authoritative than others. That may turn out to be an essential quality with France, a national team that became notorious between their two World Cup triumphs for ill-discipline, with the scandals of Seoul in 2002 and thestrike at Knysna in 2010.Kylian Mbappé leaves Nike after 20 years to sign boot deal with Swiss brand OnRead moreWhatever doubts there may be about whether Deschamps’s caution was counterproductive – until at the last, in that semi-final against Spain, he wasn’t cautious enough – over his 14 years in charge he prevented the sort of breakdowns of discipline that had undermined his predecessors, despite some extremely challenging situations.Perhaps this is not such a troubled or troublesomeFrancesquad as some of the past decade have been, but that Zidane has taken the unusual step of banning the press from covering the arrival of players at their Clairefontaine base suggests he is eager to make a bid for control early.His squad features a number of new faces. This is not continuity Deschamps. In the greater autonomy national coaches have compared with their club counterparts, perhaps, with France, the true nature of Zidane the coach will emerge and the great enigma will develop a face.Explore more on these topicsZinedine ZidaneInside footballFranceReal MadridcommentShareReuse this content

title: Everton hold off Ipswich thanks to Thierno Barry goal despite VAR controversy | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Thierno Barry was denied a second goal by VAR but his opener was enough for Everton to beat Ipswich 1-0, with the visitors having Abdul Fatawu sent off
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Thierno Barry was denied a second goal by VAR but his opener was enough for Everton to beat Ipswich 1-0, with the visitors having Abdul Fatawu sent off
Content: Thierno Barry celebrates opening the scoring after 11 minutes for Everton against Ipswich.Photograph: Luke Williams/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThierno Barry celebrates opening the scoring after 11 minutes for Everton against Ipswich.Photograph: Luke Williams/Every Second Media/ShutterstockPremier LeagueEverton hold off Ipswich thanks to Thierno Barry goal despite VAR controversyAndy Hunterat Hill Dickinson StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 12.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the trials and tribulations of the transfer window,Evertoncan be content with fifth place, an unbeaten start and five clean sheets in seven games. There will also be relief, for Pro Ref as well as David Moyes, that another controversial call from a video assistant referee did not impede their progress against Ipswich.Brighton demolish champions Arsenal 3-0 to mark anniversary in styleRead moreThierno Barry decided a close-fought contest with his fifth goal of the campaign. He should have had a sixth but an offside Brennan Johnson was adjudged to have impacted Ipswich goalkeeper Christian Walton’s ability to save a ball he made no attempt to save and was nowhere near saving. Unlike last weekend’s Manchester derby, however, referee Stuart Attwell’s decision would not prove decisive. The game turned in Everton’s favour minutes later when Abdul Fatawu received a second yellow card for diving but, having failed to kill off Gary O’Neil’s 10 men, they ended up hanging on. VAR was therefore spared Moyes’s wrath.“They said it affected his ability to save it which I don’t think was the case,” said the Everton manager, far more relaxed than he would have been had Ipswich levelled late on. “It’s really difficult for referees, we understand that. Do I think we will get consistency from that decision through all the season on the same thing? I’ll be doubtful of that. There is no doubt Brennan was offside but did he really interfere, was the goalkeeper ever going to save it?”O’Neil took a differing view, and also claimed his visitors controlled the game. That was stretching it. Everton were extremely careless in possession with the usually reliable Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, Jarrad Branthwaite, James Garner and Harrison Armstrong among those responsible. But they created enough chances to have rendered Ipswich’s stirring finale irrelevant, 21 in total, though managed only two on target. “I am ratting the players like you wouldn’t believe,” added Moyes. “Why are we not scoring more? I think that’s one of the things we are missing from being a half-decent side.”Johnson missed a gilt-edged chance from an Armstrong pass before Barry delivered an early lead with his strangest goal of the season. The striker reacted sharply to divert James Tarkowski’s 25-yard volley into the net after Walton and the lively Jack Clarke had cleared a cross from Dewsbury-Hall. The Ipswich keeper had Tarkowski’s shot covered only for Barry to leave him wrong-footed by chesting the ball into the opposite side of the goal. The striker clearly moved to play the ball with his chest, so gets the benefit of the doubt over his intention.Fatawu was a persistent threat down Ipswich’s right flank, making his dismissal all the more galling for O’Neil as his team chased an equaliser. The Ghana international forced a fine save from Jordan Pickford after Everton made a hash of clearing his corner and attempted to beat the England goalkeeper from inside his own half. The long-range effort was drifting wide but Pickford, unawares, took no chances and scampered back to save. Fatawu should also have claimed an assist when floating a cross over the Everton defence to Leif Davis. The left-back, perhaps surprised to find himself onside and unmarked in front of goal, scuffed his shot badly wide of the far post.View image in fullscreenStuart Attwell shows Ipswich’s Abdul Fatawu (centre) a second yellow card for simulation.Photograph: Alex Dodd/ShutterstockIpswich started the second half on top with Pickford saving from Julio Enciso and Abdoul Ouattara in quick succession. But it was Everton who converted next when Barry rose between four static Ipswich players and headed Dewsbury-Hall’s corner in off the far post. Walton was nowhere near the ball and did not appeal any infringement by the offside Johnson. Referee Attwell, sent to the pitch-side monitor, infuriated the home crowd by disallowing the goal on the basis Johnson was offside and affecting the keeper’s ability to save the ball.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFatawu foolishly helped Everton recover. Booked for hauling down Dewsbury-Hall in the first half, the winger invited a second yellow card when diving to win a free-kick against Garner. He became only the third player in the last sixPremier Leagueseasons to receive a second yellow card for simulation.Everton had numerous chances against Ipswich’s ten men but Johnson, Dewsbury-Hall and Armstrong all miscued while Walton produced a fine save to deny impressive substitute Tyler Dibling. Their profligacy made for a nervy finale as the visitors piled forward in search of an equaliser. Branthwaite, launching himself in the way of Diop’s goal-bound shot, helped Everton over the line.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueEvertonIpswich TownVideo assistant referees (VARs)match reportsShareReuse this content

title: Newcastle back to winning ways as Willock and Hall end Hull’s unbeaten start | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Newcastle held on to beat Hull 2-1 after Yoane Wissa failed with a penalty that could have put them 3-0 up, five days after their 4-1 humbling at Leeds
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Newcastle held on to beat Hull 2-1 after Yoane Wissa failed with a penalty that could have put them 3-0 up, five days after their 4-1 humbling at Leeds
