Content: Lewis Hall celebrates scoring Newcastle’s second goal, which proved decisive.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAView image in fullscreenLewis Hall celebrates scoring Newcastle’s second goal, which proved decisive.Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PAPremier LeagueNewcastle back to winning ways as Willock and Hall end Hull’s unbeaten startLouise Taylorat St James' ParkSat 19 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHull always knew, sooner or later, they would lose aPremier Leaguegame, but no one can say they did not do everything in their power to try to delay that inaugural top-tier defeat.After conceding two goals in the opening seven minutes, Hull could easily have folded but they are made of sterner stuff than that. Tellingly, they also sensed the inherent fragility of a gifted, but injury-hit and extremely youthful Newcastle.Brighton demolish champions Arsenal 3-0 to mark anniversary in styleRead moreOnce Matthias Jaissle was forced into a late switch to an unloved three at the back and Mohamed-Ali Cho narrowed the scoreline, the visitors assumed control and it almost seemed a minor miracle that Newcastle clung on for a morale-boosting victory.“I’m very proud of how we played this game, especially the second half,” said Sergej Jakirovic. “We made mistakes in the first 10 minutes and Newcastle were clinical on the counterattack, but after that, I think we showed our mentality and our character. Over 90 minutes, we deserved a point. My team showed they will not be beaten easily.”Jaissle had harsh words for his players afterMonday’s 4-1 defeat at Leedsand it seemed they had the desired effect. Sure enough, Joe Willock swiftly lashed the ball beyond Konstantinos Tzolakis. Three minutes were on the clock and it was only the third goal Hull’s £20m Greece goalkeeper had conceded since arriving from Olympiakos.It came after John Egan blocked Willock’s initial shot, but Hull’s subsequent failure to clear permitted Harvey Barnes to pick out the midfielder.Four minutes later, Barnes was once again the creator as he exchanged passes with the excellent Lewis Hall before the left-back, recalled to the England squad on Friday, swept the crispest of shots low into the bottom-left corner. Significantly, it had all begun with Hall dispossessing Oli McBurnie deep in Newcastle’s half.Tino Livramento, too, was included in Thomas Tuchel’s latest squad, but the right-back’s chances of joining up with England receded when an injury collected in training ruled him out here. Livramento was one of nine home absentees, but, undeterred, a youthful starting XI initially delighted in a spot of tiger taming.As much as Hull struggled to second-guess the dynamic Willock and the impressive 18-year-old Sean Steur in the home midfield, they were not subdued entirely. Hull came close to reducing the deficit when Sorba Thomas almost turned in a Matt Crooks cross at the near post.When, deep in first-half stoppage time, Thomas slipped before pulling the advancing Jacob Murphy back by an ankle, a penalty was awarded. Yoane Wissa stepped up, but his rather under-powered kick was saved by Tzolakis.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJoe Willock slots Newcastle into a third-minute lead from close range.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersNewcastle’s substitutes featured five academy players including the winger Kyran Thompson, a first year scholar who left school this summer, but when, midway through the second half, Jaissleturned to his bench he introduced the 34-year-old Fabian Schär in place of a tiring Steur.This change prompted a switch to a back three, featuring Schär at its heart. That configuration is, as Jaissle has made abundantly clear, far from his favourite formation and that feeling probably crystallised when, almost immediately, Hull scored.Cho’s goal was created when Lewis Miley – relocated from right-back to midfield – was caught in possession, enabling Mohamed Belloumi to play in the summer signing from Nice. Cho, a former England youth international turned France Under-21 forward, duly revelled in whipping a close-range left-foot shot past Lukas Hornicek.From then on Hull blitzed Newcastle’s area with a barrage of crosses, corners and shots from all angles. Newcastle were under siege and, among assorted other saves, their goalkeeper did particularly well to extend a foot and somehow divert Robinio Vaz’s half-volley.“It was an intense game,” said Jaissle, whose backroom staff exchanged words with their Hull counterparts. “We started at a really high level, it was the right reaction to Leeds. But the missed penalty changed momentum. We tired and we needed to suffer, but the commitment to win this game was exceptional. It made me proud. It was something special.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueNewcastle UnitedHull Citymatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: European football: Martínez double gives Inter comeback draw at Roma | European club football | The Guardian
description: In Serie A Inter fought back after Manu Koné had given Roma a 2-0 half-time lead, while in France Paris FC’s Liam Rosenior was abused by Strasbourg fans
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In Serie A Inter fought back after Manu Koné had given Roma a 2-0 half-time lead, while in France Paris FC’s Liam Rosenior was abused by Strasbourg fans
Content: Lautaro Martinez celebrates after scoring a second goal for Inter.Photograph: Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLautaro Martinez celebrates after scoring a second goal for Inter.Photograph: Giuseppe Maffia/NurPhoto/ShutterstockEuropean club footballEuropean football: Martínez double gives Inter comeback draw at RomaRoma lead 2-0 after Manu Koné’s first-half doubleStrasbourg fans abuse Rosenior; Salah hits hat-trickAgence France-Presse and ReutersSat 19 Sep 2026 17.12 EDTFirst published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 12.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLautaro Martínez rode toInter’s rescue as theSerie Achampions fought back from 2-0 down to force a 2-2 draw atRoma, in a meeting of what had been the last two sides with 100% records.Manu Koné’s double had givenRomaa 2-0 lead at half-time but for the second time in a week Cristian Chivu’s side, inspired by Martínez, showed mettle as the champions fought back from such a deficit.After the announcement earlier in the day of the death of Sandro Mazzola at the age of 83, both sides paid homage to the former Inter and Italy playmaker prior to kick-off, with theNerazzurrialso sporting black armbands.Roma raced out of the blocks as Koné sent them ahead with less than six minutes on the clock when he readjusted his body well to rifle home Nahuel Molina’s knockdown.View image in fullscreenRoma supporters hold up scarves during their match against Inter.Photograph: Ciro De Luca/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe champions had bounced back from being 2-0 down inside the opening 16 minutes at home to Udinese to emerge 5-3 winners on Monday. But Inter were not at the races for most of the opening period at the Stadio Olimpico as Paulo Dybala twice threatened to double the hosts’ advantage.However, just as Inter slowly seemed to be waking up, Koné had the ball in the net again when he tucked in from close range at the back post on 37 minutes. His celebrations were initially cut short by the assistant’s flag before the video assistant referee intervened and, after a lengthy review, Davide Massa pointed to the centre circle as the 25-year-old skipped off in delight after notching the sixth Serie A goal of his career.Martínez halved the deficit less than a minute after the interval with a scuffed finish from Thuram’s pull-back that just crept perfectly into the side-netting of Mile Svilar’s far post.Just as the match appeared to be petering out going into the final 10 minutes, a sudden goalmouth scramble saw Svilar make a sharp save before Martínez headed on to the bar under pressure. Inter, however, managed to recycle the ball and it came back to the Argentinian inside the box and this time he made no mistake as he controlled with his thigh and arrowed a finish past the Serb to ensure the spoils were shared.Laziojoined their city rivals Roma and Inter on 13 points after beating bottom-sideVenezia, who remain pointless, 2-0. A 51st-minute Mattia Zaccagni penalty, coupled with a Tijjani Noslin goal on the hour, was enough to earn Gennaro Gattuso’s team a fourth win from five outings.Paris FCextended their unbeaten start to theLigue 1campaign, beating Liam Rosenior’s old chargesStrasbourg2-1 in a match marred by abusive chants towards the Englishman from visiting fans.View image in fullscreenLiam Rosenior raises his arms in jubilation to celebrate victory in front of the Strasbourg supporters.Photograph: Matthieu Mirville/DPPI/ShutterstockThe game was halted in the second half as Rosenior was targeted by his former supporters. There were also ugly scenes after the final whistle as Rosenior motioned to remonstrate with the away fans and had to be pulled away by his players.He said later: “A small section of the fans, and I want to stress that it was only a small section, because Strasbourg is a fantastic club, were disrespectful. They insulted my family. My bench was very angry. So, for me, celebrating like that was obviously sending a message. I won’t say anything more about this.”Goals from Ilan Kebbal on 18 minutes and Pablo Pagis 12 minutes into the second half were enough for the capital club to add a third win to their two draws so far this campaign, despite conceding a late own goal by Moustapha Mbow.The game betweenLyonand ⁠Stade Rennaiswas also disrupted after ⁠Lyon ​fans ‌displayed an ‌offensive banner ‌directed at their rivals St Etienne.Lyonwere leading 2-0 ‌through two goals from ​Ernest Nuamah when the banner ⁠was unveiled, prompting ​officials to ​suspend ​the match ​briefly ‌before ​play ​resumed. They went on to win 4-0.Barcelonamaintained their ⁠100% record this season with a 3-1 La Liga ⁠victory overSevilla, as captain Raphinha scored a hat-trick ⁠to continue his remarkable start to the campaign. Sevilla opened ⁠the scoring after 18 minutes ​through a ‌Youssouf Fofana header, ‌butBarcelonahit back with ‌a Raphinha strike four minutes later.Seven minutes into the second half, Raphinha headed in a Lamine Yamal cross and the pair combined again ​as the Brazilian completed his hat-trick in the 69th minute, his 12th league goal in ⁠seven games this season. Barcelona are ​provisionally ​six points clear ​at the top of ​La Liga, with ‌second-placed Real ​Madrid, ​who have a game in hand, playing Atlético Madrid on Sunday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMaximilian Beier’s 70th-minute winner securedBorussia Dortmunda 1-0 victory atStuttgartas they moved to the top of the early Bundesliga table. Beier tapped in from Jobe Bellingham’s low cross to send Dortmund to the summit for the first time since May 2023, a run of 1,212 days since they threw away the title with a final-day home draw against Mainz.View image in fullscreenMaximilian Beier (centre) celebrates with teammates after scoring Borussia Dortmund’s winner against VfB Stuttgart.Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPAThe victory also marks the first time in a decade Dortmund have won their opening four league matches. “Sounds good to me,” Beier told Sky Germany. “We’ll take that.”Earlier,Freiburghad missed a chance to return to the top of theBundesligaafter being held to a 2-2 draw atEintracht Frankfurt. Bayern Munich’s ruthless 7-0 win over Union Berlin on Friday had put them top overnight.Harry Kane smashes record for fastest to 100 Bundesliga goals in 98th gameRead moreSeveral new members of Jürgen Klopp’s 44-man Germany squad shone on both sides in a see-sawing encounter. Frankfurt’s Younes Ebnoutalib finished off a lovely team move to score 10 minutes in, two days after a surprise first call-up.Derry Scherhant, another of Klopp’s lesser-known new additions, levelled forFreiburg, but Jonathan Burkardt edged Frankfurt back in front. Scherhant created a second for Yuito Suzuki to grab Freiburg a point and leave them level with Bayern on 10 points.Mohamed Salah scored a hat-trick and set up another ⁠goal asTrabzonsporthrashedGalatasaray4-0, handing the ⁠defending champions their first defeat of the Turkish Super Lig season.Salah opened ⁠the scoring in the fourth minute, running through from midfield and finishing calmly, ⁠before he turned provider to set up Noah ​Saviolo, who struck ‌from inside ‌the penalty area in the 39th. Salah added a ‌third in the 44th minute with a clinical finish from a Franculino Dju assist. He completed his ‌hat-trick in the 80th minute, running more than half the length of the ​pitch unchallenged to score with a trademark side-foot finish.Galatasaray’s coach, Okan Buruk, was sent to the stands in the 71st minute while Lesley ⁠Ugochukwu was shown a red card in the ​87th. Trabzonspor are fifth in the table with 10 points from six games, three points behindGalatasaray.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballSerie ALigue 1BundesligaFreiburgBorussia DortmundStuttgartnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kanté and Mavropanos rescue late point for West Ham in derby thriller at Millwall | Championship | The Guardian
description: West Ham, who had Mohamadou Kanté sent off in the 89th minute, hit back from two goals down to secure a 2-2 draw at Millwall
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: West Ham, who had Mohamadou Kanté sent off in the 89th minute, hit back from two goals down to secure a 2-2 draw at Millwall
Content: Konstantinos Mavropanos roars in delight after scoring West Ham’s equaliser.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKonstantinos Mavropanos roars in delight after scoring West Ham’s equaliser.Photograph: Richard Pelham/Getty ImagesChampionshipKanté and Mavropanos rescue late point for West Ham in derby thriller at MillwallBarney Ronayat The DenSat 19 Sep 2026 10.06 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWelcome back, then,the Dockers Derby. We really must do this again. On a lovely soft September afternoon on the Bermondsey peninsula, watched by an outrage-ready media multiverse, something unexpected happened at the Den. A really good football match broke out.Not wild or violent. No shameful scenes that nobody (trans: everybody) wants to see. Not in the stands or the streets at least: the only really sour note was an allegation of spitting against West Ham’s Taty Castellanos, which will now presumably be investigated.Fear and loathing linger as Millwall and West Ham resume ferocious rivalryRead moreOtherwise this was a thrilling, high-quality 2-2 draw betweenMillwalland West Ham, a game where for the full 90 minutes nothing outside the Den’s rattly corrugated stands seemed to exist, right down to the sleepy London commuter trains chugging past the open corners.Alex Neil’s evolving team produced a first half of sustained and artful intensity to take a 2-0 lead. West Ham reminded everyone why they were relegated last season by forgetting to turn up, before dominating the second half and scoring twice.There was even a moment of late drama, controversy and, let’s face it, blatant cheating, as Kyrell Lisbie robbed Mohamadou Kanté then ran through on goal all alone, only to be pulled to the floor by the same opponent. It was an obvious but also essentially useless red card. Lisbie had a fair chance of scoring the winner. A free-kick outside the box was rich reward for an act of cynicism.In the end a draw was a fair result in a game where football, of all things, was the winner. Half an hour before kick-off the Den was already crackling with a rare kind of energy. But then this is an authentic derby, a game with context and hinterland, albeit that original source of tension hasn’t existed since the docks were abandoned and then rebuilt.Quick GuideChampionship roundup: Swansea top; pressure mounts on HayenShowSwanseamoved to the top of the table after Stephen Eustaquio’s first goal for the club earned a 2-1 victory atLincoln. The Swans turned the game on its head after half-time and, barring a big win for West Brom over Wolves on Sunday, Vítor Matos’s (pictured) side will head into the international break top of the pile.Middlesbroughneeded a late equaliser from Adilson Malanda to salvage a point and a 2-2 draw atBirmingham. The defender was on hand to punish Birmingham goalkeeper James Beadle’s handling error when the home side seemingly had the game won after coming from a goal down.Burnleywere denied a first league victory since February as Mohammed Fuseini’s dramatic stoppage-time equaliser earnedDerbya 1-1 draw at Turf Moor. Zeki Amdouni’s 34th-minute far-post header looked to have given Burnley a much-needed victory to ease the pressure on their new head coach Nicky Hayen, but Fuseini’s equaliser leaves Burnley winless and bottom of the table.Asked if he expected to be in charge when Burnley return from the three-week international break for their next league match, away to Watford on 10 October 10, Hayen said: “I don’t know. You have to ask this question to other people, but I speak a lot with those people also. I know the fans are disappointed.  But I’m always resilient. I’m always a fighter. Tomorrow I come back with a new positive energy."Paul Smyth scored a 90th-minute equaliser for 10-manQPRas they came back from two goals down to draw 2-2 with strugglingPreston. Johnny Kenny’s first goals for North End – including an opener after 64 seconds – left them in a great position, but Kwame Poku pulled a goal back and Smyth’s late strike rescued a point for the west London side.Stokestaged a fine comeback to stunSheffield Unitedwith a 2-1 win at the Bet365 Stadium despite Kalvin Phillips's first league goal for five and a half years. Two goals in the space of 11 second-half minutes from Jack McGlynn and Sam Gallagher enabled the home side to make it four wins in their past five league fixtures.Wrexhamsecured a smash-and-grab 2-1 victory against wastefulSouthamptoncourtesy of Keven Schlotterbeck’s late own goal. Phil Parkinson’s men headed into the game reeling from a 6-0 hammering at West Ham and desperate to kickstart their campaign, and they edged a late win as Schlotterbeck turned in Jacques Ekomie’s cross.Cardiff’s long wait for a first win on their Championship return is over after Jack Moylan scored twice in their 3-1 home victory overCharlton, while Colby Bishop struck his first goal since April to givePortsmoutha 2-2 draw withBlackburnat Fratton Park.Press AssociationPhotograph: Greig Cowie/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The deep history is real: a battle for work on the docks, a river in between, a club that moved from your actual back yard (the mill wall in question is just over the Thames). Even if these days it’s more a matter of muscle memory, familial tradition, internet blather. Even the docks are quays now. Although there are some really good artisan coffee shops around the place if you look.Otherwise this was also a self-contained media event. When the West Ham bus arrived at 11.30am it felt like there were more influencers with collar mics, more rubbernecking reporters than actual enraged docker-descendants. Disappointingly for some, perhaps, the only real threat of violence around the ground all day was the danger of an accidental mass entangling from the endless Stone Island shoulder badges on show.West Ham were always favourites to win here. Their most recent annual turnover was £226m. Millwall are on a tenth of that. Chronic mismanagement gave us this game. Boardroom incompetence made it happen. And playing squads aside, Millwall were hugely focused from the first thunderously claimed loose ball.View image in fullscreenCamiel Neghli doubles Millwall’s lead from close range in first-half stoppage time.Photograph: Tom Cusden/PPAUK/ShutterstockNeil has introduced a more fluid passing game in the last year, but this was all about energy and tempo. Early on Zak Sturge left Jarrod Bowen on the floor to vast approving roars, then slid a pass to Taïryk Arconte, who couldn’t get his shot away.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd with 16 minutes gone Millwall took the lead with a goal that came in stages. First Mads Hermansen made a brilliant one-handed save from Mark Sykes, then another one, leaping up, from Arconte. The ball looped across the six-yard box to Caleb Taylor, who half-volleyed it elegantly into the net.Quick GuideLeagues One and Two: Peterborough sack Williams after latest lossShowPeterboroughhave sacked manager Luke Williams (pictured) following a 2-0 League One defeat to fellow strugglersDoncaster. Alfie May opened the scoring for Rovers after 15 minutes before Isaac Hutchinson wrapped up the victory with two minutes remaining.Posh have just one league win to their name this season and sit 23rd in the table. A club statement read: “This is not a decision the club has taken lightly. However, the team’s form  has not matched the Board’s expectations, particularly given the significant investment made in the squad … the Board felt it had no other choice.”Ryan Harley has been asked to take interim charge. After the defeat, he said: “The situation is very difficult.  He’s a brilliant manager, a brilliant coach. I’ve never seen anyone coach like him is my honest opinion, and I’ve seen a lot of coaches. But, as we know, it’s not quite worked recently for loads and loads of different reasons, so I get it, but it’s difficult."The under-pressureLeicestermanager Russell Martin was left furious about his side’s failure to kill off 10-manBarnsley. The Foxes had to settle for a 1-1 draw, despite having a man advantage for more than an hour after the sending-off of Luca Connell. The hosts came close to winning it through Patrick Kelly in added time, and the Leicester fans who travelled to South Yorkshire booed the players and Martin off at full-time.Martin said: “Winning would have made everyone feel a bit better and would have energised people. But we haven’t done it. It’s a missed opportunity for everyone – the players, us, the fans, to feel good going into the break.”Bradfordclimbed to the top of the table with a 1-0 victory overLutonat Kenilworth Road. The only goal of the game arrived in the fourth minute when Bobby Pointon nodded the Bantams in front from close range and secured a third straight win, while Jack Wilshere’s Hatters made it back-to-back defeats.Huddersfieldsaw their unbeaten start to the season come to an end with a 2-1 defeat atBromley. JJ McKiernan gave the Ravens an early lead before Ashley Fletcher equalised for Huddersfield on the stroke of half-time, but Mickel Miller hit the winner for Bromley – their first victory since the opening day of the season.Plymouthpicked up a third successive victory with a 4-2 victory atBlackpoolcourtesy of a brace from Oli Irow and further efforts from Harvey White and Bim Pepple, whileSheffield Wednesdaystretched their unbeaten run to five matches as they shared a goalless draw withStockport.Barnetstayed top of League Two with a 3-1 victory overFleetwoodcourtesy of goals from Kabongo Tshimanga, Charlie Lakin and Idris Kanu despite having Nnamdi Ofoborh sent off late on. James Connolly and Andrew Dallas scored in each half to giveWalsalla 2-0 victory over strugglingPort Vale.First-half goals from Iwan Morgan and Kieran Green gaveGrimsbya 2-0 win over rock-bottomCrawleyto extend their unbeaten start to the campaign.Salfordstretched their unbeaten run to four games following a poor start with a 1-0 win overSwindonthanks to a second-half effort from Joe Powell.Press AssociationPhotograph: MI News/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Den erupted with a noise so visceral the Lewisham council incinerator at the Cold Blow Lane end (it is, Millwall fans will tell you, a world-class incinerator) must have shivered on its foundations. And they kept on coming. Arconte made and then spurned another good opportunity. Jenson Metcalfe spanked a loose ball from 35 yards that dipped and swerved and pinged back off the crossbar. And in first-half added time it was 2-0, again from a long throw from the right. This time the ball fell to Camiel Neghli, who took a nice touch from under his feet and smashed it into the net.Pablo and Kanté came on at half-time and West Ham began to turn the screw. Bowen drew a fine save from Filip Marschall. Arne Engels spanked a shot hard into the head of Jake Cooper, who staggered once, remembered where he was, then just walked it off.On 74 minutes West Ham pulled one back via Kanté’s powerful low drive. They were hunting this now. Bowen seemed to be running every element of the game. A series of corners were bundled away, until finally Konstantinos Mavropanos headed the equaliser.Millwall held on until the red card, then West Ham held on to the end. At the final whistle there was even some minor chest-bumping stuff between Bowen and Mathis Servais, traditions preserved, the family line respected, followed by a chorus of “you’ll run out of Bermondsey” from the Millwall fans. It will be more a case of regional trains these days, back to the places beyond the riverside high-rises. But this was a wonderful game, and a fitting tribute to the enduring power of all that.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipMillwallWest Ham Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘They deserved to win’: Mikel Arteta left humbled by Brighton defeat | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: After Arsenal’s 100% start to season came to end in a 3-0 defeat at Brighton, Mikel Arteta said the team put themselves in trouble from the start
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: After Arsenal’s 100% start to season came to end in a 3-0 defeat at Brighton, Mikel Arteta said the team put themselves in trouble from the start
Content: Mikel Arteta cuts a frustrated figure as Arsenal lose 3-0 at Brighton.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta cuts a frustrated figure as Arsenal lose 3-0 at Brighton.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersArsenal‘They deserved to win’: Mikel Arteta left humbled by Brighton defeatArsenal’s 100% start to season comes to an endManager says team put themselves in trouble from startEd Aaronsat the Amex StadiumSat 19 Sep 2026 13.34 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 14.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta admitted Arsenal were taught a lesson by free-scoring Brighton as their 100% start to the seasonwas abruptly ended on Saturday. Not since 10 May 2023 – 1,224 days ago – whenthe same opponents won 3-0at the Emirates Stadium had the Premier League champions lost by three goals. But they were second-best throughout as Pascal Gross, Charalampos Kostoulas and Chema Andrés rounded off a comprehensive victory.“They deserved to win the game and it’s a big lesson for us,” said a disappointed Arteta, who felt his players were not their usual combative selves. “From the first throw-in you could sense it, it was so clear.Brighton demolish champions Arsenal 3-0 to mark anniversary in styleRead more“We put ourselves in trouble one time, two times, three times and we need to get out of that much quicker than that. That’s one of the biggest lessons that we have to take from the game.“We knew how tough it was going to be and the first thing we had discussed was about the first part. If you don’t get out of that first part as winners, it will be extremely difficult to dominate the game and to have any probability of winning the game. At this level, it’s extremely important to respect and to understand [that] before anything else.”Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Asked whether this was a wake-up call after nine straight league wins that included them being crowned champions for the first time in 22 years in May, Arteta said: “For us it’s crystal clear. We knew and we talked for two days about what we have to do here. We played the fourth away game in a really short period of time.“We know what it takes to win every single match and we know what it’s going to take to win against Leeds when we come back. That’s not a surprise, but it doesn’t take away the disappointment and emotional state we have”Brighton have recorded victories over the reigning champions in the past three seasons and with 16 goals from five matches are all but certain to go into the international break as the division’s top scorers. Fabian Hürzeler compared the 35-year-old Gross to “a good wine” after he was instrumental in the win and praised his team’s collective efforts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Everyone has this mindset today: ‘I need to defend first and we defend as a team,’” he said. “We wanted to approach this game by getting small wins. Everyone speaks about a goal is a win, but a small win can be the first throw in, the first corner, win the first header, win the first tackle.“If you win these small steps, if you celebrate them individually as a win then you can grow into the game. Then you can gain bigger and bigger wins.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetaBrighton & Hove AlbionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rory McIlroy gives himself a chance to repeat history at PGA Championship | European Tour | The Guardian
description: Rory McIlroy is two behind the leaders, Filippo Celli and Manuel Elvira, at the PGA Championship after three rounds
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Rory McIlroy is two behind the leaders, Filippo Celli and Manuel Elvira, at the PGA Championship after three rounds
Content: Rory McIlroy acknowledges the crowd after setting up a tap-in for an eagle at the last.Photograph: Chris Roll/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRory McIlroy acknowledges the crowd after setting up a tap-in for an eagle at the last.Photograph: Chris Roll/Action Plus/ShutterstockEuropean TourRory McIlroy gives himself a chance to repeat history at PGA ChampionshipNorthern Irishman two behind Celli and ElviraUnlikely leaders birdie 18th to reach 13 underEwan Murrayat WentworthSat 19 Sep 2026 12.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEighteen holes sit betweenRory McIlroyand an impressive piece of symmetry. In September 2025, McIlroy claimed a second Irish Open title in euphoric scenes at the K Club. Five months earlier, he had won the Masters.At Wentworth on Sunday, McIlroy will take off in hot pursuit of a second PGA Championship crown. As was the case last year, he is the reigning Masters champion. Another season that will inevitably be defined by Augusta National could find itself with a cherry on top.“I’d certainly like to win again,” said McIlroy. “The Masters feels like quite a long time ago. I have had half-chances here and there since then, but tomorrow is a great opportunity.“It is a tournament and a place that means a lot to me. I first came here as a 10-year-old to watch the World Match Play with my mum and dad. I have played this tournament so many times, I have been able to win this event and now I have a house on the estate. I have a lot of history here, a 27-year history.” Indeed, the 2014 point at which McIlroy won at Wentworth feels like a lifetime ago.On a wonderfully compacted leaderboard, McIlroy will begin round four two shots adrift of a pair of unlikely lads. Filippo Celli and Manuel Elvira are 358th and 294th in the world rankings, which makes their 54-hole prominence here rather extraordinary. Both made birdies at the last to reach 13 under par.Alejandro del Rey, Johannes Veerman and JJ Spaun are one shy of the lead. Spaun arrived in Surrey with a point to prove after being overlooked for the United States Presidents Cup team. Del Rey and Veerman shot 64 on day three. So, too, did Kristoffer Reitan, who has Joaquin Niemann, Adam Scott and Davis Bryant for scoring company alongside McIlroy at minus 11. For the second time in three days, Scott missed an apparently straightforward eagle opportunity on the 18th green.View image in fullscreenJoint-leader Filippo Celli plays out of the rough on the 17th hole at Wentworth.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAIn testing conditions, McIlroy’s day was the slowest of burners. He was one over through 11 holes and irritated by subsequent missed opportunity before closing with a bang. McIlroy birdied the 17th in straightforward fashion. At the last, he fired a 230-yard four iron to tap-in range. With that eagle secured, McIlroy signed for a 69.“It was a frustrating day,” he said. “It was hard to get the ball close to the hole, but if you look at the last few groups, I think everyone has struggled. We had the most of the wind and those first 11 holes were very, very difficult.“It was a day when you really needed patience. That patience I tried to show all day was rewarded with the birdie and eagle.”How the galleries roared. This is a fine tournament to attend if you fancy a close-up view of some of the best in the world who are not McIlroy. It feels as if 95% of the gallery follow him. “The crowds and the atmosphere have been absolutely incredible,” McIlroy said. “Great tournaments need great crowds and, honestly, this is one of the best atmospheres we play in all year.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA bigger picture is in play. If McIlroy finishes solo second, he will overtake Patrick Reed in the DP World Tour’s order of merit race.It would be folly to discount those at 10 under, who include Ludvig Åberg and Robert MacIntyre. The latter was amusingly candid when assessing a 66 that included 14 single putts. “Thankfully I can putt because I can’t hit an iron shot to save my life,” he said. “I hit some unbelievable shots, but I also hit some of the worst possible shots you can hit.“There’s signs of it being there, but it’s frustrating. I’ve shot six under through putting unbelievable and you can’t complain about that, but I would like it a little bit more stress-free.”Nine under and four shots back means a share of 16th place. Round four predictions feel like a fool’s errand.Explore more on these topicsEuropean TourRory McIlroyGolfnewsShareReuse this content

title: GB take command of Ecuador Davis Cup tie on Arthur Fery’s London return | Davis Cup | The Guardian
description: Great Britain lead their Davis Cup qualifier against Ecuador 2-0 after day-one wins for Toby Samuel and Arthur Fery
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Great Britain lead their Davis Cup qualifier against Ecuador 2-0 after day-one wins for Toby Samuel and Arthur Fery
Content: Arthur Fery celebrates his 7-5, 6-0 victory over Álvaro Guillén Meza of Ecuador at the Copper Box Arena.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenArthur Fery celebrates his 7-5, 6-0 victory over Álvaro Guillén Meza of Ecuador at the Copper Box Arena.Photograph: John Walton/PADavis CupGB take command of Ecuador Davis Cup tie on Arthur Fery’s London returnToby Samuel beats Andrés Andrade 4-6, 6-4, 6-1Wimbledon semi-finalist wins for 2-0 day one leadTumaini Carayolat the Copper BoxSat 19 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArthur Fery’s return to competition on home soil for the first time since his glorious summer at Wimbledon took place on a different surface, in a different format and on the opposite side of London. The emotions it generated were all the same as the British No 1 led his team to a 2-0 lead over Ecuador by defeating Álvaro Guillén Meza 7-5, 6-0 in Great Britain’s Davis Cup qualifier tie in the Copper Box Arena.The victory for Fery, aWimbledon semi-finalist, was preceded by a solid debut for the British No 5, Toby Samuel, a late injury replacement for Cameron Norrie. Samuel opened the tie by overcoming a nervous start to set the tone with a 4-6, 6-4, 6-1 win over Ecuador’s No 1, Andrés Andrade.Alex de Minaur roars back to life as Australia and Poland share spoils in Davis CupRead moreA successful opening day means Britain stands one win away from theDavis CupFinal 8, the decisive knockout stage of the competition, which takes place in Bologna between 18 and 23 November.“You get goosebumps walking out,” said Fery. “I don’t know how many people that was, but it made a lot of noise. It was great playing here in London. A lot of support from everyone.“It’s always different playing Davis Cup. You’re playing for a whole nation. There’s more responsibility on your shoulders. You know that it’s going to impact the team result as well, how you play. It’s a weight I can carry on my shoulders and I felt confident. It was never too much of a burden.”Great Britain will now call on its impressive doubles team, the world No 1, Henry Patten, and last week’s US Open champion, Neal Skupski, to seal the tie in the first of three potential matches on Sunday.As a result of Norrie’s late withdrawal, a packed and forceful British crowd witnessed a new Great Britain singles lineup, with Fery’s singles victory in Poland last September the only Davis Cup match he or Samuel had played. Despite their inexperience, the home team, in favourable conditions, was heavily favoured to defeat an Ecuador team without a player inside the top 200.Still, no tennis competition springs surprises like the Davis Cup and Ecuador had already showed it should not be taken lightly. They earned their place at this stage with a 3-1 win against Australia in Quito on clay in February. An away tie in east London on indoor hard courts, however, is a different challenge.Last February, Samuel was ranked outside the top 1,600 and was competing on the lowest rung of the WorldTennis(formerly ITF) Tour as recently as November. He has been one of the fastest-rising players since then, winning nine titles in the past year at all levels, including five ATP Challenger titles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenToby Samuel battled back from a set down to defeat Andrés Andrade.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersAs a result of qualifying and winning a round at the US Open, Samuel broke into the top 100 for the first time this week, reaching a career-high ranking of No 95 and deservedly earning his first Davis Cup call-up. Things did not start ideally for him as he looked understandably nervous and tense, losing the first four games. As he relaxed, Samuel began to dominate the underpowered Andrade with his big serve and forehand, winning 10 of the final 11 games from 4-4 in set two.Ranked No 293, Álvaro Guillén Meza was as high as 175 last year, but has rarely played on hard courts since his professional debut in 2018, let alone won matches on the surface, compiling a 1-9 pro record. The 23-year-old hung tough in the first set, remaining solid against an unusually erratic and frustrated Fery who struggled with his forehand.At 5-5, 0-30, Fery looked tight, but grinding through a long point with his defence allowed him to settle down. He recovered to hold serve and began to overpower Guillén Meza from the baseline, immediately breaking serve to take the set.Fery closed out his first Davis Cup win with the final eight games to extend his team’s lead to 2-0 after the first day.Explore more on these topicsDavis CupArthur FeryTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tottenham 2-3 Aston Villa: Premier League – as it happened | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Spurs scored their first goals of the season but Johan Manzambi, Nicolas Jackson and Emi Buendía earned the win for Villa
Author: Daniel Gallan

Content: 11h ago10.05 EDTMatch reportAnd here’s the report.Well done to Villa. title: China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: Silicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanity
Content: Alvaro Dominguez / Guardian Design / Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenarioSilicon Valley China hawks, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei among them, fear the country surpassing US’s AI lead as much as superintelligence destroying humanityNick Robins-EarlySat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTShareWhen reporters asked Donald Trump this week if he supported calls to slow down the development of artificial intelligence out of growing fears for cybersecurity, public safety andthe fate of humanity, he said no. His argument:China.“We’re leading China in AI,” Trump said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to ⁠keep it that way, because whoever wins AI, wins.”Trump was echoing a message the AI industry has put out for years. The US is in a heated technological race with China, companies including Anthropic andOpenAI have argued, and any regulation that would cede the contest risks incalculable economic and political harm.Even as Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO,led an industry-wide call this weekto “pace the frontier”, he declared that the US could only slow down to the point where China could not catch up.“If we greatly restrain our AI capabilities in the belief that China will do the same, and then China defects, AI could be so powerful that such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance,” Amodei warned.Feeling overwhelmed by the AI doom loop? Here’s the essential reading list to make sense of it allRead moreThe AI industry’s concerns about China may come with self-serving economic incentives, but they also reflect a strain of hawkish foreign policy toward Beijing that has become entrenched in tech.In recent years, parts of Silicon Valley have positioned themselves as the vanguard in a new cold war with China, arguing fiercely that the industry’s technological advancements are essential to both US hegemony and the liberal world order. This view has taken hold across tech’s different ideological camps, creating strange bedfellows of AI safety advocates, techno-militarists and neoconservatives, all of them fearful of Beijing.AI companies have hired former top US government staffers from both the Biden and Trump administrations to shape public strategy and analyze geopolitical risk, setting up in-house policy teams. Influential tech leaders have meanwhile written essays and policy documents calling for efforts to deter and degrade China’s AI capabilities, sometimes advocating for threatening armed conflict if necessary, in an attempt to influence foreign policy.As public calls for reining in the AI industry intensify and the risks associated with the technology increase, various industry forcesare trying to ensure they are the ones with the answer to the question “what about China?”.Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this article.Amodei’s worst China fearsFew have been more vocal about the threat of Chinese state-controlled artificial intelligence than Amodei. The Anthropic CEO has argued for years that one of the reasons he’s so animated to advance AI is to ensure that the technology falls into the hands of Democratic governments and not oppressive regimes such as China.Amodei’s position has made him one of Silicon Valley’s most vocal critics of China’s tech industry, separating him from fellow AI leaders such as OpenAI CEOSam Altmanor Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, who frame the competition more in corporate or economic terms; and people such as Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, who have encouraged the use of Chinese AI models. Demis Hassabis, the leader of Google Deepmind, has made few public remarks on China in comparison with his peers.“Sam Altman doesn’t have especially strong views when it comes to China. Anthropic is a totally different story,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. “Amodei is really, really focused on a particular view of the risk from AI and what he frames as basically a struggle between a world dominated by authoritarian AI versus democratic AI”.Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous propositionRead moreAmodei’s argument, which he has laid out over a series of essays, is that China acquiring superpowered AI is one of the most severe threats posed by the technology. He believes humanity is approaching the creation of an ultra-advanced AI, and that such a tool would give an authoritarian state the ability to create a “swarm of millions or billions of fully automated armed drones” that would be “capable of both defeating any military in the world and suppressing dissent within a country by following around every citizen”.“There are a number of possible arguments against the severity of these threats, and I wish I believed them, because AI-enabled authoritarianism terrifies me,” Amodei wrote in January in an essay called The Adolescence of Technology.Amodei has long asserted that in order to stop China’s advancement, the US and its allies should take aggressive action to limit Chinese AI companies’ growth – most notably blocking the sale of advanced semiconductor chips and manufacturing equipment necessary for improving AI. (Huang of Nvidia has bristled at this position,calling export controls a failureand urging Trump to ease restrictions.)But Amodei’s position was perhaps most on display last weekend, in his response to warnings from a young Anthropic researcher who resigned, predicting human extinction by the end of the decade at the digital hands of AI. The apocalyptic string of tweets by Jacob Coxon did not mention China. But the specter across the Pacific looms so large in the Anthropic CEO’s mind that, when outlining how to prevent human extinction, beating Beijing was paramount.Amodei has built a team that shares his views. He for example hired Tarun Chhabra, former Biden-era national security council staffer, as Anthropic’s head of national security policy. Chhabra has campaigned against the sale of chips to China and has called for a full-scale government effort to curb the Chinese Communist party’s AI advancements.“The CCP does not seek complementarity or coexistence or comparative advantage with the United States or our allies. Instead, the CCP seeks run-the-table dominance and control of the most critical technologies and supply chains,” Chhabra told a Senate hearing last year, adding that he believed the Biden administration did not take decisive or rapid enough action to maintain the US lead against China.View image in fullscreenDario Amodei speaks at Dreamforce 2026 summit in San Francisco, California, in September.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAmodei’s concern over export controls has also placed him in the company of other influential China hawks. He wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal last year with Matt Pottinger, the architect of Trump’s first-term China policy, urging the administration to clamp down on chip exports. Pottinger, a visiting fellow at the conservative Hoover Institution and author of a book on how to defend Taiwan against a Chinese attack, argued in 2024 that the US and China were in the “foothills of a great-power hot war”.Anthropic and Amodei’s stance on China puts the company in strange tension with its own domestic policy. The company has spent millions lobbying for increased government oversight and safety measures. At the same time as Anthropic advocates for more safeguards, it has made clear that it will aggressively oppose any policy it perceives as giving China the chance to overtake the US.“There’s something that’s really important that everyone hears from Anthropic,” Sarah Heck, the company’s head of public policy, said ata Politico eventon Wednesday. “The United States needs to stay in the lead on AI and you cannot do safety from second place.”Understanding the beliefs of AI companies and CEOs such as Amodei is particularly important, experts say, because the Trump administration’s laissez faire policy towards the AI industry has meant that private companies are the primary actors in shaping public policy.“It would be akin to having the entire pharmaceutical industry be just completely unregulated,” Chan said. “It’s kind of amazing and ultimately boils down to one thing, which is Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economy.”Anthropic is not the only company to hire and align with former top policy staffers, withOpenAIhiring the author of Trump’s AI action plan Dean Ball as “head of strategic futures” earlier this year. While Ball has criticized Amodei’s framing of the competition with China,, he has expressed a similar pessimism on US-China cooperation.double quotation mark... Trump has been very reluctant to want to regulate because he doesn’t want to slow down the AI boom and the effect that it’s having on the economyKyle Chan“There was a time when it was possible to believe we could each pursue our strengths, enrich our respective economies, and grow together. Alas, such harmony now appears impossible,” Ball wrote of China last year. “We are locked into a structural conflict.”Silicon Valley’s ChinahawksAlthough Amodei is the AI industry’s most prominent voice on China, fears of Beijing gaining advanced AI capabilities and using them for global domination run through Silicon Valley.Several of the tech figures focused on Chinahave connections, like Amodei himself, to the effective altruism movement – a quasi-utilitarian idea that society should focus on projects that maximize the good and reduce the most harm for humanity. The movement tends to overlap with AI safety advocates who worry about the longterm, existential risks of the technology.Leopold Aschenbrenner, a 25-year-old former OpenAI researcher, founder of an influential AI hedge fund, and husband to Amodei’s chief of staff, called for a government-led effort to reach super-intelligent AI before China in a 165-page paper.“Super-intelligence will give a decisive economic and military advantage. China isn’t at all out of the game yet. In the race to AGI, the free world’s very survival will be at stake,” Aschenbrenner wrote in 2024.The position of Aschenbrenner, who made headlines earlier this year when his hedge fund lost $35bn in less than a month, was echoed in Washington. When the typically hawkish US-China cconomic and security review commission issued its annual report to Congress a few months after Aschenbrenner’s manifesto, the congressional advisory committee’s number one suggestion was to “establish and fund a Manhattan Project-like program dedicated to racing to and acquiring an Artificial General Intelligence”.Grand strategy proposals from the AI industry on China are not solely contained within the effective altruist movement. In 2025, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, Alexander Wang, Scale AI founder (now head of AI at Meta), and Dan Hendrycks, Center for AI Safety director, wrote a wide-ranging strategic deterrence doctrine called Mutual Assured AI Malfunction (Maim). Their paper applies the cold war framework of Mutually Assured Destruction (Mad) with nuclear weapons and applies it to AI, proposing that the US and China could achieve geopolitical stability through threatening espionage, cyberattacks and potential military strikes against each other if either state pursues a monopoly on AI.“A nation with sole possession of super-intelligence might be as overwhelming as the Conquistadors were to the Aztecs,” the paper warns.Nuclear considered an optionSome leading AI thinkers have argued for extreme measures to deal with AI advancement from nations such as China. Eliezer Yudkowsky, one of the earliest and loudest voices of the AI safety movement, has argued that the US should be willing to carry out airstrikes against foreign data centers and risk nuclear war in order to make rival states comply with a global AI moratorium.“Make it explicit in international diplomacy that preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange, and that allied nuclear countries are willing to run some risk of nuclear exchange if that’s what it takes to reduce the risk of large AI training runs,” Yudkowskywrote in a 2023 Time Magazine essay.Yudkowsky founded the Machine Research Intelligence Institute, which has received more than $10m in funding over the past decade from Open Philanthropy, a non-profit associated with the effective altruism movement. Open Philanthropy’s cofounder and former CEO Holden Karnovsky is married to Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei.View image in fullscreenAlex Karp, Palantir CEO, at the G20 Innovation summit in North Carolina, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersOther China hawks in the tech and AI industry tend to have ties to the military industrial complex and an economic incentive in the competition, such as Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Palantir CEO Alex Karp. Luckey has claimed that his defense tech firm has an internal policy that any of its projects need to be built with the assumption China will launch hostilities against Taiwan in 2027.Karp has meanwhile framed the AI competition with China as a fight for geopolitical supremacy and suggested Americans should accept tradeoffs to their civil liberties to win.“We are going to be the dominant player or China is going to be the dominant player. And there will be very different rules depending on who wins,” Karptold Axioslast year. “When people are worried about surveillance, of course there are huge dangers there, but it’s like, you will have far fewer rights if America is not in the lead.”The view from ChinaWhile Amodei and other US AI leaders frame competition with China as a race to reach a super-powerful artificial intelligence first and worry about AI breaking free of human control, experts say that most Chinese firms and their government don’t view the technology the same way. Instead, loss of control debates are relatively new in China, and the government’s primary concern is how AI could lead to domestic social unrest.As China and the US are set to hold talks this month on AI cooperation, experts say Beijing is primarily approaching the talks from a place of distrust that the negotiations are merely a way to suppress its growth under the guise of safety. Amodei’s essay has fueled that concern.“They’re very much paying attention to Amodei’s essay and they’re also conflating his essay with potential US approach in the upcoming AI safety talks,” said Kenton Thibaut, senior resident China fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab.Trump is set to meet with Xi Jinping in less than a week in Washington, with AI high on the agenda.China’s state-backed media properties have aggressively criticized Amodei,accusing himof running a “cold war playbook” against China through his support for an AI slowdown. Experts say Anthropic’s dual calls for both strict export controls on China and safety agreements have also had the effect of combining the discourse around two arguably separate subjects: AI safety and economic competition around AI.“Anthropic has played quite a strong role here in linking those issues together in a way that they maybe didn’t need to be linked,” Brookings’ Chan said. “To put it really bluntly, it made it much harder to get the Chinese to want to talk about these things and not see it purely as a veiled way to slow them down.”A race to the bottomWhile the Trump administration negotiates with China, the growing domestic backlash to the AI industry in the US may force lawmakers to take action regardless of how it affects global power dynamics. Nationwide opposition to datacenters and recent cybersecurity incidents such as OpenAI’s modelshacking into outside organizationshave become midterm election topics, adding incentive for lawmakers to to address the immediate harms related to AI.“You can go ahead and wield the China arms race argument, but at some point this industry will also have to deal with the consequences of fueling a race to the bottom,” said Amba Kak, co-executive director at the AI Now Institute and former senior adviser on AI for the Federal Trade Commission.Although experts and diplomatshave expressed little hopethat upcoming US-China talks will lead to major agreements, it is also possible that the increasingly real risks of AI being used for autonomous weapons, cyberattacks and other destabilizing technologies may force countries to shift the AI race’s course even if they don’t stop building it.“We don’t win if we develop the killer robots first. Nobody wants killer robots,” Thibaut said. “There should be powerful incentives on both sides to stop this.”

title: Google says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companies | Google | The Guardian
description: Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: Disclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI models
Content: Google said the hacks highlighted the importance of training its AI models to ‘act responsibly’.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGoogle said the hacks highlighted the importance of training its AI models to ‘act responsibly’.Photograph: John Angelillo/UPI/ShutterstockGoogleGoogle says its Gemini AI model hacked three other companiesDisclosure comes after OpenAI and Anthropic hacks amid fears that tech firms unable to control powerful AI modelsJohana BhuiyanFri 18 Sep 2026 20.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 20.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a first forGoogle, the company confirmed that its AI model, Gemini, breached the security of three other companies in May. The hacks occurred during a cybersecurity evaluation by AI-security firm Irregular.Irregular, an Israel-based startup that scrutinizes the security of advanced AI systems, was also at the center of some of the recentOpenAIandAnthropichacks of third-party entities, including OpenAI’sbreachof AI software company, Hugging Face.The circumstances that enabled the models to hack other companies in some of these cases are similar: Irregular was testing the models in a closed testing environment with fake companies. The testing environment was not supposed to be internet enabled, but internet access was made available unintentionally,according tothe Wall Street Journal. Once connected to the internet, the models unexpectedly hacked into real firms.Irregular disclosed the hacks to Google at the end of July after discovering OpenAI hacked into Hugging Face. Google confirmed to the Guardian that the hacks occurred, but that the company did not feel it required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies. The Wall Street Journalfirst reported on the breachesand revealed for the first time that they occurred.“In a standard evaluation, the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test,” Heather Adkins, vice-president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement. “In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”In one of the security breaches, Irregular was testing Gemini’s cybersecurity capabilities by prompting the AI model to obtain information from a fake company’s software. The fake company had the same name as a real company. When the model unintentionally gained access to the internet, it correctly guessed the password of and breached a real company’s service, Irregular told the WSJ. Google said once it figured out it had hacked a real company, and not the simulated one, it stopped.In two other tests, the model searched the web for and found public repositories containing credentials to two other companies. The model used those credentials to access real companies. When it figured out they were real companies, it stopped, according to Google.Anthropic and OpenAI chose to voluntarily disclose the hacks but Google did not. However, the company said it ensured the three companies that were hacked were made aware.“These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly,” Adkins, the Google spokesperson, said.Anthropic and OpenAI’s disclosures prompted the independent senator Bernie Sanders to demand the companies pause development of their technology, saying it signaled the company was no longer able to control their models.OpenAI paused development of their models fortwo weeks, while Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei hascalled for a collective slowdownof AI development to ensure that its most advanced models are being built with enough safeguards.Explore more on these topicsGoogleAI (artificial intelligence)AlphabetnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners | Transport | The Guardian
description: Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group
Content: The Blade Runners group began attacking traffic infrastructure in 2023.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Blade Runners group began attacking traffic infrastructure in 2023.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyTransport‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scannersSensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ groupEsther AddleySat 19 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, inDevon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers.A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.”Posted to social media after the incident on 28 August, the footage rapidlyattracted attention. To some, it was an act of straightforward vandalism; a woman in her 60s and man in his 70s werelater arrestedand bailed on suspicion of criminal damage and causing danger to road users.Others, however, believed the woman should be lauded. “Not all heroes wear capes,” reads one Facebook comment on a supporter’s page. “Bideford and Barnstaple next, please,” reads another.Most people view traffic lights as helpful landmarks that keep road and pavement users safe. To a group who call themselves “Blade Runners”, however, the traffic scanners installed above them increasingly conceal a sinister purpose: to install “phased array electronic assault weapons” on city streets that they claim can carry out mass surveillance and even cause cancer, dementia and sudden death.Previous activists claiming affiliation to the movement havetargeted Ulez camerasin London, resentful at their surveillance and the resulting emission zone charges; there have also been sporadicattackson 5G mobile network towers, inspired by conspiracy theories that include the suggestion theyspread Covid.View image in fullscreenA vandalised Ulez camera in west London targeted by ‘Blade Runners’ in 2024.Photograph: Maureen McLean/AlamyIlfracombe is not the only town where traffic scanners have been attacked. In May, police in Cambridgeappealed for informationabout a suspect after nearly 200 traffic detector units were damaged. In the same month inSleaford, Lincolnshire, 10 units were vandalised in a week, with the council describing the conspiracy claims as “ridiculous”. In County Durham, apensioner is facing trialafter allegedly damaging units on eight sets of traffic lights.To Susan Grant-Muller, a professor of technologies and informatics at the University of Leeds’s Institute forTransportStudies, hostility to traffic scanners is puzzling because “this technology, in its most basic form, has been around since the late 70s”. Activists targeting traffic lights do not generally damage the familiar green, amber and red stop-go systems, but instead target additional sensors installed on top that monitor vehicle volume and, in some cases, pedestrian numbers, to allow lights to be phased to help traffic flow smoothly.“The cameras aren’t recording any personal information at all,” says Grant-Muller. “They aren’t recording faces or any details about the car. They just detect that there is something there, a car or person, and the length of the queue that people are waiting in.”They are generally only installed at junctions with a history of traffic flow problems, she says – often at the request of concerned local residents – and are welcomed byLiving Streets, which promotes pedestrian safety. “Better monitoring technology improves pedestrian safety at traffic lights and crossings, [particularly] when enforcement technology is used as part of a wider approach to road safety,” says Tanya Braun, the charity’s director of external affairs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDrivers ignoring roadwork closures to skip queues ‘wilfully putting lives at risk’Read moreNone of this convinces those who see a more nefarious purpose behind them. Conspiracies about these scanners fits into a broader fear of surveillance and limits to individual freedom. This is part of a“super-conspiracy” that believers call “the great reset”, says Clare Birchall, a professor of contemporary culture at King’s College London, who has written extensively on technology and conspiracist thinking.“These super-conspiracies draw all sorts of different things together to give some kind of shape to a whole bunch of different anxieties and fears,” says Birchall. “We’re all worried about technological overreach. Lots of people are worried about datacentres. And I often read conspiracy theories as a vernacular form of critique. It’s an everyday version of what we’re all trying to grasp.“I’m not surprised at all that [some] people need to find a narrative to find their way through it, because we’re so disenfranchised when it comes to the collection of our data or what happens to that.”Conspiracies often form in response to frightening events, agrees Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor and chair in cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, “and if you can assign that to a bunch of evil-doers who are responsible, that can provide psychological comfort for certain people, because they’d rather have bad people do bad things, then realise that the world contains effectively random events that you can’t control”.Explore more on these topicsTransportCrimeRoad safetyMotoringDevonLondonSurveillancefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Domestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your home | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Energy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save money
Author: Shane Hickey
Headline: Energy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save money
Content: More companies are working on ways people can heat their homes in different and cheaper ways.Photograph: Jamie Grill/Getty Images/Tetra images RFView image in fullscreenMore companies are working on ways people can heat their homes in different and cheaper ways.Photograph: Jamie Grill/Getty Images/Tetra images RFEnergy billsDomestic datacentres: how computer power can help heat your homeEnergy bills are scheduled to rise next month but there are innovative ways to heat your home and save moneyShane HickeySat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Giles Gibson turns on the hot tap in his home, the water that comes out of it is not heated by gas but by the tiny datacentre strapped to the tank.Attached to the hot water cylinder in his London home is a compact computer server that generates heat and then transfers it as it operates.Gibson gets the benefit of hot water when he needs it at a reduced cost, while the heat that is generated by the server is not lost into the air, a big environmental problem with large datacentres around the world.“As soon as I read about it, I thought: ‘This is obvious – why wouldn’t you do this?’”he says. “It just makes sense to take a computer out of a datacentre and to strap it next to your water tank and get free heat.”View image in fullscreenGiles Gibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom home have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the datacentre system installed last year.Photograph: Giles GibsonGibson estimates that the hot water bills for his four-bedroom house in south-east London have fallen by between £10 and £15 a month since he had the system installed last year.“So over a year, it adds up, and it’s just another little extra that helps,” Gibson says. “Having one of these units is a no-brainer.”Saving waste heatWithdomestic energy bills set to rise again next month, and growing disquiet about the impact of large-scale datacentres on the environment, there are lots of projects looking at how to harness the heat being thrown out by computers.Gibson’s system, supplied by the Surrey-based companyheata, is one of a number of innovative ideas on the market that aim to tackle the problem of waste heat on a domestic scale.Heata operates a sustainable cloud computing business that sends processing jobs from its clients to the servers in people’s homes. The devices have the combined power of about eight laptops.“What the home gives us is effectively somewhere to put a server that has a power connection, and a fibre connection, and a place for heat to go,” says Charlie Beharrell, commercial director of heata.View image in fullscreenThe heata unit in Giles Gibson’s home.Photograph: HeataHe says the company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water. “The water in their hot water cylinder will effectively be heated by our server, and they might have to use the gas boiler for the peakier moments in the day, like when they have a bath,” Beharrell says.“The idea is that the primary heating system is working a lot less hard to heat the water than it would normally have to do if our system wasn’t in place.”How it worksIt can only work in homes with vented, unpressurised water cylinders, typically recognisable by the blue insulation around the outside.A container with the server in is attached to the front of the cylinder after engineers cut a hole in the insulation.It is glued to the boiler with a thermal paste so the unit can conduct heat to the cylinder with no plumbing involved. There is no cost for the installation.View image in fullscreenA heata unit being installed in a home.Photograph: Heata“It takes a couple of hours and we retrofit it to the domestic water system,” Beharrell says.Heata pays for the electricity that is used to keep the server running, while the homeowner pays for the fibre broadband connection that is necessary.Beharrell says that millions of homes are fitted with vented water cylinders, while the units can also work with heat pumps.However, the system is not suitable for homes with combi boilers. A version for unvented cylinders is in development.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHeata’s units are now in 100 homes and there are 3,000 people on the waiting list for installation.Anyone interested in having one can sign up on the company’s website, heata.co.The company says hundreds more are expected to be installed next year.Easy as Raspberry Pi?In aseparate project in Essex, two households are testing a concept where almost 500 matchbox-sized computers are stored together to form a mini datacentre, and the heat generated from them is converted into energy.The freezer-sized HeatHub units are made by the Wales-based companythermifyand, like heata’s, also recycle the energy created when computers process tasks.They work differently from the heata system and the makers say they could one day replace domestic boilers.The heat created by the rows of Raspberry Pi computers warms a mineral oil that surrounds them.“The computers get the mineral oil hot,” says thermify’s chief executive, Travis Theune. “We send that through a heat exchanger. The heat exchanger heats up the water that’s going through a radiator, and the radiator delivers heat to the room. It’s the same basic concept as an induction heater.”View image in fullscreenHeata company aims to provide about 80% of the heat needed for a home’s hot water.Photograph: Soho Studio/AlamyThe existing units have 480 computers in them, which carry out tasks for companies that buy time to process the work they want done.Theune says that the company plans to make a range of units to cater for different-sized homes. For example, a three- to four-bedroom house will have a unit which is about the size of a washing machine, while a flat could have one the size of a microwave.He says that the thermify systems will cost homeowners £90 a month, based on an average-sized home. A bigger house, that requires more energy, will cost more, and a flat less, he says.The planned cost includes installation, leasing the unit, repairs, and will have a minimum 10-year contract.The company claims that the device will lead to a 14% reduction in bill costs compared with homes with a gas boiler, and 34% for those households with a heat pump, over a 15-year period.The savings come from not having to pay for the installation of a boiler or the heat pump.Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHome improvementsSaving moneyConsumer affairsHousehold billsEnergy industryDatacentres - UKfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Maga wants more babies. But they don’t seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detention | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Officials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they need
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Officials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they need
Content: ‘It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers; the agency, and the Trump administration, is normally very big on surveillance.’Photograph: AlamyOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)Maga wants more babies. But they don’t seem too worried about miscarriages in ICE detentionArwa MahdawiOfficials lack data on miscarriages after October 2025. Detained women aren’t getting the prenatal healthcare they needSat 19 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTShareMaga men have babies on the brain. They may not all be interested inchanging diapersor hands-on parenting, but they’re very keen on population growth. “[W]e want more babies, to put it very nicely,” Donald Trump saidlast year.Trump, who has called himself the “father of IVF” andjokedthat he will be known as the “fertilization president”, surrounds himself with people who profess a similar fondness for children. Only afew daysafter being sworn in as vice-president, JD Vance declared he wanted “more babies in the United States of America” and went on to make pronatalist policies a theme of his time in office.Meanwhile, the administration’s favourite moneyman, Elon Musk, is doing his own part to increase the population. Ashley St Clair, the mother of one of his many offspring, has claimed he once told her hewanted to have“a legion of children before the civil war”. At least one of Musk’s kids hasdenounced him, so I’m not sure he’s considered that they might not all be fighting on the same side.While the Trump administration may want a baby boom, it won’t shock you to hear that, when you take a closer look at their particular brand of pronatalism, they don’t actually seem to want “more babies”. What they really want, judging by the way in which pregnant immigrants are being treated, is more of the “right” type of baby.AGuardian investigationpublished this week revealed that ICE is arresting a record number of pregnant women and teenagers. These detained women are reportedly not receiving the prenatal healthcare they need and, alarmingly, ICE does not seem to have records of how many of these women have suffered miscarriages.“ICE recorded 18 miscarriages during the first nine months of the Trump administration,” the Guardian writes. “[B]ut the agency has no data on miscarriages after 3 October 2025.” Let me just reiterate that: we have no idea how many women in ICE detention have lost their babies over the past 11 months.It’s very strange that ICE seems to have just stopped tracking miscarriage numbers;the agency, and theTrump administration, is normally very big on surveillance. Last year, the Guardianreportedthat pregnant immigrant women were turning up to hospitals to deliver their babies wearing location-tracking smartwatches as part of an ICE monitoring program. One of these women was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia, which can cause major swelling, and hospital staff were worried that the smartwatch would cut off her circulation. “She was in tears about [the idea of taking the surveillance device off],” a hospital staffer told the Guardian. “She had this deep fear that ICE was going to come to the hospital and take her baby.”Surveillance also extends to the broader pregnant population.
