When Dr Erica Schwartzwas confirmedby the US Senate as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) earlier this year, sheemphasized: “Abortion surveillance is absolutely a critical component of what the CDC is currently doing.” While the CDC doesn’t require states to collect data on abortions, 44 states plus Washington DC have some sort of mandated abortion reporting, according to theGuttmacher Institute. This isn’t necessarily sinister but, following the overturning of Roe v Wade, there has been growing concern that this data might be weaponized to punish abortion patients and providers, who are increasingly being treated like criminals.And that concern is hardly unfounded. In the first two years after Roe was overturned, prosecutors in 16 states charged more than 400 people with pregnancy-related crimes, a2025 reportby the group Pregnancy Justice found. The report also noted that there are likely far more cases of miscarriage criminalization than have made headlines.Funny, isn’t it? If you suffer a miscarriage in ICE detention, possibly because of systemic medical neglect, the US government will apparently shrug and look the other way. But if you have a miscarriage in a state that hasfetal personhood languagein its abortion laws, you may find yourself facing a police investigation and criminal charges. Once again, there is nothing pro-life about this administration. They are solely pro-control.FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles“These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” an internalFBI memo warns. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online.” Oh dear, my heart bleeds for these poor ICE agents.Turkey is targeting LGBTQ+ activists and journalistsStarting last Sunday, Turkish police raided the offices of LGBTQ+ rights organizations and HIV-advocacy groups. Then they arrested peopleprotestingagainst the raids and journalists covering the protests. “This is thewidest crackdownon LGBTQ+ people in recent years,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, of Human Rights Watch. Homosexuality isn’t illegal in Turkey, but the government seems to be weaponizing “obscenity” laws to target the community.Israeli ‘double tap’ strike kills child and medic in GazaThe “ceasefire”continues.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWomen ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’ than men with the same conditionNew research from the University of St Andrews found that women have significantly unequal medical care. Men are far more likely to be offered treatments such as strong painkillers or surgery,according to the analysis.Joe Rogan calls Trump supporters ‘nuts’ and ‘rabid’Does thepodcasternot realize that his supporthelpedget Trump elected? Lack of self-awareness aside, it’s amusing to watch some of Trump’s former supporters turn on the president.Michigan high school asks girls to share details of menstrual cyclesFemale students who miss swimming because of their periods need to have a parent submit a note “stating the length of the menstrual duration” so they canmake up the day. If you don’t comply,your grade is at risk.Indonesia’s all-female firefighting team are battling peatland blazes and patriarchal attitudesOne hundred and forty-six women, aged between 20 and 58,make up the Power of Mama, which protects the biodiverse region of Indonesian Borneo. “Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most,” one member said of what motivated her to fight fires. “I thought I had to do something about it.”Kash Patel defends new FBI bestiality policyPatel told a Senate judiciary committee oversight hearing that the FBI “did not want to punish victims of bestiality” byautomatically disqualifying them. At one point of this absurd hearing, a senator from Louisiana asked Patel whether the change “disqualified the animal” from FBI service. Just when you thought US politics couldn’t get any more stupid, it goes and surprises you.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)OpinionSurveillanceFBITurkeyLGBTQ+ rightsIsraelGazacommentShareReuse this content

title: By fixating on immigration numbers, are our leaders missing the bigger picture for working Australians? | Sanmati Verma | The Guardian
description: It can be tempting to blame grievance politics or the rise of One Nation for the tenor of current debate, but these are symptoms of a deeper malaise
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: It can be tempting to blame grievance politics or the rise of One Nation for the tenor of current debate, but these are symptoms of a deeper malaise
Content: Tony Burke’s address at the National Press Club ‘was a message for all working people – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us’, writes Sanmati Verma.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenTony Burke’s address at the National Press Club ‘was a message for all working people – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us’, writes Sanmati Verma.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionAustralian immigration and asylumBy fixating on immigration numbers, are our leaders missing the bigger picture for working Australians?Sanmati VermaIt can be tempting to blame grievance politics or the rise of One Nation for the tenor of current debate, but these are symptoms of a deeper malaiseSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.05 EDTShareWhen the immigration minister,Tony Burke, approached the National Press Club podium on Thursday, the eyes of every migrant in the country would have been fixed on him. But, in fact, Burke’s address was a message for all working people across the country – and a signal of the times ahead for all of us.The past 12 months have seen all sides of politics cohere around the consensus articulated in theintroductionto Burke’s address by the press club’s president, Tom Connell: “there is furious agreement over a need for a cut to immigration.” The only difference across the political spectrum is in the detail: who deserves to be cut, and who is valuable or otherwise deserving enough to remain.The fight over immigration could decide the next election. Labor has to take the gloves off | Tom McIlroyRead moreIn fact, judging by the tenor of current debate, it would be easy to think that immigration is theonlyeconomic lever available to the government to address housing affordability, falling wages and cost-of-living pressures. To test that theory, consider whether, over a Sunday lunch, your uncle is more likely to proffer an opinion on tax settings driving housing speculation, the corporate supermarket duopoly or immigration levels? There is an attractively simple supply-and-demand logic underlying the assumption that fewer people will automatically mean more to go around.But migrants didn’t design – and then implement over 20 years – thetax breaks that transformed housing into an asset, allowing investors to drive up prices and control distribution through property hoarding. And it wasn’t migrants, sitting in state and federal legislatures, who chose to wind back investment in public housing that previous generations had benefited from.Migrants didn’t mastermind theattacks on collective bargainingthat have seen union membership and real wages plummet over the past two decades. And they didn’t invent the supermarket duopoly or dictate the eye-watering profits that Coles and Woolworths maintain, driving upgrocery prices while wages remain stagnant.But as long as public debate remains fixated on immigration numbers, the bigger policy questions that could actually transform the lives of working people will remain unanswered. And there will be an endless, self-fulfilling cycle of blame targeting our friends, neighbours and co-workers born overseas for problems not of their making.Burke set the scene for future blame-shifting. Design features of our migration program are ascribed to temporary migrants as a kind of collective moral failing. For decades, governments have re-geared the migration system towards temporary migration and shifted the goalposts on permanent residency. The natural result of this – that people transition between temporary visas to realise their hopes of permanent migration – has been recast as an illegitimate form of “visa-hopping”.International students and graduates will no longer be able to migrate with their partners and children because, according to Burke, they should not receive special treatment compared with permanent residents and citizens forced to wait years for family reunion. But family visa processing blowouts are the direct result of ministerial directions thatdeprioritise and slow down some applications.Labor visa overstayer detention centre plan branded a ‘Donald Trump twist’ on immigrationRead moreThe path has been cleared for more “comprehensive” measures to come, when political and economic pressures demand them. The government has repeatedly floated the idea of legislating a 30-day window on asylum applications, requiring new migrants to make a claim immediately or miss out. This would, of course, force people seeking asylum who have missed the eligibility window to remain in the community without a visa, exposing them either to destitution, exploitative work in the cash economy or being rounded up in immigration raids.As tempting as it might be to blame grievance politics, far-right organising or the electoral rise of One Nation for the current impasse, these are just symptoms of a much deeper malaise. It will always be in the interests of our political leaders and their backers to deflect blame for economic conditions away from themselves and on to people who cannot speak back at the ballot box.By continuing to allow immigration to be the scapegoat for economic grievance, we not only abandon refugees and migrants to endless cycles of blame – we abandon working people to the very conditions that produced the grievances in the first place.Sanmati Verma is the legal director of the migration justice program at the Human Rights Law CentreExplore more on these topicsAustralian immigration and asylumOpinionAustralian politicsTony BurkecommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia has done precious little to prepare for the dangers of AI. Where is brilliant leadership when you need it? | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: Australia faces stark choices about the most significant technological development since the splitting of the atom in the 1930s
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: Australia faces stark choices about the most significant technological development since the splitting of the atom in the 1930s
Content: The Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, has warned that rogue AI agents, like those from OpenAI that escaped their test environment in July, are ‘capable of taking over the entire internet’ within six to 12 monthsPhotograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, has warned that rogue AI agents, like those from OpenAI that escaped their test environment in July, are ‘capable of taking over the entire internet’ within six to 12 monthsPhotograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Australia has done precious little to prepare for the dangers of AI. Where is brilliant leadership when you need it?Zoe DanielAustralia faces stark choices about the most significant technological developmentsince the splitting of the atom in the 1930sGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastSat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 17.25 EDTShareThere’s nothing like a threat of human extinction to focus the mind.The threat of AI to the existence of humanity has long been raised.But with the rapid mainstreaming of artificial intelligence,warningsfrom three researchers from Anthropic have landed differently, with the prediction that the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade.As if people didn’t have enough to worry about with the cost of living, shortage of housing, climate change, resulting escalating mental health issues, the drift to rightwing populism and fraying of democracy, now this.If the expected question from the grandkids was “What did you do when the world was burning and democracy was failing?”, it’s now “What did you do when we got to the brink of outsmarting ourselves out of existence?”Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?Read moreThere are deep community concerns about datacentres, jobs and livelihoods, privacy and the very future of human creativity.Tech journalistsare already claiming AI agents are “harassing people, making spam and sales calls, deleting your inbox, cancelling flights, giving control of Instagram accounts to hackers, deleting companies’ databases, filling music streaming platforms with slop, hacking companies, running scams, and snatching up dinner reservations. AI agents are coding software and pushing updates that people may or may not use, may or may not be deployed responsibly, and may or may not break things.”TheAnthropicchief executive, Dario Amodei, has warned that rogue AI agents, like those from OpenAI that escaped their test environment in July, are “capable of taking over the entire internet” within six to 12 months.Agentic AI is also capable of doing much good, including, among other things, identifying network vulnerabilities, responding nimbly to threats and threading knowledge across sectors.And while much of the focus is on the risks that AI poses to democracy, there is immense potential to use it toincreasecommunity engagement and participation if deployed well.It’s the risk/reward matrix that’s at the core of the policy and regulation struggle around data, mis- and disinformation and community trust, national security and finance, as well as the overall impact on communities, for good and bad.Anew studyfrom MIT FutureTech and the University of Queensland identifies five risks as the most likely to produce the most severe harms; dangerous capabilities, competitive pressures, weapons and cyber-attacks, concentrated power and false information: “Under the business-as-usual scenario, experts judged that 18 of the 24 AI risk domains had at least a 10% probability of catastrophic outcomes over the next five years.”So, what now?The researchers emphasise the need to treat AI as a new paradigm with “ecosystem-wide, society-wide opportunities and vulnerabilities.”The Albanese government has recently taken some initial steps but, as Western Australian independentKate Chaney notesin her recent discussion paper on AI, Australia has done “remarkably little to prepare” not for what’s coming but what’s already here.Several nations are attempting to transition to their own “native” systems amid concerns that a “kill switch” could be deployed as a weapon. This could crash economies and cause untold death and destruction by shutting down healthcare, education, transport, energy and all other communications reliant systems.One of my definitive reflections on covering disasters as a foreign correspondent is that once the communications fail all other systems break down, including law and order. This threat is dire.In the UK,there are calls fora new, multinational AI treaty.OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, has said: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”Anthropic lands deal in $31bn datacentre in western Queensland, David Crisafulli saysRead moreThe Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, is a proponent of stronger alliances between middle powers. He is advocating for cooperation with like-minded democracies to avoid dependence on global tech giants, through “strategic autonomy”.The US president, Donald Trump, meanwhile, whowill meetthe Chinese president, Xi Jinping, in Washington this week, says: “We’re leading China on AI ... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.”Right now, more than 30% of the US Standard and Poor’s top 500 index sits with a handful of tech companies. Nvidia alone represents 8% of the S&P.Both OpenAIand Anthropic are preparing to list on the Nasdaq.If ever we needed sensible, collaborative and timely leadership, it’s now.There is no other option but to proactively and thoughtfully manage both the risks and opportunities that come with what looks to be the most significant technological developmentsince the splitting of the atom in the 1930s. That brought with it both profound benefits and mass destruction.And, if you thought the world was already ruled by the tech bros, it’s about to go nuclear.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionOpenAIAnthropicAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Ed Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he was | Jason Okundaye | The Guardian
description: Twenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking out, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Author: Jason Okundaye
Headline: Twenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking out, says Guardian columnist Jason Okundaye
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at Coachella in California on 19 April 2025.Photograph: Timothy Norris/Getty Images for CoachellaView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at Coachella in California on 19 April 2025.Photograph: Timothy Norris/Getty Images for CoachellaOpinionEd SheeranEd Sheeran thought fans didn’t want artists to be politically engaged. He’s finding out how wrong he wasJason OkundayeTwenty years ago, even Madonna faced radio blacklisting for being overtly political. But in our age of streaming, there’s less excuse for not speaking outSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 07.14 EDTShareIt must have come as a surprise to Ed Sheeran when all of hissupport acts withdrewfrom the remainder of the US leg of his tour. The American rapper Macklemore had triggered the walkout when he gave an impassioned speech calling for a “free Palestine” on stage and was dropped for doing so. The decision by the remaining acts to drop out in solidarity exposed a deep divide in the modern music industry.Some artists still insist on keeping politics out of music, while others expect music to speak to our perilous times.After he was dropped,Macklemore wrotethat Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before”, to which Sheeranresponded: “I am not complicit” and “those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum”.Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row - The LatestRead moreI think that the concept of expectation is worth probing. The idea that artists should make their political sentiments known is often dismissed as a parasocial delusion, one particularly rampant among young people on social media who “call out” musicians for their silence (indeed, young people are far more likely to be in favour of musiciansusing their concerts to make political statements). Artists aren’t politicians, the criticism goes, and to consider them as such distracts from, even compromises, the purpose of art as a forum for personal expression and of escapism. In other words, why not just enjoy the music instead of expecting activism from musicians, too?The problem with that idea is that it treats a separation of art and politics as natural rather than something determined by historical convention. It wasn’t so long ago that expectations were quite different. There used to be a neater division between countercultural musicians who were relegated to the periphery and mainstream artists who would be disciplined if they spoke up.The MTV era of music in the 2000s prioritised blockbuster, spectacle and glamour, while avoiding political, social and economic controversies. Artists were generally expected to keep politics out of their music. When Madonna challenged that idea in 2003 with her single American Life, which opposed US foreign policy and jingoism at the onset of the Iraq war, the backlash was heavy: she wasforced to dumpits “un-American” music video, and faced heavy radio blacklisting. It took years forthe Chicks, then known as The Dixie Chicks, to recover commercially from the backlash they faced to their criticism of the Iraq War and George W Bush around the same period.Today, theexpectations that audiences have of artistsare different from two decades ago. Partly, this is because the economics and the technology behind the music industry has changed. In the age of streaming, it is harder to silence artists who have made politically problematic statements – radio station blacklisting is far less fatal than it was before people discovered music through their phones and algorithms.Interestingly, this greater political autonomy also means that the biggest artists take less of a commercial hit in their worst moments. After Kanye West’s antisemitic rants (which the rapper apologised for), his albumVultures still reached No 1on the Billboard charts in 2024. On his most recent tour, he performed at AT&T stadium in Arlington, Texas, one of the venues that banned Macklemore from performing.In any case, this greater autonomy pushes young fans to ask: why not take the risk? Why not speak? Particularly in the case of Palestine, it has often been smaller and less influential artists who have done so. Think of how the scale of Sheeran’s commercial reach, by contrast, dwarfs that of the artists around him who have risked more by speaking out.Artists, both alternative and mainstream, have also set this expectation for each other. The stances a musician has taken on pressing issues are no longer just cudgels used against them. Rather, silence on these matters has become a source of shame.Billie Eilishrebuked her fellow celebrities for not taking a stance against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the US and itskilling of civilians. The Irish singer-songwriter CMAT, who I saw at Glastonbury last year leading a “free Palestine” chant on the Pyramid Stage, had this to say while receiving the award for best album at theIvor Novello Awardsthis year: “I have a very specific idea of what songwriting is supposed to be for, and I think it is to reflect the times through your own personal view so that everybody can have something to connect to and something to learn from years later. And now I would compel my fellow artists in the room, it is not the time to sit on the fence.”The political shift in music also reflects a tonal shift. Artists have become more emotionally intimate with their audiences. I was struck by ananalysispublished earlier this year by the music data company Musixmatch for the Economist, which assessed lyrics from the Billboard charts to conclude that pop music has become “gloomier”. The most popular songs increasingly invoke sadness, angst and heartbreak.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA study in the Times also found that the musical mood hasbecome more downbeat. This is in itself not surprising – listeners increasingly wantauthenticityfrom musicians and depend on it for a sense of connection. Think of the music of Eilish and CMAT, both of whom are popular with young audiences and praised for filterless emotion. They invoke that gloom, vulnerability and emotion – in other words, they communicate pain as a central tenor of their sound.As CMAT said of her music, which muses on isolation, capitalism and disillusionment: “Everyone has the same wants and desires, and if you’re really honest as an artist with your pain, it will always connect.” For many young people, part of the pain they have felt in the past few years has been in witnessing the events in Gaza, as well as the rising global tide offar-right populism, the climate crisis and instability. So for a generation that is increasingly accustomed to having their despair made audible through gloomier music, why would they not increasingly expect artists to draw connections between their personal pain and what is causing it?Artists, then, cannot assume that the old bargain still holds. Sheeran’s insistence on an apolitical arena of music is increasingly anachronistic – a position that has exposed the faultlines of modern music. Many listeners increasingly seek emotional clarity as well as moral clarity. Whether popular music has risen to that moment will be judged by history. But for now, as the expectation changes, it is down to artists to decide if they change with it.Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the GuardianDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsEd SheeranOpinionMacklemoreActivismYoung peopleMusic industryPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: After 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properly | Jamie Oliver | The Guardian
description: This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful, says chef and campaigner Jamie Oliver
Author: Jamie Oliver
Headline: This week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful, says chef and campaigner Jamie Oliver
Content: Children wait to be served dinner at a school in Swindon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreenChildren wait to be served dinner at a school in Swindon.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyOpinionSchool mealsAfter 20 years of my school dinners campaign, I’m a happy man. At last, we’re going to feed kids properlyJamie OliverThis week’s government announcement on school food standards is huge. It’s based on common sense and science. Beautiful!Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 13.20 EDTShareMore than 20 years ago, when I started thecampaign and TV series School Dinners, I couldn’t believe that we had standards for dog food but no standards for the food we fed our children at school. I have never, and will never, stop banging that drum – even after this week’smomentous announcement on school food standardsin England. Because it is so important we remember where we started from.Children in the state sector are at school for 190 days a year. And if they’re eating breakfast and lunch there, the majority of what they consume each day is in the hands of their school. When we know that children are consuming less than half the recommended fruit and vegetables, buttwice the recommended sugar, school food is a massive opportunity to directly improve diets at scale.But eating good food around a shared table isn’t just important for children’s health. It’s a core part of a child’ssocial connection and sense of belonging. Well-fed kidsare happier, have more energy and fewer days off school due to sickness, andtheir learningandbehaviour improve, too.It’s no surprise that80% of teachers agreethat unhealthy food at lunch and breaktime can lead to disruptive behaviour, and 85% say diet affects pupils’ ability to concentrate.But we didn’t need scientific evidence to tell us that – who doesn’t feel and perform better when their bellies are full of the good stuff? Get school food right and the prize is massive. Not just for children today, but for the adults they will become. Feed children well and we give them a better chance of healthier lives, greater productivity and less long-term pressure on the NHS and social care from diet-related disease. That’s no small change when current estimates are that obesity, and its knock-on consequences, costs the UK economy about£126bn each year.That is why it’s so great to see the government announce new standards, based on the latest science. It’s the first time in a decade. And it means, for this generation of kids, they will be nourished with more fruit and vegetables, fibre-rich proteins and whole grains. Beautiful stuff.It’s a big and much-needed update, but we know that amazing schools, caterers and chefs can rise to the challenge. Through myGood School Food awards, we have shown amazing school food is possible and affordable, and it’s happening right now in schools across the UK.TakeChef Russ in Bournemouth. Working out of a cupboard-sized kitchen, he has transformed the food at his school. Not only has the school increased the uptake of meals from 28% to 98%, there’s a waiting list of parents keen to nab their kids a place there.We see this pattern in schools up and down the country, and we have to keep telling these stories again and again because it goes against what many people think they know – that kids simply won’t eat the “good stuff”. We have heard that for decades. And we get it, because the food environment we all struggle with makes it hard to eat well, and so this seems to chime with our experience. But school is different. It’s a rare, protected space where that noise can be stripped away.And when it is, remarkable things happen. Children eat – and enjoy – delicious, nutritious food. The evidence is clear: when the food is good and the environment is supportive, over time school meal uptake increases.View image in fullscreenJamie Oliver serves up a healthy school dinner.Photograph: Andy Butterton/PAWhat makes me excited is these standards won’t just sit on a piece of paper. There will be proper monitoring to make sure they are actually followed. Not to nit-pick. Not to catch schools out. But so we know what’s working, where schools are doing brilliantly, and where we need to deploy care, love and support to help them get it right. That’s where theSchool Food Projectcomes in. We know not all lunch trays are created equal, which is why we are partnering with Bite Back, Chefs in Schools, School Food Matters and the Food Foundation to help to make sure these new standards can really be for everyone.These new school food standards will finally fix what is on children’s school plates, but it’s only half the job we have to do. A delicious lunch nourishes a child for the afternoon, but teaching them how to cook nourishes them for the rest of their life. You can serve the best meals in the world, but if a child leaves school without knowing how to feed themselves, that’s where it stops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionServing up salad success at school dinners | LettersRead moreThat is why food education must be absolutely central to transforming school food. And it’s why I’m passionate about giving kids (and adults) the skills, knowledge and confidence to cook from scratch. My dream has always been simple: I want every single child to leave school knowing 10 core skills that will save their life.My free10 skills food education programmeteaches kids basic, bulletproof culinary foundations – how to chop safely, balance flavours, cook a nutritious staple meal from scratch, and stretch simple, fresh ingredients into something delicious. If kids leave school knowing how to cook a fast vegetable stir-fry, a simple soup, or how to make a loaf of bread, not only will they be healthier now, but they have options in the future.With this cooking superpower they can feed themselves, and their future families, on a budget. That isn’t just a life skill: it’s health insurance for life.Jamie Oliver is a chef, restaurateur and campaignerExplore more on these topicsSchool mealsOpinionSchoolsObesityNHSHealthNutritionHealth & wellbeingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles | Anna Ivanenko | The Guardian
description: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Author: Anna Ivanenko
Headline: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Content: Illustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianOpinionUkraineMeditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missilesSometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming backAnna IvanenkoSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTShareSometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours afterUS Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow.Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time.I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen

title: Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answer | Timothy Garton Ash | The Guardian
description: Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Author: Timothy Garton Ash
Headline: Instead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watching, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Content: A protester holds up a placard reading ‘Nazis raus’ (Nazis out) during rival rallies at Koenigsplatz in Munich, Germany, 12 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protester holds up a placard reading ‘Nazis raus’ (Nazis out) during rival rallies at Koenigsplatz in Munich, Germany, 12 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)Here’s how Germany can defend its democracy. Banning the AfD isn’t the answerTimothy Garton AshInstead, constrain it legally and fight it politically. The world is watchingSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.08 EDTShareFar-right nationalist populist parties are making the running everywhere from Washington to Warsaw. So why be so alarmed about a littleregional electoral victoryfor one such party, the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), in one federal state, Saxony-Anhalt? “Because it’s Germany!” is the almost instinctive answer in many heads around the world.But that “because it’s Germany” needs to be taken apart, like the segments of an orange. Yes, because of Adolf Hitler, two dictatorships (NaziGermanyuntil 1945, communist-ruled East Germany until 1989) and two world wars. And yes, some of the language used by the AfD will give anyone familiar with Nazi rhetoric a cold shudder down the spine.Then there’s the fact that Germany is Europe’s central power. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel says that when her party gets into government after the federal election scheduled for 2029, Germany will abandon the euro and leave the Schengen border-free travel area. What would be left of the EU then?The great German liberal social and political thinker Ralf Dahrendorf,who died in 2009, told me more than once that he would only feel really confident of the resilience of German democracy when it had withstood the test of a big economic crisis. Well, the country is close to that now.The final segment of “because it’s Germany!” is perhaps the most interesting. The federal republic’s entire constitutional, political and educational system is designed to prevent anything like the collapse of the Weimar republic into Hitler’s dictatorship in 1933. The federal republic should be awehrhafte Demokratie– a democracy capable of defending itself.So how Germany will defend its democracy is a question not just of European but of global significance. Looking at all the answers being frenetically canvassed in Berlin, I think the most convincing formula is: neither ban the AfD nor embrace it, but instead constrain it legally and fight it politically.The German constitution provides for political parties that are “hostile” to its basic liberal democratic principles to be banned. Senior German politicians have called for an application to be made to the constitutional court to ban the AfD, or at least its most extreme parts, on those grounds. But it’s too late for that. The AfD has been a major force in the Bundestag since its success (off the back of the migration crisis)in the 2017 general electionand, like Reform UK in Britain, has led nationwide in opinion polls. To suddenly tell so many citizens “you’re not allowed to vote for the party you support!” would itself be an assault on democracy.But this is not democracy as the tyranny of the majority: the people have spoken, off with your head! It’sliberaldemocracy, meaning the outcome of any popular vote is constrained by the rule of law, human and minority rights, and pluralist, anti-majoritarian institutions. The real threats to German democracy today are less like Weimar in 1933than Budapest in 2010(when Viktor Orbán took over) and Washington DC in 2025. The mini-Donald Trumps of the AfD have reportedly been quietly exploring Trump-like executive and administrative devices they might use toconsolidate their control. The Federal Republic of Germany has the right, the power and the duty to stop them.Article 37 of the constitution, which allows federal authorities to overrule anti-constitutional behaviour by the states, has never been used in the 77-year history of the republic. Assuming, as now seems likely, the AfD forms the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, all federal powers, up to and including article 37, should be used wherever necessary. For example, they should prevent sensitive intelligence about Russia’s increasing aggression being shared with a Saxony-Anhalt branch of the domestic security service controlled by the pro-Russian AfD; secure the independence of courts and prosecutors, as well as the neutrality of police and civil service; and, I would add, stop any extreme politicisation of education and public service broadcasting. Of course, AfD politicians will cry “foul!”; tough. If, as they say, they want “another republic”, they can go and live in Russia.Yet even more important than these legal and administrative constraints is the political response. At the opposite end from those calling for the party to be banned are Christian Democrats calling forthe “firewall” to be abandoned and AfD politicians to be embraced as part of the normal political process. Letting them take responsibility in a state government will, it’s argued, expose their incoherence, incompetence and lack of real policy answers.Talking and working with them will end up moderating them, as apparently happened with Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. I’ve been tempted by these arguments myself. But evidence collected bypolitical scientistssuggests that a strategy of inclusion is just as likely to put more wind in the nationalists’ sails. And AfD activists are themselves warning against the danger ofMelonisierung(Melonisation).So Christian Democrats should not be tempted to get half into bed with the AfD, like a middle-aged man nervously edging into an extramarital affair. Instead, starting already this weekend with elections in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, they should more effectively combat it politically. Rather than defining Christian Democracy by what it’s against (the AfD and the far-left Linke), they should say what it’s for. To renew Germany’s social market economy, they should implement all the labour market, pension, tax and other reforms agreed this summer with their Social Democrat coalition partners – and more. Faced with huge external challenges, from Russian aggression to US and Chinese AI, the Christian Democrats – historically the party of Europe – should boldly advocate the European-scale answers which alone will give any European country the strength to stand up to giants.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut besides AI, Germany’s mainstream parties badly need EI (emotional intelligence). The key to the success of the AfD’s Ulrich Siegmund in Saxony-Anhalt, as with Trump and Britain’s Nigel Farage, is a kind of emotional communication. I’m here with you; I hear you and see you; I share your anger. With me, you can say what you really think and be yourself, because – whether or not I’m a millionaire – deep down I’m a normal bloke like you. So let’s all have a beer and march forward to an imagined past.It’s fascinating to re-read the exiled German political scientist Karl Loewenstein’s influential1937 articleon “militant democracy” and find him insisting that democracy cannot “devise emotional formulas capable of competing with the fascist Pied Pipers”. Hence the emphasis on constitutional constraints. But in our transformed information environment, with its premium on attention, drama and passion, democracy can’t be defended simply by legal constraints and rational policies. Democrats everywhere need to compete with today’s Pied Pipers on the emotional plane, too. Constant presence on social media and physical presence on the ground are both essential.Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, and to some extent the UK’s, Andy Burnham, have shown how it can be done. So much will now depend on German democrats, and especially Christian Democrats, proving they can do the same.Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book,Europe in 7 1/2 Chapters, is published in OctoberDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)OpinionThe far rightGermanyEuropeReform UKGiorgia MelonicommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?  | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievement
Content: ‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Andrew Scott in London earlier this month.Photograph: LounisPhotography/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Andrew Scott in London earlier this month.Photograph: LounisPhotography/ABACA/ShutterstockMoviesAnalysis‘He’s simply astonishing’: will Andrew Scott become the first out gay man to win the best actor Oscar?Catherine ShoardThe Irishman seems a dead cert for his performance as Ian Charleson in Elsinore. And his ability to avoid being pigeonholed while embracing queer stories, from Pride to All of Us Strangers, is a remarkable achievementSat 19 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.31 EDTShareThis Sunday, the curtain falls on theToronto film festival, the last of the three big autumn showcases – alongsideVeniceandTelluride– that are launchpads for award campaigns. And as the dust settles on the red carpets, one name rises above the others as destined for sure-fire glory: Andrew Scott.The Irish actor, 50 next month, is now not only considered a lock for a leading actor Oscar nomination but almost certain to take the prize next spring. Should he win, he will become the first out gay actor to do so in the Academy’s almost 100-year history.If that’s a fact that seems astonishing today, it would have felt an inevitability in 1989, when the film for which Scott has been so praised is set. InElsinore, he plays Ian Charleson, the dashing Scottish star of films including Chariots of Fire and Gandhi. Charleson had been given his first role three years before Chariots by Derek Jarman, but excised it from his CV (leading to a lifelong rift, depicted in Elsinore). Muting his sexuality was then considered essential in the pursuit of stardom. Yet despite such curation – and his undeniable talents – Charleson never reached the level of fame he felt he deserved.View image in fullscreenOscar buzz … Scott as Ian Charleson in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony DickensonUntil December 1989, that is, when he took over the role of Hamlet from Daniel Day-Lewis at the National Theatre, despite secretly having Aids. His performance wasreckoned to be one of the finest ever, and he died six weeks after the final show, aged 40. His family then went public with his diagnosis and sexuality: this was the first celebrity death in the UK attributed to Aids, and did much to boost awareness and acceptance.Elsinore review – Andrew Scott is astonishing as Ian Charleson in devastating Aids dramaRead moreThe film is a passion project for Scott, who also produced and rallied together funding alongside Stephen Beresford, screenwriter of Scott’s big-screen breakthrough, 2014’sPride, another real-life story of 1980s gay history, about an unlikely alliance of LGBTQ+ activists and striking Welsh miners. Scott was galvanised to get Elsinore off the ground by the death of his mother, Nora, in 2023. “When you’re in that grief state,” he said, “you feel like you’ve got nothing to lose.”The actor’s own path to stardom makes for a curious contrast with the man he plays. Born in Dublin in 1976, Scott shot his first film aged 17 before studying drama at Trinity College Dublin and moving to London aged 22. Despite playing gay characters, he, too, was advised to remain silent on his own sexuality, to avoid pigeonholing. Speaking after Elsinore’s Toronto premiere last week, Scott said such a climate gave him “a horrible feeling that I perhaps wasn’t going to be able to speak a language I was desperate to speak”.View image in fullscreenAnother real-life story … Scott with Imelda Staunton, Bill Nighy and Dominic West in Pride (2014).Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyHe came out publicly in 2013 aged 37, shortly after his small-screen breakthrough as Moriarty opposite Benedict Cumberbatch’s Sherlock. In the 13 years since, Scott has arguably done more than any man since Ian McKellen to refute the idea that publicly gay actors cannot plausibly play straight roles. His part in Fleabag is the most lusted after example, yet thehot prieststands alongside numerous other heterosexual characters he’s taken on: Richard Rogers inBlue Moon, Anthony Julius inDenial, 10 different people in hisone-man Uncle Vanya. Still in cinemas is his sturdy and scowling Group Captain James Stagg, meteorological hero of D-day and new dramaPressure.“The war is never over,” said Scott of the debate over LGBTQ+ casting in Toronto, “but there have been significant advances in what I believe is stopping the underestimation of audiences. They’re smart and they want to see representation and also transformation.”Andrew Scott is right – it’s time to retire the phrase ‘openly gay’ | Ryan GilbeyRead moreAnd yet alongside his more conventional career choices, the actor has also consistently sought to engage with the pricklier aspects of the debate – railing against the use of the phrase “openly gay” while doing the rounds forAll of Us Strangersin 2023, for instance. His next role, in Leo Reich’s forthcoming sitcom It Gets Worse, pushes the envelope further.A teaserappears to shows him as a toxic therapist who instructs his much younger client that he’s “just a hole for daddy” before spitting into his mouth.View image in fullscreenA devastating performance … Paul Mescal with Scott in All of Us Strangers (2023).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyFor Guy Lodge, chief critic of Variety, Scott is “essentially carving an unprecedented career path for an out gay leading man in the industry. One where he isn’t pigeonholed into queer roles, but where he doesn’t have to avoid them either, in order to prove his mainstream viability.”While some of his highest-profile roles have been gay or queer men – Pride, All of Us Strangers, the Netflix seriesRipleyand now Elsinore – Lodge points to the lack of other commonalities between these parts. “In defiance of the restrictions and stereotypes that would, not all that long ago, have limited his options, Scott is showing us that there are many ways to embody queerness on screen.”And it is this forward-thinking integrity that has come to mark the actor’s persona. His gentle, uncompromising candour – paired with an elegant discretion about his private life – has meant he is held in high regard and affection both by the public and his collaborators.“I love him,” says Johnny Flynn, who plays the director Richard Eyre in Elsinore, and previously starred opposite Scott in Ripley. “He’s a dear friend and I think he deserves everything for Elsinore. He always puts his whole soul into whatever he does but this was something else. Watching him channel and hold Ian Charleson was such a privilege.”View image in fullscreen‘He puts his whole soul into whatever he does’ … Scott with Ethan Hawke in Blue Moon (2025).Photograph: Sabrina Lantos/APScott, Flynn adds, is “one of our greatest actors. He’s got such a unique quality – a beauty in the deftness of his thinking; darkness and humour and power with heartbreaking fragility. He is such a gorgeous human being – so quick to laugh and wicked fun.”This sort of write-up is seemingly echoed by everyone who works with him. “He is an actor of incredible emotional insight,” says Simon Stephens, who scripted Scott’s one-man Vanya. “His linguistic and physical nuance are balletic. He thinks with relentless curiosity and he works with equal amounts of ferocious energy and care.” Stephens knew he had found a new favourite actor back in 2000, “since I saw him in Conor McPherson’s Dublin Carol. I’m glad I was 26 years ahead of the curve.”In fact, given Scott’s pedigree, his awards run so far has been surprisingly patchy. He won Oliviers for A Girl in a Car With a Man andPresent Laughter, and a TV Bafta for Sherlock, but nothing major for Fleabag – and, at the 2020 Sag awards, shortly after losing, he had to crawl from the auditorium in agonyafter passing a kidney stone mid-ceremony.View image in fullscreen‘I was 26 years ahead of the curve’ …  Scott with Brian Cox in Dublin Carol at the Royal Court in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianFurther indignity came in 2024, when his devastating performance in All of Us Strangers was snubbed at nomination stage at the Baftas (unlike those of his castmates Claire Foy and Paul Mescal). The movie, considered by many to be one of that year’s finest, then failed to score a single Oscar nod – a slight which may end up working in Scott’s favour, as his name will now be synonymous to voters with embarrassment as well as excellence.It may also be worth considering that actors make up the largest branch of the Academy’s votership – and they may respond especially favourably to Elsinore’s celebration of the profession’s inclusivity, courage and camaraderie.The film positions Charleson’s achievement – not unfairly – as a vital fightback against the final curtain that is common to us all, whether or not we tread the boards. “I’d rather die of Hamlet than of Aids,” the character tells his doctor (Olivia Colman), trying to persuade her to help him build up the stamina needed to take on theatre’s most challenging role (1,500 lines, four hours, swordfight in hour three).And in promoting the film so far, Scott has sought to highlight the universal bravery of Charleson’s actions, as well as the sports movie-style achievement of someone weeks from death exhibiting such commitment and athleticism. Those around the actor have, meanwhile, emphasised the sheer graft involved in pulling off a performance of the stature of Hamlet, or Charleson, or both.View image in fullscreen‘I struggle to think of a better performance’ … Scott in Elsinore.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/Focus FeaturesAndrew Haigh, who directed him in All of Us Strangers, calls Scott’s turn “simply astonishing. I struggle to think of a better performance. Andrew embodies the character so completely it feels as if we are watching lived experience. But make no mistake, this is a performance of incredible skill. Andrew is completely fearless in the role.”Likewise, Elsinore director Simon Stone says that “every time I rewatch the film I can’t see Andrew – it’s just Ian. The way he surrenders to the character, to the world, the situation, is beyond compare. Sure, it’s also an effortlessly brilliant performance in terms of technique. But what is most astonishing is how he matches this technique with raw truth.“Where other actors may perform an emotion or a state, Andrew presents us with a character surprised by what he is going through. That shock helps the audience be surprised and heartbroken with him and we can feel empathy in the truest sense.”The Academy has spent 98 years giving out leading performance Oscars to gay actors who never or only later publicly spoke their whole truth, as well as to a parade of straight stars for playing LGBTQ+ characters. Their failure to recognise Scott’s remarkable achievements, both professional and personal, seems unlikely.Explore more on these topicsFilmAndrew ScottanalysisShareReuse this content

title: From ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: As Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaign
Content: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the special jury prize award for NAZA at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Laurent Hou/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesNAZAFrom ovations in Venice to death threats in Israel: the extreme responses to NAZA documentaryAs Gaza documentary wins cinematic acclaim, its directors face vitriol in Israel amid a febrile election campaignPeter BeaumontSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFirst there was a moment of stunned silence. Then, in the Sala Grande, the main screening hall of the Venice film festival within the Palazzo del Cinema, the audience stood almost as one and turned to applaud the film-makers for 25 minutes.The film the audience had watched for 80 harrowing minutes was theGazadocumentary NAZA, which has been produced by the Guardian.The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to the civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.Unfolding against the background of Tel Aviv at night, the participants – intelligence officers and other soldiers –describe a series of systems, some powered by AI, that select the thousands who should die in strikes, often at night and surrounded by their families.Perhaps most challenging for Israel’s political elite is that it is a story told exclusively in Hebrew by 24 anonymised Israeli military insiders, many of them from elite units.The documentary depicts a wide variety of viewpoints that all lead to the same conclusion: participation in a programme of mass killing where there were few boundaries between combatant and civilian, in a war where more than 73,000 Palestinians have been killed. Some describe being shamed by their experience. Some are neutral. Others describe excitement, and a sense of “fun” as they justify their actions.It will open in US cinemas from 30 September, with international distribution plans to be announced shortly. The ripples of ovation gathered in volume among the few who have seen the film before its New York premiere, but in Israel the film provoked a very different response.Rightwingpolitical figures have rushed to accuse its directors – the Oscar-winning Israeli film-makers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor – of “treason”. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, who has long harboured an antipathy to critical media, declared on Wednesday he wouldseek new laws to strip citizenshipfrom people who he said “smear” Israeli soldiers.Demonstrators and members of far-right groups went further still, calling for violence against the pair and the demolition of their homes. Outside Szor’s parents’ house in central Israel, protesters called for the “death penalty for traitors”.An editorial in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretzwarnedthat their lives were credibly endangered. Dozens of human rights and peace organisations in Israel rallied to defend the film-makers, as didinternational press freedom organisations.The whiplash ferocity of the response, even in the midst of a febrile election campaign where Israeli attitudes to the war in Gaza are a central issue, has surprised even those in the Israeli leftwing and human rights community who have long been on the receiving end of such denunciations.The pushback to the documentary is both a testament to its power and evidence of how the Israeli right is exploiting a film, as yet unseen by most, to craft its own version of what it says it represents.Critics in Israel seized on the longstanding idea that Israelis should not criticise their country in front of foreign audiences.Ofer Winter, a controversial former rightwing army officer turned politician, told an election rally for his People of Israel in Rishon LeZion: “An Israeli citizen, a Jew, receives thunderous applause for going out and smearing and defaming his own people.“I understand that you are afraid to return to Israel,” he taunted the directors. “You are right. You have nothing to return to. It is a disgrace and a shame to return after you spat in the faces of your own people.”View image in fullscreenA protest against the NAZA film-makers in Savyon, Israel.Photograph: Sharon Eilon/Sopa Images/ShutterstockThe rightwing journalist Yehuda Schlesinger of Channel 14, a station regarded as being a mouthpiece for Netanyahu, went further still, saying Abraham and Szor should be “pursued” and “hunted”, prevented from returning to Israel, and describing the ovation in Venice as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause”.By Wednesday, Netanyahu had decided to weigh in, announcing he would promote two bills to legislate against the “defamation” of Israeli soldiers and the state of Israel.“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket.”At points, the threats of violence have been realised.On Wednesday, the journalist Haggai Matar, a director of the left-leaning independent +972 Magazine and Sicha Mekomit (Local Call), where Abraham’s first reporting on the allegations appeared in collaboration with the Guardian, said their offices had been broken into by rightwing activists who had filmed the intrusion.“The discussion aboutNAZAhas been a million times more prominent than the UK sanctions announcement,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli political and polling expert who writes a column for Haaretz, adding that the right was exploiting the current inability of Israelis to see the film and make their own judgment.“While it is unseen, it can be turned into something electorally potent that at present Israelis aren’t able to demystify.”The film has also arrived in the midst of a markedly worsening atmosphere towardsdissenting views, acute since Hamas’s deadly attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, with the film challenging a long-held expectation that Israel’s media self-censor in times of conflict.As Israel has become increasingly isolated internationally over both Gaza, where an independent UN inquiry foundIsrael continues to commit genocide, and growing settler violence in the occupied West Bank, the film also appears to have touched a more complex nerve in Israel’s collective psyche.‘This should be condemned by any thinking human’: film industry rallies behind NAZA directorsRead moreIsrael’s forthcoming elections in October have acted as an accelerant for the country’s rightwing parties, whose language has become more hardline and extreme under Netanyahu’s far-right coalition.Human rights activists, critical journalists, the left more broadly and even the notion of an independent judiciary have long been presented as an enemy within by the far right, who appear to be seeking to weaponise the film against a wider community of critics of Israel and its military.The extreme response from Netanyahu and his allies has itself been condemned.The Yedioth Ahronoth columnist Nahum Barnea described the calls to strip the film-makers of their citizenship as “delusional”.The former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, Yaakov Katz,wrote: “Not only does such a move not make Israel look stronger, but it creates the impression that we have something to hide and are afraid of criticism. It makes it seem like we fear to stand up for our truth and what we believe in.”And for Haaretz’s Etan Nechin, who saw the film at a press screening in New York earlier this week, the reaction to NAZA is a symptom of a serious malaise.“In a healthy democracy, NAZA would be shown on the evening news, its allegations would cause a public outrage and the state would promise a thorough investigation,” hewrote. “Instead, following the film’s Venice premiere, Abraham and Szor have effectively been pushed into exile.”Explore more on these topicsNAZAIsraelGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Revel review – broken Barbies and a splash of Swan Lake as older dancers limber up | Dance | The Guardian
description: Warm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated show
Author: Róisín O'Brien
Headline: Warm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated show
Content: Stage bright … Kally Lloyd-Jones and Steinvör Palsson in Revel.Photograph: Brian HartleyView image in fullscreenStage bright … Kally Lloyd-Jones and Steinvör Palsson in Revel.Photograph: Brian HartleyDanceReviewRevel review – broken Barbies and a splash of Swan Lake as older dancers limber upByre theatre, St AndrewsWarm-up routines lead into a reverie about life on the stage in Company Chordelia’s funny, carefully calibrated showRóisín O'BrienSat 19 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe inevitable aches and sprains of an ageing body take on heightened significance for a seasoned dancer turning up to work each day. Revel by Company Chordelia is a whimsical rumination on these changes, and a personal riposte to the fear that you might “make a spectacle of yourself” if you don’t stop at the “right” moment.It is conceived and staged by the artistic director Kally Lloyd-Jones, who performs with the co-creator Steinvör Palsson, a well-known teacher and choreographer in the Scottish dance community.Revel opens on an apparently empty dressing room, until Lloyd-Jones suddenly appears from underneath a discarded puffy dress, and Palsson creeps out of a storage crate. The backstage PA system delivers a message: they have – only! – nine hours to get ready.View image in fullscreenLong stretch … the pair must prepare properly for their performance.Photograph: Brian HartleyEach dancer’s warm-up manifests differently: Palsson serenely wafts through her qigong routine, while Lloyd-Jones prefers a strenuous running, lunging, shaking approach. They must do their checklist (but first get their reading glasses). Multivitamins? Check. Alternate nostril breathing? Check. HRT patch? Check.‘How incredibly stimulating!’ Retirees on discovering a new world through danceRead moreAs the clock counts down, they get lost in dreamlike dance recollections, ranging fromSwan Laketo marching gestural sequences, before resuming the crossword with a banana and two chocolate digestives.Highlights in this stately procession to their curtain call include Palsson’s juicy rendition of Whatever Lola Wants, indulged while Lloyd-Jones runs to the bathroom. They bring out Barbies to demonstrate their former abilities (“I don’t think you could ever do that, Kally”) before smashing the dolls to bits. No amount of exaggerated hunching, however, can hide the dancing histories in their bodies; Lloyd-Jones bounds around the stage with clarity, Palsson hovers delicately on her toes. They have a great comic rapport, every word and beat finely calibrated.Time runs out, costumes are donned for one last practice; there’s no resisting these performers, aches and all.Touring until 23 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDanceOlder peopleSwan LakeBalletreviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’ | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concrete
Content: John Wilson in The History of Concrete.Photograph: Photo courtesy of Magnolia PicturesView image in fullscreenJohn Wilson in The History of Concrete.Photograph: Photo courtesy of Magnolia PicturesDocumentary filmsInterviewJohn Wilson on his unlikely concrete movie: ‘There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way’Adrian HortonThe creator of How To with John Wilson has returned with his first film, a documentary about how to sell a documentary about concreteSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 06.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs mayor of New York City, Zohran Mamdani has frequently demonstrated impressive media savvy, but arguably nothing has proved his genius for in-the-know promo more than avideo, released in April, with the documentarianJohn Wilson.The History of Concrete review – John Wilson’s first movie is an absurd triumphRead moreThe spot, in support of the mayor’s plan to reduce the presence of the city’s ubiquitous sidewalk sheds, suggested that either he or someone on his team was a fan of How To With John Wilson, the film-maker’s cult-beloved HBO series that remains a taste signifier for alt-humorous New Yorkers. And for good reason: over three near-perfect seasons, Wilson, armed with his ever-present camera and diffident, memoiristic narration, explored the city’s disintegrating streets with a singular eye for the weird and unintentionally hilarious, turning the most mundane of NYC preoccupations – public restrooms, parking spots, scaffolding – into profound meditations on the glories, indignities and absurdities of modern life.It was because of that scaffolding episode, released in October 2020, that I, like some smart Mamdani staffers, began to perceive the sidewalk shed shadowing my block not as an inevitable fixed entity but an obtrusive, if well-intentioned, symptom of neglect. Shortly after the mayor’s video, said scaffolding miraculously came down – revealing, to my shock, a three square-wide swath of concrete that had not seen the sun in six years.When I credit Wilson for this upgrade, in person at a film office in Manhattan, he reacts with a modest “I’ll take it,” as dry as the dusty footprints of the recently departed metal poles. Fitting, for though that newly revealed concrete, speckled with old gum and anonymous residue, is certainly better, if not exactly beautiful, perhaps only Wilson could see it as cinematic. His debut feature film,The History of Concrete, takes on the granddaddy of all urban materials, tugging wry insights on our terminal human condition out of the crumbling facades of New York’s most pervasive substance.Concrete is many things: a mixture of cement, water, sand and crushed stone; arguably ancient Rome’s greatest invention; the second-most used substance on earth, behind water; the foundation of buildings and bridges and “everything I’ve done before” Wilson says, a “Marvel supervillain origin story” to How To’s many bricolages of unfortunately named streets (“Titman Road”) and sidewalk characters. But it is not what one might call a marketable idea. The general response on pitch calls was crickets – “an absolute emotional flatline,” Wilson tells me during a break from signing film posters featuring a single giant cinderblock.It didn’t help that Wilson, languishing in a post-How To malaise and without the structure of an HBO contract nor writer’s room, didn’t have much of an idea what it would be about, beyond realizing, through a poor DIY attempt to fix the cracked foundation of his Queens apartment, how strange it is to know so little about the dominant element of your visual environment. Wilson initially tried pitching it as an environmental doc, a new riff on the enshittification of American infrastructure. The response was, roughly, “I don’t want to think about this,” he laughs. “And it’s hard to say that I don’t want to make that movie I just told you about either. I want to try, and then experiment and get lost along the way as I usually do.” A strike-era Writer’s Guild of America workshop on how to make a Hallmark movie offered salient advice – “trauma is FINE, if it ends on a high note” – and a pressing question: if Hallmark could make movies about property developers, why not concrete?View image in fullscreenJohn Wilson at the New York Premiere of The History of Concrete.Photograph: Dave Allocca/Starpix/ShutterstockSo goes the 100-minute film, which plays like an extended episode of How To and, in true Wilson fashion, is as much about the difficulty of figuring out your next thing, let alone making and selling it, as it is about the composite material (though he does visit one science lab and, naturally, a corporate meet-up for “the women of concrete”). The film finds Wilson in a strange place after the high of How To’s 2023 – directionless, anxious, famous enough to be the $2,000 Jeopardy question no one gets but not to secure financing for his dream of a feature-length documentary.“I was having a lot of strange thoughts, crazy problems with self-esteem, especially when nobody wanted to take a chance with something like this, at least at first,” he recalls in the same halting, nasally speech of both his How To narration and, as seen in the film, someone’s AI-generated ad to sell gutters on TikTok (“I would’ve done it for free, if they asked,” he deadpans). The pressure to follow but not repeat the show was creatively dead-ending. “There was a lot of frustration when I started to pitch this idea because everyone seemed to want something different than How To, and that just felt like an arbitrary requirement to me,” he explains. The show’s digressive style “wasn’t a shtick. This is how I think. I just think this is the right way to do things. I like essay films, I like shooting things from my perspective.”Resistant to do something different for difference’s sake and in the absence of financing, Wilson went back to basics: pick up camera, leave house. “I just started to do things the way that I always did, and that was the most fluid way to get myself out of the house and, like, have anything to do and work on, because I was depressed,” he recalls. “For some reason, I need to keep reminding myself of the same basic idea, that you should not wait for anyone else to make the thing that you want. You just need to do it.”“I was just caught in this trap again, of thinking that I needed permission,” he continues, eyes grazing the cinderblock poster. So I just went out to try to make it, and then I decided to incorporate all of these voices that were trying to get me to change and do whatever the market would reward.”View image in fullscreenA still from The History of Concrete.Photograph: John WilsonSaid advice includes: make it sexy (he attends a brick-laying competition, where the winner receives a very sleek blue truck); make it a rock-umentary (he meets and follows an aging rocker at a liquor store); make it topical (expert testimony will leave you wary of driving under the crumbling Brooklyn Queens Expressway); make it celeb-adjacent (Wilson is among the few documentarians less comfortable in a room with Kim Kardashian than with a man preserving tattooed human skin). As with any Wilson project, the narrative wanders far away from the initial premise; Wilson wanders from Rome to the Sri Chinmoy Self-Transcendence race in which runners loop around a single block in Queens for a month, from an Ohio driver’s ed class to the set of Marty Supreme (whose director, Josh Safdie, served as an executive producer of Wilson’s doc).All become avenues for Wilson’s sly explorations of far less solid material, from the struggle to find motivation to cyclical self-doubt, our desire to at once move forward and make something last. “I’m thankful for the resistance that I got, because the very thing that you are resisting, or that’s resisting you, ends up becoming the skeletal system or the spine of your work in certain ways, if you let it,” he says, slipping into the show and film’s standard second-person voice.Such challenges could cause you to give up, to quit the project of your dreams for something else, to abandon the sly attempts to convince people to pay more attention to the ever weirder world around them. “There might be a kind of sickness in shooting things this way,” he tells me, reflecting on the uphill climb to a concrete movie. “But it’s the kind of imagery that I want to see, because I don’t see it anywhere else.”The History of Concrete is out in select US cinemas now and will premiere at the London film festival next month with an Australian release planned for 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsComedy filmsComedyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: From Shaun the Sheep to The Split Up: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Aardman’s woolly hero reckons with a mysterious beast and Abi Morgan’s lawyers-in-love TV drama gets a Manchester-set reboot
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Aardman’s woolly hero reckons with a mysterious beast and Abi Morgan’s lawyers-in-love TV drama gets a Manchester-set reboot
Content: Vial bodies … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Richard DaviesView image in fullscreenVial bodies … Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom.Photograph: Aardman/Richard DaviesGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Going out, staying inCultureFrom Shaun the Sheep to The Split Up: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadAardman’s woolly hero reckons with a mysterious beast and Abi Morgan’s lawyers-in-love TV drama gets a Manchester-set rebootSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out: CinemaShaunthe Sheep: The Beast of Mossy BottomOut nowThe beloved Wallace and Gromit spin-off character returns to topline another film, with a Halloween-themed adventure involving the destruction of a pumpkin patch and a mysterious beast on the loose. Naturally, our hero turns to weird science to address matters.Bad ApplesOut nowA splendidly deranged combination of weird-wave European arthouse sensibility and the aesthetic of a classic British debut sees Saoirse Ronan as a teacher who improbably but deliciously takes justice into her own hands when one of the kids pushes her too far. There are also stunning child-actor performances from Eddie Waller and Nia Brown.Queen at SeaOut nowAn acting tour de force, Lance Hammer’s hit from this year’s Berlinale stars the heavyweight trio of Juliette Binoche, Tom Courtenay and Anna Calder-Marshall (the latter two reunited almost 60 years after they played Hamlet and Ophelia together on stage) in a nuanced exploration of dementia and sexual consent.Resident EvilOut nowDirector Zach Cregger has been on a run of form with Barbarian (2022) followed by his Oscar-winning horror Weapons (2025).
