It may be unfair to expect him to bring quite the same level of flair to the eighth live-action Resident Evil film, but at least it’s a standalone: no need to wade through endless lore before you go in.Catherine BrayGoing out: GigsView image in fullscreenFlowered up … Patrick Wolf.Photograph: Emma JonesHow the Light Gets InKenwood House, London,19 & 20 SeptemberThe London leg of the world’s largest (only?) philosophy and music festival returns with an intriguing lineup of brainy talkers and brainy singers. The latter group includes indie pop duo Prima Queen and the recently rejuvenated Patrick Wolf, who released his seventh album, Crying the Neck, last year.Michael CraggNiall Horan22 Septemberto 16 November; tour starts BirminghamNiall Horan and his trusty soft-rock bops arrive in the UK and Ireland for a tour in support of June’s fourth album, Dinner Party. Expect a handful of new tunes to sit nicely alongside hits such as Slow Hands and the gently epic Heaven.MCLinda May Han Oh & Melissa AldanaWigmore Hall, London,21 SeptemberBassist-composer Linda May Han Oh, a subtle collaborator with jazz giants including Pat Metheny, shares an exquisitely lyrical and intuitive duo stage partnership here with Chilean saxophone star Melissa Aldana – on both an original and classic repertoire including timeless themes by Charlie Parker, Wayne Shorter, Billie Holiday and many more.John FordhamBluebeard’s Castle + Oedipus RexWales Millennium Centre, Cardiff,20 & 25 September, 2 October;touring to 28 NovemberRebranded and determined to thrive, Welsh National Opera launches its new season with a double bill that pulls no punches, pairing powerful one-acters by Bartók and Stravinsky. The casts feature soprano Christine Rice, tenor Peter Hoare and bass-baritone Nathan Berg. Joe Hill-Gibbins directs, with conductor Lidiya Yankovskaya in the pit.Flora WillsonGoing out: ArtView image in fullscreenA still from Amar Kanwar’s Such a Morning, 2017.Photograph: Courtesy Amar Kanwar/Marian Goodman GalleryAmar KanwarSerpentine North, London,23 Septemberto 3 JanuaryLyrical Indian artist Amar Kanwar is best known as a film-maker. This show functions as a site-specific installation of video work touching on themes of displacement, nationalism, violence and memory.Raqib ShawCompton Verney, Warwickshire,19 Septemberto 21 FebruaryShaw’s dense, super-intricate, mythologically influenced fusion of Indian motifs and classical western art references is instantly recognisable, but he hasn’t had a major show of new work in the UK since 2017. Until now, that is, with this exhibition of atmospheric nocturnal paintings and tapestry.Jenkin Van ZylSomerset House Studios, London,24 Septemberto 29 NovemberOne of the UK’s most interesting young artists returns with another disturbingly surreal immersive film installation, this time filled with holograms and inflatable cocoons, all about celebrities and obsolete technologies.Rae Yen SongFact, Liverpool, to 14 FebruaryThe glowing pond at the centre of Rae Yen Song’s exhibition is filled with microscopic life and organic matter. It’s a living ecosystem that allows the artist to explore woozy ideas of mythology, ancestry and spirituality.Eddy FrankelGoing out: StageView image in fullscreenTour de force … Celya AB.Photograph: Sonja Horsman/The GuardianCelya ABGlasgow,23 September; Newcastle upon Tyne,24 September; Sheffield,25 September; touring to 1 NovemberThe cast may have received the bigger profile boost, but it was actually members of the SNL UK writing team who dominated this year’s Edinburgh fringe (including main award winner Chris Cantrill). French comedian Celya AB is among their number: a master joke-constructor whose latest show grapples with standup’s darker side.Rachel AroestiBirmingham Royal Ballet: Swan LakeBirmingham Hippodrome,23 Septemberto 31 OctoberSometimes you just want to see a classic. No need for boundary-breaking, head-scratching new inventions, just a tried-and-tested hit. That’s where Swan Lake comes in. With a perfectly matched corps de ballet and Tchaikovsky’s score, Birmingham Royal Ballet’s production of Swan Lake ticks every box.Lyndsey WinshipWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?@sohoplace, London,21 Septemberto 19 DecemberThe prospect of Gillian Anderson blasting her way through Edward Albee’s boxing match of a play – with husband and wife sparring brutally throughout – is quite something. She plays Martha opposite Billy Crudup’s George in an intimate/intense production that’s staged in the round.Miriam GillinsonDeath of a SalesmanLiverpool Everyman,19 Septemberto 10 OctoberArthur Miller’s heartbreaking tragedy is reimagined by director Tristan Fynn-Aiduenu (For Black Boys Who Have Considered Suicide …). Cyril Nri stars as Willy Loman: a family man at breaking point, exhausted by his lifetime’s pursuit of the American dream.MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in: StreamingView image in fullscreenMum’s the word … Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey in Brothers.Photograph: Ryan Green/AppleBrothersApple TV,23 SeptemberIn 2023, Matthew McConaughey revealed there was a chance he and his close friend Woody Harrelson could be siblings after his mother hinted at a dalliance with the latter’s father. Cue this Curb-style comedy in which the actors play versions of themselves who begin to wonder if they’re more than merely buddies.YouthHBO Max,21 SeptemberCoupling covered footloose singledom, Catastrophe explored marriage and motherhood, and now Sharon Horgan returns to wring bitter laughs from midlife in this eight-part autofictional dramedy about parenting confused teenagers, caring for elderly parents and post-divorce dating.The Split UpBBC iPlayer & BBC One,20 September, 9pmThe Split, Abi Morgan’s supremely soapy drama about a family of divorce lawyers, gets a glitzy Manchester-set spin-off starring Sanjeev Bhaskar as the head of a (different) family of divorce lawyers. Ritu Arya, Jane Horrocks, Lenny Henry and Mawaan Rizwan also appear.American HostageMGM+,20 SeptemberCertain true-crime stories can suddenly find themselves in vogue. Earlier this year Gus Van Sant’s Dead Man’s Wire dramatised the 1977 kidnap of a mortgage broker by Tony Kiritsis; now this series does the same with a cast that includes Jon Hamm, Giovanni Ribisi and William Jackson Harper.RAStaying in: GamesView image in fullscreenServe chilled … Silent Hill: Townfall.Photograph: Screen BurnSilent Hill: TownfallPS5, PC; out 24 SeptemberAtmospheric and creatively chilling, this is the latest in a peerlessly mind-bending series of horror games. Arriving on a mist-wreathed island town off the Scottish coast, you must reckon with what has happened to its inhabitants – and revisit your past mistakes.RivagePS5, Xbox, PC; out 22 SeptemberYou are stuck in a time loop on a space station in this sci-fi puzzler. The station resets each time you retire to your bunk, but your memories do not. Put together the clues to figure out what has happened to you and the crew.Keza MacDonaldStaying in: AlbumsView image in fullscreenThat’ll be the day … Carly Rae Jepsen.Photograph: Vince AungCarly Rae Jepsen – Day and NightOut nowHaving released companion albums to go with her last five records, the Canadian pop star cuts to the chase this time around, releasing a 24-track double. As the title suggests, the album is split into two moods, with the bubbly, synth-driven Motivation a late-night anthem.Beck – Ride LonesomeOut nowThe musical polymath returns to the more sombre setting of 2002’s Sea Change and 2014’s three Grammy-winning Morning Phase for his 15th album. Full of the rustic joys of autumn, its 12 songs are built around delicate acoustic figures and, on the lovely title track, elegant touches of slide guitar.Miley Cyrus – Bass PersuadesOut nowFollowing the commercially disappointing Something Beautiful, the Pablow the Blowfish hitmaker returns with a bigger sound, as showcased on the Lady Gaga-esque title track. Co-produced by Kid Harpoon (Harry Styles), and featuring US art-rockers Model/Actriz, it should see her return to pop’s upper echelons.Beabadoobee – PylonOut nowThe Filipino-British singer-songwriter follows up 2024’s chart-topping This Is How Tomorrow Moves with her fourth album of alt-rock heaters. On the pogoing Sun Has Set she’s a coiled spring of emotion over lacerating guitars, while the softer Memories rides a gorgeous indie pop melody.MCStaying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenVittlesPodcastFood publication Vittles’ audio series delves deeper into its long-form features, providing insights into the changing world of British hospitality. Recent highlights include writer Stephen Buranyi on the economics of food influencers.Big Think ClipsYouTubeTypically running between 20 and 30 minutes, this curated selection of video essays presents excerpts of longer lectures discussing everything from the phenomenon of “self-loneliness” to the ways our phones can stifle creativity.Caught in the CrackdownPBS America,25 September, 9.40pmPBS’s Frontline series investigates the ongoing violence perpetrated by the US’s Immigration Customs and Enforcement agency (ICE). We see how community legal action and grassroots activism are fighting the force that embodies Donald Trump’s anti-immigration rhetoric.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Beabadoobee to 70 Up: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter’s new album sprinkles her 90s alt fuzz with sweet melodies, while Asif Kapadia wraps up the seminal series. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The singer-songwriter’s new album sprinkles her 90s alt fuzz with sweet melodies, while Asif Kapadia wraps up the seminal series. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews

Sure, it doesn’t carry the intensity or the existentialism of its edgier counterparts. But I was surprised by how long I wanted to stay with these characters and inhabit their island bubble. It kept subverting my expectations. I didn’t want to go home.”Micha Frazer-CarrollRead the full reviewMy Brilliant CareerNetflix; available nowSummed up in a sentenceA joyous, witty and beautiful adaptation of the classic feminist novel about a young woman in 1890s Australia who rebels against society’s expectations.What our reviewer said“Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine, is played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFurther readingInside Netflix’s teenager who was the youngest girl ever charged with terror offences in the UK, and who later killed herself after the charge was dropped.What our reviewer said“By the end of the hour you feel like you have sat through a nightmare, watching [her mother] Emily and others who loved Rhianan shout into voids that were supposedly filled with people trained and ready to help those in exactly their title: Jay-Z in 8 review – the rapper’s interminable interview show should have been a podcast | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Rick Rubin’s eight-part interview series with the MC is irritatingly unstructured, has portions that feel like filler and would hugely benefit from a different medium – which encourages use of the pause button
Author: Shaad D'Souza
Headline: Rick Rubin’s eight-part interview series with the MC is irritatingly unstructured, has portions that feel like filler and would hugely benefit from a different medium – which encourages use of the pause button
Content: ‘Borders on the interminable’ … Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiView image in fullscreen‘Borders on the interminable’ … Jay-Z and Rick Rubin in Jay-Z in 8.Photograph: MubiTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewJay-Z in 8 review – the rapper’s interminable interview show should have been a podcastRick Rubin’s eight-part interview series with the MC is irritatingly unstructured, has portions that feel like filler and would hugely benefit from a different medium – which encourages use of the pause buttonShaad D'SouzaSat 19 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJay-Z in 8 does what it says on the can: the docuseries, released by Mubi, finds influential, mercurial superproducerRick Rubininterviewing rap titan Jay-Z over the course of eight meandering, freeform episodes. Directed by Rubin himself and shot in black and white, the series is ostensibly designed to give viewers a look inside the brain of a godlike musical figure as he celebrates 30 years in music.As it makes eminently clear, this is a deeply reflective time for Jay-Z: in any given episode, he is liable to make reference to old collaborators such as Biggie and Jaz-O, reminisce on his upbringing in the Marcy Projects (the public housing units in Brooklyn where he grew up), and speak with astonishment about his rapid rise from crack dealer to generational rapper, often swinging between anecdotes with free-associative ease.Therein lies the problem with Jay-Z in 8. It’s remarkable to see someone of his stature talk so openly about his life and career without adornment, but there is no narrative or thematic structure to this show. Aside from the moments when Jay and Rubin listen to entire songs together – which then spark more anecdotes and interview questions – it is lacking connective tissue to hold together Jay’s stories for a casual fan.For a relative Jay-Z agnostic like myself – I like the classic records well enough but didn’t grow up with his music, and generally have a fairly superficial relationship with that era of rap music – Jay-Z in 8 borders on the interminable. Each conversation is interesting, but there’s something profoundly abrasive about being dropped into such unstructured chat. The format is clearly modelled on longform interview shows such as David Letterman’s My Next Guest Needs No Introduction, but where Letterman is an incisive, journalistically minded interviewer with decades of experience steering conversations, Rubin is famous for his terseness. After he and Jay listen to one song, for example, Rubin simply says, “I don’t know how you did that” – a statement of fact, perhaps, but hardly a guiding idea for a casual viewer who sees the show on their Mubi homepage and decides to dive in.At one point, Rubin offers a theory: “I don’t know that people really know how to listen to hip-hop,” he says. “It’s so dense with information, and a lot of people kind of hear the hook and the beat.” But that’s the thing about a hook and a beat: they can help draw in a listener who otherwise might not think they’re equipped to take in the rest of the information the song is providing. Jay-Z in 8 is a track without hook or beat: it is pure, dense information, and it can prove challenging at times.Within that framework, certain little Jay-Z-isms act like anchors – “I’ve always thought like I was a businessman,” he says at one point; at another, he compares Jail, his latest collaboration with Kanye West, to a Johnny Cash song – and it’s nice enough to hear the songs themselves, which have proven durable over the course of his career.But, ironically, the show’s most legible moments end up feeling like pure filler. Whenever Jay explains his lyrics, time seems to stop. His unpacking of the lyrics to Jail in episode six is simplistic: “No cap,” he says (of a term that has become extremely heavily used in modern hip hop), means you’re not lying; an invocation of “The Throne” refers to the collaborative album he and Kanye made. In another episode, while explaining his verse on the Notorious BIG’s I Love The Dough, he pauses to explain that “hit” means “kill.”Most of Jay’s line-by-line lyric breakdowns, which occur a couple of times in each episode, reveal an oxymoronic quality to Jay-Z in 8: anyone watching who doesn’t know what “hit” means, or that Jay-Z and Kanye released an album called Watch The Throne, will probably be lost during most of the conversations. If you like Jay-Z enough to find the show compelling, you’ll likely be left wondering why, exactly, so much of the show’s runtime has been dedicated to this specific kind of exposition.Jay-Z in 8 may not warrant such scrutiny. Or it wouldn’twarrant such scrutiny if it had been released in the format it so clearly wants to be: a podcast. This high-budget, artfully shot television show would work a lot better in a form that doesn’t demand its audience consume each episode in one go. Or which is so easily paused if you need to Google a reference. And, ultimately, if there’s one thing more enjoyable than watching Jay-Z and Rick Rubin listen to a Jay-Z song, it’s just listening to that song without the visual accompaniment of two guys nodding along and smiling knowingly.As a producer, Rubin is known for his ability to cut things back, reveal the heart and true intention of a song. His first work as a director is pure excess.Jay-Z in 8 is on MubiExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewJay-ZRick RubinMusic TVHip-hopreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #261: There is so much good telly this autumn you may never go outside again | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like me
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like me
Content: Knowingly trashy and super smart … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesView image in fullscreenKnowingly trashy and super smart … Dominic West and Sienna Miller in War.Photograph: Justin Downing/Sky/HBO/New PicturesThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #261: There is so much good telly this autumn you may never go outside againIn this week’s newsletter:From HBO’s incredible divorce drama War to the hilarious return of The Paper, there’s too much TV to choose from even for a confirmed addict like meStuart HeritageSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor those of us who like to stay indoors, it has been a bad summer. The World Cup ate up all traditional television scheduling, and the streamers apparently declined to counterprogramme. The Bear came and went before anybody noticed, and House of the Dragon conclusively disappeared up its own bottom.If you’re anything like me then you clung to the good stuff (basicallyDisney’s Furiousand nothing else) like a life raft, eking out new episodes like someone in a desert sucking condensation off the underside of a tarpaulin. But forget summer. It is now autumn, and television is back. In fact, I can’t remember a time when television has come roaring back with quite the same ferocity as it has this month.Everywhere you turn there is something new and unmissable. And I suspect you haven’t even seen your favourite TV show of the year yet.For me, the big one is Sky and HBO’s new divorce dramaWar(main pic). Watching it feels like scratching an itch I didn’t know I had. About the messy divorce between a fading Hollywood star (played by Sienna Miller) and a tech billionaire (played by Dominic West), and the warring lawyers who represent them, it sits precisely at the midpoint between Rivals and Succession – knowingly trashy, but also hugely smart. It’s so unbelievably propulsive, every episode ends with a whopper of a cliffhanger scientifically engineered to give you whiplash. And on top of that, Pip Torrens gets to play the haughtiest lawyer in all of recorded media. It is an absolute joy of a thing.But also –Slow Horsesis back! And that performs a little miracle of its own, too. The show is so long in the tooth that you would probably expect a significant drop off in quality. And yet its new run (its sixth) may very well be its strongest yet (despite theless than enthusiastic viewsof my colleague Jack Seale). Its plot has been slimmed down to its barest essentials – the whole thing is basically just a chase – and it is far more muscular as a result. Everyone is brilliant in it. The writing still sparkles, despite the departure of show-runner Will Smith. There’s a chance that there might not be much more of it to come, especially if Jack Lowdenends up becoming James Bond, so we really need to relish it while we can.View image in fullscreenAn ensemble coming into its own … Domhnall Gleeson, Chelsea Frei, Melvin Gregg and Eric Rahill in The Paper.Photograph: Peacock/SkyEven the remakes and spin-offs are unnecessarily good. I found myself watching the second season ofThe Paper– Greg Daniels’ cousin to The Office – with a mixture of ticklishness and irritation. Ticklishness because it’s warm and funny, and has an ensemble cast (pictured above) that has really started coming into its own; and irritation because it’s only 10 episodes long. The show has the potential to be one of those all-timers, like Friends or Cheers, that you can stick on years from now as you go about your business because you’re so familiar with – and fond of – the characters. At this rate, though, it’ll take 20 years to build up enough episodes to let that happen. There is a possibility that I’m just being greedy, but it’s only because I like it so much.And in the remake department,Reckless(ITVX here, SBS in Australia) is a spin on Neil Forsyth’s impeccable Guilt, that manages to retain all the tension and momentum of that show while adding layers of interesting new dimensions.But there are so many other things to look forward to. Rivals is back soon. So is The Celebrity Traitors. Sharon Horgan has a new show, in the form of Youth. Apple’s Brothers, about Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson, looks incredibly diverting. Even if it ends up being bad, Amazon’s Blade Runner 2099 series should be absolutely fascinating. And, if you’re my dad, then the new Reacher spinoff Neagley is essentially the moment your entire life has been leading up to.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have barely scratched the surface here, which is slightly terrifying. For the first time in ages, there might be more good television than spare hours in the day. What an unusual feeling that is.To read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Youth: Sharon Horgan’s comedy about dating at 50 is utterly hilarious  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painful
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: The perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painful
Content: Adulting … Sharon Horgan and Aran Murphy in Youth.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenAdulting … Sharon Horgan and Aran Murphy in Youth.Photograph: HBOThe watcherTelevision & radioYouth: Sharon Horgan’s comedy about dating at 50 is utterly hilariousThe perils of ageing and the horrors of finding post-divorce romance are laid bare in the new show from the creator of Motherland. It’s humungously funny, and so acutely observed it’s painfulRhik SamadderSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAgeing has changed, hasn’t it? There’s a generation of middle-aged and perimenopausal elder millennials and xennials who refuse to do it. We’re young enough to be part of an online world that puts a premium on appearance, too old for such narcissistic self-branding to be achieved without unsustainable effort. Dating apps and social media connect people across generations, so it’s easy to become confused about how old we actually are. Here’s a tip: ask your knees.This brings us to Youth (from Monday 21 September, HBO Max),Sharon Horgan’s dramedy about being 50. That perky title is a quip about the decade being known as “the youth of old age”. Horgan is Alex, a divorcee in her sandwich years, caring for teenage son Ruarí and ageing parents. There’s a lot going on in her life, and some doom. She’s falling forwards in a semi-successful career as a literary agent, getting back into dating under pressure. She needs someone to fall in love with her immediately, as she points out to her best friend. Not for romantic myth-making, but “so there’s a bit of time with the present version of me, before the ‘old me’ is here”.I’ve made it sound not funny; it’s very funny. The world of publishing is ripe for satire, and the show wields more skewers than a kebab shop. On the walls of Alex’s office are posters for prestige titles: Life After Death – A Memoir of Guilt, Babyfingers and Where the Daylight Falls. I’ve seen all of them on the Richard and Judy Book Club. And then there’s Goblin Seed.Goblin Seed is a ludicrous romantasy in the Twilight or Fifty Shades of Grey mould. (I think that title is a pun, too.) It’s written by one of Alex’s former authors, a smug creep who self-published after rejection, and has since enjoyed runaway success with his horny, badly written prose (“The goblin seed was gold, and soon the sheets were glittering”). Tasked with wooing him back, every interaction has Alex looking as if she wants to throw up in her mouth.Youth fires shots across the creative arts. Ruarí’s dad, Lorcan, is an actor. Not quite absent, but so self-involved he’s not so much phoning it in as texting. He’s about to move to Canada to film a lucrative “spaceship show”, and has re-recorded his answer-machine message in its alien language, while feeling above the project. He’s also dating the young landlady he met when he moved out of Alex’s. Oh God, the humanities.‘I didn’t know if I’d ever have sex again’: inside Sharon Horgan’s excruciating post-divorce comedyRead moreThankfully, Ruarí has a number of unsuitable father figures to choose from. There’s Alex’s ex, Patrick, a handsome and “institutionally single” 47-year-old who specialises in sending mixed messages. There’s older love interest Michael, played with generous sensitivity byTim McInnerny. He’s stable, kind, attentive. But Alex can’t stop staring at his loose chin, and ducks his kisses like Neo dodges bullets.Sex scenes in Youth are the antithesis of Hollywood gloss, hilarious and penetratingly insightful. “I don’t know you well enough to be selfish in bed,” Alex confesses to one lover. How has the gap between sex and intimacy widened in her lifetime? It’s easy to kid yourself about this at 25, twice as hard at 50.Horgan’s gift is vérité. The friend groups and workplaces are diverse in a way that’s London-real, rather than box-ticking from above. Youth is mordantly funny, yet never betrays character. As you’d expect from the creator of Motherland, it’s superb on mum stuff. Alex often mutters the word “dick” to herself when Ruarí is being particularly teenage, yet their love is clear. He’s played byAran Murphy,son of Cillian, who delivers a beautifully unforced performance. At points I felt as if I were watching Boyhood.Then there’s the parental subplot, which could carry a series alone. A million miles from saccharine depictions of elderly people, Youth shows the uninspiring, Sisyphean grind of care-giving, which is mostly navigating confused, false-crisis phone calls, sibling resentment and travelling 25 miles to demonstrate the position of the volume button on an iPad. However much we deny our age, life has its own plans. Thank God for Sharon Horgan: chronicler of all our journeys, like a foul-mouthed, funnier 7 Up. This painfully relatable, brilliant show made me feel a bit tired at times. Then again, I’m always tired.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioThe watcherTelevisionSharon HorganDramafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a new era of Strictly begins in typically sparkling style | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Johannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis prepare their takeover.Photograph: Guy Levy/PAView image in fullscreenJohannes Radebe, Josh Widdicombe and Emma Willis prepare their takeover.Photograph: Guy Levy/PATV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a new era of Strictly begins in typically sparkling styleEmma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe take over hosting duties in the hoofing extravaganza. Plus: John Bishop’s new gameshow asks a lot of its audience. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 19 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStrictly Come Dancing7.25pm, BBC OneIt’s time for the new Strictly era to begin, with Emma Willis, Josh Widdicombe and Johannes Radebe ebulliently taking over (sparkling) hosting duties. EastEnders stalwart Lacey Turner, footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips, Aussie singer Delta Goodrem, Gavin and Stacey’s Melanie Walters and previous dropout Dani Dyer are some of the 15 celebrities meeting their dance partners in this curtain-raiser. Alongside them, as is now customary in celebrity-based reality TV competitions, there’ll be some “media personalities” you’ll probably need to Google. But it’s not all change: the usual four judges are back with their scoring paddles. All that’s left to do is get ready to rumba!Hollie RichardsonWisdom of the Crowd9.15pm, BBC OneFrancis Galton’s groundbreaking century-old statistics theory is the inspiration behind this new gameshow. (No mention here of him also being widely considered the originator of eugenics though …) John Bishop puts contestants against the audience to ask: is the crowd better than the individual? Anyone who beats the theory could win £30k.HRThe Voice UK6.10pm, ITV1It’s a double Willis weekender, as she returns to host this next round of the singing competition. So far, Kelly Rowland has been left in tears after Aaren James’s emotional performance of How Do I Say Goodbye, while Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones used the show’s first Rewind button to bring back Phantom of the Opera singer Finlay McKillop. Who’s next?HRParis Police 19109pm, BBC FourIt’s the third season of this stylish fact-based French period drama, and the past of courtesan turned informant Meg Steinheil (the charismatic Evelyne Brochu) has caught up with her. However, even as she processes the loss of her husband, her statement isn’t adding up. Meanwhile, Dreyfus has returned, bringing trouble.Phil HarrisonDolly Parton Night9.15pm, BBC TwoView image in fullscreenDolly Parton wows Worthy Farm in 2014.Photograph: Will Oliver/EPAAn evening-long celebration of the country-pop goddess. First, her 2014 Glastonbury triumph. Then, a documentary in which KT Tunstall explores the parallel careers of Parton, Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris. Finally, Dolly’s appearances on the BBC.PHSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneLive from London, the homegrown SNL offshoot roared back last week, with a brand new Andy Burnham (George Fouracres) and a seamless debut from Freddie Meredith. This week sees Stath Lets Flats mastermind Jamie Demetriou on hosting duty, with music from rock duo Royal Blood.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceHamlet (Aneil Karia, 2025), 10.05am, 6pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenRiz Ahmed and Timothy Spall Ham it up.Photograph: NBCUniversal/2026 NBCUniversal All Rights ReservedThere is little Riz Ahmed can’t turn his hand to, so it’s no surprise that he gives a bravura performance as Shakespeare’s tragic hero in Aneil Karia’s modern-day adaptation. The royal Danes are now a wealthy British Hindu family of property developers, but the film retains the Bard’s language while cutting down the text to focus exclusively on Hamlet’s trauma. It’s a bold move that largely pays off, as we follow the heir to the firm as he descends into angst, rage and revenge after discovering his uncle Claudius (Art Malik) murdered his father.Simon WardellLive sportGolf: PGA Championship, 9am, Sky Sports GolfDay three from Wentworth.Premier League Football Tottenham v Aston Villa, 11am, TNT Sports 1Nottingham Forest v Coventry is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Championship Football: Millwall v West Ham, noon, ITV1A local derby from the Den.T20 International Cricket England v Sri Lanka, 2pm, Channel 5The third match, from Old Trafford.Super League Rugby, 5.15pm, BBC TwoWarrington Wolves v Hull KR in the second elimination play-off.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’ | Books | The Guardian
description: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: The author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’
Content: Jonathan Franzen.Photograph: Cayce Clifford/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJonathan Franzen.Photograph: Cayce Clifford/The GuardianBooksInterviewJonathan Franzen: ‘It’s still mysterious to me that I was angry for so long’Sophie McBainThe author of The Corrections talks about a new TV adaptation, the future of reading and why creating new work is ‘horrible’Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 04.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen HBO dropped its plan to adapt Jonathan Franzen’s bestselling novel The Corrections in 2012, the author was so relieved he says he performed his first and last cartwheel on the lawn of his home in Santa Cruz, California. There had been an attempted film adaptation before that, but he had been unsurprised by its failure, having warned that it was impossible to condense his densely plotted doorstopper of a novel into a feature-length film. This time, Franzen had signed up as co-writer, with filmmaker Noah Baumbach. He says that HBO was “excluded from the development process. Mistake, because we didn’t know how to do TV.” Franzen himself hadn’t even owned a telly until a few years earlier and certainly didn’t have cable, so as he was wrestling with the script, he began renting box sets. Around three episodes into one drama series, he realised “we have no idea what we’re doing. This is not how you do TV. This is bad,” he recalls. The result, he says, was “one of the worst pilots anyone has ever made”.Franzen used to think TV was the “enemy” of the serious novelist. In a well-known 1996 essay for Harper’s Magazine about the decline of high literature he had complained bitterly about the “banal ascendancy of television”. But after the HBO series failed, he watched Breaking Bad, Nurse Jackie and Silicon Valley and loved them. In the age of social media, AI and the endless scroll, TV has started to look like a “friend”, he says now. And The Corrections is finally being adapted into an eight-part Netflix series, with Meryl Streep playing Enid Lambert, the matriarch clinging to dreams of hosting a perfect last family Christmas, even as her husband Alfred is in terminal decline with Parkinson’s and dementia and their grownup children’s lives are falling apart in terrible, comical ways. Once Streep announced she was in, Franzen felt the “chances of making this show have gone up above 50%”. He says he’s a month away from finishing the script.We are meeting at his home on the edge of Santa Cruz, in his office where the blinds are pulled down low against the bright sunshine. He is 67, tall and slightly stooped, and although his hair has turned white he still looks boyish when he laughs, wide smile and little snub nose, a wicked glint behind his trademark dark-framed spectacles. He has settled into a chair that seems too small for his lanky frame and frequently squirms with discomfort. Should we try switching places, I ask at one point? “No, I’m just physically expressing discomfort with repeating myself,” he replies. He likes to edit his speech as he goes along: “strike that word!” he orders at one point, and “this needs to be underlined”. When he loses his thread he announces, grandly, “you can redirect”.View image in fullscreenMaggie Gyllenhaal and Ewan McGregor on HBO pilot of The Corrections.Photograph: Bang Media International/AlamyThe Corrections, Franzen’s third novel, won the 2001 National book award for fiction in the US, and remains one of the bestselling works of literary fiction of recent decades. It was published a few days before 9/11 and distils the materialism, anxieties and complacency of America’s long 20th century. It is also Franzen’s most “autobiographical novel”, drawn loosely from his own midwestern upbringing: Franzen was raised in an affluent suburb of St Louis, Missouri. Like Alfred, his dad, who was an engineer, developed Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, while Enid is a “cartoon version” of his own mother. “There are not very many incidents from my life in the book but those two: the personalities and the self-deception about the gravity of the mental deterioration – that’s all drawn from my own experience,” he says.Franzen says he learned his “psychology as a novelist” from his family. His parents were “powerful characters”: they were “hilarious” and “terrifying” and also “thoughtful”, with rich interior lives. “They created not only Enid and Alfred, but really the notion of a character … the combination of intellectual substance, emotional wanting, emotional needs and comedy,” he explains. His father died before The Corrections was published. His mother lived long enough to know that an extract had appeared in the New Yorker, as part of a special issue dedicated to American writers under 40.“My annoying aunt, her sister, called her up and said: ‘Irene: do not read Jon’s piece in the New Yorker,’” Franzen recalls. His mother was ill with cancer and had been given months to live. He visited her a few days after that phone call, when inevitably her question was “Why shouldn’t I read your piece in the New Yorker?”. He summarised the story for her, “making some small omissions, but basically just describing what the thing was”. When he was finished, she said: “Thank you, I don’t need to read it.” It was one of their last long conversations. She died 10 days later. “My parents gave us kids everything – including a lot of criticism. But then they just exited, and I was still in my 30s and could write whatever I want,” he says. He could not have published The Corrections had they been alive. Most of his subsequent novels – includingCrossroadsandFreedom, two other big, ideas-filled books – have also centred on dysfunctional midwestern families. “It always puzzles me that people find it remarkable that I have characters who are related through family in my books,” he says, sounding a bit put out. “Because it’s like, well, the Bible is a book of family stories. The Old Testament, it’s all family stories. The Greek myths, Homer …”Franzen initially studied science at university: “That was a bit of a beard to get my parents to pay for college,” he says. They were not happy when he switched majors, “but at least I did something serious like German literature as opposed to a frivolous English major, which they literally would not have paid for.” After graduating from Swarthmore, a liberal arts college in Pennsylvania, in 1981, he won a year-long Fulbright scholarship at the Freie Universität in Berlin. His first novel, The Twenty-Seventh City, was published six years later, in 1988. He has worked full-time as a writer ever since. “I made nothing but mistakes as a young person but actually was lucky enough to realise, this is what you’re good at,” he says.Franzen describes The Corrections as an “angry comedy” and he has a reputation for being, well, an angry guy. Where does his anger come from, I wonder? “It’s still mysterious to me, having so many privileges – not really economic privilege, but every other imaginable kind of privilege – that I was angry for so long. There’s 14 years of being in a marriage that should have ended after two years. That explains a lot, actually,” he says. He married a fellow writer, Valerie Cornell, soon after graduating, and they divorced in 1994. “Then there’s you know, I’m a bright guy, and the stupidity of the world makes me angry.” Oh, and in the 90s, he spent a lot of time “angry that people were seen to be losing interest in the kind of novels that I wrote”. But, he adds, “I don’t know why people think of me as angry now, because I haven’t really been angry in that way since a year after The Corrections was published.”That first year, he concedes with a wry smile, was a little “bumpy”. Many will remember his spat with Oprah Winfrey, who picked The Corrections for her book club and invited him on to her show, only to rescind her invitation after he described her other picks as “schmaltzy”. The pair later made up – she picked Freedom for her book club in 2010, and they hugged on live TV. One of his problems, he points out, is that he cannot “start a thought without injecting a counterthought to it”. Read only half the quote and he comes across like an “asshole”. While criticising her picks, he also praised Oprah for promoting reading, for instance. He can see now that she was right to be annoyed. But, counterthought: “Well, some of her earlier picks were …” theatrical pause “… schmaltzy.”Other spats have followed, with the writerJennifer Weinerover the disproportionate attention given to Franzen’s work. Thought: Weiner is “freeloading” on the gender debate and “asking for a respect that not just male reviewers, but female reviewers, don’t think her work merits”. Counterthought: the gender bias in literature is a genuine problem. He got into trouble for saying he consideredadopting an Iraqi orphanto better understand young people. Counterthought: that mad idea lasted six weeks at the most. Franzen says he has learned to become more circumspect. “I didn’t know what I was doing. I didn’t know how to talk to people in an interview. I didn’t know how to do TV. I would just say whatever I was thinking about and then I would get into trouble and I would feel like: ‘Oh, unfair! I’m getting into trouble.’ Well, you know, dude, wise up, learn how to protect yourself. Don’t say those things.”In 2010, following the publication of Freedom, Franzen appeared on the cover of Time magazine, a rare achievement for any writer. The piece described him as the “Great American Novelist”. He says it was his suggestion that he should be the cover. He got his publicist to contact Time to say they hadn’t had a writer as a cover star for ages, and Franzen would be great. Wait, what, I ask, shuffling through my notes, doesn’t that piece describe you as “singularly ungifted at what you might call brand management”? “Isn’t that hilarious?” he asks, his eyes widening in delight. “It’s hilarious!”He doesn’t think much of the phrase “great American novel”, though. “It’s usually not said kindly. It’s sort of mocking,” he says. He puts on a bullying sneer: “Oh, the great American novelist. Oh, you’re going to write the great American novel, are you?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation mark‘People don’t read Steinbeck any more? It’s sad, but nothing lasts for ever’Franzen is not as down on the future of the literary novel as he used to be. That Harper’s essay? His real complaint at the time was “people weren’t buying books like mine”, he says, pretending to sob. “Actually, they were. They were just not buying my novels. That was my complaint in the 90s, and of course I blew that up into some huge cultural problem.” These days, he thinks those who bemoan the decline of reading need some perspective. “I think the doom-criers about the novel tend to make a fundamental mistake. They imagine some golden age when everyone read Flaubert. There was never a time,” he says. It’s true, he continues, that modern technology does little to help cultivate a love of reading. “It’s easy to imagine a time soon when there is no reason to be able to read, because text can be converted into spoken language and you don’t have to write because you just speak and it can be written for you,” he says. But that hardly feels like the worst thing happening in the world right now. “That’s the other thing I feel about the doom-criers of the novel, it’s like, really, this is a world historical problem? People can’t read Steinbeck any more? It’s sad, but nothing lasts for ever. What do you want?”Franzen says he doesn’t want to comment on American politics because “nobody cares what the novelist thinks”, plus he did an interview with the German newspaper Die Welt before Donald Trump’s second term in which, like many pundits, he predicted that the president wouldn’t follow through on most of his promises and “it’s like no, I was all wrong”. He was, however, on to Trump early. He wrote about the future president in his 1992 novel, Strong Motion, and in various essays that decade. “He symbolised a certain kind of horribleness, a crass, narcissistic, bullying side of American life that, yeah, I noticed early and I hated. I didn’t even live in New York when I wrote Strong Motion and I could feel that odious presence,” he says.He’s more open to weighing in on environmental issues, having written several feather-ruffling essays for the New Yorker on the climate crisis. He angered climate crisis activists by arguing that humankind needs to accept that global warming is going to happen and start refocusing on local projects devoted to conservation and biodiversity. A passionate birder himself, in 2015 hecriticised the bird conservation organisation Audubonfor falsely claiming that climate change is the main threat faced by birds, rather than collisions with glass windows and hunting by cats, two more fixable problems. Audubon responded by accusing him of “extreme intellectual dishonesty”. “They’ve apologised,” he says when I ask him about it, “full stop.”Franzen discovered his passion for birds soon after The Corrections was published. He goes on birding trips whenever he can, but he can also spot a lot from his home: there are violet-green swallows nesting next door, and hooded orioles in the back garden. If it wasn’t so hot, and his blinds weren’t drawn so low, we’d probably see a family of quail running past his office window. “If you want to see quail, this is one of the best places in the world,” he says.He shares his home with his longtime partner, the writer Kathryn Chetkovich. In a corner of his office there is an electric guitar. He picked up the guitar while working on Freedom, and has this morning been practising with the band, Shady Characters, which he formed with Chetkovich’s brothers. It’s a purely private hobby. “I have never performed in public, and I never will,” he announces.Last June, Franzen published a new story in the New Yorker about an aspiring teenage actor suffering an unwanted pregnancy and a crisis of faith. It will form part of his next novel, a sequel to Crossroads, which was published in 2021 as the first book in a proposed trilogy. Does that mean his next book is imminent? “This is not, ‘I’ve delivered the manuscript and we’re getting a little teaser.’ No, this is a ‘I’ve gone deep into the cave and I need to send a sign of life,’” he says. It takes Franzen many years to write a novel, and the years before he has settled on a new project are often “horrible”, he says. He tries to distract himself, often by writing nonfiction, and then “I periodically go back and beat my head against the proverbial brick wall”. “It’s not fun,” he confirms: “Some other day, another idea. Yeah, that one didn’t work either. Wake up in the middle of the night. Yeah, I got it. No, you don’t.”Franzen believes the most difficult part of writing a new novel is that it requires him to change: he needs to become “the kind of person who can write the novel. I’ve had to become a different person in some significant way to get each book written.” To move from The Corrections to Freedom he had to let go of his anger. To write Crossroads, he had to become more forgiving. Right now, he says, “I’m waiting to wake up as the person who is alive again and not the same person he was five years ago.”Does this mean he sees writing as a means of self-improvement? God, no! When he’s working on a scene, trying to capture a character or get the tone right, he’s not thinking in moral terms. “If you’re really engaged with that, it’s not a matter of morality, but a matter of getting at something true. So I prefer truth as a goal to morality, to self-improvement, to the betterment of one’s soul,” he says. “I don’t really care about bettering my soul. I care about getting it right,” he adds. And then, the reflexive edit: “Which is a pretty good ending line.”A 25th anniversary edition of The Corrections is published by 4th Estate.Explore more on these topicsBooksJonathan FranzenFictioninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky review – the bell tolls for Patrick Hamilton’s lost Londoners | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettling
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettling
Content: Deftly suggesting turmoil … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Jordan Scowen as Bob in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky at Southwark Playhouse Borough.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDeftly suggesting turmoil … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Jordan Scowen as Bob in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky at Southwark Playhouse Borough.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewTwenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky review – the bell tolls for Patrick Hamilton’s lost LondonersSouthwark Playhouse Borough, LondonThe sequence of richly atmospheric novels about lonely souls in the capital is condensed into an engrossing play that could be more unsettlingChris WiegandSat 19 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatrick Hamilton’s 1929 novel The Midnight Bell unfolds over a series of weeks but has the air of one winding night on the tiles in London. The waiter Bob starts out flush, with £80 to his name, as he opens up the eponymous Euston Road pub for business alongside barmaid Ella. At the end of the novel, he wakes with a brutal hangover and loose change, thoroughly undone by his obsession with a sex worker, Jenny. In two later novels, Hamilton reframed each of these women’s stories in turn. His trilogy, Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky, gains great power through separating out their lives, giving each a concentrated interior monologue.Simon Reade’s adaptation instead interweaves them throughout and opens in medias res, diluting the elements of surprise and downward spiral yet drawing out parallels between the relationships. When Ella muddles into a union with a better-off older suitor, Ernest, it raises not dissimilar issues of class, shame and control to Jenny and Bob’s own stumbling, equally imbalanced affair. Each couple is formed by the lonely seeking out the lonely.View image in fullscreenDisquiet … Rosalind Lailey as Ella and Michael Maloney as Ernest in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHamilton’s set of characters is pruned and Matthew Iliffe’s well-blocked, in-the-round production forTroupeemphasises the isolation, heightened by Ellie Wintour’s sparse set design with a bar counter lowered by a pulley system and stools rearranged into a bed. Elizabeth Purnell’s soundscape captures what Hamilton described as the “grim, yet burdened and plaintive” noise of a busy city that is here impervious to these personal crises. Alex Musgrave’s lighting gives us an interwar London of fog, smoke and gas lamps as the cast swirl around each other.The central young characters are each shown to seem old before their time. It’s there in the way Yanexi Enriquez’s Jenny uses a world-weary “dear” and how Rosalind Lailey’s Ella must dig deep not to make do with the fastidious and appropriately named Ernest, whom Michael Maloney turns into a study of later-life disquiet. Maloney excels at a nice bit of comic business with a hat and there is a vein of uneasy humour but more menace is needed across the production, which never fully captures the trilogy’s jaundiced prose or more squalid locations. Jordan Scowen’s Bob switches well between being intoxicated, crestfallen and disgusted with Jenny but should plumb greater depths of despair.View image in fullscreenSadistic encounter … Yanexi Enriquez as Jenny and Alex Bhat as George in Twenty Thousand Streets Under the Sky.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianAs a playwright, Hamilton is best known for two thrillers of cruelty – Rope and Gaslight – and Reade draws out Jenny’s formative sadistic encounter with a stranger, George (Alex Bhat), in a flashback heightened by queasy lighting from Alex Musgrave and Sam Spencer-Lane’s sharp movement direction. The physicality is often astute: there are several prolonged embraces that grow uncomfortable for one of those involved.Iron review – a real-life mother and daughter add extra dimension to prison dramaRead moreYou miss the obsessive inner wrangling over social status in the novels, although Enriquez deftly suggests Jenny’s turmoil about what even a choice of drink may signify about her when she meets George through another sex worker, Prunella (Lucy Gray). The minimal setup also denies the chance to pore over a detailed design for the Midnight Bell, whose personal and public atmospheres Hamilton likened to a theatre itself. But this engrossing production mostly gets the measure of the trilogy.AtSouthwark Playhouse Borough, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreSouthwark PlayhousereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tristan & Yseult review – Kneehigh’s lovers still soar with giddy glory | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistible
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistible
Content: Aerial shenanigans … Nandi Bhebhe as Yseult and John Leader as Tristan.Photograph: Steve TannerView image in fullscreenAerial shenanigans … Nandi Bhebhe as Yseult and John Leader as Tristan.Photograph: Steve TannerTheatreReviewTristan & Yseult review – Kneehigh’s lovers still soar with giddy gloryTheatre Royal BathThis heady mix of circus mayhem, cabaret sexiness, comedy antics and medieval tragedy is utterly irresistibleArifa AkbarSat 19 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKneehigh’s take on this medieval legend was first staged in 2003, in the Cornish setting from which the story of knights, love potions and infidelity arose. It earned cult status and a breathless following of balloon-blowing audience participants, returning to just as much acclaim for a10thanniversary outing.Adapted and directed byEmma Rice, here it is again, in all its giddy, fourth-wall trampling glory, with its army of anorak-clad unloved, and its circus-tricked mayhem. We are once again invited to blow up balloons for the wedding between King Mark (Edward Rowe) and Yseult (Nandi Bhebhe) while her lover, Tristan (John Leader), simmers with secret passion in the wings.View image in fullscreenHow can anyone fail to be enraptured? … Tristan & Yseult’s live band.Photograph: Steve TannerWell, I suppose some things just never get old. This is one of the greatest hits of theformer companybut the young crowd at press night is perhaps some proof that it still has sex appeal. But then, how can anyone fail to drink the potent Kneehigh potion as Tristan and Yseult glug back the magic elixir that makes them fall in love and take off for their staggering set-piece of aerial shenanigans? Or fail to become enraptured with the live band on one side of the stage, with compositions by Stu Barker providing accompaniment between a soundtrack of Wagner, Nick Cave and Roy Orbison, all spinning on the record player on the other side? Or not fall in love with the blend of circus, cabaret, comedy and tragedy, which all run ingeniously alongside each other?‘It was like running away with the circus’ – the thrills, shocks and genius of KneehighRead moreThere is wonderful humour from Yseult’s maid Brangian (Tom Fox) and King Mark’s spurned right-hand man, Frocin (Matthew Churcher). The king brings emotional depth; Yseult and Tristan add a physicality that is both comic and sensuous. The love story makes you cry, even if writers Carl Grose and Anna Maria Murphy choose the most benign ending (the myth has several outcomes but there is no brutal kingly command to burn anyone at the stake here).It is a still marvel of theatrical innovation, a blueprint for dealing with an old story in a new way, bringing bathos to romance but without undercutting its power. Yes, it’s a revival of a surefire hit with the whiff of bums-on-seats ambition, and it does not feel as dangerous all these years later. But neither has it sagged with time. The potion still seduces.AtTheatre Royal Bathuntil 19 September. Thentouringuntil 17 AprilExplore more on these topicsTheatreKneehighTheatre Royal BathEmma RiceCircusCabaretImmersive theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture war | Ed Sheeran | The Guardian
description: Moment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaire
Author: Nadia Khomami
Headline: Moment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaire
Content: Ed Sheeran performing at BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend in Liverpool last year.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/Zuma/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEd Sheeran performing at BBC Radio 1's Big Weekend in Liverpool last year.Photograph: Andy Von Pip/Zuma/ShutterstockThe Saturday readEd Sheeran‘A maelstrom of his own making’: how Ed Sheeran’s tour turned into a full-blown culture warMoment of reckoning for ‘Mr Nice Guy’ of music, who embraced Macklemore’s political cred only for pro-Palestine rapper to be dropped under pressure from billionaireNadia KhomamiSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.02 EDTShareEd Sheeran has long been known as the “Mr Nice Guy” of music. His is an unthreatening kind of pop stardom; he looks and talks like the bloke who might be standing behind you in a pub, rather than someone selling out stadiums. He champions other artists, he celebrates different cultures. His songs are about love, heartbreak and friendship. People get engaged at his concerts.But this week, one of the most successful musicians in the world faced the biggest controversy of his career, and found himself dragged into exactly the kind of political row he has spent his career avoiding.It began whenMacklemore, the Grammy-winning rapper supporting Sheeran on the US leg of his Loop tour, used his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey to call for a “free Palestine”. He performed Hind’s Hall, his 2024 protest song for a five-year-old girl killed by Israeli forces, while footage of pro-Palestine student demonstrations and destruction in Gaza played behind him.The backlash was immediate. The StopAntisemitism group accused Macklemore of “ambushing” fans with “anti-Israel propaganda”, a post amplified by the singer Pink. The Israeli-American Council called for him to be pulled from the tour, asking where the line should be drawn “when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda”. There was extra heat given Macklemore’s history: in 2014 he performed in a fake beard, wig and prosthetic nose widely read as a Jewish caricature. He was soon dropped from the remaining tour dates.But then Macklemore turned the story on Sheeran, accusing his friend of a “determination not to take sides publicly”, and claiming Robert Kraft – owner of the New England Patriots – had pressured Sheeran by threatening to pull his stadium from the tour dates and urging other venues to do the same. Sheeran’s team confirmed multiple venues had objected to Macklemore staying on the bill. Kraft, a prominent supporter of Israel and founder of the Foundation to Combat Antisemitism, has a personal relationship with Sheeran, who sang at his 2022 wedding. In a phone call with Sheeran, the billionaire reportedly acknowledged the sensitivity ofGazabut argued Macklemore’s remarks crossed into hate speech.“Taking a side can cost you,” Macklemore said. “Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I’ve lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed.”View image in fullscreenSheeran and Macklemore pictured in 2014. The US rapper claimed the British singer was pressured by the billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesSheeran’s own statement, published a day later, did little to calm things. He said dropping Macklemore was not his decision and he was “deeply disappointed” by it, but made clear he was not using the moment to declare a position on Israel andPalestine.He was “appalled by the conflict”, he wrote, adding that the “suffering and pain caused on both sides” was “a human tragedy”. “I am not complicit. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have [personal views], and it doesn’t mean that I don’t care.” He wanted his concerts to stay places of “safety and sanctuary”, where people could gather regardless of politics.View image in fullscreenPalestinian artists put the finishing touches on a mural depicting Macklemore on the ruins of homes in Gaza City – the rapper has been vocal in his support for Palestinians.Photograph: Majdi Fathi/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) was unconvinced: Sheeran’s statement, it said, “attempts to ‘both-sides’ Israel’s ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza” and its appeal to “peace” left out “its crucial condition – justice”.“The stakes for him would have been very, very high,” said Dorian Lynskey, the author of 33 Revolutions Per Minute: A History ofProtestSongs. “Taking a stand meant potentially cancelling the rest of your tour, with all the refunds, people who work on the tour losing their work. It’s an enormous thing.”View image in fullscreenThe far-right activist Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersLynskey, who has interviewed Sheeran several times, has “a lot of sympathy” for him, but he thinks the attempt to frame the decision as something that simply happened around him, rather than a choice he made, has backfired. “He may end up being put in another position which is further away from where his sympathies lie. He’s now being seen as a supporter of genocide, when he obviously isn’t.”Within days, every other support act on the US tour pulled out, including Finneas, Lukas Graham, the Irish band Beoga and Aaron Rowe. Sheeran’s Instagram following dropped by almost 150,000 in 24 hours; Macklemore gained more than 750,000. The actor Hannah Einbinder, Irish musician CMAT and Zara Larsson spoke up for Macklemore. Then Tommy Robinson tweeted his support for Sheeran, yanking the singer into a political camp about as far as possible from where he would want to be.Suddenly, one rapper’s decision to speak from a concert stage had ballooned into a full-blown culture war. Many were asking: how does a man who has built a fortune on being liked by everyone end up here?Subtly progressiveThe answer partly lies in the distinction Sheeran has always drawn between having political views and making them part of his public identity. He has never been entirely apolitical. In 2017, he said he was supporting Jeremy Corbyn at the general election, while also saying he did not want to tell other people how to vote. He has campaigned on music education and copyright and supported charities including Crisis. In 2022, he performed at the Concert for Ukraine alongside other artists, raising more than £13.4m for humanitarian relief after Russia’s invasion.Paloma Faith, who also played at the Concert for Ukraine, highlighted what she perceived as a hypocrisy. “He wasn’t apolitical by doing that and I don’t really understand why one felt more political than the other,” she told Channel 4 News.View image in fullscreenThe songwriter and actor Paloma Faith, pictured here at a pro-Palestine protest in 2025, notes that Sheeran took a stand over Ukraine.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAThe difference, said Lynskey, is that Ukraine reads in the west as a “consensus position” – “like Chris Martin wearing the pride flag, subtly progressive without risk of a massive backlash. That’s the realm Sheeran exists in: generally on the right side of things without talking about them too much. This time he’ll have had people around him going ‘this is how much money you lose’ or ‘this is how you could be tarred as antisemitic’.”Musicians speaking out is nothing new, from Dylan and civil rights to punk and anti-apartheid – and neither is the price of doing so.In 2003, the Dixie Chicks faced boycotts, radio bans and death threatsafter Natalie Maines criticised George W Bush over Iraq. What sets Sheeran apart is that he did not say the controversial thing himself – someone he chose to put on his stage did. Choosing Macklemore was not the same as endorsing everything he says. But Macklemore’s politics are not incidental to who he is.View image in fullscreenEd Sheeran’s people knew that Macklemore’s music was ‘explicitly political’, says Billy Bragg.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters“He can’t say: ‘I didn’t know Macklemore was going to do that’,” said Billy Bragg, who has spent decades making explicitly political music. “Macklemore has been speaking out about Palestine and the war in Gaza for quite some time now. His song Hind’s Hall and its accompanying video are a central aspect of his set. Ed’s people must have seen that on every other night of the tour.”Stephen Millar, the author of Sounding Dissent, calls it “a maelstrom partly of Sheeran’s own making”. Sheeran had chosen an artist whose politics were well established, he said. “By doing that you could say that was his effort to the cause. But to pull that back is almost like wanting your cake and eating it.”David Hesmondhalgh, a professor of media, music and culture at the University of Leeds, said while artists should not be compelled to take a position on everything, “Sheeran arguably gains credibility from associating himself with an act like Macklemore whose star persona is based on strong political commitments … So his declarations of neutrality look a bit spineless”.‘A real S-storm’The episode also points to a broader shift in what people expect of celebrities. Social media and the sheer weight of feeling over Gaza have made the old split between public image and private politics much harder to hold. “If you’re not using your platform, you’re seen as doing something wrong,” Millar said.At the same time, artists have become proxies for arguments much bigger than themselves. Lynskey pointed to figures such as Gal Gadot and Mark Ruffalo, who have become stand-ins for opposing sides of the Israel-Palestine debate. “There is this sort of proxy war fought out with celebrities. People have been protesting for almost three years and it doesn’t seem to have made any difference, so I think they’re getting more and more angry and frustrated.”The journalist Lulu Garcia-Navarro made a similar point to CNN: “There’s an increasing antipathy towards Israel, regardless of left or right, and popular culture gives people a way in – they’re not talking about what’s happening in Congress, but this they can understand.” She pointed to a second layer, too: “Both the left and right feel like they don’t have control over their free speech … today there’s a perception that pro-Palestinian voices get censored. So it’s become a real S-storm.”View image in fullscreenCelebrities like the actor Gal Gadot, pictured, and Mark Ruffalo have become proxies in the Israel-Palestine debate.Photograph: Amazon MGM StudiosLisa Nandy, the UK culture secretary, said she had “enormous sympathy” for Sheeran, calling his position “really difficult and impossible” – he wanted to platform his support acts, she said, while promoters were warning himthey would cancel shows over politics on stage.Bragg also acknowledged the practical realities. “Undoubtedly Ed has contractual obligations, and he’d get sued and it would cost him money,” he said. “I can understand it.” But he believes Sheeran could have drawn a cleaner line between defending Macklemore’s right to speak and endorsing every word of it.“He doesn’t have to come out and say ‘free Palestine’. Put purely on the grounds of free speech, he can say an artist must be able to express their view. He needs to let people know how he feels about billionaires deciding what can and can’t be said from a stage,” he said.“Of course, someone like Kanye West should be banned because of the antisemitic things he’s said. But drawing attention to the suffering of civilians in Gaza is not a reason to lose your gig. Culture has to entertain, but it can also challenge.”The point found an echo on the American left. “When you see what Robert Kraft did, to line up all of the stadiums to censor speech in that one specific way, it’s become clear this isn’t about one or two music artists – it’s about how a handful of stadium owners and the elite can bury an entire massive issue. In this case, the genocide in Gaza,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez told TMZ. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is.”Lynskey worries about the wider lesson. “Are you just going to vet your support act for politics? Is the lesson that big artists learn that you don’t book anybody who might be a bit spicy? That would be terrible.”Taking a standSheeran is due back onstage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln Financial Field on Saturday – with no support acts and no band. “I can’t think of a clear precedent where a star of that size has been put in that kind of situation because of support acts,” Lynskey said. It’s a sharp contrast to his last tour, one of the best-attended of all time; this time thousands of tickets sit unsold, some going for $65 online. Classic Hits Radio in Ireland has dropped him from its playlist “for the foreseeable future”, citing listener reaction.View image in fullscreenFinneas is among the musicians who have pulled out from the Loop tour, leaving Sheeran to perform alone.Photograph: Jerod Harris/Getty Images“In Ireland, rebel songs were used to resist against British occupation for centuries, so the fact that Sheeran makes so much of his Irishness makes his stance all the more jarring,” Millar said.Sheeran has tried to answer the controversy on his own terms: through money instead of words. Macklemore has pledged $1m of his Loop tour earnings to humanitarian organisations in Gaza; Sheeran and Kraft have each promised $2m for “aid in the region”. It is a way of showing he cares about the human cost without making any overt political statements – but whether it satisfies the people who wanted him to speak is another matter.Paul Rieckhoff, the founder of Independent Veterans of America, who was inside MetLife Stadium with his two young children on the night of Macklemore’s statement, told CNN Sheeran might be better placed than most to do some good here: “Maybe Ed Sheeran is the person who can actually bring people together around this. But it’s not going to be by throwing Macklemore under the bus or by appeasing Bob Kraft.”Bragg said: “By trying to be Mr Nice Guy and not take sides, he’s in danger of becoming a pariah himself. And that would be a shame, because it’s not his fault. He does need to make a choice here, and it’s one I think that will define him in the eyes of the public for a long time.”

title: Deep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraud | Vinyl | The Guardian
description: Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings
Author: John Harris
Headline: Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings
Content: The lucrative trade in vintage and new vinyl LPs online has spawned a shadow market of bootleggers trying to cash in.Photograph: MarekUsz/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenThe lucrative trade in vintage and new vinyl LPs online has spawned a shadow market of bootleggers trying to cash in.Photograph: MarekUsz/Getty Images/iStockphotoVinylDeep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraudThousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stingsJohn HarrisSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom 2017 onwards, Rehan Ahmed styled himself as a savvy business owner. But behind the facade of a successful entrepreneur lurked one stark fact: his empire was built on fakery.On Friday, the man behind the biggest-ever UK case of producing fraudulent vinyl, who sold counterfeit copies of records by some of the world’s biggest artists including Taylor Swift, Coldplay andKendrick Lamar, was jailed.Ahmed, a 40-year-old father of three from Southall, westLondon, pleaded guilty to two charges of breach of artists’ copyright, and acquiring and using criminal property. On the first count, Judge Darren Reed sentenced him to two years and eight months in prison, while the more serious second charge led to a custodial penalty of three and a half years. The sentences will be served concurrently, meaning that the second will dictate the time Ahmed spends in prison.In a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Friday, the judge highlighted the “sophisticated and planned nature of the enterprise”, and the fact that Ahmed had caused “wider harm to the music industry”.Operating under the company names Phoenix ofVinyland Paragon Music, Ahmed produced counterfeit vinyl albums that he supplied to record shops or sold directly to consumers through online platforms such as Discogs and eBay. In 2025, eBay removed about 7.9m potentially counterfeit or prohibited items from the platform.A spokesperson said: “Counterfeits are strictly prohibited on eBay. Where listings violate eBay policies, we act swiftly to remove them and may take action against the seller’s account.” Discogs did not respond to a request for comment.Phoenix of Vinyl was no minor operation. When police raided Ahmed’s factory, they found 15,000 records. His previous business endeavours, around which there is no suggestion of criminality, had focused on takeaway food and bodybuilding supplements. But the booming vinyl industry appears to have lured him into the illicit market.3:04Police uncover warehouse involved in the biggest counterfeit vinyl records business – videoIn 2025, UK vinyl sales increased by 13.3% to 7.6m units, maintaining 18 years of constant growth. Led by Swift’s 2025 release of The Life of a Showgirl, the total retail value of vinyl in the US that yearreached over $1bn for the first time in four decades.Rising prices of records inevitably followed this increased demand: some high-profile albums, particularly in “limited edition” versions, are now regularly priced at about £40.View image in fullscreenIllicitly produced vinyl at Ahmed’s factory including albums by Kanye West and De La Soul.Photograph: BPIWhile “bootlegs” of rare and unreleased material have long been part of the music landscape – originally on vinyl and now largely eclipsed by the internet – Ahmed was part of a growing underground industry making counterfeit copies of officially released albums. Over the last two years, the music business umbrella organisation the British Phonographic Industry (BPI) says it has been involved in the execution of 43 search warrants centred on illegal counterfeit vinyl and CDs, and seized about 600,000 items estimated to have a street value of up to £8m.View image in fullscreenPolice officers inspecting piles of counterfeit vinyl.Photograph: BPIThe fakes can be easily spotted when it comes to particular artists. The American star Frank Ocean, for example, digitally released his Grammy-winning debut Channel Orange in 2012, but only put out a vinyl edition in 2025, leaving a huge gap for the counterfeiters to fill. In my experience reporting on counterfeit vinyl, Ocean’s work is ubiquitous in impounded batches and the stash found at Ahmed’s HQ was no exception.Ahmed employed “three or four” people at his factory, which operated exclusively at night. When officers from the Police Intellectual PropertyCrimeUnit (Pipcu), a national taskforce based within the City of London force, raided the premises, they found a squalid mess, with chemicals stored in fridges next to cans of lager. Machinery, some of which was believed to be at least 70 years old, and stock were haphazardly arranged over three floors, suggesting little quality control. Receipts and order documents were found randomly scattered around.In footage of the raid viewed by the Guardian, a framed silver disc apparently presented to Ahmed by “the God of Vinyl” is visible.
