A representative from the BPI can be heard expressing surprise at the absence of a cutting lathe, the very expensive piece of machinery that commences record manufacturing by producing the “master” disc, from which everything else is copied, which indicated Ahmed’s “masters” were existing records.View image in fullscreenVinyl press moulds used in the knock-off factory.Photograph: BPIAmid the chaos, officers, assisted by vinyl experts from the BPI, found albums with a street value of about £1m alongside production equipment that is considered a relative rarity among illegal British record specialists, who tend to outsource manufacturing. The only things Ahmed did not produce himself were labels and sleeves, which he had printed by a factory in Gravesend, Kent.Iwas led to Ahmed while reporting on what appeared to be a sprawling counterfeit vinyl trade across the UK. In summer 2024, I was writing a feature about the case of Richard Hutter, a Hampshire-based rogue trader who avoided a spell in prison, despite having been found to have made £1.2m from selling illicit records by artists including Amy Winehouse and the US metal band Tool under the company name Vinyl Groove UK.While researching his case, I was told about a Midlands-based inquiry called Operation Typhoon, which had come to life with the seizure of 529 counterfeit vinyl records from a shop in Stoke-on-Trent.Then there was an enticing new development. The Stoke discovery was followed by a new police inquiry called Operation Imatra, which had started with forced entry into “a three-storey industrial unit in west London”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTen days before Ahmed was sentenced, I met DC Daryl Fryatt, who led the investigation. A relative newcomer to the byzantine world of vinyl, he was clearly fascinated by his new line of work. Midway through the investigation, he bought his first turntable, which he used to indulge his love of modern country music.Phoenix of Vinyl, he explained, had already been issued with a legal cease and desist order in 2017, but blithely carried on its activities for another seven years – something Fryatt put down to the fact that systems designed to detect counterfeits were new, allowing Ahmed’s records to slip through the net.By the time raids took place on Ahmed’s business and family home – a pebble-dashed semi in nearby Southall – at 6am on 20 February 2024, Fryatt and his team still hadn’t grasped the scale of his operation. “Then we searched the premises and we seized a huge amount of records. We found all the production equipment there. And clearly, the factory did the whole lot: made the vinyl, distributed it. Everything,” Fryatt said.View image in fullscreenSome of the extensive equipment used in Ahmed’s factory to produce the records.Photograph: BPIPolice and BPI experts faced an arduous task before they were able to bring charges. They needed to contact 108 record labels or artists’ legal representatives to formally confirm that copyright had been breached.It took until 5 February this year for Ahmed, along with his brother and sister, to be charged with copyright infringement and acquiring, using or possessing criminal property. At a hearing a month later at Westminster magistrates’ court, Ahmed’s siblings pleaded not guilty and the charges against them were later dropped.When Ahmed was first interviewed under caution by the police in May 2024, he painted an illusory picture of his operation, identifying a number of supposed business partners and presenting the police with packs of their supposed ID documents.“One of them didn’t exist,” said Fryatt. “One was a heroin addict who struggled with life and the other one was a guy in America that may or may not have been involved, but there were no records on any phone to show he was. So we discredited his account, basically.”‘It brings me joy’: how young people are making CDs cool againRead moreIn a second police interview, Fryatt recalled that Ahmed “decided to give us another version: ‘Forget all that: it’s my business, I’m the mastermind behind it all and I’ll take the punishment.’”Between the first and second interview, Fryatt said, “his demeanour was completely different: he started out confident and cocky, but in interview two he was kind of crushed.”He said he would now plead guilty.Fryatt believes Ahmed’s motivation for his crime was simple: “Money, getting rich quick … There was no kind of siphoning it off and investing it. It was all just spent.”Peter Ratcliffe, the BPI’s new director of content protection, appointed nine months after Ahmed’s operation was raided, said there were “absolute shockers” among the seized stock. “They were warped: there were bumps in them. The sound was dreadful. The printing quality was awful.”The ex-Pipcu officer, himself a vinyl enthusiast – the last album he bought was The Cure’s Songs of a Lost World – is ambivalent about the soaring cost of records, viewing his role as more about protecting quality and ensuring money made from counterfeit records isn’t used to fund other serious crime.On 22 April, thanks to information provided by BPI vinyl specialists who were present at the subsequent raid, officers from Pipcu forced their way into a warehouse in Luton, where they found counterfeit albums estimated to be worth £260,000, by artists including The Beatles, Queen and David Bowie.Ratcliffe said that at least 10 other counterfeit vinyl investigations are also taking place. “We’re going to find more,” he said, “and I think we’re going to have bigger finds as well. Just the industrial scale now and the increased popularity of vinyl … It’s all going to lead to very big seizures.”Explore more on these topicsVinylCrimeTaylor SwiftKendrick LamarLondonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Meditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missiles | Anna Ivanenko | The Guardian
description: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Author: Anna Ivanenko
Headline: Sometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming back, says artist Anna Ivanenko
Content: Illustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianOpinionUkraineMeditating by the Dnipro: I’m an artist in Ukraine, searching for peace and a life between the missilesSometimes, you can remember what ordinary life was like before Russia’s invasion. Then reality comes screaming backAnna IvanenkoSat 19 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTShareSometimes, where I live in Kyiv, I hear people say: “This feels pre-war.” It refers to situations that remind us of what life was like before. You could call it a “sense of normalcy”.For example, it refers to being able to walk around at night, travel abroad or plan your life at least six months in advance. Simple, everyday things have become a lost luxury.Sometimes people say this phrase simply because they feel that the war isn’t completely occupying their entire mental space: while attending a play at the theatre, for example, or reading arguments about Eurovision. But this ability to mentally transport yourself back in time doesn’t remove the reality that will never let you forget where you are. We are in a place where a theatre performance is overshadowed by the threat of ballistic strikes. Where musicians who could have gone to Eurovision are serving in the army. Where a drone yesterday crashed into the coffee shop that people are used to getting their morning coffee from. But today the coffee shop is reopening, and people head over to their new location for a cappuccino, scanning the QR codes posted everywhere, codes that can be used to donate to the military units the coffee shop supports. It’s a place where the missiles and drones strike suddenly. Just this week, another salvo in Kyiv and other cities. More than two dozen injured only hours afterUS Congress passed a sanctions bill allowing the country to target Moscow.Recently, I had the opportunity to visit Poland for a few days. The seaside in Sopot, located very close to Gdańsk, is now a very peaceful place. In 1939, Hitler was here with his army. A hotel on the shore served as his headquarters during the invasion of Poland. It is well known that he adored this region. Was this his “happy place”? In 2009, Putin stayed at the same hotel to mark the 70th anniversary of the start of the second world war. All of this, against the backdrop of carefree tourists, made me reflect on the fact that every place has different stories associated with it over time.I began to think about it when I returned to Kyiv. Sitting on the banks of the Dnipro River one day, I recalled my feelings in Sopot. I thought that a place has as many versions as it has witnesses, and these versions can exist in the same place at the same time.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anna Ivanenko/The GuardianView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen

title: Henry Harris’ recipe for tomatoes, creme fraiche and herbs | Summer food and drink | The Guardian
description: Sumptuous, late-summer tomatoes cooked with cream and served on toast? Supper is served in 10 … OK, maybe 15 minutes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sumptuous, late-summer tomatoes cooked with cream and served on toast? Supper is served in 10 … OK, maybe 15 minutes
Content: ‘A great favourite’: Henry Harris’ tomatoes creme fraiche and herbs.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘A great favourite’: Henry Harris’ tomatoes creme fraiche and herbs.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The GuardianSummer food and drinkHenry Harris’ recipe for tomatoes, creme fraiche and herbsSumptuous, late-summer tomatoes cooked with cream and served on toast? Supper is served in 10 … OK, maybe 15 minutesHenry HarrisSat 19 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 01.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForty years ago, an antiquarian bookseller recommended to meEdouard de Pomiane’sLa cuisine en dix minutes, a selection of recipes that could be cooked at home in less than 10 minutes. A scientist and food lover, de Pomiane stripped back what was then viewed as a very complicated craft, and also gave the time-poor an opportunity to cook and enjoy a good meal made from good ingredients. This was the first recipe I cooked from that book, and it is still a great favourite that has punctuated my menus ever since.Tomatoes, creme fraiche and herbsThis is a perfect end-of-summer supper that I have never quite managed to do at the speed of de Pomiane – it usually takes me about 15 minutes. Use proper creme fraiche for this, ideally a French one, because there are some very poor British-made equivalents out there that have no natural tang and tend to coagulate when heated.Prep5 minCook15 minServes21 goodtbspunsalted butterSalt and black pepper4ripe plum tomatoes, cut in halflengthways200g creme fraiche, or more if you like a lot of sauce2thick slicessourdoughA few basil leaves, or 1 small handful mixed soft herbsMelt the butter in a medium frying pan until foaming. Generously season the tomatoes, then put them cut side down in the hot butter and leave to cook on a medium heat for at least five minutes, until the butter colours to a light nut brown (if at any stage it looks as if it may be going too dark and at risk of burning, turn down the heat and proceed more gently).Spoon the creme fraiche into the pan, bring up to a low simmer and cook for another two minutes. Turn over the tomatoes, cook for a further minute or two, then taste the tomato-rich cream and adjust the seasoning as required. Meanwhile, toast the sourdough.Put four tomato halves on each slice of toast, spoon the sauce all over the top and serve topped with torn or roughly chopped basil.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go toguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsSummer food and drinkTomatoesFoodFrench food and drinkStarterSnacksBreadrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘An intense caramelised toffee flavour’: the best supermarket maple syrup, tasted and rated | Dessert | The Guardian
description: Which supermarket syrups ooze with potential? We put 10 of the finest, grade-A bottles to the test
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Which supermarket syrups ooze with potential? We put 10 of the finest, grade-A bottles to the test
Content: The dearest bottles taste divine, but then, so do the cheapest.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenThe dearest bottles taste divine, but then, so do the cheapest.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterDessertReview‘An intense caramelised toffee flavour’: the best supermarket maple syrup, tasted and ratedWhich supermarket syrups ooze with potential? We put 10 of the finest, grade-A bottles to the testThe best supermarket runny honeyTom HuntSat 19 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThough today’s maple syrups vary dramatically in intensity, complexity and taste, they’re all of decent quality and have that classic and unmistakable flavour. I avoided blended or maple-flavoured syrups for this test, and instead tried only 100% pure, grade-A maple syrups, usingAgriculture Canada’s flavour wheeland four-step tasting process as a guide. I poured a small shot into a glass to observe the colour. Then I followed the tasting process: I smelled the syrup with three quick sniffs, took a small sip and swirled it around my mouth before contemplating the flavours. Step four is to assess the flavour intensity. Alongside appearance, aroma, texture and taste, I awarded extra points for specific provenance and organic certifications, as well as for value.Prices vary greatly, and although the dearest bottles taste divine, so do the cheapest. Each pure maple syrup is unique in flavour, with nuanced notes from mild clove tones to intense, woody and almost menthol-like piney flavours. Like wine, maple syrup has the tang of its terroir: it’s an artisanal product that tastes of the land.The best supermarket maple syrupBest overall:Maple Shack maple syrupView image in fullscreen£4.90 for 250g at Ocado (£1.96/100g)★★★★☆A deep mahogany colour, and noticeably sweet on the nose, with complex forest notes and a hint of roast chicory smokiness. Medium viscosity, with a pure, intense, caramelised toffee flavour and a lingering sweetness. Sourced from the “top 200 maple farms” in the Bas-Saint-Laurent region of Quebec.Best bargain:Waitrose No 1 Canadian amber maple syrupView image in fullscreen£5.60 for 330g at Waitrose (£1.70/100g)★★★★☆Tapped early in the season, this has a classic light amber colour and an intense, sweet-caramel aroma with a subtle floral acidity. Thick and viscous, with a mild intensity, a buttery and balanced flavour, and a hint of cinnamon.And the rest …M&S Collection Canadian maple syrupView image in fullscreen£5.50 for 330g at Ocado (£1.67/100g)★★★★☆Light amber with a beautiful copper-red tone and a hint of molasses and honeyed acidity on the nose. Deeply caramelised with notes of brown butter, toffee and woody undertones. Medium-strong intensity, finishing on a high acidity.Asda Exceptional Canadian amber maple syrupView image in fullscreen£4 for 250g at Asda (£1.60/100g)★★★★☆A deep ochre colour and an intense, sweet butterscotch aroma. Medium viscosity. A deep, complex, umami flavour with notes of brown sugar, butterscotch and vanilla and, for an amber, a bold character.Buckwud organic classic Canadian maple syrupView image in fullscreen£4.50 for 250g at Morrisons (£1.80/100g)£4.85 for 250g at Waitrose (£1.94/100g)★★★★☆A mahogany amber-red, and an earthy, rounded aroma with classic notes of wet wood and maple. Medium viscosity. Wonderfully balanced, and with a lighter acidity than most, giving it higher flavour notes of caramel, toffee and firewood, with a nice, light butterscotch. Two Great Taste stars in 2023. Soil Association organic-certified.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBiona organic pure amber maple syrupView image in fullscreen£6.80 for 330g at Ocado (£2.06/100g)★★★★☆A deep amber-sienna colour, with a mild aroma, medium body and a subtle, low-intensity flavour of butterscotch with a hint of pine. Delicate, with a woody, creamy, butterscotch taste. From Quebec’s Bas-Saint-Laurent region, and certified organic by theOrganic Food Federation.Tesco Finest amber maple syrupView image in fullscreen£6.85 for 330g at Tesco (£2.08/100g)★★★☆☆A burnt sienna colour, darker than most. A very simple, mild aroma, and full-bodied viscosity. Very sweet, woody and earthy, with a subdued fudge flavour and a note of toasted grain. Well-balanced, and mild in intensity.Aldi Specially Selected Canadian maple syrupView image in fullscreen£3.99 for 330g at Aldi (£1.21/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A whisky-coloured syrup, with a very sweet but grounding, earthy rye aroma. Candied on the tongue, light and viscous, with a butterscotch flavour and a hint of vanilla. Mild, yet full of flavour.Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference Canadian maple syrupView image in fullscreen£5.20 for 250g at Sainsbury’s (£2.08/100g)★★★☆☆A classic, amber-yellow bourbon colour, with a distinct, sweet marshmallow-vanilla aroma. Thick viscosity, with a balanced caramel flavour and hints of acidity, toast and leafy earthiness. Medium intensity.Co-op pure Canadian maple syrupView image in fullscreen£5.25 for 250g at Co-op (£2.10/100g)★★★☆☆A light mahogany colour, and a subtle, sweet and mildly woody aroma. Medium viscosity. A sweet, well-rounded syrup, medium intensity with a balanced, earthy flavour of dandelion root and a classic maple-caramel taste. Intriguingly plain packaging, too.For more, read thebest supermarket double creamand thebest supermarket balsamic vinegarExplore more on these topicsDessertThe FilterFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Everyone assumed it represented a poo emoji!’ 27 writers on the greatest cake of their life | Cake | The Guardian
description: From the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressions
Content: Catherine Shoard’s eerie-looking Sorting Hat cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Catherine ShoardView image in fullscreenCatherine Shoard’s eerie-looking Sorting Hat cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Catherine ShoardCake‘Everyone assumed it represented a poo emoji!’ 27 writers on the greatest cake of their lifeFrom the blissful threat of ‘death by chocolate’, to a book made of sponge and the lemon drizzle to end them all, these are the bakes that left the biggest impressionsSat 19 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Sorting Hat sponge cakeThe Sorting Hat sponge I made for my son’s Harry Potter party is not the best cake I’ve ever tasted. That would be anything baked by my granny, or the coffee religieuse (a choux pastry puff) I ate in Boulogne-sur-Mer with my mum. But it’s the most surprisingly edible cake I’ve ever made – a vaguely Jamie-Oliver recipe with buttercream filling and tinned mandarin slices. It didn’t only work; it tasted great, and wasn’t quite as teeth-screechingly sweet as expected. My one regret is that I over-pimped the decoration: it looked so sinister in the fridge with its cold, Sorting Hat stare that the next day I stuck on googly eyes and further sparkles. This perhaps explains why everyone assumed it was a poo emoji cake, despite it being a Harry Potter party with heavy-touch theming. That people thought I actually wanted children to eat shit is a shame, but it still remains my greatest culinary success.Catherine ShoardA perfectly piped 35th birthday cakeView image in fullscreenA knockout 35th birthday cake from Lily Vanilli.Photograph: Courtesy of Hollie RichardsonMy dreams of a cake fit for Marie Antoinette came true on my 35th birthday: with a single baby-blue tier, whimsical white piping and glace cherries for a welcome dash of gaudy. After taking it home in a taxi from Lily Vanilli bakery in London, I proudly displayed her for all to marvel at. Inside, the vanilla sponge had a raspberry and buttercream filling. It felt like my wedding day when I cut the first slice. By the end of the night, after everyone had tucked in and I was about 10 tumblers of prosecco deep, I fulfilled another lifelong dream: face-planting a cake. (Well, half of one.) I picked at those sugary remains for days afterwards.Hollie RichardsonAn orange cream gateauMy most treasured Christmas present of 1992 was the Hamlyn All Colour Cook Book. While I don’t remember cooking any of the savoury recipes – sherried kidneys and turkey in aspic weren’t quite to my 10-year-old tastes – the “family favourite cakes” chapter was a different story. I started with Mary Berry’s classic Victoria sandwich and graduated to her triple-decker chocolate button cake. But I found the ultimate in sophistication, decadence and all-round deliciousness in Audrey Ellis’s “fancy cakes” section: a glorious orange cream gateau. I lovingly baked two orange-zest sponges, sandwiched and smothered them with orange-juice buttercream, and decorated the top with jellied orange and lemon slices. It looked, and tasted, like pure sunshine.Rachel DixonNigella’s pear, pistachio and rose cakeView image in fullscreenA post-dip Viv Groskop with her 51st birthday cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Viv GroskopThe monumental creation is Nigella’s pear, pistachio and rose cake, expertly reinterpreted by my friend Sian. This entity represents the three all-important ingredients of the perfect bake. First, it was made by someone whose cakes always taste as good as they look (a difficult achievement), the kind of person who is tired of everyone saying to them: “You should go on Bake-Off. No, but really, you should.” Sian very much ticks this box. (She really should.) Second, it is part of the grand tradition of “birthday swim” cakes to be eaten with friends at 7am after a freezing cold dip. And third, it features the inventive use of a single candle to represent the numeral “one”. (It is a 51st birthday cake.) No cake could compete on taste, suitability-for-occasion or creativity.Viv GroskopAn iced gingerbread cakeBefore my father died, I had never had to organise a funeral. The strangest element was choosing items for a funeral buffet when I was so choked with tears that I could barely swallow. But my mother was keen that we offered a good spread for my foodie father’s send-off. I chose iced gingerbread mainly because my dad loved ginger. But a mass-catered cake sounded unpromising. Imagine our surprise when it turned out to be one of the most heavenly bakes I’ve ever eaten. Tasting as if it was homemade, it was perfectly moist, with a good kick of ginger and cinnamon. The showstopper was the melt-in-the mouth lemon icing. There was loads left over and it offered us some solace in the gloomy days afterwards.Anita ChaudhuriThe Forg meme cakeView image in fullscreenMadévi Dailly’s generous Forg cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Madévi DaillyThe best cake I ever had was a replica of the notorious “Forg cake” meme, surprise delivered to my door by a friend who had never baked before. I was in the middle of a full nervous breakdown, and had been hooked up for a 24-hour blood pressure test the day before that had brought me to the edge of sanity – so this gentle, generous act of friendship restored my faith in better things to come. It was delicious, too: a superlative victoria sponge hidden underneath droopy pastel icing.Madévi DaillyA Swiss-meringue buttercream chocolate cakeView image in fullscreenThe ‘vintage’ cake at Cafe Lewi, Sydney, Australia.Photograph: Courtesy of Yvonne C LamIt’s not my fault I’m not a cake person. When I was growing up, after the birthday kid had blown out the candles, my saturated-fat-fearing aunties (it was the 90s) would scrape off the cream before serving the naked cake slices to my unimpressed cousins. One upside of adulthood is cake (and cream) whenever I want. On a recent child-free day with my husband, we went to Cafe Lewi, a tiny venue in Lewisham, Sydney, where they serve homemade bakes and pastries, as well as enticing meals and drinks. Their “vintage” cake is a thing of beauty – layers of chocolate sponge with a sultry crumb, sandwiched together with a chocolate ganache and raspberry curd, and thickly slathered on all four sides with a snow-white Swiss meringue buttercream, all embellished by someone who knows their way around a piping bag. We ate it for breakfast.Yvonne LamA Kirby birthday cakeEvery year since my son’s third birthday, I’ve put together a fancy fondant based on one of his fleeting interests: on my first attempt, when the theme was Pokémon, my Pikachu was so lumpenly misshapen that my son burst into tears. It turns out, though, that if you practise something once a year (with a few clay modelling sessions) and watch alotof videos, you do improve. This cake, made by my wife, was a victoria sponge with buttercream and jam filling, but the wrapping – modelled, of course, on video game hero Kirby when he turns into a car – was all me. It tasted like triumph.Joel SnapeMy mum’s chocolate hedgehog birthday cakeView image in fullscreenRich Pelley’s mum, with her hedgehog cake.Photograph: Courtesy of Rich PelleyAs a child, I had one currency: chocolate. The more the better. Nowhere offered a better exchange rate than my mum’s cakes, not least her chocolate hedgehog birthday cake: chocolate sponge, chocolate buttons for spikes and a chocolate-icing face. It became the best bit of birthdays, until I got too old for candles, left home and somehow went 30 years without a birthday cake from Mum, hedgehog or otherwise. Luckily, I’ve corrected this terrible injustice by telling her that all Guardian journalists are now required to have their mum bake them a cake … and she believed me. Thanks, Mum. Happy birthday to me.Rich PelleyThree fourth birthday cakesIn April 2000, I turned four while on a family holiday to Nepal to visit my grandparents, who were living there. My parents had explained that it might not be possible to get me a birthday cake while we were away. For an almost-four-year-old, this was a huge tragedy, a fact that I shared with almost everyone we met. When the big day arrived, the hotel staff surprised me with a huge cake decorated with green, pink and yellow icing. I was overjoyed. I can’t remember what it tasted like, but I know I’ve never been so excited about eating a cake. My tiny mind was blown again soon after, when it turned out that my grandparents had also arranged a cake for me. Then my mum baked another when we got home. I couldn’t believe my luck –threebirthday cakes! I was on a high for weeks.Lucy KnightThe perfect vegan chocolate gateauView image in fullscreenAnastasia’s handmade vegan chocolate gateau.Photograph: Courtesy of Ann LeeIt was my friend Anastasia’s birthday party. We were watching Eurovision and had just finished stuffing ourselves with pizza when she brought it out. A vegan chocolate cake, covered in edible purple flowers, plump strawberries and juicy blackberries, it was more a work of art than a simple gateau. She had baked it using a recipe by Nigella (who else?) and the glossy chocolate icing oozed on to the plate. From the first spoonful, I knew I had finally found it – a vegan cake that didn’t taste like a vegan cake.
